PREFACE.


It has been the object of the Authors of this Work to produce a more
complete and more perfect <sc>English-Latin Dictionary</sc> than has
hitherto existed; and the long delay in its publication has been owing
to the time and labour necessary to execute this intention.

When the announcement of a new English-Latin Dictionary was
first made, the extent of the labour involved in such a work was far from
being adequately estimated. Had we anticipated that nearly fifteen years
would have elapsed before the enterprize could be completed, we should
probably have shrunk from the toil. Yet this has been the time
expended upon the Work. The first announcement of this Dictionary
was made in 1855; the completed work issues from the press in 1870.

In order to appreciate the nature and extent of the labour undertaken,
three things require to be kept in view.

/#
1. There was no existing English-Latin Dictionary, from which any
considerable amount of help could be derived. The English-Latin
Dictionary published under the joint names of Messrs. Riddle and
Arnold is avowedly based upon the German work of Georges; but,
though containing valuable matter, it is confused in arrangement, and
in general does not indicate the different classical sources from which
its Latin phraseology is derived. It was therefore of no use to us except
in the way of suggestion; and, moreover, the whole of its material could,
in most cases, be found by a simple reference to the pages of Georges,
or, in a much more satisfactory and complete form, to those of Kraft.

Thus the lines of the work had to be laid <i>de novo</i>, as much so as if
no other Dictionary of the kind existed. An entirely new plan was
accordingly adopted; a new classification of the meanings of the
English words had to be elaborated; and new examples and illustrations
adduced.
#/

/#
2. In order to ensure the pertinency of the examples, it was
necessary to use special care in the verification of references. Very
many quotations, at first sight applicable, were found on actual reference
to the context from which they were detached to be not exactly
in point, or, if available at all, available only by way of suggestion.
Only those who have had similar experience can appreciate the labour
which such a task as this entails. Not a few works, in themselves
excellent, have yet many false references; as, for example, the extremely
valuable Ciceronian Lexicon of Nizolius; while even the most accurate
are, of course, sometimes found fallible. In some cases an error of
#/
-----File: a0004.png-------------------------------------------------------
/#
this kind has been painfully tracked from one authority to another;
and after appearing in every successive edition of Forcellini's great
work, has met with its correction--probably for the first time--in our
pages. Doubtless incorrect references are to be found here also, in spite
of the extreme care which has been exercised; and the Authors will be
grateful to any persons who will kindly communicate such should they
be discovered; but it is believed that they are extremely few in
proportion to the total number. And even in the case of these, the
student may feel assured that the verification has been actually made,
in spite of a clerical or typographical error in recording it.
#/

/#
3. The Work has grown and developed under our hands in such a
way as to demand greatly increased time and labour. Owing chiefly to
modifications of plan, not less than half of the book certainly--perhaps,
it may safely be said, two-thirds--has been executed thrice over. It is
hoped that in the improvement which the work has thus undergone
exists an ample compensation for the delay which has occurred.
The earlier part of the book will be seen to contain fewer exact
references than the latter. In fact, it was not until a large portion of
it had been printed, and a still larger portion prepared for the press,
that the plan of specifying the precise place in an author where each
example is to be found, was--from a growing sense of its advantages--adopted.
This course involved an immense addition of labour, and was
attended by the slight anomaly indicated;[**;?] which may perhaps be
allowed to mark the development of an enterprize more than ordinarily
trying to patience and industry. From the very beginning, however,
exact references had been introduced in cases where the special importance
or interest of any illustration appeared to require it.

Every article in the book is the result of original and independent
research; and it is not too much to say that a single column often
represents the hard labour of several days. The progress of the work
has been often delayed for hours by the difficulty of finding a passage
in a Latin author wrongly quoted, or of meeting with a suitable Latin
equivalent for an English word.
#/

Some features of the plan of the Work require a brief exposition.

/#
1. Great pains have been taken in classifying the different senses of
the <i>English words</i>, so as to enable the student readily to find what he
wants. The facilities afforded by the use of different kinds of type have
been freely used; and those senses of words have been brought forward
most prominently, and treated most fully, which appeared likely to
cause perplexity to the student, minute subdivisions of meanings being
avoided. At the same time, the logical order has been as far as
possible followed; and even senses which have become obsolete have
been noted where this appeared necessary to the proper development of
the use of any particular word. The leading meanings of the English
words are marked by black Roman numerals (I., II., III.,[**also exclude from bold markup?] &c.), a brief
#/
-----File: a0005.png-------------------------------------------------------
/#
definition being in all such cases added in Italics. The work is
thus to a large extent a Dictionary of the English language proper,
as well as an English-Latin Dictionary.
#/

/#
2. Where there are several Latin equivalents, these are kept quite
distinct, and marked with black Arabic numerals (1, 2, 3,[**bold?] etc.). To
distinguish synonyms, short explanations of different Latin words are
added in brackets. Each meaning is illustrated by examples from the
classical writers, and those phrases are as a general rule given in both
English and Latin. This Work--it must be borne in mind--is not
a Latin-English, but an English-Latin Dictionary. Moreover, it is one
professing to deal not only with English words considered by themselves,
but with those words as occurring in their most frequent combinations
with other words, and especially in characteristic and idiomatic phrases.
The English given in any case is not therefore to be regarded as a
mere translation of the Latin example--which any one might make for
himself--but as furnishing a specimen of such combinations. Besides
this, the presentation of English and Latin together--even when not
absolutely needed for phraseological purposes--was thought likely to be
of use to the student, by giving him a firmer grasp of the meaning
of the Latin. A mere Latin extract is often passed over by the young
student. The vehicle is foreign; and the extra time consumed in reading
it, and, what is quite another matter, in bringing home to the mind
a clear impression of its force, is a consideration not to be overlooked.

Further, and to this point the Authors attach great importance,
the course adopted appeared to furnish a test of the pertinency
of the illustrations, of the most decisive and even crucial nature.
If the Latin equivalent in any given example could without harshness
be translated by the English word under treatment, conclusive proof
was thus afforded that the correspondence between the two was real and
not merely apparent; and the laying of both together before the
student seemed to be the plan best calculated to give him the fullest
satisfaction on the point.
#/

/#
3. The Vocabulary of English words treated is for the most part
limited to words in actual use or occurring in authors generally read.
Should the student require the Latin equivalent of an obsolete English
word, his obvious course will be to look under its current modern
equivalent. Very many of the unnecessary Latinisms which crowd the
columns of Webster and Richardson are omitted altogether. On the
other hand, the student will find here many derived forms--especially
the participial adjectives--which are not to be met with in any similar
work. Technical terms of Art, Science and Theology have been given
when such appeared to possess that kind of general interest which brings
them within the range of all persons of culture, apart from their own
special field. In representing theological terms, the language of
theologians has been adopted. The nomenclature of Christian Theology--Catholic
and Protestant--is itself mainly Latin; and must often be
#/
-----File: a0006.png-------------------------------------------------------
/#
used apart from all questions of elegance or classicality. To write
a treatise on the Sacraments in words known only to Cicero would be
as absurd as for an English author to attempt to describe a railway or
a steam-engine in the phraseology of Shakspeare and Bacon. So on
the principle--<i>artifici in sua arte credendum</i>--the authority of the
Scriptores rei rusticae has been chiefly appealed to in matters relating to
farming, gardening, and the management of stock; that of Priscian and
the authors embraced in the copious collection of Putschius, in matters
grammatical and verbal; that of the Scriptores gromatici, in the case of
some terms relating to geometry and mensuration; and that of Pliny
the Elder, for the miscellaneous vocabulary of the natural sciences. In
the case of words for which there neither is nor can be any classical
equivalent, recourse has been freely had to more modern sources. Such
words are marked by an asterisk. But while special terms have been
taken from writers of various ages, in all that relates to the complexion
of sentences involving questions of taste or style, the aim of the Authors
has been to follow in the steps marked out by Cicero and his contemporaries[**like-break hyphen didn't print],
or the writers of what is called the Augustan age.
#/

/#
4. In dealing with English words nearly synonymous, the Authors
have carefully sought to avoid needless repetition. They have aimed
to bring their matter in each case under its natural head; that is,
under the English word by which the Latin equivalent in question
is oftenest represented. When the same equivalent has to be adduced
again under another English word, it is for the most part less fully
treated, or the student is simply directed to another place for illustrations
of its use. Mere cross references have, however, been avoided
as far as possible; and pains have been taken to present under every
article enough to be of service to the student, who may perhaps lack
time for a prolonged consultation. Nothing is more vexatious than
to be sent unprofited from article to article; on the other hand, no
reasonable person will complain if, at times, his first consultation is
rewarded by only an instalment of the information of which he is in
quest, when a little further search will discover all he wants.
#/

It is difficult in a work of this kind to express properly the obligations
under which the Authors lie to previous labourers. But in the
foremost rank, mention must be made of the German-Latin Lexicon of
Kraft, which has been consulted throughout, and drawn upon for very
many illustrations which might not have been otherwise arrived at.
The briefer and inferior work of Georges supplies little that is not to
be found in its predecessor. The French-Latin Dictionary of Quicherat
furnishes perhaps a more extensive vocabulary than either, and has
often been found extremely useful in the conversion of rarer and more
technical words; the only drawback to its utility being the entire absence
of precise references. The work of Riddle and Arnold, to which allusion
has already been made, has also been consulted; and some examples
and suggestions have been derived from it. These, however, when
-----File: a0007.png-------------------------------------------------------
appearing to be the original property of the work in question, are
acknowledged, <i>in loco</i>, thus [R. and A.]. In most cases however they are
derived from Georges. The excellent treatise of Nägelsbach (Die Lateinische
Stilistik) has furnished some valuable hints for the conversion
of various modes of speech in which German and English alike differ
from Latin; also of some words partaking in an especial manner of
the complexion of modern thought. The synonym books of Habicht
and Döderlein have also been carefully consulted. To express indebtedness
to the great work of Forcellini--the German edition of which has
been chiefly used--is almost superfluous; while the indispensable
Lexicon of Nizolius (before referred to), the 'Lexicon Quintilianeum' of
Bonnell, the 'Lexicon Taciteum' of Bötticher, and the copious indexes
to almost all classical authors of any importance to be found in the
great standard Editions, have furnished aids without which our labour
would have often been multiplied many fold. For scientific words we have
derived valuable assistance from Mayne's 'Expository Lexicon of the
Terms, Ancient and Modern, in Medical and General Science,' London,
1860. On lexical and grammatical points frequent reference is made to
Dr. Smith's Latin-English Dictionary, and to the Student's Latin
Grammar by the authors of the present Work.

<tb>

It remains to notice the assistance which the Authors have received,
and the part which they themselves have taken in the preparation of the
Dictionary. It was projected by Dr. Smith, and upon him has mainly
devolved the editorship and general superintendence of the work, in
addition to the composition of various portions. He was originally
associated in his labours with Mr. Robson, who had rendered valuable
aid in the preparation of the Latin-English Dictionary. Mr. Robson
devoted two years exclusively to making preparations for the work,
taking as his basis Webster's quarto Dictionary, supplemented by other
standard Dictionaries, and assigning from the best sources the ordinary
Latin equivalent for each word and every meaning of each word.
Having completed this laborious task, Mr. Robson proceeded to draw
up the separate articles in detail, and had reached as far as nearly the
end of C[**bold, or just heavily inked? (next pg not so much)], when other engagements compelled him to resign his share in
the undertaking[**period failed to print] Dr. Smith then obtained the assistance of Mr. Hall,
whose name now appears on the title-page along with his own. Mr
Hall originally entered on the work as a contributor; and as such has
completed more than one half of the entire book--from the beginning
of D to nearly the end of P, besides other detached portions. But prolonged
association with Dr. Smith in the undertaking led naturally to
a participation in the care and responsibility of the work as a whole.
Notwithstanding the unremitting exertions of Dr. Smith and Mr. Hall,
it was found necessary to call in further assistance in order to finish
the Work in any reasonable time. Accordingly the Authors have to
acknowledge their obligations to the following scholars: Mr. F. Millard,
M.A., of the International College, London, and of Queen's College,
Oxford, who has executed under their superintendence portions of R
-----File: a0008.png-------------------------------------------------------
and S, and the greater part of T; to Mr. Philip Smith, B.A., who contributed
the articles from "Pull" to the end of Q; and to Mr. C. A. F.
Fennell, M.A., Fellow of Jesus College, Cambridge; Rev. C. E. Graves,
M.A., Classical Lecturer and late Fellow of St. John's College, Cambridge;
Rev. W. C. Green, M.A., late Fellow of King's College, and
Classical Lecturer, Queen's College, Cambridge; Rev. H. W. Phillott,
M.A., Rector of Staunton-on-Wye, and late Student of Christ Church,
Oxford; Mr. E. B. Rand, B.A., late Student of Caius College, Cambridge;
and Mr. Evelyn S. Shuckburgh, M.A., Fellow of Emmanuel College,
Cambridge; for very valuable aid in preparing the later letters of the
Alphabet. But strenuous exertions have been made by the Authors to
secure the homogeneity of the work, and it is hoped that the student
will in no part seriously miss that unity of treatment which is so essential
to the utility of a work of this nature.

<tb>

In conclusion, the Authors would commend the fruit of their long
labour to the candid and favourable consideration of English scholars
and students. It is inevitable that a work of such magnitude should
have not a few blemishes and imperfections; but they nevertheless
trust that it will be received as supplying, in a manner not altogether
unworthy, a long and deeply felt want in our English schools and
colleges.

/#
<i>January 1st, 1870.</i>
#/

-----File: b0001a.png------------------------------------------------------




AN

ENGLISH-LATIN DICTIONARY.
-----File: b0001l.png------------------------------------------------------




A.


<b>A</b>, <i>first letter of the alphabet</i>. A,
<i>indecl. f.</i> (sc. littera), more frequently
<i>n.</i>, Cic.: Prisc.: <i>to make the mark
of the letter A</i>, litteram A imprimere, Cic.


<b>a</b>, or (before vowels) <b>an</b>:

I. As
the indefinite article prefixed to a substantive
employed to designate <i>any-*one</i>[**F2: not hyphenated on following pg]
of a species, it has no representative
in Latin, which in such cases
employs the singular number of the
substantive alone: <i>he bore pain as a
man</i>, tulit dolorem ut vir, Cic.: <i>a Greek</i>,
Graecus; <i>a Roman</i>, Romanus.

II.
Even when a <i>definite</i> single object is
spoken of, the indefinite article is usually
unrepresented in Latin:[** : conf. in TIA] <i>there was
a great plain, and in it a tolerably large
earthen elevation</i>, planities erat magna et
in ea tumulus terrenus, satis grandis,
Caes.

III. Sometimes, however, when
special attention is to be directed to the
object, aliquis or quidam is employed in
a sense nearly equivalent to our expression,
<i>a certain</i>: <i>the Peripatetics maintain
that there is in the minds of men,
as it were, a divine voice</i>, Peripatetici
censent esse in mentibus hominum tanquam
oraculum aliquod, Cic.: <i>a (certain)
soldier of the tenth legion</i>, quidam ex
militibus decimae legionis, Caes.

IV.
When used distributively, as in the
phrases <i>once a year</i>, <i>so much a head</i>, etc.,
it must be expr. with the help of a distributive
numeral: as <i>the price of corn
had now risen to 50 denarii a bushel</i>, jam
ad denarios L in singulos modios annona
pervenerat, Caes.: <i>he promises to the
soldiers four jugers a man</i>, militibus
pollicetur quaterna in singulos jugera,
Caes.: <i>if ye are willing to quit Saguntum
unarmed with two dresses a piece</i>,
si inermes cum binis vestimentis velitis
ab Sagunto exire, Liv. Phr.: <i>twice a
day</i>, bis in die, Cic.; bis die, Tib.:[** : ?|conf. in TIA] <i>once
a month</i>, semel in mense, Cat.: <i>twice
a month</i>, bis in mense, Plin.: <i>twice a
year</i>, bis in anno, Varr., Cic.; bis anno,
Plin.

V. When referring to a <i>particular</i>
thing: is, ĕa, ĭd: <i>a certain reward and
not a small one</i>, certa merces nec ea
parva, Cic.: <i>a thing which was easy to
be done</i>, id quod facile factu fuit, Cic.:
<i>at such a time</i>, id temporis, Cic.: <i>of such
a kind</i>, id genus, Cic.--<sc>Note.</sc> The ordinary
<i>indef. art.</i> must on no account be
translated by <i>unus</i>: v. <f>SINGLE</f>, <f>INDIVIDUAL</f>.

B. Adverb.:

I. Of Place: in
combination with verbs: as, <i>to walk
about</i>, <i>ride about</i>, etc. These are in
reality compound verbs, and expr. in
Latin by a single word, as dĕambŭlo,
circumvĕhor, etc. See <f>TO WALK</f>, <f>RIDE</f>,
etc.

II. Of degree: <i>nearly</i>: circā
(rare): <i>the victors slew ab. 500 Romans</i>,
c. quingentos Romanorum victores ceciderunt,
Liv.

2. circĭter: <i>he reached
the frontiers of the Belgae in ab. fifteen
days</i>, diebus c. quindecim ad fines Belgarum
pervenit, Caes.: <i>ab. a fourth

c. pars quarta erat militaribus
armis instructa, Sall.

3. fĕrē: <i>ab.
the fifth hour</i>, quinta fere hora, Caes.:
<i>for ab. 600 years</i>, sexcentos f. annos,
Cic.

4. fermē: <i>this happened ab.
two years ago</i>, hoc factum est f. abhinc
biennium, Pl.: <i>ab. a half</i>, pars f.
dimidia, Liv.

5. fortassĕ (like our
<i>perhaps</i>): <i>out of many books of Isocrates

multis Isocratis libris triginta f. versus,
Cic.

6. quăsĭ (prop. <i>as it were</i>): <i>I
have collected ab. fifteen talents</i>, quasi

the bottom of the page</i>, q. in extrema

7. instar (prop. a <i>neut.

<i>Tiro has ab. seventy of my letters</i>, habet

Cic.: v. <f>AROUND</f>. Phr.: <i>to have

Cic.: <i>to seize one ab. the middle</i>, medium
aliquem arripere, Ter.--N.B. The
two languages do not exactly correspond
in the uses of these words, and
hence the English adverb is sometimes
expressed by a Latin preposition, but
the examples are classified in accordance
with the English.

-----File: b0006m.png------------------------------------------------------
<i>*ceptus</i> stands to <i>gratus</i> in the same relation
as an effect to a cause. He who
is <i>gratus</i>, that is <i>dear</i> to me, is for that
reason <i>acceptus</i>; <i>I accept</i> or <i>receive</i> him
with pleasure. Hence we always find
<i>gratum</i> atque <i>acceptum</i>: never the
contrary order. Quod approbaris, id
gratum acceptumque habendum, Cic.
Tusc. 5, 15, 45: munus eorum gratum
acceptumque esse, Nep. Hann. 7.

of Gabinius</i>, Gabinii a., Cic.: <i>a. from a
charge of high treason</i>, majestatis a.,
Cic.

2. lībĕrātĭo: <i>most arbitrary
a.s of defendants</i>, libidinosissimae reorum
liberationes, Cic. Phr.: <i>to give
verdicts of a.</i>, absolutorias sententias
ferre, Sen.: <i>verdicts of a.</i>, absolutoria
judicia, Gai.


<b>acquittance</b> (legal):

1. acceptĭlātĭo
(i. e., accepti latio), Dig.

2.
ăpŏcha: v. <f>ACKNOWLEDGMENT</f>.


<b>acre</b>: jūgĕrum, i; but in <i>plu.</i> usu. as
of 3rd decln. The Roman jugerum was
about ·625[** decimal is ·|fixed/F2] of an English acre, so that
it is only in a very loose way that the
Latin word can be employed as equivalent
to the English one. Where exactness
is necessary, the number of acres
must be expressed in accordance with
the above ratio: <i>e. g.</i>: <i>an estate of 100
acres</i>, fundus jugerum centum sexaginta.


<b>acrid</b>:

1. ācer, acris, acre: <i>a.
things, as mustard, onion, garlic</i>, acria,
ut est sinapi, caepa, allium, Varr. ap.
Non.: <i>a. humours</i>, a. humores, Cic.

2. asper, ĕra, ĕrum: <i>the a. taste of
sea-water</i>, a. sapor maris, Plin.: v.
<f>PUNGENT</f>, <f>SHARP</f>, <f>SOUR</f>.


<b>acrimonious</b>, i.e.[** i. e.] <i>bitter or severe in
temper or expression</i>:

1. ăcerbus:
<i>an a. tongue</i>, a. lingua, Liv.: <i>on that
day we found Curio a.</i>, eo die a. habuimus
Curionem, Cic.

2. ămārus: <i>old
age makes me more a.</i>, amariorem me
senectus facit, Cic.: <i>a. words</i>, dicta a.,
Ov.: <i>a. wit</i>, a. sales, Quint.: v. <f>BITTER</f>.

3. asper, ĕra, ĕrum: <i>a savage, a.,
abusive orator</i>, orator truculentus, a.,
maledicus, Cic.: <i>a. Juno</i>, a. Juno, Virg.:
v. <f>SEVERE</f>, <f>SEVERITY</f>.


<b>acrimony</b>, <b>acrimoniousness</b>, i. e.
<i>bitterness or sharpness of temper or expression</i>:

1. ăcerbĭtas: <i>a. and plenty
of wit</i>, acerbitas et abunde salis, Quint.:
<i>severity I approve of; a. not by any
means</i>, severitatem probo; a. nullo
modo, Cic.

2. ămārĭtūdo: <i>the a. of
the poems of Hipponax</i>, Hipponacis carminum
a., Plin.: v. <f>BITTERNESS</f>.


<b>across</b>:

I. Prep.:

1. trans (with
<i>acc.</i>): <i>to lead a multitude of men a. the
Rhine</i>, hominum multitudinem t. Rhenum
transducere, Caes.: <i>they hasten a.
the sea</i>, t. mare currunt, Hor.: <i>to purchase
gardens a. the Tiber</i>, t. Tiberim hortos
parare, Cic.

2. transversus (in agr.
with that which <i>crosses</i> or <i>is crossed</i>):
<i>we saw Manilius walking a. the forum</i>,
Manilium nos vidimus transverso ambulantem
foro, Cic.: <i>I come now to that
line which is written a. at the end of
your letter</i>, nunc venio ad transversum
illum extremae epistolae tuae versiculum,
Cic.: <i>he will make a black mark
upon the unpolished verses by drawing
his pen across them</i>, versibus incomptis
allinet atrum transverso calamo signum,
Hor.

II. Adv.:

1. transversus (in
-----File: b0011m.png------------------------------------------------------
agr. with the subs. to which it refers):
<i>to carry a moat a.</i>, transversam fossam
ducere, Caes.: <i>to rush a. against</i> (fig.),
transversus incurrere, Cic. Esp. as
adv. phrase, in transversum (cf. in obliquum,
<f>OBLIQUELY</f>, q. v.): <i>a peninsula
stretching a. in the form of a sword</i>,
paeninsula ad formam gladii in tr. porrecta,
Plin.: <i>the stone is marked a. with
a white line</i>, gemma in tr. alba linea
praecingitur, Plin.: also poet. transversă:
v. <f>ATHWART</f>.

2. trans, in comp. with
a verb: as, <i>to go a.</i>, transire, transgredi,
etc.: for which see <f>TO GO</f>, etc.


<b>acrostic</b>, i. e. <i>a poem in which the
first letter of every line being taken forms
the name of a person or thing</i>: no Latin
word: ea quae ἀκροστιχίς dicitur, Cic.
Div. 2, 54, 111.: Suet. Gr. 6, appears to
use parastĭchis, ĭdis, <i>f.</i> in the same sense:
versus quorum primae litterae sensum
reddunt, Aug.: <i>to make out</i> or <i>read an
acrostic</i>, litteras, quae sunt in capitibus
omnium versuum, connectere, Aug.


<b>act</b> (<i>v.</i>):

A. Intrans.

I. <i>To be
active</i>: ăgo, ēgi, actum, 3: <i>there is one
time for acting, another for rest</i>, aliud
agendi tempus, aliud quiescendi, Cic.:
<i>Maecenas was a man who knew how to
act</i>, erat M. agendi sciens, Vell.

II.
<i>To conduct oneself, behave</i>:

1. ăgo:
<i>we act handsomely towards them</i>, praeclare
cum iis[**unclear] agimus, Cic.: with <i>acc.</i> to
denote the character in which a person
acts: <i>to act as a friend</i>, amicum a.,
Tac.: <i>to act as a subordinate</i>, ministrum
a., Suet. Also with <i>refl. pron.</i>:
<i>to act haughtily</i>, ferociter se a., Tac.:
Sall.

2. făcio, fēci, factum, 3 (esp.
with <i>adv.</i>): <i>to act well or ill</i>, recte aut
perperam f., Cic.: <i>Licinius a.'d like a
gentleman in coming to me</i>, fecit humaniter
L. quod ad me venit, Cic.: v. <f>TO
DO</f>.

3. gĕro, gessi, gestum, 3 (with
<i>refl. pron.</i>): <i>to act honourably</i>, honeste
se g., Cic.: <i>to act as a citizen</i>, se pro
cive g., Cic.: <i>to act shamefully upon an
embassy</i>, turpiter in legatione se g.,
Plin.: v. <f>TO BEHAVE ONESELF</f>. Phr.:
<i>to act in such a way that</i>, committere
ut (also with <i>inf.</i> poet.): <i>it is not like
me so to act as to seem to have been
negligent in correspondence</i>, non est
meum committere ut in scribendo negligens
fuisse videar, Cic.: Caes.: <i>to act
cruelly towards any one</i>, crudeliter in
aliquem consulere, Liv.: Sall.: <i>to act
under the influence of passion and
anger</i>, cupidine atque ira grassari, Sall.:
Tac. (v. <f>TO PROCEED</f>).

III. <i>To perform
on the stage</i>: in scena esse, Cic.;
in scenam prodire (the latter strictly <i>to
appear upon the stage</i>): Nep. Pref. 5:
Suet. (agere <i>alone</i> is simply <i>to deliver</i>,
whether of an <i>actor</i> or an <i>orator</i>).
Phr.: <i>Domitian forbade players to act
in public</i>, D. interdixit histrionibus scenam,
Suet.: <i>to act and gesticulate upon
the stage</i>, gestum agere in scena, Cic.
Or. 2, 57: v. <i>infr.</i> (trans.).

IV.
Of medicine: v. <f>TO OPERATE</f>.

B.
Trans.: <i>to sustain</i> a certain part, <i>on
the stage</i> or fig.:

1. ăgo, ēgi, actum,
3: <i>to act a comedy</i>, comediam a., Pl.: <i>to
act the principal part</i>, primas partes a.,
Ter. (v. <f>PART</f>): <i>Laberius acted his own
farce</i>, Laberius mimum suum egit,
Suet. Hence fig.: <i>to act the part of a
principal</i> or <i>subordinate</i>, principem,
ministrum a., Suet[**.]: Tac.: v. <i>supr.</i>
(intrans.). <i>To act frequently</i>, actĭto,
1: <i>Aeschines, when a young man, had
often acted tragedies</i>, Aeschines adolescens
tragoedias actitaverat, Cic. ap.
Aug.: <i>Valens often acted farces</i>, Valens
mimos actitavit, Tac.: v. <f>TO PLAY</f>.

2.
sustĭneo, tĭnui, tentum.[**,?] 2: <i>I act three
parts all alone</i>, tres personas unus s.,
Cic.: Suet.


<b>act</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

I. <i>The thing done</i>:

1. factum: <i>he is not only innocent
of the act, but free from even the suspicion
of being accessory to it</i>, non modo
a facto sed etiam a conscientiae suspicione
abest, Cic.: <i>I am glad that my
act is approved by you</i>, meum factum
abs te probari gaudeo, Caes. ap. Cic.:
<i>illustrious and glorious acts</i>, facta illus-*
-----File: b0011r.png------------------------------------------------------
*tria et gloriosa, Cic.: v. <f>ACTION</f>, <f>DEED</f>,
<f>EXPLOIT</f>.

2. acta, orum (esp. <i>acts
of public functionaries</i> or <i>which partook
of a public character</i>): <i>and do ye, who
are overturning Caesar's laws, defend
his acts?</i> et vos acta Caesaris defenditis
qui leges ejus evertitis? Cic.: <i>the acts
of your tribuneship</i>, acta tui tribunatus,
Cic.: <i>plans first, then acts, afterwards
results</i>, consilia prima, deinde acta,
postea eventus, Cic.

3. actĭo (chiefly
of <i>official proceedings</i>)[** :|P2: yes, in my copy] <i>the acts of the
tribunes</i>, actiones tribunorum, Caes.:
Liv.: v. <f>PROCEEDINGS</f>.

4. actus, ūs
(rare): v. <f>ACTION</f>. Phr.: <i>our friends
the Stoics deny that to flee is the act of
a wise man</i>, Stoici nostri negant fugere
sapientis, Cic.: <i>for me now to inquire
closely into these things is the act of an
unreasonable father</i>, nunc ea me exquirere
iniqui patris est, Ter.: <i>to commit
hostile acts</i>, hostilia facere, Sall.: <i>Indutiomarus
was caught in the very act of
crossing the river</i>, in ipso fluminis vado
Indutiomarus deprehensus est, Caes.:
<i>when the soldiers were in the very act of
scaling the walls</i>, cum jam in eo esset,
ut in muros miles evaderet, Liv. (the
esset is <i>impers.</i>) <i>An act of parliament</i>
(v. <f>PARLIAMENT</f>): <i>the acts of the
Apostles</i>, acta Apostolorum, Vulg.

II.
<i>A division of a drama</i>; actus, ūs: <i>the
fourth act</i>, quartus actus, Cic.: <i>let not
a play either close before or extend beyond
the fifth act</i>, neve minor neu sit
quinto productior actu fabula, Hor.
Fig.: <i>the last act of life</i>, extremus
actus aetatis, Cic.


<b>action</b>:

I. <i>The putting forth of
power</i> or <i>exercise of faculty</i>:

1. actio,
ōnis, <i>f.</i>: <i>to divest the gods of motion
and of divine a.</i>, spoliare deos motu
et a. divina, Cic.: <i>the a. of the body</i>, a.
corporis, Cic.: <i>vital a.</i>, vitae a., Cic.: <i>in
undertaking every a. three things are to
be observed</i>, in omni a. suscipienda tria
sunt tenenda, Cic. Hence of definite
things done: <i>a.s right or honourable</i>, a.
rectae, honestae, Sen.

2. actus, ūs:
<i>a head liable to tremble with the least a.</i>,
caput in quantulocunque a. tremulum,
Suet.: <i>to die in a.</i>, in actu mori, Sen.: <i>to
be engaged in some kind of a.</i>, in aliquo
a. esse, Lact. Hence of <i>particular a.s</i>:
<i>good and bad a.s</i>, recti pravi a., Cic.
(but the reading is doubtful, and no
other example of such usage appears to
occur in Cic.): Sil.: Claud.

II. <i>Something
done</i>: v. <f>DEED</f>, <f>ACT</f>, <f>CONDUCT</f>.

III. <i>In works of art</i>: esp. dramas:
actio: <i>the play has much a.</i>, fabula multas
actiones habet, Cic.

IV. <i>Gesticulation
in the delivery of a speech</i>:

1.
actio: <i>a. is a kind of bodily speech</i>, est
a. quasi sermo corporis, Cic.: <i>varied
and vehement a., full of spirit</i>, a. varia,
vehemens, plena spiritus, Cic.

2.
actus, ūs: Quint.: Suet.

V. <i>A
course of legal proceedings</i>, or <i>the right
to institute them</i>:

1. actĭo: <i>to bring
an a. against any one</i>, a. alicui intendere,
Cic.: Quint.: a. inferre cum aliquo,
Dig.: <i>to arrange the proceedings of
an a.</i> (as an advocate), a. instituere,
Cic.: <i>an a. for personal injuries</i>, a. injuriarum,
Cic.: <i>an a. for theft</i>, a. furti,
etc.: <i>to allow an a.</i> (of the praetor), a.
dare, Cic.: <i>to name the kind of a[**.?]</i>
(which was done by the plaintiff), a[**.?]
edere, Ulp.: <i>to have a right of a.</i> (in
case of injury), habere actionem, Cic.
Actio sometimes means "<i>a formula of
action</i>:" <i>Cn. Flavius, a scribe, made the
fasti public, and drew up the forms of
actions</i>, Cn. Flavius, scriba, fastos protulit
actionesque composuit, Cic.: v.
<f>CAUSE</f>, <f>SUIT</f>.

2. dĭca (δίκη: only of
<i>an action in a Greek court of law</i>): <i>to
bring an a. against any one</i>, alicui
dicam scribere, Cic.: Ter.: d. alicui subscribere,
Pl.: d. alicui impingere, Ter.
<sc>Note.</sc> The word is used by Cic. in
speaking of a Sicilian court, and by the
comic writers with reference to those
of Greece. Phr.: <i>To bring an action</i>:

1. ăgo, ēgi, actum, 3: esp. with
lege: <i>to bring an a. at law for an inheritance</i>,
a. lege in hereditatem, Cic.
-----File: b0012l.png------------------------------------------------------
<i>to bring an a. on an agreement</i>, ex sponso
a.[**assumed], Cic.: <i>to bring an a. at civil law</i>, ex
jure civili a., Cic.

2. litem, actionem
intendo, etc.: v. <f>LAWSUIT</f>, and <i>supr.</i>
(V.).

VI. <i>An engagement, battle</i>: q. v.


<b>actionable</b>:

1. cujus rei actio est:
<i>I enquire whether this is a. or not</i>, quaero

Cic.: v. <f>ACTION</f> (V. 1).

2. obnoxius
(only of persons): <i>my conduct is a.

<b>active</b>:

I. <i>Full of action; of a
nature to exert power</i>:

1. actŭōsus:
<i>virtue is a.</i>, virtus a. est, Cic.: <i>a. life</i>, a.
vita, Cic.

2. actīvus: <i>a. philosophy</i>
(opp. to that which is purely contemplative
or theoretical), a. philosophia, Sen.:
Quint. <i>To be a.</i>, agere: v. <f>TO ACT</f>
(I. 1).

II. <i>Capable of quick movement</i>[** :]

1. ălăcar, cris, cre: <i>he vied
with the a. in leaping, with the swift in
running</i>, cum alacribus saltu, cum velocibus
cursu certabat, Sall. ap. Veg. (rare
in this sense: v. <f>CHEERFUL</f>, <f>BRISK</f>).

2. ăgĭlis, e: <i>an a. right hand</i>, a. dextra,
Stat.: <i>the a. goddess</i> (i. e. <i>Diana</i>),
a. dea, Ov.: v. <f>AGILE</f>, <f>NIMBLE</f>.

3.
impĭger, gra, grum: <i>a. with one's hand</i>,
i. manu, Tac.: Cic.

4. Fig. of <i>activity
of mind</i>: vĕgĕtus: <i>nor could the

III. <i>Busy, industrious</i>:

1. ĭmpĭger, gra, grum: <i>a.
service in the field</i>, i. militia, Liv.: <i>a.
tongues, sluggish souls</i>, i. linguae, ignavi
animi, Sall.: with a <i>gen.</i>: <i>a. in the
field</i>, i. militiae, Tac.

2. ăgĭlis, e:
<i>anon I became an a. man</i>, nunc a. fio[**unclear]
(i. e., <i>a man of action</i>), Hor.: <i>the mind
is by nature a.</i>, natura animus a. est,
Sen.

3. ācer, acris, acre: <i>a. in the
transaction of affairs</i> (said of Caesar),
a. in rebus gerendis, Coel. ap. Cic.: <i>the
a. husbandman</i>, a. agricola, Virg.[**:] v.
<f>KEEN</f>, <f>VIGOROUS</f>.

4. gnāvus or nāvus:
<i>an a. and industrious man</i>, homo

5. ŏpĕrōsus: <i>a. old
age</i>, o. senectus, Cic.

6. industrĭus:
<i>peace keeps the a. and the inactive upon

take a man away from a. life</i>, a rebus
gerendis abstrahere, avocare, Cic.: <i>to
be ever a.</i>, semper agere et moliri aliquid,
Cic.: <i>to be more a.</i>, plus agere, Cic.
<sc>Note.</sc> Impiger signifies <i>readiness to undertake</i>;
agilis, <i>busy activity</i>; acer, <i>keenness
and vigour of enterprise</i>; gnavus
and industrius, <i>activity in general as
opp. to indolence</i>; operosus, <i>a disposition
to undertake many works</i>: v. also
<f>VIGOROUS</f>. Join: acer et diligens:
acer et industrius: gnavus et industrius,
experientissimus et diligentissimus: vigilans
et industrius, Cic.

<b>actor</b>:

I. <i>One who acts</i>: actor:
<i>a speaker of words and an a. of things</i>,
orator verborum actorque rerum, Cic.:
v. <f>DOER</f>.

II. <i>A performer of plays</i>:

1. actor (which also denotes <i>a
pleader</i>, etc., and should not be used
unless it is clear from the context that
<i>a stage-actor</i> is meant): <i>good poets and
diligent a.s are wont to be most careful
in the last act</i>, poetae boni et a. industrii
in extremo actu diligentissimi esse
solent, Cic.: <i>a first-rate a.</i>, a. summus,
Cic.: <i>to tolerate bad a.s on the stage</i>, in
theatro malos a. perpeti, Cic.: Hor.
Also a. scenicus, Quint.

2. histrio,
ōnis, <i>m.</i> (used of all kinds of <i>theatrical
performers</i>: v. inf. 5): <i>as to
the a. a certain delivery, to the dancer
a certain movement is assigned</i>, ut[** speck not punct.]
histrioni actio, saltatori motus certus
est datus, Cic.: <i>to hiss an a. off the
stage</i>, h. exsibilare, explodere, Cic.: <i>a
miserable a.</i>, pessimus h., Cic.: <i>an a. of
tragedies or comedies</i>, comoediarum aut
tragoediarum h., Plin.

3. lūdius and
lūdio, ōnis, <i>m.</i> (<i>an inferior kind of
dancing player</i>): Liv.: Cic.

4. <i>an
actor in a tragedy</i>: trăgoedus, <i>m.</i>: <i>the
orator needs the voice of a tragic a.</i>, vox
tragoedorum est requirendus (oratori),
Cic.: Hor.

5. <i>an actor in a comedy</i>:
cōmoedus, <i>m.</i>: <i>the man who was not
even reckoned among the worst of theatrical
performers, became the first of
comic a.s</i>, qui ne in novissimis erat
histrionibus, ad primos venit comoedos,
Cic.

6. mīmus, <i>f.</i> mīma: only used
of <i>performers in pantomime</i>: Cic.: Ov.

7. artĭfex scēnĭcus: Sen.: Gell.


<b>actress</b>: <sc>Note.</sc> As females were
not employed in the Roman regular
drama, there is no word exactly suitable:
mĭma signifies <i>a low kind of theatrical
dancer</i> and pantomimic performer:
scēnĭca (for scenica mulier)
occurs in Cod. Justin. Lūdia (Juv.:
Mart.) is apparently equiv. to mima.


<b>actual</b>: vērus: v. <f>REAL</f>, <f>TRUE</f>.


<b>actuality</b>: metaphys. t. t., opp. to
<f>POTENTIALITY</f>:[**:?] actus, ūs (ἐντελέχεια,
Arist.): Apul.


<b>actually</b>: re verâ, v. <f>REALLY</f>, <f>TRULY</f>.


<b>actuary</b>: *actŭārius (prop. a sort of

<b>admissibility</b>: expr. by <i>gerund.</i> of

co-optandus esset (or co-optari

1. dēnuo

2. ĭtĕrum (a <i>second</i>

-----File: b0021l.png------------------------------------------------------
<i>Caesar sends ambassadors to him a.</i>,

3. rursus <i>and</i> rursum: <i>the Helvetii

Phr.: <i>I must lose as much a.</i>, alterum

II. <i>Further</i>, in addition:

1. autem: v. <f>MOREOVER</f>.

2. jam: <i>a., how sensible his advice

3. porro: <i>I have often heard

4. rursus <i>and</i> rursum: <i>what-*ever

<b>against</b>:

I. <i>Upon</i> (usu. with an
implication of force):

1. ĭn (with <i>acc.</i>):
<i>he runs and falls a. me</i>, in me incurrit
atque incidit, Cic.: <i>the Gauls rush a.
the Romans</i>, Galli in Romanos incurrunt,
Liv.

2. ăd (with <i>acc.</i>): <i>to strike
one's head a. an arch</i>, caput ad fornicem
offendere, Quint.: <i>they lean a. the trees</i>,
se ad arbores applicant, Caes.: v. <f>UPON</f>.
(In this sense <i>against</i> is usu. expr. by
prefixes to the verbs, as, <i>to run a.</i>,
incurro, occurro, etc.: for which see the
several verbs.)

II. <i>In opposition</i>;
denoting <i>hostility, contradiction, disapprobation,
injury, protection from</i>:

1.
contrā (with <i>acc.</i> in all the above
senses): <i>to conspire a. the Roman
people</i>, conjurare c. populum R., Caes.:
Cic.: <i>one man can do nothing a. many</i>,
nihil unus potest c. multos, Cic.: <i>a. any
one's judgment</i>, c. alicujus judicium, Cic.
(v. <f>CONTRARY TO</f>): <i>evidence which is a.
any one</i>, testimonium quod c. aliquem
est, Cic.: <i>this is not only not in my
favour, but is a. me</i>, hoc non modo non
pro me sed c. me est, Cic.: <i>a protection
a. cold</i>, tutela c. frigora, Plin.: Cic.

2. ĭn (with <i>acc.</i>: esp. of <i>direct
attack upon</i>): <i>to inflame the people a.
evil men</i>, populum inflammare in improbos,
Cic.: <i>to inveigh a. the tribunes</i>,
in tribunos incurrere, Liv.

3. adversŭs
<i>or</i> adversum (with <i>acc.</i>: of <i>direct
hostility</i> and of <i>remedies a.</i>): <i>I will
follow you a. my old allies</i>, sequar vos
adv. veteres socios meos, Liv.: <i>I will
not contend a. you</i>, non contendam ego
adv. te, Cic.: <i>remedies a. poisons</i>, remedia
adv. venena, Cels.

4. ăd (with
<i>acc.</i>: rare): <i>they dare to go a. any
number of horse-soldiers</i>, ad quemvis
numerum equitum adire audent, Caes.:
<i>to prepare for war a. the enemy</i>, ad
hostes bellum parare, Liv.: v. also,
<f>CONTRARY TO</f>, <f>FROM</f>, <f>FOR</f>.

III. <i>In a
contrary direction</i>: contrā (with <i>acc.</i>):
<i>the beams turned a. the force and current

<i>a. the stream</i>, adverso flumine <i>or</i> in adversum
flumen, Caes.: Liv.: <i>the winds

<b>agent</b>:

I. <i>An actor, he that acts</i>:

1. actor: <i>Cato was the a. in those
things</i>: Cato a. illarum rerum fuit, Cic.

2. auctor: <i>the inquiry refers both
to the act and to the a.</i>, quaeritur et de

nunquam fuit, Cic.

II. <i>One who

1. prōcūrātor (in

or in person</i>, nihil interest utrum per

Cic.: <i>the a.s of Dolabella</i>, Dolabellae
p., Cic.: <i>a legally-appointed a.</i>, legitime
p. dictus, Cic.: Quint.

2. cūrātor
(with some limiting word): <i>he
had a faithful a.</i>, erat ei negotiorum
curator fidus, Sall.: <i>a. of the commonwealth</i>
(said by Bocchus of Sulla), c. reipublicae,
Sall.

3. auctor (rather rare):
<i>that admirable a. of his state!</i> praeclarus
iste a. suae civitatis.[**P2: ,] Cic.: <i>the a.
of many societies</i>, multarum societatum
a., Cic.

4. interpres, ĕtis (esp. in <i>bad</i>
sense): <i>a.s for corrupting the administration
of justice</i>, interpretes corrumpendi
judicii, Cic.: Liv.

5. mĭnister,
tri: <i>the freedman of Fabricius had been
his a. in a crime</i>, Fabricii libertus m.
in malefacto fuerat, Cic.: <i>the a.s of
their wickedness were arrested</i>, sceleris
ministri comprehensi sunt, Liv.: v.
<f>ABETTER</f>.

6. admĭnister, tri: <i>a.s
and abetters of Naevius</i>, a. et satellites

preceding are general terms, and must
not be used for <i>agent</i> in its strict and
legal sense.) Phr.: <i>to be a. for any
one</i>, alicui procurare, Dig.: <i>to be a. for
distributing provisions</i>,[**P2: ,] alimentis dividendis
procurare, Capit.

III. <i>An active

<b>alter</b> (<i>v.</i>):

A. Trans.:

1. mūto,
1 (<i>to modify, change partially</i>): <i>to a.
a will</i>, testamentum m., Cic.: <i>to a.
one's opinion</i>, sententiam m., Cic.: <i>Tarquinius
did not a. the centuries of
knights at all</i>, nec T. de equitum centuriis
quidquam mutavit, Liv.: v. <f>TO
CHANGE</f>.

2. immūto, 1: <i>to a. the
arrangement of words</i>, i. verborum
ordinem, Cic.: <i>to a. the arrangements of
another</i>, aliquid de alicujus institutis
i., Cic.

3. dēmūto, 1 (<i>partially to
change</i>: hence closely corresponding to
the Eng.): <i>they resolved that nothing
should be a.'d in the institution of the
flamens</i>, placitum instituto flaminum
-----File: b0029m.png------------------------------------------------------
nihil demutari, Tac.: <i>to a. one's opinion
about a matter</i>, sententiam in aliqua re
d., Gell.: <i>I must a. my style of speech</i>,
oratio mihi demutanda est, Pl.--<sc>Note.</sc>
<i>Muto</i> must not be used for <i>to alter</i>, unless
the context shows that only a <i>part</i>, not
the whole is changed: thus mutare vestitum
is <i>to change one's dress altogether</i>,
esp. of <i>going into mourning</i>: <i>to a[** .] one's
style of dress</i> may be expr. by aliquid
de vestitu solito mutare, immutare: v.
<f>TO CHANGE</f>[** .] Phr.: <i>to a.</i> (<i>a will</i>, etc.)
<i>by falsifying</i>, corrumpere, vitiare, etc.:
v. <f>TO FALSIFY</f>: <i>to be very much a.'d</i>, i. e.
<i>in personal appearance</i>, *specie oris
vultuque multum immutatum esse.

B.
Intrans.: <i>to undergo change</i>: mūtor,
immūtor, dēmūtor, used reflectively;
as, <i>times a. and we a. with them</i>, tempora
mutantur, et nos m. in illis, Hor.:
v. (A.) and <f>TO CHANGE</f>.

<b>although</b>:

1. etsi (i. e. <i>even if;
notwithstanding</i>: with the <i>Indic.</i> when

gaudeo etsi nihil scio quod gaudeam, Pl.:
<i>a. you had deprived Sulla of nothing but
the consulship, yet you ought to have
been satisfied with that</i>, etsi nihil aliud

eo vos contentos esse oportebat, Cic.

2. ĕtĭamsi (same constr. as etsi,
but more emphatic): <i>a. the truth is not
pleasant, yet</i>, etc., veritas e. jucunda
non est, tamen, etc., Cic.: <i>with your aid,
a. we were fearful, yet we would cast
away all fear</i>, tuis opibus, e. timidi
essemus, tamen omnem timorem abjiceremus,
Cic.

3. lĭcĕt (only hypothetical,
and strictly <i>a verb</i>: with <i>subj.</i>)[** : ?] <i>a.
all dangers may threaten me, yet I will
assist (my client) and encounter (them)</i>,
licet omnia in me pericula impendeant,
succurram atque subibo, Cic.: <i>life is
short, a. it should exceed a thousand
years</i>, vita brevis est, licet supra mille
annos exeat, Sen. (v. <f>IT IS ALLOWED</f>.)

4. tămetsi <i>or</i> tămĕnetsi (= <i>notwithstanding</i>;
of actual facts, hence
usu. with <i>Indic.</i>): <i>I should not really
believe what I am saying, a. I had generally
heard it</i>, non mehercule haec quae
loquor crederem, tametsi vulgo audieram,
Cic.: <i>and a. Caesar understood
these things, yet he summons the ambassadors</i>,
quae tametsi Caesar intellegebat,
tamen legatos appellat, Caes.

5.
quanquam (constr. same as preceding):
<i>a. he is wicked</i>, q. est scelestus,
Ter.: <i>a. you are in haste, the delay is
not long</i>, q. festinas, non est mora longa,
Hor.: esp. used by a person correcting
himself, where it forms a kind of sentence
in itself: <i>a. (were it so), even that
would give rise to no suspicion of a
coalition</i>, q., ne id quidem suspicionem
coitionis habuerit, Cic.

6. ŭt (with
<i>subj.</i>: esp. in sense <i>granting that</i>: q.v.):
<i>but a. it be so, yet you cannot predicate

haec omnia ut invitis ita non
adversantibus patriciis transacta, Liv.:
<i>they go together to the waters of the
Cephisus, a. not yet clear, yet already

pariter Cephisidas undas, ut nondum
liquidas, sic jam vada nota secantes, Ov.

7. quum (with <i>subj.</i>): <i>he says that
a. these things are so, yet he will make
peace with them</i>, dicit quum ea ita sint,
tamen sese cum iis pacem facturum,
Caes.: Cic.

8. quamvīs (prop. <i>however
much</i>: hence esp. in connection
with adjectives: constr. same as 1, 2).[** : ?]

gesserat q. reipublicae calamitosas, attamen

tibi q. infesto animo perveneras, ingredienti

<b>always</b>:

I. <i>Perpetually</i>: whether
in strictly philosophic sense, or colloquially:
sempĕr: <i>what a. moves is
eternal</i>, quod s. movetur aeternum est,
Cic.: <i>nor does Apollo a. bend the bow</i>,
neque s. arcum tendit Apollo, Hor.: of
that which is <i>regularly done at stated
times</i>: <i>country-folks always harrow
before they hoe</i>, s. occant priusquam
sarriunt rustici, Plin.: <i>I a. shudder when
I begin to knock at this door</i>, horresco s.
ubi pultare hasce occipio fores, Ter.
Phr.: <i>he was almost a. in the country</i>,
ruri fere se continebat, Ter.: <i>when the
sky was stormy, he a. wore a laurel
wreath on his head</i>, turbatiore coelo
nunquam non coronam lauream capite
gestavit, Suet. Tib. 69: v. <f>CONSTANTLY</f>,
<f>PERPETUALLY</f>.

II. <i>Without exception</i>:
this sense occurs chiefly with superlatives;
when it may be expr. by quisque:
<i>the best speakers are a. the most alive to
the difficulty of speaking</i>, ut quisque
optime dicit, ita maxime dicendi difficultatem
timet, Cic.: <i>the newest things
are a. the most correct and free from
faults</i>, recentissima quaeque sunt correcta
et emendata maxime, Cic.

<b>and</b>:

1. ĕt: et properly joins
words or sentences which have, or are
represented as having, only a fortuitous
or temporary connection: (i) the simple
conjunction: <i>cold and hunger and thirst</i>,
frigus et fames et sitis, Cic.: <i>Caesar
orders Divitiacus to be summoned to him
and converses with him</i>, Caesar Divitiacum
ad se vocari jubet et cum eo colloquitur,
Caes.--<i>Obs.</i> When several substantives
are connected in English by
<i>and</i>, as in the first of the above examples,
the et must either be repeated
with each additional member, as there
(πολυσύνδετον), or else omitted altogether
(ἀσύνδετον): as, <i>honour, faith,
intellect, concord</i>, honos, fides, mens,
concordia, Cic. When a number of
words are connected, the latter mode is
usually preferred unless special emphasis
is needed. (Cic. has in one place, composite,
ornate, copiose loqui; and in
another, prudenter <i>et</i> composite <i>et</i> ornate
<i>et</i> memoriter dicere (Or. 1, 15, 64):
the several words being in the latter
case brought out with more distinctness
and emphasis.) <i>Que</i> (v. <i>inf.</i> 3) is however
frequently used with the last member
of a series, when that member
gathers up a number of particulars: as,
<i>in astronomy, the rising, setting, and
movements of the stars</i>, in astrologia,
ortus, obitus, motusque siderum, Cic.
(ii) the conj. emphasized = <i>and indeed</i>:
<i>you were wrong and indeed exceedingly
wrong</i>, errabas, et vehementer errabas,
Cic. (iii) = <i>and then</i> (indicating an
immediate result): <i>he said, and then instantly
perceived that he had fallen into
the midst of the enemy</i>, dixit, et extemplo
sensit medios delapsus in hostes,
Virg.: (iv) = <i>and yet</i> (subjoining an emphatic
question or exclamation): <i>and
yet are there people who complain about
the Appian way?</i> et sunt qui de via
Appia querantur? Cic. (v) = <i>and so
too, and also</i>: <i>these things themselves
are a source of pleasure to me, and so
too were those to the Torquati</i>, haec ipsa
mihi sunt voluptati, et erant illa Tor-*
-----File: b0033r.png------------------------------------------------------
*quatis, Cic.

2. atquĕ <i>or</i> āc (the
latter in classical prose gen. only before
consonants): this conj. differs from et
in denoting a closer connection between
the ideas represented by the connected
words or clauses: hence it is often employed
to join two substantives which
together represent a single complex
idea. (i) the simple conj.: <i>to speak
from the heart and truly</i>, ex animo ac
vere dicere, Ter.: <i>the dangers of this
city and empire</i>, pericula hujus urbis
atque imperii, Cic.: <i>with your virtuous
feeling</i>, isto animo atque virtute, Cic.:
<i>Caesar gave the signal for joining battle,
and having set out for the other wing,
he fell in with those actually engaged</i>,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed, clear on TIA]
Caesar proelii committendi signum dedit,
atque in alteram partem profectus,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed, clear on TIA]
pugnantibus occurrit, Caes. (ii) the
conj. emphasized = <i>and indeed</i>, <i>and
even</i>, <i>and especially</i>: <i>a difficult affair,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed, clear on TIA]
and indeed the most difficult of all</i>, res
difficilis atque omnium difficillima, Cic.:
<i>great thanks are due to the immortal
gods, and especially to this very Jupiter
Stator</i>, magna diis immortalibus habenda
est gratia atque huic ipsi Jovi
Statori, Cic.: <i>the river can be crossed on
foot in one place only, and even in this
with difficulty</i>, flumen uno omnino loco
pedibus atque hoc aegre transiri potest,
Caes.

3. quĕ, an enclitic which connects
words rather than sentences, and
words usually standing in the same relation
to the rest of the sentence, and
representing things very closely connected,
either naturally and generally,
or at least under the circumstances
spoken of; hence such words often denote
a single complex idea. <i>Que</i> must
be affixed to the <i>second</i> of the two
words; and it is to be specially observed
that it is rarely added to
words ending in a <i>short</i> vowel, especially
ĕ: <i>that force overcame all the
allurements of pleasure and ease</i>, ea vis
omnia blandimenta voluptatis otiique
vicit, Cic.: <i>the Aulerci and Lexovii shut
their gates</i>, Aulerci Lexoviique portas
clauserunt, Caes.: <i>having collected twigs
and underwood they go straight to the
camp</i>, sarmentis virgultisque collectis
ad castra pergunt, Caes.: <i>the arrangement
and order of the line of march</i>,
ratio ordoque agminis, Caes.: <i>a shout
and din arose, and some rushed one
way, some another,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed, clear on TIA] panic-stricken</i>, clamor
fremitusque oriebatur aliique aliam
in partem perterriti ferebantur, Caes.
<i>Que</i> may be used after a substantive
preceded by a preposition: as, <i>he went
to Rome and began to appear in the
forum</i>, Romam demigravit, in foroque
esse coepit, Nep.: Cic.--N.B. (i) When
a connected clause contains a <i>negative</i>,
the conjunction "and" and the negative
are often expressed by <i>neque</i> or <i>nec</i>,
especially where the former clause contains
a correlative conjunction: <i>you perceive
that he both had presence of mind
and was not wanting in prudence</i>, intelligitis
et animum ei praesto[** unclear|P2: Google likes] fuisse, nec
consilium defuisse, Cic.: <i>at that time
games were celebrated during ten days,
and nothing was omitted with a view to
appeasing the gods</i>, tunc et ludi decem
per dies facti sunt, neque res ulla quae
ad placandum deos pertineret praetermissa
est, Cic.: <i>he saw that affairs were
in a critical state and that there was no
reserve that could be sent up</i>, rem esse
in angusto vidit, neque ullum esse subsidium
quod submitti posset, Caes. (ii)
"And" connected with a demonstrative
or personal pronoun may often be expressed
in Latin by the relative pronoun
alone: <i>and Caesar having been informed
of these things orders ships of war to be
built</i>, quibus de rebus Caesar certior factus
naves longas aedificari jubet, Caes.:
<i>the soldiers were endeavouring to board
the enemies' ships, and when the barbarians
observed this, they strove to save
themselves by flight</i>, milites transcendere
in hostium naves contendebant. Quod
postquam barbari fieri animadverterunt
fuga salutem petere contenderunt, Caes.
-----File: b0034l.png------------------------------------------------------
(iii) In many cases where "and" is
employed to connect single words, it
must or may be omitted in Latin, especially
in enumerations;[**P2: : ?] but as it is impossible
to reduce such cases to rule,
they must be left to observation. It
frequently happens also that where we
employ two or more co-ordinate sentences
or clauses, connected by "and,"
the Latin language expresses the sense
of one or more of the clauses by a participial
or relative clause, attached to
one of the terms of the principal sentence,
and therefore forming part of the
latter, so that a conjunction is not required.
But the grammar rather than
the dictionary must be consulted on
such points: v. also <f>BOTH</f> (<i>conj.</i>).

Respecting the Latin conjunctions
above spoken of, see Allen's Doctrina
Cop. Ling. Latinae.

<b>another, one</b> (reciprocal): usu. expressed

on <i>inter</i>: <i>they give a pledge and

<b>antiquity</b>:

I. <i>Ancient times</i>:

1.
antīquĭtas: <i>stories derived from the remotest
a.</i>, fabulae ab ultima a. repetitae,
Cic.: <i>an extravagant admirer of a.</i>, antiquitatis
nimius admirator,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed, clear on TIA] Quint.: <i>a
knowledge of a.</i>, antiquitatis notitia,
Suet.: <i>a lover of a.</i>, antiquitatis amator,
Nep.

2. vĕtustas: <i>history, the messenger
of antiquity</i>, historia nuntia vetustatis,
Cic.: <i>all the precedents of a.</i>,
omnia vetustatis exempla,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed, clear on TIA] Caes.--<sc>Note.</sc>
Antiquitas is used of things simply as
<i>belonging to ancient times</i>; vetustas of
what has remained and become old (cf.
<f>ANCIENT</f>, 1, 2): the difference is brought
out in the following passage of Cic.: errabat
multis in rebus <i>antiquitas</i> (<i>bygone
ages</i>) quam vel usu jam ... vel vetustate
(<i>through having become old</i>, and so
<i>obsolete</i>) immutatam videmus, Div. 2,
33, 70.

3. aetas vetus, Cic. Join.[**P2: .: ?]
vetus illa atque antiqua aetas.

II. <i>The
people of ancient times</i>:

1. antīquĭtas:
<i>a. fabulously related</i>, a. fabulose narravit,
Plin:[**P2: Plin.:] Cic. (l. c.[**prev. ital.] supr.).

2.
vĕtustas: <i>who would believe this, if
a. were not its witness?</i> quis hoc
credat, nisi sit pro teste vetustas?
Ov. Met. 1, 400.

III. <i>The remains
of ancient times</i>:

1. antīquĭtas (but
antiquitas is much more extensive in its
application than the English <i>antiquities</i>,
including <i>history and the origin of nations</i>):
<i>the Greeks were fond of a.s</i>, laetum
antiquitatibus Graecorum genus,
Tac.: <i>Roman a.s</i>, [**P2: missing asterisk?]antiquitates Romanae.

2. monumenta antiquitatis
(al. vetustatis): Cic. dom. 32, 86; but
here too the reference is to <i>records</i>, not
existing remains: the phrase however
will include all that preserves the
memory of antiquity.

IV. <i>Ancientness</i>:

2. vĕtustas
(<i>i. e.</i> old standing): <i>the reputation and a.
of a state</i>, nomen et v. civitatis, Caes.:
<i>they defend themselves by the a. of their
possession, not by their right</i>, vetustate
possessionis se non jure defendunt, Cic.

<b>any</b>: <b>any one</b>, <b>any thing</b>:

1.
quis <i>or</i> qui, quae, quod <i>or</i> quid (usu. with
si, ne, or num: the forms quis and quid
are for the most part used <i>substantively</i>,
while qui and quod are used adjectively;
so in the compounds aliquis, aliqui, etc.:
quis is less <i>emphatic</i> than quispiam or
quisquam, and less <i>definite</i> than aliquis.
It is precisely = Gr. τίς): <i>the question
is whether any one duty is greater than
another</i>, quaeritur num quod officium
aliud alio majus sit, Cic.: <i>if any one
had fallen from his horse</i>, si qui equo
deciderat, Caes.: <i>if any one bring an
action against you</i>, si te in judicium
quis adducat, Cic.: <i>if I have committed
any offence against you, forgive it</i>, si
quid in te peccavi, ignosce, Cic.: <i>lest
any danger might befal</i>, ne quod periculum
incideret, Cic.

2. ălĭqui <i>or</i> ălĭquis,
ălĭqua, ălĭquod <i>or</i> ălĭquid (usu. emphatic,
and opposed either expressly or
impliedly to such words as <i>all</i>, <i>much</i>,
<i>none</i>, <i>&c.</i>): <i>this or any (other) condition
of the republic</i>, hic aut aliqui status reipublicae,
Cic.: <i>name any one</i> (or <i>some
one</i>) <i>person</i>, unum aliquem nominate,
Cic.: <i>any one</i> (or <i>some one</i>) <i>of you</i>,
aliquis ex vobis, Cic.: <i>any</i> (or <i>some
amount of</i>) <i>strength</i>, aliquid virium,
Cic.: <i>if any one</i> (or <i>some one</i>) <i>person
out of many excels</i>, si aliquis excellit
unus e multis, Cic.: <i>anything final</i>, aliquid
extremum, Cic.: v. <f>SOME</f>, <f>SOME ONE</f>.

3. ecqui or ecquis, ecquae <i>or</i> ecqua,
ecquod <i>or</i> ecquid (interrog.): <i>is there any
shame?</i> ecqui pudor est? Cic.: <i>does any
one ask for breakfast?</i> ecqui poscit
prandio? Pl.: <i>will any one open this
door?</i> ecquis aperit hoc ostium? Pl.:
Cic.: Virg.

4. quispiam (not differing
materially from the simple quis, but
rather more emphatic: usu. with si):
<i>what if any god has willed this?</i> quid
si hoc voluit q. deus? Ter.: <i>when any
cohort had left the circle</i>, cum quaepiam
cohors ex orbe excesserat, Caes.: <i>if fortune
has deprived any one of money</i>, si
cuipiam pecuniam fortuna ademit, Cic.

5. quisquam (i. e. <i>any single one</i>,
as opp. to quivis, <i>any one at random</i>):
<i>is there any one in the whole world so
unfortunate?</i> an quisquam usquam
gentium est aeque miser? Ter.: <i>this
tyrant was more hateful than any one
of the preceding</i>, tetrior hic tyrannus
fuit quam q. superiorum, Cic.: <i>is there
any human being of whom you have a
better opinion?</i> estne q. omnium mortalium
de quo melius existimes tu?
Cic.

6. ullus (equiv. in force to quisquam.[** , ?]
only used <i>adjectively</i>, whereas
quisquam is used <i>substantively</i>): esp. (i)
-----File: b0038r.png------------------------------------------------------
in sentences conveying a negation, expressed
or understood: <i>in no other state
has freedom any abode</i>,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed, clear on TIA] nulla alia in civitate
ullum domicilium libertas habet,
Cic.: <i>to march through the province
without doing any damage</i>, sine ullo
maleficio iter per provinciam facere,
Caes.: <i>he says that he cannot grant a
passage to any one</i>, negat se posse iter
ulli dare, Caes. (ii) in interrog. and
hypoth. sentences: <i>is then anything of
so much value?</i> est ergo ulla res (= quicquam)
tanti? Cic.: <i>if any recommendation
of mine has had weight with you</i>,
si ulla mea apud te commendatio valuit,
Cic.

7. omnis, e (only with <i>sine</i>:
when <i>any</i> = <i>all</i>): <i>without any danger</i>,
sine omni periculo, Ter.: <i>without any
wisdom</i>, sine omni sapientia, Cic.
Phr.: <i>hardly any one</i>,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed, clear on TIA] nemo fere, non
fere quisquam, Cic.: v. foll. article.


<b>any soever</b>, <b>any you please</b>:

1.
quīlĭbĕt: <i>any the most trifling circumstance
soever</i>, quaelibet minima res,
Cic.: <i>any name whatever</i>, quodlibet nomen,
Hor.

2. quīvis: <i>they, however
few, dare to encounter any number of
horsemen</i>, ad quemvis numerum equitum
quamvis pauci adire audent, Caes.:
<i>not any one you please taken at random,
but an accomplished connoisseur</i>, non
quivis unus ex populo, sed existimator
doctus, Cic.--<sc>Note.</sc> Quilibet and quivis
are opp. to quisquam, ullus; and signify
<i>any one at random, all alike</i>: thus, <i>I
doubt whether any (single) man can do
this</i>, is, dubito num quisquam hominum
hoc facere possit; whereas, <i>any man</i>
(i. e. <i>all indiscriminately</i>) <i>can do this</i>,
is, cujuslibet, cujusvis est hoc facere.

5. ŭbīvīs (<i>anywhere

<b>apologist</b>:

I. <i>A person who excuses

1. dēprĕcātor
(strictly, <i>one who begs off</i>): <i>not only his

<f>INTERCESSOR</f>.

2. excūsātor: app.
only in Augustine.

3. expr. by verb:

atque extenuare; *vitiis excusandis
atque extenuandis servire: v. <f>TO EXCUSE</f>,
<f>PALLIATE</f>.

II. <i>One who writes

2. dēfensor:
<i>i. e.</i> <f>CHAMPION</f>, <f>DEFENDER</f>: q. v.

<b>appeal</b> (<i>v.</i>):

I. <i>Legal t. t.</i>:

1.
appello, 1 (from one magistrate or court
to another: in the best writers appello is

<i>ad</i>): <i>to a. from the praetor to the

2. prōvŏco,
1 (to the populus in a matter

de majestate damnati ad populum provocant,
Cic.: <i>leave is given to a. from every

II. <i>To

1.

2.
prōvŏco, 1: <i>how right this is you shall

3. cĭto,
1 (with testis): <i>Salamis is a.'d to as

testimony of all Sicily to this fact</i>, in

Cic.: Liv. (similarly, teste uti aliquo;
testimonio alicujus uti, etc..[**P2: .:] v. <f>EVIDENCE</f>,
<f>WITNESS</f>).

4. testor, 1 (used
chiefly in poet. and passionate language:

7. exŏrior (only of that which

3. sisto,

and slaves</i>, opifices atque servitia, Sall.:
Liv.

3. artĭfex, ĭcis (v. <f>ART</f>, II. 2: only
of <i>skilled</i> occupations): Nep. Att. 13.


<b>artist</b>:

I. <i>One who practises any
of the fine arts</i>: artĭfex, ĭcis (more comprehensive
than the Eng. word; yet
<i>chiefly</i> used of <i>painters</i>, <i>sculptors</i> and
<i>actors</i>: v. <f>ART</f>, II. 2): <i>stage a.s, i.e.
actors</i>, scenici artifices, Cic.: Suet.:
<i>Apelles and Lysippus, a.s</i>, Apelles et
Lysippus, artifices, Cic.: <i>the same a.
made that Cupid which is at Thespiae</i>,
idem a. Cupidinem fecit illum qui est
Thespiis, Cic.

II. i. q. <i>painter</i>: q. v.:
pictor.


<b>artistic</b>:

1. artĭfex, ĭcis: <i>a. gesticulation</i>,
a. motus, Quint.: <i>a man of a.
genius</i>, vir artificis ingenii, Plin. (This
passive use of artifex appears not to be
found in Cic.: for artifex stilus [Brut.
25, 96] signifies not "an artistic style,"
but "<i>a stilus</i> or <i>pen that is itself a
master of art</i>:" stilus in the sense of
"<i>style</i>" is of later usage than Cic.).

2. artĭfĭcĭōsus: <i>most elegant and a.
rhetoricians</i>, rhetores elegantissimi et
artificiosissimi, Cic.: v. <f>INGENIOUS</f>.


<b>artistically</b>:

1. artĭfĭcĭōsē: <i>what
the hand effects in the productions of
our arts, that nature effects much more
a.</i>, quod in operibus nostrarum artium
manus efficit, id multo artificiosius natura
efficit, Cic.

2. affabrē: <i>a statue
a. made</i>, signum a. factum, Cic.


<b>artless</b>:

I. <i>Destitute of art</i>:

1. incomptus: <i>a. oratory</i>, oratio i.,
Cic.: <i>the countrymen amuse themselves
with a. verses</i>, coloni versibus incomptis
ludunt, Virg.: Hor.

2. incondĭtus:
<i>a. songs</i>, i. carmina, Liv.: <i>to give forth</i>
-----File: b0049l.png------------------------------------------------------
<i>a. strains</i>, i. jactare, Virg.

3. incompŏsĭtus:
<i>to sport with a. verses</i>, versibus
i. ludere, Virg.

II. <i>Simple, frank,
guileless</i>: q. v.: simplex, ingenuus.


<b>artlessly</b>:

I. <i>Without art</i>: incomptē:
<i>to praise a.</i>, incompte laudare,
Stat.

II. <i>Simply, frankly, guilelessly</i>:
q. v.: ingenue, sine dolo.


<b>artlessness</b>: simplĭcĭtas: v. <f>SIMPLICITY</f>,
<f>FRANKNESS</f>.


<b>as</b>:

I. As a particle of comparison,
denoting <i>equality</i> or <i>similarity</i>:

1. atquĕ, <i>or</i> āc (after the <i>adv.s</i> juxta,
aeque, similiter; the <i>adj.s</i> idem, talis,
similis,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed, clear on TIA] aequus; and other words denoting
<i>identity</i>, <i>equality</i>[**one markup? or keep as list?/F2] or <i>resemblance</i>):
<i>my disposition towards you is the same
as it was</i>, est animus te erga idem ac fuit,
Ter.: <i>the Gauls have the same way of
attacking towns as the Belgae</i>, Gallorum
eadem atque Belgarum oppugnatio est,
Caes.: <i>you will avenge your uncle's
death by the same right as he punished
that of his brother</i>, simili jure tu ulcisceris
patrui mortem atque ille persequeretur
fratris sui, Cic.: <i>he pays as
much respect to me as to his own patron</i>,
me colit et observat aeque atque patronum
suum, Cic.: <i>they made an attack
upon the enemy as soon as they gained a
footing on the beach</i>, simul atque in
arido constiterunt, in hostes impetum
fecerunt, Caes.

2. et (only so used to
imply that what is true of one thing is
true of another <i>also</i>): <i>we love our friends
as well as ourselves</i>, aeque amicos et
nosmet ipsos diligimus, Cic.: <i>the question
is, whether obstinacy is the same as determination</i>,
quaeritur idemne sit pertinacia
et perseverantia, Cic.

3.
quam (esp. as correlative to tam, answering
to the English <i>as ... as</i>: it
denotes a comparison of <i>degree</i> between
two things: v. Habicht, § 79): <i>I was
formerly as free as your son</i>,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed, clear on TIA] tam ego
fui ante liber quam gnatus tuus, Pl.: <i>a
tyrant can be as merciful as a king can
be severe</i>, tam esse clemens tyrannus
quam rex importunus potest, Cic.: <i>he
lived as long as he could</i>, vixit tam diu
quam potuit, Cic.: <i>as much as each one
can</i>, quam quisque potest, Ov.: esp. with
<i>superl.</i>: <i>to give thanks as great as possible</i>,
quam maximas gratias agere,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed, clear on TIA] Cic.:
<i>nothing frightened them so much as the
vigour and complexion of the general</i>, nihil
aeque eos terruit quam robur ac color
imperatoris, Liv. (in this instance <i>quam</i>
is probably used in preference to <i>atque</i>,
<i>ac</i> [v. supr. 1], because of the following
ac): <i>they do not act as they proposed</i>,
contra faciunt quam professi sunt, Cic.

4. qui (only after idem; = atque,
v. supr. 1): <i>the slaves had the same manners
as their masters</i>, servi moribus
iisdem erant quibus domini, Cic.: <i>all
the Gauls must do the same thing as the
Helvetii have done</i>, omnibus Gallis idem
faciendum est quod Helvetii fecerunt,
Caes.

5. prō (<i>prep.</i> with <i>abl.</i>): <i>I
loved him as my own (child)</i>, hunc amavi
pro meo, Ter.: <i>to state as a fact</i>, pro
certo ponere, Caes.

6. quemadmŏdum
(or as separate words, quem ad
modum = <i>in the same manner as</i>): <i>he was
elated by the promises of my colleague,
as he himself said</i>, inflatus est collegae
mei, quemadmodum dicebat ipse, promissis,
Cic.: <i>if you were to discuss
friendship as you are in the habit of
doing with other subjects</i>, si, quemadmodum
soles de ceteris rebus sic de
amicitia disputaris, Cic.

7. ŭt (=
quemadmodum, v. supr.): <i>go on as you
have begun</i>, perge ut instituisti, Cic.:
<i>the army was drawn up as the nature of
the position required</i>, instructus est
exercitus ut loci natura postulabat,
Caes.: <i>I have spoken of these things as
briefly as possible</i>, haec ut brevissime
dici potuerunt, ita a me dicta sunt, Cic.:
rarely and late = atque: <i>in pleading
nothing pleases him so much as brevity</i>,
ei nihil aeque in causis agendis ut brevitas
placet, Plin.

8. sīcŭt (= quemadmodum,
ut: only more emphatic than
the last): (i) in comparisons: <i>as I have
said I will do</i>, sicut dixi faciam, Pl.: <i>as</i>
-----File: b0049m.png------------------------------------------------------
<i>had formerly been done</i>, sicut erat antea
factum, Cic.: <i>I now take no pleasure as
I used formerly in writing trifling
verses</i>, nihil me sicut antea, juvat scribere
versiculos, Hor. (ii) to confirm
a statement = <i>as indeed</i>: <i>let your
affair be important, as it is indeed</i>, sit
ista res magna, sicut est, Cic.: <i>which he
saw would take place, as really happened</i>,
quod fore, sicut accidit, videbat, Caes.
(iii) to introduce a simile: <i>nature has
placed the reasoning faculty in the head,
as in a citadel</i>, natura rationem in
capite sicut in arce posuit, Cic. (iv)
to introduce illustrations: <i>in all which
causes, as in that of M'. Curius itself,
there was very great difference of opinion
on points of law</i>, quibus in causis omnibus,
sicut in ipsa M'. Curii, fuit summa
de jure dissensio, Cic.

9. vĕlut,
vĕlŭti (used to introduce a <i>parallel</i>
case) (i) in comparisons: <i>as the fall of
Saguntum had given confidence for the
war to Hannibal, so had the destruction
of the people of Abydos to Philip</i>, velut
Sagunti excidium Hannibali, sic Philippo
Abydenorum clades ad bellum animos
fecerat, Liv. (ii) to introduce a simile:
<i>Sipylus was giving the rein, as when
the captain of a ship spreads out the
sails</i>, frena dabat Sipylus veluti quum
carbasa rector deducit, Ov.: Hor.:
Quint. (iii) to introduce illustrations:
<i>there is something wonderful in those
aquatic animals which are born on land,
as for example, crocodiles</i>, est admiratio
nonnulla in bestiis aquatilibus iis quae
gignuntur in terra, veluti crocodili, Cic.
(iv) in hypotheses (usu. with si): <i>they
shuddered at the cruelty of Ariovistus
though absent, as if he were before them</i>,
absentis Ariovisti crudelitatem, velut si
coram adesset, horrebant, Caes.: <i>this, as
if obtained by valour, he hoped would
bring him great credit</i>, hoc veluti virtute
paratum, speravit magnae laudi
fore, Hor.

10. īta (in asseverations
and oaths, there being probably an ellipsis
of ut, which, however, is sometimes
expressed): <i>as true as I live, I
thought so</i>, ita vivam, putavi, Cic.: <i>as
true as I live, I am incurring great
expenses</i>, ita vivam ut maximos sumptus
facio, Cic.

11. quālis, e (usu. as
correl. to talis): <i>show yourself to us
such as you formerly displayed yourself
to the Roman people</i>, qualem te jam
antea populo R. praebuisti, talem et
nobis imperti, Cic.

12. quantus (usu.
as correl. to tantus): <i>a contest as great
as has never yet been</i>, tanta dimicatio
quanta nunquam fuit, Cic.

13. quum
(usu. as correl. to tum): <i>fortune, as it
has very great influence in other affairs,
so has especially in war</i>, fortuna quum
in reliquis rebus, tum praecipue in bello
plurimum potest, Caes.: v. <f>JUST</f>.

II.
<i>While, during, just as</i>: q. v.: dum.

III. <i>Since, inasmuch as, seeing that</i>:
q. v.: quŏniam.

Phr.:

(A) <i>As if</i>: (i) ceu (in similes):
<i>flying through the open seas, as
if free from the reins</i>, per aperta
volans, ceu liber habenis, aequora,
Virg.: Suet. (ii) tanquam (= <i>just as
if</i>: sometimes with si): <i>there was
darkness there, as if (it had been)
night</i>, tenebrae ibi erant t. nox, Pl.:
<i>I was at his house, just as if in my
own</i>, apud eum sic fui, t. domi meae,
Cic.: <i>he knows every thing, as if he
were admitted to the king's secrets</i>, t.
regis arcanis interesset, omnia scit, Liv.:
<i>whatever pen comes into my hands, I use
it as if it were good</i>, quicunque calamus
in manus meas venerit, eo sic utor t.
bono, Cic. (iii) quăsĭ (less[**P1: typo for "less"?] emphatic
than tanquam: equiv. to <i>as though, as
it were</i>): <i>I fastened as greedily upon
Greek literature as if I were desirous of
satisfying my long thirst</i>, Graecas literas
sic avide arripui quasi diuturnam sitim
explere cupiens, Cic.: <i>philosophy, the
parent, as it were, of all praiseworthy
arts</i>, philosophia laudatarum artium omnium
quasi parens, Cic.

(B) <i>As being</i>:
(i) utpŏtĕ (usu. with <i>relat. pron.</i>, but
also with participles and adjectives): <i>I</i>
-----File: b0049r.png------------------------------------------------------
<i>am worthless enough, as being one who
have to-day begun to be in love</i>, satis
nequam sum, utpote qui hodie inceperim
amare, Pl.: <i>when I was a very little
boy, as being not more than nine years
old</i>, puerulo me, utpote non amplius
novem annos nato, Nep.: <i>a people that
can be counted, as being small</i>, populus
numerabilis utpote parvus, Hor. (ii)
quippe (usu. with a <i>relat.[**P2: .|P3 fixed, clear on TIA] pron.</i> or <i>adv.</i>):
<i>nor was it a disgrace to Cimon to wed
his sister, as his fellow citizens followed
the same custom</i>, neque Cimoni fuit turpe
sororem habere in matrimonio, quippe
cum cives ejus eodem uterentur instituto,
Nep.: v. <f>INASMUCH AS</f>,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed, clear on TIA] <f>SINCE</f>.

(C) <i>As to</i> or <i>for</i>: (i) ăd (with
<i>acc.</i>): <i>as to all other things we grow
wiser by age</i>, ad omnia alia aetate
sapimus rectius, Ter.: v. <f>IN RELATION
TO</f>, <f>CONCERNING</f>. (ii) dē (with <i>abl.</i>)[**P2: :]
<i>as to wool-work, I am not afraid of
anybody</i>, de lanificio, neminem metuo,
Pl.: Cic. (iii) quod (= <i>as to what</i>): <i>as
to what you write, that you will come to
me</i>, quod scribis te ad me venturam,
Cic.: Caes.: <i>as far as depends on me</i>,
quod ad me attinet, Cic.

(D) <i>As follows</i>:
ĭtă: <i>he negotiated with Caesar as
follows</i>, is ita cum Caesare egit, Caes.
(For <i>as far as</i>, <i>as soon as</i>, <i>as great as</i>,
<i>etc.</i>[**one set of markup?/F2], v. <f>FAR</f>, <f>SOON</f>, etc.)--N.B. "<i>As</i>" is
often not to be translated into Latin: (i)
when it connects two substantives in
apposition, or a subst. in apposition to
the subject of the verb, or introduces a
factitive accusative: e. g.: <i>they send as
ambassadors to Caesar the most illustrious
men of the state</i>, legatos ad Caesarem
mittunt nobilissimos civitatis,
Caes.: <i>I have sat as juryman, I have
conducted the investigation as praetor</i>,
judex sedi, praetor quaesivi, Cic.: <i>Servilius
alone as consul had authority to
appoint a dictator</i>, uni consuli Servilio
jus fuit dicendi dictatoris, Liv. (ii) when
it is used with such verbs as "<i>to regard</i>,"
"<i>to consider</i>," "<i>to esteem</i>:" where it is
usu. an expletive even in English: e. g.:
<i>you regard him as faithful to you</i>, eum
tu habes fidelem tibi, Pl.


<b>asafoetida</b>: lăser, ĕris, <i>n.</i>: Plin.:

5. succēdo, cessi, cessum, 3

6. sŭbeo, īvi

7. ēgrĕdĭor, gressus, 3 (= <i>to make

<i>*tain</i>, ad summum montis e., Sall.

<b>ascribe</b>:

I. <i>To refer to, as to a

1. adjūdĭco, 1[** :?] <i>Pompey often

<i>Opem</i> or <i>auxilium ferre</i>, <i>opitulari</i>, and
<i>auxiliari</i> are to bring help to a person
in difficulty or danger, and are opposed
to <i>deserere</i>, <i>destituere</i>, etc. <i>Juvare</i> and
<i>adjuvare</i> are to help a person striving
to do something, and are opposed to <i>impedire</i>.
Also <i>adjuvare</i> signifies the assistance
given by an equal to an equal:
<i>opitulari</i> the assistance given by the
strong to the weak.
