<b>at</b>:

I. <i>Of place</i> (for <i>proper</i> names,
v. 5):

1. ăd (with <i>acc.</i>): <i>to be at
market</i>, ad forum esse, Pl.: <i>at the end</i>,
ad extremum, Liv.: <i>the alarm at (before)
Veii assumed various forms</i>, ad
Veios terror multiplex erat, Liv.: <i>the
battle at the Trebia</i>, pugna ad Trebiam,
Liv.

2. ăpŭd (<i>i. e.</i> strictly <i>near</i>; q. v.:
with <i>acc.</i>): <i>we stayed one day at Alyzia</i>,
nos a. Alyziam unum diem commorati
sumus, Cic.: <i>he is at your house</i>, a. te
est, Cic.

3. ăb (= <i>on the side of, by</i>:
with <i>abl.</i>): <i>the camp was not fortified
at the main entrance</i>, castra ab decumana
porta munita[**P1: n?|P3, yes] non erant, Caes.: of
a letter, <i>(written) at Appii Forum</i>, ab
Appii Foro, Cic. (= <i>dispatched from</i>).

4. in (with <i>abl.</i>: usu. with names of
towns, and in the best writers only with
those of such places as had harbours):
<i>there is a ship in readiness for us at
Caieta</i>, navis in Caieta est parata nobis,
Cic.: <i>he had ships made at Hispalis</i>, naves
in Hispali faciendas curavit, Caes.: also
to designate the <i>house</i> at which anything
is done: <i>I am at my Formian villa</i>, in
Formiano sum, Cic.: <i>I shall see you at
my villa at Arpinum</i>, te in Arpinati
videbimus, Cic.

5. the <i>locative</i> of proper
names and of domus (domi): (N.B.[** spaced?|F2: no]
The rule as usu., and for practical purposes
correctly, stated, is, that sing.
nouns of the first and second decl. are
put in the <i>genitive</i>, all others in the
<i>ablative</i>, v. L. G. § 257): <i>the philosophers
who were at Athens</i>, philosophi qui
-----File: b0055l.png------------------------------------------------------
Athenis fuerunt, Cic.: <i>this lenity is
popular at Rome</i>, haec lenitas grata
Romae est, Cic.: <i>to sit at home</i>, domi
sedere, Cic.: <i>I said the same at my own
house</i>, haec eadem locutus sum domi
meae, Cic.--<sc>Note.</sc> Such expr. as ad,
apud, Cannas, <i>in the neighbourhood of
Cannae</i>, must be carefully distinguished
from the simple locative Cannis, <i>at
Cannae</i>. Similarly, ad urbem esse is the
technical phr. to denote waiting <i>at the
gates of</i> the city (for a triumph). Concerning
the constr. of a subs. like urbs,
oppidum, etc. along with a proper name,
v. L. G. § 257, <i>Obs.</i>, § 259, <i>Obs.</i>

II. <i>Of
time</i>:

1. By the <i>abl.</i> (the most usu. and
exact mode of expression): <i>at daybreak
he sent the cavalry in advance</i>, prima
luce equitatum praemisit, Caes.: <i>at the
same time</i>, eodem tempore, Caes.: <i>there
are flowers at every period of the year</i>,
sunt flores omni tempore anni, Cic.

2. ăd (esp. of that which <i>arrives at
the time</i>): <i>at the appointed hour</i>, ad
horam destinatam, Cic.: <i>at the time</i>, ad
tempus, Cic.: <i>at last</i>, ad postremum,
Pl.; ad extremum, Caes.: <i>at present</i>, ad
praesens, Tac.

3. ăb (strictly <i>all
along from</i>): <i>at the beginning of this
defence</i>, ab initio hujus defensionis, Cic.

4. cum (with <i>abl.</i>: denoting a
point of time with which some action
<i>coincides</i>): <i>he is said to have come home
at daybreak</i>, cum prima luce domum
venisse dicitur, Cic.: <i>Crassus went out
at the same time as the messenger</i>, exiit
cum nuntio Crassus, Caes.

5. in (only
in certain phr.): <i>at the right time</i>, in
tempore, Ter.: <i>at present</i>, in praesentia,
Caes.: Cic.; in praesenti, Cic.

III. <i>Of
cost or price</i>: when this is denoted by a
subst., or by a subst. and adjective, these
words are in the <i>abl.</i>: <i>to farm the taxes
at a small price</i>, vectigalia[**checked in Perseus|& TIA] parvo pretio
redimere, Caes.: but when, as is usu. the
case, the subst. is omitted, the adj. may
often be in either the <i>abl.</i> or the <i>genitive</i>:
vili, however, is always in the <i>abl.</i>, and
the following words always in the <i>gen.</i>:
majoris (very rare), maximi, minoris,
pluris, tanti, quanti (v. L. G. § 281).

IV. When "<i>at</i>" is used after an
intransitive verb as its complement, by
which it is made transitive, it is not expressed:
e. g. <i>to aim at anyone[** any one?]</i>, aliquem
petere, Virg.: <i>I laugh at your jokes</i>, tua
joca rideo, Cic.: v. <f>TO AIM</f>, <f>LAUGH</f>, etc.
For <i>at all</i>, <i>at once</i>, etc., v. <f>ALL</f>, <f>ONCE</f>,
etc.

<b>away</b>[** : missing? p1] when this word qualifies
-----File: b0061r.png------------------------------------------------------
verbs, it is generally expr. in Latin by
the prefix ā or ăb: e. g. <i>to carry a.</i>,
auferre; <i>to snatch a.</i>, abripere; <i>to be a.</i>,
abesse. It is sometimes used in commands
elliptically for "<i>go away</i>," "<i>take
away</i>;" and must then be translated by
the imperative of the proper Latin verb:
e. g.: <i>a. with you, scoundrel!</i> abi hinc,
scelus! Ter.: <i>a. with tears</i>, aufer abhinc
lacrimas, Lucr.: <i>a. with the barbarous
fashion</i>, morem tollite barbarum, Hor.
For such sentences as "<i>I cannot away
with this trifling</i>," where the meaning
is "<i>I cannot endure</i>," v. <f>ENDURE</f>.

generally expr. by the prefix re <i>or</i> red;
as <i>to go b.</i>, redire; <i>to fall b.</i>, recidere;
<i>to push b.</i>, repellere: for which v. <f>TO
GO BACK</f>, etc.

<b>be</b>:

1. sum, fui, esse:

A. De-*
-----File: b0068r.png------------------------------------------------------
*noting simple existence: (i) In a
simple proposition: <i>there is a river
Arar</i>, flumen est Arar, Caes.: <i>the most
worthless fellow of all who are, have
been, or shall be</i>, homo nequissimus omnium
qui sunt, qui fuerunt, qui futuri
sunt, Cic. (ii) When a relative clause
follows, its verb is in the <i>indic.</i> when
it states a fact; but in the <i>subj.</i> when
it expresses a mere conception, or implies
contingency: <i>there are some who
do not dare to say what they think</i>,
sunt qui quod sentiunt non audent
dicere, Cic. (with reference to <i>certain</i>
persons): <i>yet there are offences which</i>
(= <i>of such a kind that</i>) <i>we should be
willing to forgive</i>, sunt delicta tamen
quibus ignovisse velimus, Hor. (iii)
The perfect tenses sometimes denote
the cessation of existence: <i>we Trojans
have been, Troy has been, and the great
glory of the Teucrians</i>, fuimus Troes,
fuit Ilium, et ingens gloria Teucrorum,
Virg.: <i>they have ceased to be</i>, fuerunt
(Cic.'s announcement of the death of the
conspirators). (iv) The <i>dat.</i> is often
used with sum to denote with what the
subject of the verb is connected or to
what it belongs: <i>their private property
was scanty</i>, privatus illis census erat
brevis, Hor.: <i>the name of this place too
is Troy</i>, Trojae et huic loco nomen est,
Liv. (concerning the double <i>dat.</i>, v.
L. G. § 297). (v) The Latin verb is employed
elliptically = <i>to be the fact, to be
possible</i>, &c.: <i>what do you wish me to
say to you except what is the fact?</i> quid
tibi vis dicam nisi quod est? Pl.: <i>what
you say, Laelius, is true</i>, sunt ista, Laeli,
Cic.: <i>there is no reason why we should
say much</i>, non est quod multa loquamur,
Hor.: <i>which it is not possible to say in
verse</i>, quod versu dicere non est, Hor.

B. In connection with attributives,
denoting a definite manner of being;
the verb being merely <i>the logical copula</i>:
(i) <i>we are at leisure</i>, otiosi sumus, Cic.:
sometimes with an adv.: as, <i>that enterprise
was unsuccessful for the Volsci</i>,
frustra id inceptum Volscis fuit, Liv.
(with an <i>adv.</i> however <i>to be</i> is often
expr. by habeo: v. <i>infr.</i> 4). (ii) When
a <i>subs.</i> and an <i>adj.</i> together are employed
to describe, in connection with
the verb "<i>be</i>," they are in Latin put in
either the <i>abl.</i> or the <i>gen.</i>: <i>let your
friends and mine be of good cheer</i>, bono
animo sint et tui et mei familiares, Cic.:
<i>I confess that I have been too fearful,
spiritless</i>, nimium me timidum, nullius
animi fuisse confiteor, Cic. (iii) "<i>To be
a duty, characteristic</i>," &c. is often expressed
by sum with a <i>gen.</i>: <i>rashness
is characteristic of youth, prudence of
age</i>, temeritas est florentis aetatis, prudentia
senescentis, Cic.: <i>it is the duty
of a young man to respect his elders</i>, est
adolescentis majores natu vereri, Cic.:
<i>Ptolemy was subject to the will of others</i>,
Ptolemaeus alieni arbitrii erat, Liv.
(iv) The objector result (in Eng. simply
a predicate) is sometimes expressed by
a <i>dat.</i> dependent on sum (v. L. G. §
296): <i>you think that this country life
ought to be a reproach and subject of accusation</i>,
vitam hanc rusticam tu probro
et crimini putas esse oportere, Cic.

2. exsisto, stĭti, stĭtum, 3: <i>this is</i>
(= <i>arises</i>; q. v.) <i>chiefly the case in the
greatest intellects</i>, id in maximis ingeniis
exsistit maxime, Cic.: <i>I fear that I
am too severe towards him</i>, timeo ne in
eum exsistam crudelior, Cic.: v. <f>TO
PROVE</f>, <f>TURN OUT</f> (<i>intr</i>.).

3. versor, 1
(<i>to go in and out amongst; be engaged
or situated in any particular way</i>):
they saw that the enemy were in our
camp, hostes in nostris castris versari
videbant, Caes.: <i>nor shall I be able to
be among them without disgrace</i>, nec v.
inter eos sine dedecore potero, Cic.: <i>you
know not in what great distress I am</i>,
nescis quantis in malis verser, Ter.: <i>they
are now in peace</i>, illi nunc in pace versantur,
Cic.

4. hăbĕo, 2 (usu. with <i>pron.
reflect.</i>; but the reflect. form is sometimes
used; and the verb may be employed
as an impersonal: esp. of <i>manner</i>
-----File: b0069l.png------------------------------------------------------
of being, and hence usu. with adv.): <i>he
seemed to be not very ill</i>, videbatur se
non graviter habere, Cic.: <i>I am well</i>,
ego me bene habeo, Tac.: <i>I long to know
how the matter is</i>, scire aveo quomodo
res se habeat, Cic.: <i>as is the case with
most human affairs</i>, sicuti pleraque
mortalium habentur, Sall.: <i>it is well</i>,
bene habet, Cic.: <i>you tell great news,
hardly credible,--and yet it is even so</i>,
magnum narras, vix credibile;--atqui
sic habet, Hor. Phr.: <i>so the matter is</i>,
ita dat se res, poet. ap. Cic.: <i>just as the
time and circumstance might be</i>, prout
tempus ac res se daret, Liv.: <i>they were
within a little of being killed</i>, haud multum
abfuit quin interficerentur, Liv.:
<i>it would be tedious to relate</i>, longum est
(<i>not</i> esset) dicere, Cic. (For <i>to be well</i>
or <i>ill</i>, v. <f>WELL</f>, <f>ILL</f>, etc.)


<b>be amongst</b>:

1. intersum, fŭi,
esse (with <i>dat.</i> or <i>prep.</i>): v. <f>PRESENT AT
(TO BE)</f>.

2. versor, 1: v. <f>TO BE</f>, 3.


<b>---- between</b>: intersum (with <i>prep.</i>
or absol.): <i>that the Tiber might be b.
them</i>, ut Tiberis inter eos interesset,
Cic.: <i>the region which is b.</i>, regio quae
i., Plin.: v. <f>TO LIE BETWEEN</f>.


<b>---- in</b> or <b>upon</b>: insum (with <i>dat.</i> or
<i>in</i> and <i>abl.</i>): <i>there were 800 gold pieces
in the purse</i>, numi octingenti aurei in

<b>because</b>: N.B. The various Latin

by either the <i>indic.</i> or the <i>subj.</i> in accordance

1. quĭă: <i>the city is named Neapolis

4. pro eo quod (for pro in this

<b>before</b>:

A. Prep.:

I. <i>In front
of</i>:

1. antĕ (with <i>acc.</i>): <i>I see him
b. the house</i>, eum ante aedes video, Pl.:
<i>he sends all the cavalry b. him</i>, equitatum
omnem ante se mittit, Caes.:
<i>behind me was Aegina, b. me, Megara</i>,
post me erat Aegina, ante Megara,
Sulpic. ap. Cic.: Tac.

2. prae (with
<i>abl.</i>: of what is only <i>a little way on
before</i>: usu. with verbs of motion, and
esp. before <i>pron. reflect.</i>): <i>he drives the
herd b. him</i>, prae se armentum agit,
Liv.: <i>he sent the unarmed b. him</i>, prae
se inermes misit, Sall.

3. prō (the
most usu. prep. for <i>directly in front of</i>:
with <i>abl.</i>): <i>they were on guard b. the
gates</i>, pro portis in statione erant, Caes.:
Cic.: Tac.: v. <f>IN FRONT OF</f>.

4. ŏb
(of that which <i>presents itself</i>, esp. <i>to the
eyes</i>: with <i>acc.</i>): <i>a mist b. the eyes</i>, ob
oculos caligo, Pl.: <i>death has often appeared
b. his eyes</i>, mors ob oculos saepe
versata est, Cic.

5. adversus (= <i>opposite
to</i>: with <i>acc.</i>): <i>he dresses every day
b. a mirror</i>, quotidie ad. speculum ornatur,
Gell. (a rare idiom). Phr.: <i>he
draws up his forces b. the camp</i>, copias
ante frontem castrorum struit, Caes.: <i>I
see a ship sailing b. the wind</i>, video
navem secundis ventis cursum tenentem
suum, Cic.

II. <i>In the presence
of</i> (usu. with an implication of authority
or jurisdiction):

1. antĕ: <i>to
plead a cause b. the praetor</i>, causam
ante praetorem dicere, Cic.

2. ăd
(esp. after such words as <i>to speak</i>, <i>accuse</i>,
<i>defend</i>): <i>no one could bring you b.
the Roman people</i>, nemo te ad populum
R. adducere poterat, Cic.: <i>this is the
usual course b. a jury</i>, ad judices sic agi
solet, Cic.: <i>to accuse any one b. a praetor</i>,
aliquem ad praetorem reum facere,
Liv.

3. ăpŭd (with <i>acc.</i>: used in
similar cases to ad, but more frequently):
<i>he was brought to trial b. a
jury</i>, apud judices reus est factus, Cic.:
<i>he spoke b. the senate</i>, verba apud
senatum fecit, Cic.: <i>Caesar made an
harangue b. the soldiers</i>, Caesar apud
milites contionatus est, Caes.

4.
cōram (with <i>abl.</i>): <i>what did you dare
to say b. my son-in-law?</i> c. genero meo
quae dicere ausus es? Cic.: v. <f>PRESENCE
OF</f>, <f>IN</f>. Phr.[** :] <i>to bring any one b. a
court of justice</i>, aliquem in judicium
adducere, Cic.

III. <i>In preference
to</i>:

1. antĕ: <i>whom I love b. myself</i>,
quem ante me diligo, Cic.: <i>the Greeks
were b. the Romans in eloquence</i>, facundia
Graeci ante Romanos fuerunt,
-----File: b0072r.png------------------------------------------------------
Sall.

2. prae (with <i>abl.</i>): v. <f>COMPARISON
WITH</f>, <f>IN</f>; <f>MORE THAN</f>.

IV[**.]
<i>Preceding</i> (in time):

1. antĕ: <i>b.
this day</i>, ante hunc diem, Ter.: <i>b.
night</i>, ante noctem, Hor.: <i>b. the foundation
of this city</i>, ante hanc urbem
conditam, Cic.: <i>b. the proper time</i>, ante
tempus, Liv.

2. suprā (with <i>acc.</i>:
infrequent): <i>a little b. the present generation</i>,
paulo s. hanc memoriam, Caes.:
Liv. N.B. When "<i>before</i>" is connected
with verbs of motion, it is gen.
expressed in Latin by the prefixes of
the verbs: <i>the lictors used to go before
the praetors with two fasces</i>, lictores
praetoribus ante ibant cum fascibus
duobus, Cic.: <i>Pompey had gone b. the
legions</i>, Pompeius legiones antecesserat,
Cic.: <i>the lictors used to go b. the consuls</i>,
consulibus lictores praeibant, Cic.

B.
Adverb:

I. <i>Of time</i>:

1. antĕ
(with either an <i>abl.</i> or an <i>acc.</i> which
denotes duration, and is not dependent
on ante): <i>a very few days b.</i>, perpaucis
ante diebus, Cic.: <i>you were lost four
years b.</i>, ante quadriennium amissus es,
Tac.: <i>some years b.</i>, aliquot ante annos,
Suet.: <i>I foresaw long b. that there would
be a storm</i>, multo ante prospexi tempestatem
futuram, Cic.

2. antĕquam (a
kind of conjunction, and used to connect
clauses: sometimes written as two
separate words): <i>that he might see you
b. he died</i>, ut te ante videret quam e
vita discederet, Cic.: <i>you will have no
letter from me before I am settled somewhere</i>,
antequam aliquo loco consedero,
literas a me non habebis, Cic.: <i>I was
always his friend b. he became an enemy
to his country</i>, ei fui semper amicus
antequam ille reipublicae est factus
inimicus, Cic.

3. prĭus (rare): <i>all
things have been tried b.</i>, cuncta prius
tentata, Ov.

4. prĭusquam, or separately
prius ... quam (v. antĕquam):
<i>they are here b. it dawns</i>, priusquam lucet,
assunt, Pl.: <i>b. he attempted anything,
he ordered the brother to be called
to him</i>, priusquam quidquam conaretur,
fratrem ad se vocari jubet, Caes.: <i>nor
did they give over flight b. they arrived at
the river Rhine</i>, neque prius fugere destiterunt
quam ad flumen Rhenum pervenerunt,
Caes.: Cic. (Concerning the
mood which follows priusquam, v. L. G.)
Phr.: <i>the day b. I came to Athens</i>,
pridie quam ego Athenas veni, Cic.: v.
<f>FORMERLY</f>, <f>PREVIOUSLY</f>, <f>ABOVE</f>.

II.
<i>Of space</i>: prae: <i>go you b., maiden</i>, i
tu prae, virgo, Pl.: <i>go b., I will follow</i>,
i prae, sequar, Pl. Phr.: <i>if he come
into Gaul he will be hemmed in behind,
b., on his flanks</i>, a tergo, a fronte, a
lateribus tenebitur, si in Galliam venerit,
Cic. N.B. "<i>Before</i>" <i>as</i>[**F2: "as" doesn't seem like it s/b italics] an adverb
is very often expressed by the prefixes
of the Latin verbs: as, <i>to bear b.</i>, antefero;
<i>to go b.</i>, anteeo, etc.: for which
see the several words.


<b>beforehand</b> (<i>adv.</i>): usu. expr. by
prep. prae in compos.: as, <i>to receive
money b. from any one</i>, pecuniam ab
aliquo praecipere, Cic.: <i>this first I tell
you b.</i>, hoc primum tibi praedico, Ter..[**:]
<i>to be b. in stealing a kiss</i>, praeripere
dulcia oscula, Lucr.: <i>to fix the expense
of a funeral b.</i>, sumptum funerum praefinire,
Cic.: <i>to seize on places b.</i>, loca
praeoccupare, Liv. Phr.: <i>to be b.</i>
(with any one), i. e. <f>TO ANTICIPATE</f>:
q. v.: praeverto.

<b>burn</b> (<i>v.</i>):

A. Trans.:

I. <i>To
consume with fire</i>:

1. ūro, ussi,
ustum, 3 (the most general term: also
used of other agencies besides fire): <i>you
shall neither bury nor b. a dead man in
the city</i>, hominem mortuum in urbe ne
sepelito neve urito, xii. Tab. ap. Cic.:
<i>she b.s the fragrant cedar-oil for lights
at night</i>, urit odoratam nocturna in
lumina cedrum, Virg..[** .:] <i>to b. ships</i>, naves
ur., Hor.: <i>to b. cities</i>, urbes ur., Tac.
So the compounds of uro: (i.) ădūro,
3 (to b. <i>on the surface</i> or <i>partially</i>): <i>to
b. a person's clothes</i>, alicujus vestimenta
a., Liv.: <i>to b. (singe off) anyone's beard</i>
or <i>hair</i>, alicui barbam, capillum a.,
Cic.: v. <f>TO SINGE</f>. (ii.) ambūro, 3 (to
b. <i>all round; over the entire surface</i>):
<i>the burnt body of Hercules</i>, Herculis
ambustum corpus, Cic.: <i>to restore a
theatre that has been burnt (gutted)</i>,
theatrum ambustum restituere, Suet.
(iii.) pĕrūro, 3 (rare: <i>intens.</i>): v. <f>TO
BURN UP</f>. (iv.) combūro, 3 (stronger
than uro: <i>to burn completely; burn up</i>:
q. v.): <i>to b. anyone alive</i>, aliquem
vivum c., Cic.: Caes. (v.) exūro, 3
(= comburo): <i>he was burnt alive in
his own house</i>, domi suae vivus exustus
est, Cic.: v. also <f>TO BURN UP</f>,
<f>DOWN</f>.

2. crĕmo, 1 (to b. <i>to ashes,
completely to destroy by fire</i>: Habicht,
§ 15): <i>to b. and destroy a city</i>, c. et
diruere urbem, Liv.: <i>to b. ships</i>, c.
naves, Liv.: the most regular word to
denote the <i>cremation</i> of a corpse: <i>Sulla
wished his body to be burnt by fire</i>,
Sulla igni voluit cremari, Cic. So its
comp. concrĕmo, which is stronger:
<i>they threatened to b. them alive</i>, vivos
igni concrematuros minabantur, Liv.:
<i>to b. a city with fire (reduce it to ashes)</i>,
urbem igni c., Liv.

3. incendo, di,
sum, 3 (strictly, <i>to set on fire</i>): v. <f>TO
FIRE</f>: <i>to b. incense and perfumes</i>, tus
et odores in., Cic.: Virg.

4. inflammo,
1: v. <f>TO FIRE</f>, <f>KINDLE</f>.

A. Trans.: exūro,[** , @TIA]
3: Fig.: <i>the wickedness ingrained in

parentes? Cic.: <i>history was nothing else
but the compilation of annals</i>, erat historia
nihil aliud nisi annalium confectio,
Cic.: <i>nothing is wanting here but songs</i>,
nihil hic nisi carmina desunt, Virg.:
<i>for no other reason but that</i>, etc., non
aliam ob causam nisi quod, <i>etc.</i>, Hor.
Phr.: <i>the vineae now all but touched
the walls</i>, vineae tantum non jam injunctae
moenibus erant, Liv.: <i>promising
all but mountains of gold</i>, modo non
montes auri pollicens, Ter.: <i>he was all
but killed</i>, haud multum abfuit quin
interficeretur, Liv.; parum abfuit quin
occideretur, Cic.: <i>the last dactyl but one</i>,
dactylus proximus a postremo, Cic.

II. <i>Only</i> (q. v.): mŏdŏ, tantum.
Phr.: <i>if but</i>, dummŏdo: v. <f>PROVIDED
THAT</f>: <i>but for a time</i>, duntaxat ad
tempus, Cic.: <i>I had but just come from
my villa at Arpinum</i>, tantum quod ex
Arpinati veneram, Cic.: <i>but little</i>, părum
(i. e. <i>less than should be</i>): <i>plenty of
eloquence, but little wisdom</i>, satis eloquentiae,
sapientiae parum, Sall.: Cic.

III. <i>Conj.</i> denoting <i>contrast</i> or <i>opposition</i>:

1. sĕd (the most freq. equivalent
of the Eng. word: it stands first in
its clause): (i.) denoting distinct opposition:
<i>Pausanias was a great man, but
marked by contrasting features</i>, P. vir
magnus, sed varius, Nep.: Cic. Esp.
after negatives: as, <i>I am not your
master, but your slave</i>, non ego herus
tibi sed servus sum, Pl.: <i>this often
happens, not only to individuals, but
also to most powerful nations</i>, id non
modo singulis hominibus, sed potentissimis
populis saepe contingit, Cic.
(For <i>not only ... but also</i>, v. <f>ONLY</f>.)
(ii.) denoting limitation or correction:
<i>that is not perfect indeed, but
it is tolerable</i>, non perfectum illud quidem,
sed tolerabile est, Cic. (iii.) in
transitions and resumptions: <i>but let us
return to our subject</i>, sed ad instituta
redeamus, Cic.: <i>but enough of words;</i>
-----File: b0102l.png------------------------------------------------------
<i>attend to my orders</i>, sed satis verborum
est; cura quae jussi, Pl.: <i>but in fact</i>,
sed enim, enimvero: v. <f>IN FACT</f>.

2.
vērum (similar in force to sed: also at
the beginning of its clause): (i.) of
opposition, esp. in <i>thought</i>: <i>we are inquiring,
not what is useful to us, but
what is necessary for the orator</i>, non
nos quid nobis utile, verum quid oratori
necessarium sit quaerimus, Cic.:
<i>not only in acting but even in thinking</i>,
non modo agendo, verum etiam cogitando,
Cic.: <i>he adopts a foolish, but yet
a merciful plan</i>, consilium capit stultum,
verum tamen clemens, Cic. (ii.)
esp. in transitions: <i>the calends of January
were waited for, perhaps not
rightly--but let us say nothing about
the past</i>, exspectabantur calendae Januariae,
fortasse non recte--verum praeterita
omittamus, Cic. Esp. with the
emphatic enimvero, <i>but indeed!</i> <i>in very
truth!</i> cf. Sall. C. 20 (<i>med.</i>).

3. autem
(denoting less of opposition than the
two preceding words, being often = <i>and
then, moreover</i>: as it is less emphatic,
it <i>follows</i> the first word of the sentence
which it introduces): (i.) to introduce
a gentle contrast; esp. where a word is
repeated: <i>I myself write nothing, but I
read</i> (or, <i>I read however</i>) <i>with the greatest
pleasure</i>, ipse nihil scribo; lego autem
libentissime, Cic.: <i>Croesus thought
that he should overturn the power of his
enemies, but he overturned his own</i>,
Croesus hostium vim sese perversurum
putavit, pervertit autem suam, Cic.
(ii.) with interjections: <i>but lo! a sudden
divorce</i>, ecce autem subitum divortium,
Cic.: v. <f>HOWEVER</f>, <f>MOREOVER</f>.

4. vēro (implying, not so much
opposition, as corroboration: like autem
it <i>follows</i> the first word of its clause):
<i>the Helvetii had led three parts of their
forces across the river, but the fourth
was left on the hither side of it</i>, Helvetii
tres copiarum partes flumen transduxerant;
quarta vero pars citra flumen
reliqua erat, Caes.: Cic.

5. at (ast[** Earlier variant, presumably.]
archaic: always placed at the beginning
of its clause): (i.) to denote transition
of thought, and to introduce an addition,
which usu. modifies what precedes:
<i>the contest was carried on vigorously,
hand to hand with swords, but
the Germans sustained the onset</i>, cominus
gladiis acriter pugnatum est, at
Germani impetus gladiorum exceperunt,
Caes. (ii.) in passionate exclamations,
where it often introduces something
quite abruptly: <i>but how like they are!</i>
<i>but how beautiful both!</i> at quam sunt
similes! at quam formosus uterque!
Ov. F. 2, 395; cf. Hor. Epod. 5, 1: <i>but
by the immortal gods! what can be said
about this?</i> at per deos immortales!
quid est quod de hoc dici possit? Cic.
(iii.) to introduce the answer to an objection
which is anticipated: <i>what further
is to be inquired? whether it was
done? but it is admitted: by whom?
but it is evident</i>, quid porro quaerendum
est? factumne sit? at constat: a quo?
at patet, Cic.: <i>but (you urge), the memory
fails</i> (in old age): <i>so I believe,
unless you keep it exercised</i>, at memoria
minuitur: credo, nisi eam exerceas,
Cic.

6. atqui[** unclear.]: usu. = <i>and yet</i>, q. v.
(i.) to connect an emphatic adversative
clause: Cl.--<i>she makes you fine enough
promises</i>; Sy.--<i>but do you suppose that
she is jesting</i>?[**include question mark in italics?] <i>Cl.</i>--satis scite promittit
tibi; <i>Sy.</i>--atqui tu hanc jocari credis?
Ter. (ii.) in conditional clauses: <i>let
him come; but if he lay a finger on her,
his eyes shall be torn out instantly</i>, sine
veniat; atqui si illam digito attigerit,
oculi illi illico effodientur, Ter.: Cic.
(iii.) after an expressed or virtual negative:
Ni.--<i>you shall never carry off the
gold</i>; Ch.--<i>no, but you will give it
to me now</i>; <i>Ni.</i>--nunquam auferes hinc
aurum; <i>Ch.</i>--atqui iam dabis, Pl.:
<i>you state a wonderful thing; scarcely
credible. But it is the fact</i>, magnum
narras, vix credibile. Atqui sic habet,
Hor.: Cic. (iv.) to connect a minor
premiss: Cic.: v. <f>NOW</f>.

IV. Equi-*
-----File: b0102m.png------------------------------------------------------
*valent to the relative pronoun and a
negative: quīn (only after negative or
virtually negative sentences: v. Gell.
17, 13): <i>there is hardly a day but he
comes to my house</i>, dies fere nullus est
quin domum meam ventitet, Cic.: <i>there
was no one but said that he had heard
this</i>, nemo erat quin hoc se audisse diceret,
Cic.: <i>I cannot but send letters to
you</i>, facere non possum quin ad te litteras
mittam, Cic.: <i>there was no doubt
but that they were the most powerful</i>,
non erat dubium quin plurimum possent,
Caes.: <i>not but that an answer
might have been briefly given</i>, non quin
breviter reddi responsum potuerit, Liv.
Phr.: (i.) <i>but if</i>, quod si; also when
an alternative with si has gone before,
sin: <i>but if not</i>, quod nisi <i>or</i> quod ni: v.
<f>IF</f>. (ii.) <i>but for, but that</i>: (<i>a</i>) nisi <i>or</i>
ni, foll. by <i>subj.</i>: as, <i>me the trunk would
have cut off, but that Faunus lightened
the blow</i>, me truncus sustulerat, nisi
Faunus ictum levasset, Hor. (<i>b</i>) absque
(prep. with <i>abl.</i>; only in the colloq.
language of the comedians): <i>but for
this one thing, how fortunate am I in
everything else</i>, quam fortunatus sum
ceteris rebus, absque hac una foret,
Ter.: Pl.: so, <i>but for me, you</i>, etc.,
absque me, te: Ter.: Pl. (<i>c</i>) also sometimes
expr. by the help of quominus:
as, <i>but for Trebonius, it seemed they
would have taken the place</i>, stetisse per
Trebonium, quominus oppido potirentur,
videbatur, Caes. (iii.) <i>not but that</i>, non
quin: <i>not but that I could pay my debts
... but because</i> ..., non quin aes
alienum solvere possem ... sed quod,
<i>etc.</i>, Sall.: Cic. (the same sense may be
conveyed by non quod [quia] non ...
with <i>subj.</i>, followed as before by sed
quod <i>or</i> quia: v. <f>THAT</f>, <f>BECAUSE</f>).

III[** .]
Of other relations: as to denote the
agent, instrument, or cause; measure
of excess or defect; distribution,[** , clear on TIA] <i>etc.</i>:
(i.) of the <i>agent</i>, after a passive verb.[** :?]
ā or ăb (with <i>abl.</i>): Caes.: Cic. (<i>passim</i>).
<sc>Note.</sc>--This construction is confined
to the case of a personal agent.
We also find, instead of the prep. and
<i>abl.</i>, the <i>dative</i>, esp. after the gerundive
participle; as, <i>wisdom should be enjoyed
by us</i>, sapientia nobis (<i>not</i> a nobis) fruenda
est, Cic. After the gerund, indeed,
the prep. is only used to avoid occasional
ambiguity: thus, we should say
for <i>these men must be resisted by you</i>,
a te (<i>not</i> tibi) his hominibus resistendum
est. The dative after other forms
of the passive, and the ablative without
a preposition, belong to the poets: as,
<i>nor is she seen by any</i>, neque cernitur
ulli, Virg.: <i>thou shalt be celebrated by
Varius, a swan of Homeric tune</i>, scriberis
Vario, Maeonii carminis alite, Hor.
(ii.) of the <i>means</i> or <i>instrument</i>, after
active and passive verbs:

1. pĕr[** é or spot?] (with
<i>acc.</i>): <i>I did not hesitate to ask you for
that by letter</i>, non dubitavi id a te per
literas petere, Cic.: <i>to march through
a province by force</i>, iter per provinciam
per vim facere, Caes.: <i>Caesar
ascertained this by the scouts</i>, id per
exploratores Caesar cognovit, Caes.: <i>he
has by himself, without any helper,
mustered the forces</i>, per se, nullo adjuvante,
copias confecit, Cic.

2.
Usu. expr. by the simple <i>abl.</i>: <i>to excite
the feelings of the mob by the mere
name and recollection of his father</i>,
nomine ipso et memoria patris animos
multitudinis concitare, Cic.: <i>by a law
they fix the departure for the third year</i>,
in tertium annum profectionem lege
confirmant, Caes. Phr.: <i>by your leave</i>,[** , clear on TIA]
bona tua venia dixerim, Cic.: v. <f>LEAVE</f>:
<i>by themselves they were unable to prevail
upon the Sequani</i>, Sequanis sua sponte
persuadere non poterant, Caes. (iii.) of
the <i>cause</i>, <i>means</i>, or <i>mode</i>:

1.[**3 or small 1? out of numero order] ē <i>or</i> ex
(with <i>abl.</i>: rare, and only of that <i>out of
which</i> something arises): <i>she is pregnant
by Pamphilus</i>,[** , clear on TIA] gravida e Pamphilo
est, Ter.: <i>led into hope of victory by
the advantage of the position</i>, in spem
victoriae adductus ex opportunitate loci,
-----File: b0103m.png------------------------------------------------------
Sall.

2. expr. by the <i>abl.</i> alone: <i>a
place suitable by nature</i>, locus natura
idoneus, Caes.: <i>this has been occasioned
more by easiness than by any other
fault of mine</i>, magis id facilitate quam
ulla alia culpa mea contigit, Cic.: <i>the
consul himself, holding Lentulus by the
hand, leads him into the senate</i>, consul
Lentulum, ipse manu tenens, in senatum
perducit, Sall.: <i>pepper is bought
by weight</i>, piper pondere emitur, Plin.
Phr..[** .:] <i>he ran by stealth into the plain</i>,
furtim in campum currebat, Cic.: <i>Thisbe
saw the lioness by the rays of the moon</i>,
leaenam ad lunae radios Thisbe vidit,
Ov.: <i>by fair means</i>, recte, Hor.: "<i>by
hook or by crook</i>," quocunque modo,[** , clear on TIA]
Hor. (iv.) with words of measurement,
to denote <i>excess</i> or <i>defect</i>: this
is gen. expr. by the <i>abl.</i> of the words
denoting the excess or defect: <i>he is
taller than you by a foot and a half</i>,
sesquipede est quam te longior, Pl.:
<i>Ireland is less by a half than Britain</i>,
Hibernia dimidio minor est quam Britannia,
Caes. (v.) to denote the separate
succession of a number of items:
this sense is usu. expr. by adverbs or
distributive numerals: sometimes also
by in and <i>acc.</i>: <i>the number of the enemy
is increasing day by day</i>, crescit in dies
singulos hostium numerus, Cic.: <i>the
siege was more severe day by day</i>, erat
in dies gravior oppugnatio, Caes.: <i>to
buy pepper by the pound</i>, piper in libras
emere, Plin.: <i>they began by degrees to
leave the camp</i>, paulatim ex castris discedere
coeperunt, Caes,[** .:] <i>the waggons
were drawn one by one</i>, singuli carri
ducebantur, Caes.: <i>to engage a servant
by the year</i>, *annua mercede famulum
conducere: v. the respective substantives.
(vi.) in adjurations:

1. per
(with <i>acc.</i>): <i>by gods and men</i>, per deos
atque homines, Cic.: <i>I beseech you by
your friendship and love</i>, te per amicitiam
et per amorem obsecro, Ter.
sometimes per stands at the beginning
of the adjuration without an acc., the
object appealed to being defined by the
clause following[** s/b :] cf. Virg. A. 2, 142:
Ov.

2. prō <i>or</i> proh (prop. an <i>interj.</i>:
v. <f>AH!</f> also sometimes followed by the
<i>acc.</i>): <i>by the faith of gods and men!</i> p.
deum atque hominum fidem! Cic.: <i>by
Jupiter!</i> pro Jupiter! Ter. (but in a
formal oath it would be <i>per</i>). Phr..[** .:]
<i>by Hercules!</i> mehercŭles! mehercŭle!
mehercle! hercules! hercule! hercle!
Cic.: Ter.: of the same import is medius
fidius, i. e. me dius <i>s.</i> deus fidius
(juvet), <i>by the god of faith!</i> (Hercules)!
<i>by Castor!</i> mēcastor, ēcastor! Pl.: Ter.
(rarely used except by <i>women</i>): <i>by
Pollux!</i> ĕdĕpol! Pl.: <i>by Ceres!</i> eccĕrĕ
<i>or</i> ĕcĕrĕ: Pl.: Ter.


<b>by the by</b>: ŏbĭter, in transcursu
dicendum est: v. <f>IN PASSING</f>.

<b>can</b> (<i>v.</i>):

1. possum, pŏtui, posse
(foll. by <i>inf.</i>; and <i>used of all kinds of
ability or possibility</i>): <i>the enemy can
no longer hold out</i>, hos es diutius sustinere
non possunt, Caes.: <i>he says he
cannot grant any one a passage through
the province</i>, negat se p. iter ulli per
provinciam dare, Caes.: <i>all is now being
done which I affirmed could not be done</i>,
omnia nunc fiunt fieri quae posse negabam,
Ov.: <i>as diligently as I possibly
could</i>, ut [quam] diligentissime potui,
Cic. (v. <f>POSSIBLE</f>, <f>POSSIBLY</f>): <i>I cannot
but exclaim</i>, non possum quin exclamem,
Cic. (more freq. <i>facere</i> non possum quin,
etc.: v. <f>BUT</f>, iv.): <i>I cannot but write
to you</i>, ut nihil ad te dem literarum
facere non possum, Cic.

2. queo, quīvi,
quĭtum, 4 (less freq. than possum, and
referring rather to <i>possibility from circumstances</i>
than to inherent ability:
with <i>inf.</i>): <i>as we can, since we are not
at liberty to do as we will</i>, ut quimus,
quando ut volumus non licet, Ter.:[**Possibly ".:" or ".;"][** P3 fixed, vis. on TIA]
most freq. with negative: as, <i>I cannot
write the rest</i>, non queo reliqua scribere,
Cic.: Hor.: for which we have[** .--or something missing? or ref. to sec. 3 foll.?]

3.
nĕqueo, quīvi, ĭtum, 4, which is far
more frequent than the simple verb:
<i>I cannot but weep</i>, nequeo quin lacrimem,
Ter.: <i>ye cannot look straight at
the sun</i>, solem adversum intueri nequitis,
Cic.: Hor.[**Perhaps ":"|not before "Phr."] Phr.: <i>which cannot
be said in verse</i>, quod versu dicere non
est, Hor.: <i>do what you can to save my
son</i>, serva, quod in te est, filium, Ter.:
<i>he can do what he chooses</i>, i. e. is his
own master, suae potestatis est, Nep.:
<i>I cannot tell what to do about the children</i>,
de pueris quid agam non habeo,
Cic.: <i>I can assert that as a positive fact</i>,
illud affirmare pro certo habeo, Liv.:
"<i>what cannot be cured must be endured</i>,"
levius fit patientia quicquid
corrigere est nefas, Hor. When <i>can</i> or
<i>cannot</i> refer to knowledge or ignorance,
as of <i>an art</i>, they may be rendered by
scio, nescio: v. <f>TO KNOW HOW</f>: when
<i>can</i> signifies <i>to be at liberty</i>, it is expr.
by licet: v. <f>MAY</f>; <f>TO BE AT LIBERTY</f>.
Also <i>can</i> in combination with a passive
verb may often be expressed with an
adjective in bĭlis <i>or</i> ĭlis: as, <i>towers
which can be moved</i>, mobiles turres,
Curt.: <i>a beast that can be taught</i>, belua
docilis, Cic.: <i>a knot that cannot be
untied</i>, nodus indissolubilis, Plin.

<b>case</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

I. <i>State, condition,

1. res, rĕī, <i>f.</i>:

4. tempus, ŏris, <i>n.</i> (esp.

5.
Very often expressed by a neuter
adjective or pronoun, or left to be understood:
as, <i>since such is the c.</i>, quae
cum ita sint, Cic.: <i>the c. is as you say</i>,
sunt ista, Cic.: <i>and yet the c. is so</i>, atqui
sic habet, Hor.: <i>I was afraid that
the c. which has occurred might befal</i>
timebam ne evenirent ea quae acciderunt,
Cic.: <i>c.s often occur in which
debtors do not meet their engagements
punctually</i>, fit saepe ut ii qui
debent non respondeant ad tempus, Cic.:
<i>the same c. has not happened to me as
you write has befallen you</i>, non venit
idem usu mihi quod tu tibi scribis, Cic.
Phr.: <i>his c. is dangerous</i> (of a sick person).
periculose aegrotat, Cic.: <i>were my
c. yours you would think differently</i>,
tu si hic sis, aliter censeas. Ter.: <i>impartial
law has always been striven
after; for in any other c. it would not
be law</i>, jus semper est quaesitum aequabile;
neque enim aliter esset jus, Cic.:
<i>fear is embarrassing in both c.s</i>, pavor
est utrobique molestus, Hor.: <i>in case</i>:
v. <f>IF</f>, <f>SUPPOSING</f>.

<b>cause</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

I. <i>That which produces
an effect</i>:

1. causa: <i>a c. is
that which produces that of which it is
the c.</i>, c. ea est quae id efficit cujus est
c., Cic.: <i>an efficient c.</i>, c. efficiens, Cic.:
<i>a final c.</i>, c. finalis, M. L. 2. mātĕrĭes
<i>or</i> mātĕrĭa (<i>material</i>: q. v.): <i>the c. of
all evils</i>, materies omnium malorum,
Sall.: <i>to give c. for envy</i>, materiam invidiae
dare, Cic. Phr.: <i>Trebonius
seemed to be the c. of their not getting
possession of the town</i>, stetisse per Trebonium
quominus oppido potirentur,
videbatur, Caes.: <i>he has given you no
c. to be angry</i>, nihil fecit quod succenseas,
Ter.: <i>I will give him c. to
remember me as long as he lives</i>, faciam
ut mei semper meminerit, Pl.: <i>I hear
that you accuse us all without c.</i>, te
omnes nos accusare audio immerito,
Ter.: <i>Milo is shocked at this, and not
without c.</i>, hoc horret Milo, neque injuria,
Cic.: v. <f>REASON</f>, <f>ACCOUNT</f>.

II.
<i>A subject of litigation; a legal suit</i>:

1. causa: <i>to decide a c. in one's
favour</i>, causam alicui adjudicare, Cic.:
<i>to abandon a c.</i> (of an advocate), c. affligere,
Cic.: <i>private c.s</i>, c. privatae, Cic.:
<i>public c.s</i>, c. publicae, Cic.: <i>a c. affecting
life or reputation</i>, capitis aut famae c.,
Cic.: <i>to lose a c.</i>, causam perdere, <i>or</i>
causā cadere, Cic.: <i>to plead a c.</i>, causam
dicere, Caes.: Liv.: <i>a petty or unimportant
c.</i>, causŭla, Cic.

2. rēs, rĕi,
<i>f.</i>: <i>to speak about c.s already investigated
and decided</i>, de rebus cognitis
judicatisque dicere, Cic.: Ulp.

3.
sacrāmentum (rare; and orig. denoting
<i>the deposit</i> made by litigants): <i>the decemvirs

decemviri s. nostrum justum judicaverunt,
Cic.: v. <f>SUIT</f>, <f>ACTION</f>.

III. <i>Side,
party, object</i>: causa: <i>that he might not
seem to condemn that c. to which he had
attached himself, he came to the camp</i>,
ne condemnare c. illam quam secutus
esset, videretur, ad castra venit, Cic.:

-----File: b0112m.png------------------------------------------------------

II.

<i>a person of most infamous c.</i>,

atque facinorum catervae," Cat.

have got a c. for roguery</i>, turpi fraude
innotuisse, Phaedr.: <i>to care nothing for
c., fortune, or danger</i>, fidem, fortunas,
pericula vilia habere, Sall.: v. <f>REPUTATION</f>.

IV. <i>Peculiar</i> or <i>specific nature</i>

1. prŏprĭĕtas: <i>the c. of

v. <f>CHARACTERISTIC</f>.

2. cŏlor (fig.):
<i>what after all, said he, is that c. of refinement

3. hăbĭtus, ūs: <i>the
c. of a speech</i>, h. orationis, Cic.: v. <f>CHARACTERISTIC</f>.

V. <i>Office, capacity</i>:

1. persōna: <i>to assume the c. of a

2. partes, ium: <i>the c. of
a (single) actor</i>, actoris partes, Hor.: v.
<i>inf.</i>

3. nŭmĕrus: <i>in the c. of a

VI.
<i>A part</i> or <i>personage</i>; esp. <i>in a drama</i>:

1. partes, ium, <i>f.</i>: <i>he who will

primas p. qui aget, is erit Phormio,
Ter.: <i>the second</i> or <i>inferior c.</i>, p. secundae

2. persōna: <i>the c. of a parasite</i>,
parasiti p., Ter.: Gell.


<b>characteristic</b> (<i>adj.</i>):

1. proprĭus
(with <i>gen.</i>): <i>this vice is not c. of

id non p. senectutis est vitium,
sed commune valetudinis, Cic.: <i>to create
and to produce is chiefly c. of art</i>, artis

2. mōrātus: <i>a c. poem</i> (i. e. <i>abounding
in character</i>), m. poema, Cic.: Hor.
Phr.: <i>some traits in you are c., others

c., that is to say, dubious, fidelity</i>, sua,

<b>characteristic</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

1. proprĭum
(prop. an <i>adj.</i>: v. <i>supr.</i>): <i>this

2.
hăbĭtus, ūs: <i>the natural c.s of soils</i>,

3.
proprĭĕtas: <i>everything has its peculiar

4. Expr. by <i>gen.</i> of the subs.

humanum est).

5. chăractēr, ēris:
v. <f>STYLE</f>.


<b>characteristically</b>:

1. proprĭē:
<i>it is difficult to treat hackneyed subjects

2. ex more suo, tuo, etc: v.
<f>MANNER</f>.

<b>charge</b> (<i>v.</i>):

A. Trans.:

I.
<i>To load</i> or <i>burthen</i>: q. v. Phr.: <i>to c.
a gun</i>, *tela, missilia, glandes, pulveremque
nitratam tormento (sclopeto)
ingerere.

II. <i>To rush against, attack.</i>

1. incurro, curri, and cŭcurri,
cursum, 3 (with <i>dat.</i> or <i>acc.</i>): <i>the infantry
c.d the wings</i>, peditum signa incucurrerunt

2.
invādo, 3: v. <f>TO ATTACK</f>.

3. irrŭo,
rŭi, 3 (foll. by <i>in</i>): <i>to c. the centre</i>, in
mediam aciem ir., Cic.

4. signa infĕro,
tŭli, lātum, 3 (with <i>in</i> and <i>acc.</i>,

III. <i>To
place on the debit side; regard as a

1. fĕro, tŭli, lātum, 3 (with the
<i>perf. part.</i> expensus agreeing with the

Cic.

2. infĕro, tŭli, lātum, 3: <i>to c.
an expense to the citizens</i>, sumptum
civibus inf., Cic.: <i>to c. in accounts</i>,
rationibus inf., Col.

3. impŭto, 1:
<i>bailiffs c. for far more seed-corn than
they have really sown</i>, villici longe plus
im. seminis jacti quam quod severint,
Col.: <i>to c. expenses to any one</i>, sumptus
alicui im., Ulp. Fig.: <i>he perceives that
the days which are lost, yet c.d to us, are

atque abire sentit qui nobis pereunt et
imputantur, Mart. Phr.: <i>to c. a certain
price for goods</i>, pretium statuere
merci, Pl.: <i>to c. a fixed price</i>, pretium
certum constituere, Cic.

IV. <i>To impute
to, accuse of</i>:

1. arguo, ui,
ūtum, 3 (the offence charged is expr. by
<i>gen.</i>, <i>abl.</i>, or <i>de</i>[**"de" should be in roman type]; also by <i>acc.</i> and <i>inf.</i>):
<i>to c. dead men with the greatest wickedness</i>,
viros mortuos summi sceleris ar.,
Cic.: <i>I do not c. you with this crime</i>, te
hoc crimine non arguo, Cic.: <i>he is c.d
with this crime</i>, de eo crimine arguitur,
Cic.: <i>Roscius is c.d with having killed
his father</i>, occidisse patrem Roscius arguitur,
Cic.

2. impŭto, 1 (with <i>dat.</i>

<i>the murder should be c.d upon him who
began the quarrel</i>, ei caedes imputanda
est a quo jurgium coepit, Quint.: v. <f>TO
IMPUTE</f>.

3, insĭmŭlo, 1 (usu. of <i>false</i>
or <i>malicious</i> charges): <i>to c. any one
with treachery</i>, aliquem proditionis in.,
Caes.: Cic.: <i>to be c.d with the offence of

Liv.: <i>to c. any one falsely</i>, aliquem
falso in., Cic.: v. <f>TO ACCUSE</f>, <f>ASCRIBE</f>.

V. <i>To enjoin upon</i>: q. v.: mando,
1 (with <i>dat.</i> of person and <i>subj.</i>): <i>he
c.s Volusenus to return to him as soon

VI. <i>To
charge</i> any one <i>with</i> some duty:

1.
committo, mīsi, missum, 3 (foll. by ut

2. crēdo, 3: v. <f>TO ENTRUST</f>.

3. impōno, pŏsui, pŏsĭtum, 3 (with

<f>TO IMPOSE UPON</f>. Phr.: <i>to c. any one
with the oversight of any matter</i>, aliquem

<f>TO APPOINT</f>.

<b>clearly</b>:

I. Prop. = <i>in a clear

2. lĭquĭdē <i>or</i> lĭquĭdō

Fig.:[**P2: dot missing] <i>to judge more c.</i>, liquidius judicare,
Cic.: Liv.

3. lūcĭdē (lit. <i>brightly</i>:
q. v.). Fig. = Eng. <i>lucidly</i> (q. v.): <i>to

in meaning, but somewhat stronger, is

4. expressē (cf. <f>TO EXPRESS</f>):

5. plānē:
v. <f>PLAINLY</f>. (N.B. This and the foll.

<b>cloak</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

1. pallium, <i>dim.</i>
palliŏlum, <i>poet.</i> palla (the last esp. of

this was "the most common article of

2. lăcerna (a <i>thick</i> c.

4. paenŭla (<i>a travelling

aliae coriis tectae sunt, aliae
villis vestitae, Cic.: <i>the mountains are
c.d with forests</i>, montes silvis vestiuntur,
Liv.: <i>to c. and adorn one's discoveries
with eloquence</i>, inventa v. atque
ornare oratione, Cic.: Quint.

2. convestio,
4 (to c. <i>completely</i>: rare and
chiefly poet.): <i>the ivy has c.d everything</i>,
omnia convestivit hedera, Cic.:
Lucr.

3. vēlo, 1 (prop. <i>to veil, drape,

4. indŭo,

<b>cold</b> (adj.):

1. frīgĭdus (the most

<i>a fountain c. by day, warm by night</i>,

2. algĭdus (i. e. <i>so cold

Mart.: Plin.

3. gĕlĭdus (<i>ice-cold</i>):
<i>the (junction of) the Fibrenus makes the

also mean a <i>frozen river</i>: Virg.): <i>c.[**P2: unclear]

<b>command</b> (<i>v.</i>):

2. grex, grĕgis, <i>m.</i> (prop. <i>of animals</i>):

III. <i>An assembly of persons for entertainment

<b>comparative</b>:

I. <i>Estimated by
comparison, not positive or absolute</i>:
Phr.: <i>we may easily see the c. insignificance
of these causes</i>, *quam nullae
sint hae causae, si modo aliis conferantur,
videre palam [in aperto] est: <i>you
have great c. advantages</i>, *magna tibi
alienorum ratione habita adjumenta
sunt. N.B. Not compărātivus: which
means <i>pertaining to comparison</i>: it
must however be used in technical
sense; as, <i>c. anatomy</i>, *anatomia comparativa.

II. In Grammar: <i>the c.
degree</i>, gradus comparativus; or without
a subs.: Donat. (In the same sense
Fest. has collatio.)


<b>comparatively</b>: Phr.: <i>(they show)
c. a good deal of calculation and skill
for Germans</i>, multum ut inter Ger-*
-----File: b0138l.png------------------------------------------------------
*manos rationis ac sollertiae,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed, clear on TIA] Tac.: <i>he
was, for a Roman, c. a learned man</i>,
multae (erant in eo) ut in homine Romano
literae, Cic. Or it may be expr.
by such phrases as, *si modo cum aliis
conferatur, comparetur; ratione aliorum
habita, etc.: or, by the comparative degree:
as, <i>the good orators will be found,
by the side of the good poets,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed, clear on TIA] to be c.
few in number</i>, multo pauciores oratores
quam poëtae boni reperientur, Cic.
Phr.:[**P2: dot missing] <i>c. few persons</i>, nemo fere, Cic.
N.B. Not compărātē, which is good
Latin, but has a diff. sense: v. Cic.
Top. 22, 84.


<b>compare</b>:

1. compăro, 1 (the
word denoting the thing <i>to</i> or <i>with
which</i> another is compared, being put
in the <i>dat.</i>; the <i>acc.</i> with a prep. [rare;
and poet.]; or, very freq. in the <i>abl.</i>
with cum): <i>to c. resemblances</i>, similitudines
c., Cic.: <i>to c. things greater,

Cic.: <i>nor is this man to be c.d to the
other</i>, nec comparandus hic quidem ad
illum est, Ter.: <i>even the Gauls themselves
do not c. themselves to the Germans
in valour</i>, ne se quidem Galli ipsi
cum Germanis virtute c., Caes.: <i>and
does Ajax c. himself to me?</i> et se mihi
c. Ajax? Ov.: <i>to c. things together</i>, res
inter se c., Cic.

2. compōno,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed, clear on TIA] pŏsui,
pŏsĭtum, 3 (constr. same as 1): <i>to c.

c., Virg.: Cic.

3. confĕro, tŭli, lātum,
3 (constr. same as above): <i>c. this
peace with that war</i>,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed, clear on TIA] conferte hanc
pacem cum illo bello, Cic.: <i>to c. small
things with great</i>, parva magnis
c., Cic.: Hor.

4. contendo, di, sum and
tum, 3: <i>c. whatever you have said
on the other side with my defence</i>,
quidquid tu contra dixeris, id cum nostra
defensione contendito, Cic. Rosc.
Am. 33, 93 (where immediately after
conferre is used synonymously): <i>to c.
laws</i>, leges c.,[**P2: c.,|P3 fixed, clear on TIA] Cic.: v. <f>TO CONTRAST</f>.
N.B. <i>Comparo</i> is used of comparing
things which nearly resemble each other:
<i>compono</i> is to <i>set side by side</i>, in order
to discern resemblance or difference:
<i>confero</i> and <i>contendo</i>, esp. the latter,
are often equiv. to the Eng. <i>contrast</i>:
q. v.

5. aequĭpăro, 1: i. e. <i>to set
on an equality with</i>: Pl.: Liv.: v. <f>TO
LIKEN</f>.


<b>comparison</b>:

I. <i>The act of comparing</i>:

1. compărātio: Cic.

2.
collātio (esp. of <i>rhetorical c.s or similes</i>:
q. v.): Cic.

3. contentio: Cic. (who
uses contentio along with comparatio,

4. Expr. by means

quam quum ipsae per se aestimantur,

also foll. art.


<b>comparison, in</b>: foll. by <sc>WITH</sc>[** ? not a link] (<i>adv.

1. ăd (with <i>accus.</i>): <i>in c.

3. prae
(with <i>abl.</i>: or, when a clause follows,

<b>compilation</b>:

II. <i>A book

<b>compile</b>: Phr.: <i>to write an original

<b>compiler</b>: qui libros ex aliorum

<i>assiduous and careful c[**.]</i>, assidua ac
diligens s., Cic.: <i>this style of c. should
be not only free, but spirited and high-*toned</i>,
genus hoc scripturae non modo
liberum sed incitatum atque elatum
esse debet, Cic.

3. confectio: <i>the
c. of a book</i>, libri c., Cic.: <i>the c. of annals</i>,
annalium c., Cic.

4. Expr. by
<i>ger.</i>: <i>facility of c.</i>, pangendi facilitas,
Tac. (but a Ciceronian writer would add
the <i>acc.</i> of <i>that composed</i>).

III. <i>The
book, poem, etc., composed</i>: lĭber, scriptum

IV. <i>A sum paid in discharge of a
larger debt</i>: Phr.: <i>he paid a c. of 50

solutum est; convenit inter eos (<i>sc.</i> debitorem
et creditorem) ut debita ex
semisse solverentur: simly, with ex
triente (<i>one-third</i>), ex centesima parte
(<i>one per cent.</i>), etc.

<b>comprehend</b>:

I. <i>To contain,

2. complector, plexus, 3 (with some

5. cerno, crēvi, crētum,

6. comprĕhendo

7. intellĭgo, 3: v. <f>TO UNDERSTAND</f>.

<b>comprehensive</b>: may usu. be expr.

filia gratularis, Cic.: <i>he c.s him very
loudly on his victory</i>, ei voce maxima
victoriam gratulatur, Cic.: <i>he c.d him
on the recovery of liberty</i>, ei recuperatam
libertatem est gratulatus, Cic.: <i>I c.
you that the highest credit has attended
you</i>, tibi gratulor quod te summa laus
persecuta est, Cic.: poet. with <i>infin.</i>:
<i>I c. you that your ability has not lain
hid</i>, tibi g. ingenium non latuisse tuum,
Ov.: absol.: <i>impious citizens were c.ing
one another as if they had conquered</i>.[**P2: ,]
inter se impii cives quasi vicissent gratulabantur,
Cic.

2. grātor, 1 (with
<i>dat.</i> or <i>acc.</i>: not in Cic.): <i>I c. myself</i>,
mihi grator, Ov.: <i>he c.s them on their
return</i>, gratatur reduces,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed, clear on TIA] Virg.: <i>mutually
c.ing each other</i>, invicem inter se
gratantes, Liv.

3. congrātŭlor, 1:
i. q. simple verb: Liv. (rare in Cic.).


<b>congratulation</b>: grātŭlātio: <i>to offer

<b>congratulatory</b>: expr. by some

<b>conscience</b>: conscientia (often with

is meant): <i>great is the power of c.</i>,
magna vis est conscientiae, Cic.: <i>to take
to oneself the comfort of a good c.</i>, consolari
se conscientia optimae mentis,
Cic.; who has also, praeclara c.: <i>a bad
(guilty) c.</i>, mala c., Sall.: the plural is
often used esp. in <i>bad</i> sense: <i>bad reflections
and an evil c.</i>, malae cogitationes
conscientiaeque animi, Cic.:
<i>struck by a guilty c.</i>, maleficii conscientia
perterritus, Cic.: <i>remorse of c.</i>,
angor conscientiae, Cic.: the word is
neutral, but occurs oftener in bad than
in good sense: <i>stains on one's c.</i>, conscientiae
labes, Cic. Phr.: <i>a good c.</i>,
mens conscia recti, Virg.: <i>those who
feel the terrors of a guilty c.</i>, diri quos
conscia facti mens habet attonitos [et
occulto verbere torquet], Juv.: <i>to keep
a good c.</i>, nil conscire (= conscium esse)
sibi, Hor.: <i>cases of c.</i>, *res dubiae: <i>to
make a c. of doing something</i>, *aliquid
diligentissime observare et facere: <i>he
had no c.</i>, nulla (ei) religio (erat), Liv.
(of Hannibal): <i>I have no scruple of c.
in saying</i>, nulla mihi religio est dicere,
Ter. (see <f>SCRUPLE</f>): <i>a scruple of c. about
falsehood</i>, religio mendacii,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed, clear on TIA] Liv.


<b>conscientious</b>:

1. rēlĭgiōsus (with
ref. to some <i>religious</i> motive; as <i>an
oath</i>): <i>a nation not at all c. in giving

dicendis r., Cic.: <i>a c. judge</i>, r. judex,
Quint.: (but in gen. sense religiosus
usu. implies censure: "oportet religentem
esse non <i>religiosum</i>," Cic.).

2.
sanctus: of general <i>integrity</i>: v. <f>MORAL</f>,
<f>IRREPROACHABLE</f>. Phr.: <i>the c.
keeping of a promise, of an oath</i>, *fides
ac religio promissi, jurisjurandi.


<b>conscientiously</b>:

1. bona fide:
Cic. (who adds, et citra fraudem).

2.
relĭgiōsē (of <i>evidence, oaths</i>, etc.): <i>to give

3. (in gen. sense) sanctē: <i>to behave
most c.</i>, se sanctissime gerere, Cic.:
Quint.

4. (of a duty) dīlĭgenter:[** diacritic unclear] v.

<b>conscientiousness</b>:

<b>conscious</b>:

I. <i>Aware of one's own

<i>capable of feeling</i>; sensu praedĭtus,

<b>consistency</b>:

<b>consul</b>:

I. Roman:[**P2: unclear] consul, sŭlis:
<i>to appoint c.s</i>, consules[**P2: unclear] creare (often
used <i>of the presiding magistrate</i>), Liv.:
<i>c. elect</i> (but not actually in office), c. designatus,
Cic.: Liv.: <i>a c. chosen in the
place of one deceased</i>, c. suffectus, Liv.:
<i>c. for the second time</i>, consul iterum,
Cic.: simly. c. tertium, quartum, etc.:
<i>when Manlius was c.</i>, consule Manlio,
Hor.: v. <f>CONSULATE</f>: <i>one who has been
c.</i>, consŭlāris: Cic.: <i>an assembly for
the election of c.s</i>, comitia consularia,
Cic.: <i>a c.'s house</i>, consularis domus,
Plin.: <i>a c.'s wife</i>, femina consularis,
Suet.

II. Modern: no exact term;
the Romans relying upon the protection
of their name of <i>Roman citizens</i>, or of
their ordinary magistrates. The Greek
πρόξενος does not appear to have been
adopted in Lat.: perhaps the nearest
word is curator (not procurator, which
would be taken for a <i>governor</i>).

Messala and Piso</i>, Messala et Pisone
consulibus (Coss.), Caes.: Cic.

2.

confer, take away the c.</i>, fasces deferre,

<b>context</b>: i. e. <i>the adjoining words or

<b>contrast</b> (<i>v.</i>):

<b>coolness</b>:

I. Lit.:

1. frīgus, ŏris,
<i>n.</i> (of <i>all degrees of cold</i>): <i>there is generally
c. in the morning</i>, fere matutinis

2. refrīgĕrātio, Cic. de Sen. 14,

II. <i>Self-possession</i>: animus
sedatus, lentus et consideratus, potens

III. <i>Indifference</i>:
lentĭtūdo: v. <f>INDIFFERENCE</f>:
or expr. with lentus: as, <i>we look on

v. <f>COOLLY</f>. Frigus in this sense is rare:
used with ref. to friendship, Sen.

IV.
<i>Impudence</i>: os durum: esp. as an exclamation,
Ter.

<b>country</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

2. rūs, rūris, <i>n.</i>

II. <i>Any tract of land</i>

1. rĕgio, ōnis, <i>f.</i>: <i>but we see the

2.

3. fīnes, ium, <i>pl.</i>

5. ōra, plăga:
v. <f>REGION</f>, <f>COAST</f>.

6. The name of
the inhabitants of a country is often put

(of <i>persons</i>): as, novi mariti, "<i>a young
c.</i>," Apul. (= nova nupta et novus maritus).

<b>courage</b>:

1. ănĭmus: <i>our men's

<b>course</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

I. <i>Motion in
some particular direction</i>:

1. cursus,
ūs (in most senses): <i>the c.s of the stars</i>,
stellarum c., Cic.: so of <i>rivers</i>, Cic.:
Ov.: of <i>ships at sea</i> (esp. in phr. tenere
cursum, <i>to keep on their</i> course,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed] Caes.:
Cic.): <i>to direct one's c.</i>, c. dirigere, Nep.:
<i>to be driven out of it</i>, cursu excuti, Virg.
Fig.: <i>the c. of the times</i>, c. temporum,
Cic.

2. lapsus, ūs (<i>a gliding</i> or <i>flowing
c.</i>): <i>the rapid c. of rivers</i>, fluminum
rapidi lapsus, Hor.: <i>the stars proceed
in a fixed c. and space</i>, stellae certo l.
spatioque feruntur, Cic.: <i>to flow to the
sea by its natural c.</i> (of the water of the
Alban lake), lapsu et cursu suo ad mare
profluere, id.

3. tĕnor, ōris (a c. that
is <i>steadily kept on</i>: cf. the phr. cursum
tenere, <i>supr.</i>): <i>the spear flies, and keeps
its c.</i>, hasta volat, servatque t., Virg.:
<i>c. of life</i>, vitae t., Ov.

4. via, ĭter:
v. <f>ROUTE</f>, <f>WAY</f>: <i>to direct one's c.</i>, iter
dirigere, Cic.: <i>to alter one's c.</i>, iter
flectere, Virg.: also flectere viam velis,
id. A. 5, 28. Fig.: <i>the c. of our affection
and my attentiveness</i>, iter amoris
nostri et officii mei, Cic. Att. 4, 2, <i>init.</i>
Phr.: <i>to direct one's c. towards</i>, pĕto
(with <i>acc.</i>): v. <f>MAKE FOR</f>, <f>GO TO</f>: <i>to
run through one's c. of life</i>, decurrere
vitam, Tib.; also d. spatium vitae (for
the figure is borrowed from the circus),
Ov.: <i>that c. of study</i>, orbis ille doctrinae,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed]
Quint.: <i>the whole c. of our industry</i>,
curriculum omne industriae nostrae, Cic.

II. <i>Stated and orderly method of
proceeding</i>: esp. in phr., <i>in due course</i>:
ordĭnātim: <i>to canvass for honours (offices)
in the commonwealth in due c.</i>[**P2: ,] honores
ordinatim petere in republica, Cic.: so
also, ex ordine, per ordinem, in ordine:
<i>each according to his precedence in age
and rank gave his opinion in due c.</i>, ut
quisque aetate et honore antecedebat,
ita sententiam dixit ex ordine,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed] Cic.: v.
<f>ORDER</f> (in). <i>Out of c.</i>, extra ordinem:
<i>to decree a province to any one out of c.</i>,
extra ord. decernere provinciam alicui,
Cic.: <i>the act of going through all public
offices in due c.</i>, decursus honorum, Cic.

III. <i>Plan</i> or <i>regulated proceeding</i>:

1. rătio, ōnis, <i>f.</i>: <i>to resolve on a
certain c.</i>, r. instituere, Pl.: more usu.,
r. inire, Caes.: <i>to abandon a c.</i>, r. omittere,
Caes.: <i>my c. in speaking is accustomed
to be as follows</i>, mea r. in dicendo
haec esse solet, Cic.

2. consĭlium:
<i>nor do I know what c. now to take</i>,
neque quid nunc consili capiam scio,
Ter.: Cic.: v. <f>PLAN</f>.

3. instĭtūtum
(a course <i>resolved upon, deliberately
adopted</i>): <i>to follow one's own c.</i>, instituto
suo uti, Caes.: Cic. Phr.: <i>to let a
person take his own c.</i>, *permittere alicui
ut ad arbitrium suum, ad libidinem
suam agat, cf. <i>supr.</i> (I., <i>fin.</i>).

IV.
<i>The place where a race is run</i>: circus,
spătium[**P2: :] v. <f>RACE-COURSE</f>.

V. <i>A
course of lectures</i>: perh. *schŏlarum

habere, cf. Cic. Tusc. 1, 4, 7.

Of medicine: cūrātio: v. <f>TREATMENT</f>.

VIII. <i>Service
of meat</i>: Phr.: <i>the first, second, and

Suet.: Juv.

IX. In certain phr.:

(<i>a</i>). <i>in the course of</i>:

1. de (with <i>abl.</i>):
only of time: <i>in the c. of the night</i>, de
nocte, Caes.: Cic. (also <i>abl.</i> alone): v.
<f>IN</f>.

2. inter (with <i>acc.</i>: esp. before a
gerund): <i>in the c. of speaking</i>,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed] inter
loquendum (also in sermone, e. g. injicere,
to let fall <i>in c. of conversation</i>,
Cic.): v. <f>DURING</f>. (N.B. Iter sermonis
is the <i>drift</i> or <i>line of reasoning</i> in discourse
or conversation: Cic. Leg., 1, 13,
37.)

(<i>b</i>). <i>of c.</i>, <i>as a matter of c.</i>:

1.
contĭnuo: (only in connection with a
negative, or a question implying one):
<i>if I have mingled with a crew of assassins,
I am not, therefore, as a matter of
c., an assassin</i>, non c., si me in gregem
sicariorum contuli, sicarius, Cic.: <i>if he
is free from evil, does he, as a matter
of c., enjoy the chiefest good?</i> si malo
careat, c.ne fruitur summo bono? Cic.

2. scīlĭcet: <i>what says Naevius to this?
he laughs, of c., at our folly</i>,[**P2: ,|P3 fixed] quid ad
haec N.? ridet, scilicet, nostram amentiam,
Cic.: <i>your companions followed
the maiden, of c.?</i> comites secuti s.
sunt virginem? Ter.: <i>present my respects
to my sister.--Of c.!</i> gratulator meae
sorori.--Scilicet! Plaut.: very often
ironical: <i>people trouble themselves a
great deal about that, of c.!</i> id populus
curat s.! Ter.: v. <f>FORSOOTH</f>.

3. nīmīrum
(= <i>no doubt</i>: q. v.): very often
iron.: Hor.: Juv.

4. vĭdēlĭcet (iron.):
Cic.: v. <f>DOUBTLESS</f>.

<b>crossing</b>:

I. The verbal <i>subs.</i>:
transĭtus, transmissio, etc.: v. <f>PASSAGE</f>.

II. <i>A place where roads cross</i>:

1.
compĭtum (usu. in <i>pl.</i>, and esp. with
reference to <i>the country</i>): <i>to sell by
auction in c.s (town or country)</i>, in
triviis aut in compitis auctionari, Cic.:
Hor.: Virg. Hence <i>adj.</i> compĭtālis:
esp. in phr., lares compitales (<i>deities
having charge of c. roads</i>), Suet.

2.
trĭvium (strictly <i>of three roads</i>: applied
to <i>public places in towns</i>): <i>a copper
fastened in a c.</i>, in triviis fixus as, Hor.:
<i>bred in a c.</i> (i. e. <i>in a public part of the
town</i>), triviis innatus, id. A. P. 245:
Cic.

3. bĭvium (a place where <i>two
roads</i> meet): <i>to stop at a c.</i>, ad bivia
consistere, Liv.

4. quadrĭvium (of
<i>four roads</i>): Juv.: Cat.


<b>cross-legged</b>: poplitibus alternis
genibus impositis: Plin. 28, 6, 17.


<b>cross-purposes</b>: in phr. <i>to be at c.</i>,
errore quodam contrario duci (R. and
A.); *re parum intellecta inter se pugnare;
prave inter se intelligere.


<b>cross-question</b>: v. <f>CROSS-EXAMINE</f>.


<b>cross-road</b>: trāmes, ĭtis, <i>m.</i> (opp.
to <i>a high-road</i>): Cic.: Sall. More fully,
<i>by c.s</i>, transversis tramitibus, Liv. 2, 39.
See also <f>CROSSING</f>.


<b>cross-wise</b> (<i>adv.</i>):

1. dĕcussātim:
Vitr.: Col. (see <f>CROSS</f>, <i>subs.</i> II.).

2.
in quincuncem (i. e. <i>as the points were
set for the</i> quincunx :·:[**symbol 5 dots]): <i>rows of
trees set c.</i>, directi in q. ordines, Cic.
Simly[**. ?] quincunx is used to denote <i>a c.
arrangement</i>:[**P2: dot missing] quid illo quincunce speciosius?
Quint. 8, 3, 9. Phr.: <i>to divide
c.</i>, dĕcusssso[**~cusso],: [** , 1:] Cic.: <i>such a division</i> or
<i>arrangement</i>, decussatio, Vitr.:[**P2: dot missing] <i>lines</i>
-----File: b0173l.png------------------------------------------------------
<i>drawn c.</i>, in decusses ductae lineae,
Plin. (N.B. Not in crucis speciem:
comp. <f>CROSS</f>, <i>subs.</i> II.).


<b>crossly</b>: ămārē, īrācundē, etc.: v.
<f>PEEVISHLY</f>.


<b>crossness</b>: importūnĭtas, ămārĭtūdo:
v. <f>PEEVISHNESS</f>, <f>ILL-TEMPER</f>.


<b>crotchet</b>:

I. In music: *quadrans
[notae musicae], Kr.

II. <i>A fancy</i>:

1. lĭbīdo: v. <f>CAPRICE</f>.

2. prōlŭbium
(rare): v. <f>FANCY</f>.


<b>crotchetty</b>: i. e. <i>full of whims</i>:
(?)mōrōsus: cf. Cic. Or. 29, <i>fin.</i>, "usque
eo difficiles ac morosi sumus ut nobis
non satisfaciat ipse Demosthenes:" *putida
quadam morositate [homo]: i. e.
<i>of a temper so fault-finding as to be
offensive</i>: v. <f>PEEVISH</f>.


<b>crouch</b>:

I. <i>To stoop low</i>:

1.
subsīdo, di, 3: <i>the Spaniards c. down to
protect themselves from the missiles discharged
by the foe</i>, s. Hispani adversus
emissa ab hoste tela, Liv.: Virg.

2.
dēmitto, submitto (with <i>pron. refl.</i>):
v. <f>TO STOOP</f>, <f>COUCH</f>.

II. <i>To bend servilely</i>:
ad pedes alicujus abjicere sese,
projicere; jacēre: v. <f>CRINGE</f>, <f>COWER</f>.


<b>croup</b>: <i>a disease of the throat</i>:
*cynanche trachealis.


<b>crow</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

I. <i>The bird</i>: cornix,
īcis, <i>f.</i>: Cic.: Plin. <i>Dimin.</i>, cornīcŭla,
Hor. Prov.: <i>to pluck or pull a crow</i>,
i. e. <i>to contend about a trifle</i>, de lana
caprina rixari, Hor.

II. <i>A bar</i>:
vectis: v. <f>LEVER</f>.

III. <i>The voice of
the cock</i>: cantus, ūs: <i>the c.ing of the
cock</i>, galli cantus, Cic.: <i>at cock-c[**missing .?]</i>, sub
galli cantum, Hor.


<b>crow</b> (<i>v.</i>):

I. Lit.: of <i>a cock</i>:

1. cūcūrio, 4: Auct. Car. Phil.

2.
căno, cĕcĭni, cantum, 3 (gen. term:
used of <i>all birds</i>): <i>cocks are accustomed
to c. when victorious</i>, galli victores c.
solent, Cic.

3. canto, 1: Cic.

II.
Fig.: <i>to boast</i>: glōrior, jacto (usu. with
<i>pron. refl.</i>) etc.: v. <f>TO BOAST</f>.


<b>crow-foot</b>: rānuncŭlus, Plin.


<b>crow's-foot</b>: <i>a caltrop</i> (q. v.): stĭmŭlus:
Caes.


<b>crowd</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

I. Of people.

1.
turba (<i>a number of persons without
order</i>): <i>the praetor's house filled with
a c.</i>, domus praetoria, turbâ referta,
Cic.: <i>a c. of unknown gods</i>, t. ignotorum
deorum, Cic.: <i>a c. of disciples</i>, discipulorum
t., Quint.

2. vulgus, i, <i>m.</i> and
<i>n.</i> (<i>the common herd, the multitude</i>:
always used <i>contemptuously</i>): v. <f>MULTITUDE</f>.

3. frĕquentia (<i>a number of
persons or things close together</i>): <i>a very
great c. of people</i>, summa hominum f.,
Cic.: v. <f>THRONG</f>.

4. concursus, ūs
(of people <i>flocking together</i>): <i>a c. assembles
in the streets</i>, fit c. per vias,
Pl.: <i>great c.s assembled</i>, magni c. sunt
facti, Nep.

5. cĕlebrĭtas (strictly an
abstract <i>subs.</i>: thus Cic. has celebritas
loci in sense of the <i>crowdedness</i> or <i>fashionableness</i>
of a place: Fam. 14, 1, <i>fin.</i>):
<i>I hate a c.; I avoid men</i>, odi celebritatem;
fugio homines, Cic.: more fully
celebritas virorum ac mulierum, id.
See also <f>MULTITUDE</f>, <f>RABBLE</f>.

II. Of
other things: chiefly in fig. sense; as,
<i>a c. of thoughts</i>, *turba, frequentia, multitudo
cogitationum (?): v. <f>MULTITUDE</f>.
Phr.: <i>what a c. of thoughts come rushing
into the mind</i>, *quot res mentem
subeunt: quarum rerum in mentem
venit!


<b>crowd</b> (<i>v.</i>):

A. Trans.:

I. <i>To

II. <i>To force together into one space</i>:

2. constīpo, 1
(slightly stronger than simple verb):
<i>to c. together a number of men into a</i>

4. cŏarto, condenso,

<b>crowded</b> (<i>adj.</i>):

I. <i>Close together</i>:

1. condensus: <i>ships c. together on
the shore</i>, c. puppes litore, Virg.: Liv.
Also, densus: Ov.: Hor.

2. confertus:
<i>ships c. together</i>, naves c., Liv.:
<i>c. together in confined dwellings</i>, c. in
arcta tecta, Liv.: <i>in c. or close array</i>,
confertus (<i>e. g.</i> c. acies), <i>sup.</i> confertissimus,
Caes.: v. <f>CLOSE</f>.

II. <i>Full,
attended by many people</i>:

1. cĕlĕber,
bris, bre: <i>a very c. assembly of men
and women</i>, celeberrimus virorum mulierumque
conventus, Cic.: v. <f>FREQUENTED</f>.

2. confertus (more freq.
in sense I.): <i>the temples of the Gods c.
with a vast multitude</i>, ingenti turba c.
deorum templa,[**P2: ,|P3:yes, checked scan] Liv. Fig.: <i>a life full
and c. with pleasures</i>, vita plena et c.
voluptatibus, Cic.

3. frĕquens, ntis
(of assemblies and places <i>well-attended</i>):
<i>a c. banquet</i>, f. convivium, Suet.: <i>a very
c. theatre</i>, frequentissimum theatrum,
Cic.

4. rĕfertus (i. e. <i>full of, abounding
in</i>: with <i>abl.</i>): <i>his house was c. with
gamblers</i>, domus erat aleatoribus r.,
Cic.

5. spissus (<i>thick together</i>): <i>c.
seats</i>, s. sedilia, Hor.: <i>c. theatres</i>, s.
theatra, Hor.

6. artus, arctus (<i>too
much c.</i>): nimis a. convivia, Hor.
Phr.:[**P2: dot missing] <i>crowded state</i>, cĕlebrĭtas: <i>the c.
state of the place</i>, c. loci, Cic.: <i>of the

<b>crown</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

I. <i>Of a king</i>:

1.
insigne rēgium:[**P2: dot missing] <i>he replaced on his head
the c.</i>, insigne r. (capiti) reposuit,[**P2: ,|P3:yes, checked scan] Cic.
Sext. 27, 58: insigne r. capiti imponere,
Tac. Ann. 2, 58: for this, insigne capitis
may be used where the context shows
that a <i>king's</i> crown is meant: Sen.

2. ăpex, ĭcis, <i>m.</i> (strictly, a <i>conical
tiara worn by priests</i>): Cic. Leg. 1,[**P2: ,|P3:yes, checked scan] 1,
<i>fin.</i> (see the place): Hor.

3. diădēma,
ătis, <i>n.</i> (Gr. διάδημα) <i>a kind of
band; the sign of royalty in the East</i>):
Suet.: Hor.: Juv. The pure Latin for
this word is (candida) fascia, which is
used by Suet. in the well-known story
of Caesar's statue (Jul. 79). N.B. Corona
is not used in this sense: see Suet. l. c.;
and <i>infr.</i>

II. By meton., <i>royal power</i>:
regnum: <i>to bestow the c. on any one</i>,
alicui r. deferre, Caes.: Hor. (who
adds et diadema): <i>to aspire to the c.</i>,
r. appetere, affectare: v. <f>ASPIRE TO</f>: v.
<f>REGAL POWER</f>.

III. <i>Any honorary
wreath</i>: cŏrōna: for the diff. kinds of
coronae see Dict. Ant. <i>s. v.</i>: as <i>a constellation</i>,
Cic.: Virg. <i>Dimin.</i> cŏrolla:
v. <f>WREATH</f>, <f>GARLAND</f>.

IV. <i>The top</i>

<i>of the head</i>: vertex.[**P2: ,] ĭcis, <i>m.</i>: <i>from the
soles of the feet to the c. of the head</i>, ab

Cic.: Hor.: v. <f>TOP</f>. V. <i>Completion,

<b>crucifixion</b>:

I. Lit.: Mostly

<b>crucify</b>:

I. Lit.: in crucem agere,

as single word, belongs to later
and Christian writers.)

II. Fig.: in
theol. sense, <i>to c. the flesh</i>, *corporis
libidines omni duritia coercere et quasi

<b>crude</b>:

I. Lit.: <i>not cooked</i> or

II. Fig.:

2. rŭdis, e (<i>unfinished</i>):

<b>crudely</b>: imperfectē: v. <f>IMPERFECTLY</f>.

<b>cruelty</b>:

1. crūdēlĭtas : which

2.
atrōcĭtas (less freq. in this sense;

<f>SEVERITY</f>.

3. fĕrĭtas, immānĭtas
(cruelty as it were <i>beyond human</i>).[**s/b : ?]

4. saevĭtia
(used by Cic. for <i>severity</i> in good sense:

<b>cruise</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

I. <i>A small vessel</i>

<b>curse</b> (<i>v.</i>):

II. Abstract
for concr.: = <i>bane, plague</i>: pestis, fŭria,
pernĭcies: Cic.: v. <f>PLAGUE</f>, <f>PEST</f>.


<b>cursed</b> (as <i>adj.</i>): săcer, exsecrābĭlis,
etc.: v. <f>ACCURSED</f>. Phr.: <i>a c. tree</i>

<b>cursing</b> (<i>subs.</i>): expr. by <i>verb</i>:

under <f>CURSE</f>: as, <i>abstain from c.</i>, *exsecrationes
fuge.


<b>cursorily</b>: i. e. <i>briefly and superficially</i>:

1. strictim: <i>these things,
now said c., will be made more clear

Varr.: <i>to speak c.</i>.[** ,] s. dicere, Cic.

2.
summātim (<i>dealing only with the
heads of a subject</i>): <i>to touch upon
anything c.</i>, aliquid s. attingere, Quint.:
Cic.: v. <f>SUMMARILY</f>.

3. brĕvĭter: v.
<f>BRIEFLY</f>. Join: breviter strictimque,
Cic.: breviter ac summatim, Varr.
Phr.: <i>to touch upon a subject c.</i>, perstringere,
Cic.: v. <f>TO GLANCE AT</f>: also
sometimes percurrere, transcurrere, esp.
of <i>reading through hastily</i> or <i>c.</i>, Quint.:
v. <f>TO RUN THROUGH</f>.


<b>cursory</b>: expr. with <i>adv.</i>: as, <i>c. remarks</i>,
strictim dicta, etc.: v. preced. art.


<b>curst</b> (<i>adj.</i>): i. e. <i>shrewish</i>:

1.
mordax, Hor.: Phaedr.: v. <f>SNARLING</f>.

2. importūnus: <i>a c. shrew of a
wife</i>, uxor imp. atque incommoda, Pl.
As. 1, 1, 48.


<b>curt</b> (<i>adj.</i>): i. e. <i>short to excess</i>; only

1. abruptus: Quint.:
v. <f>ABRUPT</f>.

2. perh[** .] adstrictus: cf.
Cic. Br. 25, <i>init.</i>

3. brĕvis, brĕvior:
v. <f>BRIEF</f>.


<b>curtness</b>: abruptum loquendi genus,

(much more freq. in this sense).[** unnecessary punc|F1: why? s/b :] <f>TO
LIMIT</f>, <f>DIMINISH</f>:

<b>custom</b>:

I. <i>Frequent or habitual
using and doing</i>:

1. consuētūdo,
ĭnis, <i>f.</i>: <i>it is not my c.</i>, non est meae c.,
Cic.: <i>to adhere to or follow c.</i>, c. tenere,
uti, id.: <i>according to one's c.</i>, ex c.,
Caes.; pro (sua) c., Cic.

2. assuētūdo
(the accustoming <i>to</i> something): <i>long

by c.</i>, seu natura,[**P2: ,] sive assuetudine, Tac.

3. mos, mōris, <i>m.</i>: v. <i>infr.</i> (II.).

4. instĭtūtum (<i>regular custom or
practice</i>): Join: consuetudo et institutum
meum, Cic:[**P2: Cic.:] v. <f>HABIT</f>, <f>PRACTICE</f>.

II. <i>An usage</i>; esp. of a nation:

1. mos: <i>according to the c. and
precedent of the Roman people</i>, m. et
exemplo populi Romani, Caes.: <i>to obey
c. and law</i>, mori legique parere, Cic.:
<i>as was the c. of the kings of Bithynia</i>,
ut mos fuit regibus Bithyniae,[**P2: ,] Cic.: <i>it
is the c. of men to be unwitting, etc.</i>,
mos est hominum ut nolint,[**P2: ,] Cic.: <i>according
to the c. of their ancestors</i>, more
majorum, id.: <i>away with the barbarous
c.</i>, tollite barbarum m., Hor.

2. consuētūdo:
<i>the inhuman and barbarous
c. of offering human sacrifices</i>,[**P2: ,] immanis
et barbara c. hominum immolandorum,[**P2: ,]
Cic.: <i>according to the c. of the Greeks</i>,
ad c. Graecorum,[**P2: ,] Cic.: <i>contrary to usage
and c.</i>, praeter morem c.que, Cic. (N.B.
Mos refers esp. to <i>national customs</i>,
and thus usu. denotes something more
general and permanent than consuetudo:
v. <f>HABIT</f>.)

3. instĭtūtum (<i>an established
c.</i>): <i>they differ in language,
c.s, and laws</i>,[**P2: ,] lingua, institutis, legibus
inter se differunt, Caes.: v. <f>PRACTICE</f>
and <i>supr.</i> (4).

4. rītus, ūs (prop. of
<i>religious customs</i>; hence used generally):
<i>to perform sacred rites after the
Greek c.</i>, Graeco r. sacra facere, Liv.: v.
<f>RITE</f>. Esp. in <i>abl.</i> ritu, <i>after the c. or
manner of</i>: v. <f>LIKE</f>. Hence <i>adv.</i> rītĕ,
<i>according to (regular and proper) c.</i>,
Hor.: Cic.: v. <f>DULY</f>.

5. sollenne, is,
<i>n.</i>: <i>a ceremony</i> (q. v.).

III. <i>Business,
buying and selling</i>: expr. with phr.:[**P2: dot missing]

p., Petr.: Just.: <i>to c. off (the end of) a
whetstone</i>, cotem p., Cic.: cf. <f>TO CUT</f>
(II., <i>fin.</i>).

2[** .] abscīdo, 3 (rare, and
-----File: b0179m.png------------------------------------------------------
often confused with abscindo in MSS.):
<i>to c. off a head</i>, caput a., Virg.; <i>with
the right hand c. off</i>, abscisâ dextrâ,
Suet. Fig.: <i>to c. off hope</i>, spem a.,
Liv.

3. abscindo, scĭdi, scissum, 3
(<i>to c. or tear forcibly away</i>): <i>c.ing
away shoots from the parent trunk</i>,
plantas abscindens de corpore matrum,
Virg.: <i>Xerxes cut off Athos from the
mainland</i>, Xerxes Athon continenti abscidit,
Plin.: Hor.

4. ampŭto, 1: <i>to
c. off a (dead) man's head</i>, caput a.,
Suet.: <i>to c. off a person's hand</i>, alicui
manus a., id.

5. dēcīdo, 3 (less freq.):
<i>to c. off (clip) wings</i>, pennas d., Hor.:
Tac.

6. dēsĕco, 1: <i>to c. off hairs</i>,
crines d., Ov.: <i>ears c. off</i>, aures desectae,
Caes.

7. rĕcīdo, 3: v. <f>CUT AWAY</f>.
Phr.: <i>to c. off a man's head</i>, alicujus
collum secare, Q. Cic.; caput ense demetere,
Hor.: Ov.; caput detruncare,
Ov. (also detrunco with <i>acc.</i> of person:
Val. Fl.).

II. <i>To destroy completely
or suddenly</i>:

1. exstinguo, nxi,
nctum, 3: <i>to be c. off the sooner</i>, maturius
exstingui, Cic.; <i>in the prime of
life</i>, primo exstingui in aevo, Ov.: <i>he
was c. off by disease</i>, eum morbo fortuna
extinxit, Liv.

2. occŭpo, 1 (with
<i>suddenness</i>): <i>being off his guard he
(Caesar) was c. off by ungrateful men</i>,
incautus ab ingratis occupatus est, Vell.

3. pĕrĭmo, intĕrĭmo: v. <f>TO DESTROY</f>.

4. (in <i>pass.</i>): pĕreo, intĕreo, 4, <i>irr.</i>:
<i>the whole army would be c. off</i>, totum
exercitum periturum, Nep.: Liv.: <i>to be
c. off by disease</i>, morbo perire, Hirt.: v.
<f>PERISH</f>. See also <f>TO EXTIRPATE</f>, <f>EXTERMINATE</f>.

III. <i>To intercept, cut off
communication</i>:

1. interclūdo, si,
sum, 3 (with <i>acc.</i> and <i>dat.</i>; or <i>acc.</i> and
<i>abl.</i>): <i>to c. off the enemies' supplies</i>,
inimicis commeatum int., Pl.; [hostes]
commeatibus int., Caes. (the <i>abl.</i> is
usual in this sense): also with <i>prep.</i> a
commeatu omni adversarios int., Caes.:
Liv.

2. exclūdo, 3 (with <i>acc.</i> and
<i>abl.</i>): <i>to c. any one off from (joining)
another</i>, aliquem ab aliquo ex., Pomp.
ap. Cic.: <i>to c. off any one's return</i>, aliquem
reditu ex., Nep.: Caes.

3.
(less freq.): claudo, 3: <i>to c. off the
enemies' retreat</i>, hostibus fugam c., Liv.

4. prŏhĭbeo, 2: v. <f>TO PREVENT</f>, <f>KEEP
OFF</f>.


<b>cut open</b>: insĕco, incīdo: v. <f>TO CUT
INTO</f>. (But usu. aperire with or without
ferro will expr. the meaning more
precisely: v. <f>TO CUT THROUGH</f>.)


<b>---- out</b>:

I. <i>To remove with a
cutting instrument</i>:

1. exsĕco, 1: <i>to
c. out the bottom of a chest</i>, armarii fundum
ex., Cic.: Col.

2. excīdo, 3: <i>to
c. out any one's tongue</i>, alicui linguam
ex., Crass. ap. Cic.: <i>to c.</i> (or <i>hew</i>) <i>out
columns from the rocks</i>, columnas rupibus
ex., Virg. See also <f>TO CASTRATE</f>. (For
syn. see simple verb.)

II. <i>To shape
by cutting</i>: *secando formare: or
simply caedere: thus Quint. has toga
rotunda et apte caesa, i. e. <i>well cut
out</i>: 11, 3, 139. (N.B. Not secare,
which would be <i>to cut when made</i>: nor
formare, which is <i>to mould</i>.)

III. Vulg.
and only in <i>p. part.</i>: <i>cut out for</i>, i. e.
<i>adapted for</i>: nātus, aptus: v. <f>FIT</f>,
<f>MADE</f>.


<b>---- short</b>:

I. <i>To abridge</i>:

1.
praecīdo, 3: <i>to c. short</i> (the greater <i>part
of</i>) <i>the defence</i>, magnam partem defensionis
p., Cic.: <i>the consideration of time</i>
(i. e. <i>of the shortness of time</i>) <i>c.s short
delay</i>, temporis (<i>al.</i> mortis) ratio cunctationem
p., Plin. Ep. 9, 1, <i>fin.</i> Esp. as
<i>intrans.</i>, <i>to c. the matter short</i>, (brevi)
p., Cic.

2. intercīdo, 3: <i>to c. short
the intervening circumstances</i>, media
int., Cic.

3. ampŭto, 1: <i>to c. narrations
short</i>, narrationes a., Cic.: <i>they recommend
him to c. short delays ("to make
short work of it")</i>, amputari moras
jubent, Just. 27, 4 (for which Virg. has
rumpere moras, G. 3, 43, etc.): v. also
<f>TO CUT AWAY</f>, <f>CURTAIL</f>, <f>COMPRESS</f>.

II.
<i>To stop</i> another <i>abruptly</i>, oblŏquor, interpello:
v. <f>TO INTERRUPT</f>.


<b>---- through</b>:

I. Lit.: <i>to part
asunder by cutting</i>: intercīdo, dissĕco:
-----File: b0179r.png------------------------------------------------------
v. <f>CUT ASUNDER</f>: perfŏro, perfŏdio: v.
<f>PIERCE</f>. (N.B. Not perseco, which is <i>to

<i>the beasts c. through the snow</i> (with

II. Of troops: <i>to make a way

1.

2. Expr.
with ferro: <i>he c. a way through the

<b>cut to</b> or <b>in pieces</b>:

I. Lit.:

1. concīdo, 3: <i>to c. into small pieces</i>,
