2. consĕco, 1: <i>to c. in small pieces</i>,

Not conscindo, which is <i>to tear</i> in

3. Expr. by circuml.: as,

II.

<b>---- up</b>:

I. Lit.: <i>to c. in pieces</i>:

II. Fig.: <i>to handle severely</i> in

2.
invĕhor (with in and <i>acc.</i>): v. <f>TO INVEIGH

<b>day</b>:

I. In usual sense:

1.
dies, ēi, <i>m.</i> and <i>f.</i> (in <i>pl.</i> only <i>m.</i>): <i>holidays
and working d.s</i>, d. festi profestique,

sense), Ov.: <i>thirty</i> full or <i>legal d.s</i>,

ac noctem, Liv.; die quinetiam noctibus
(where the latter word is marked as
more extraordinary), Cic.: <i>to put off

simly with proferre[**unclear], Just.: <i>by d.</i>, de die,
Ter.: Cic. (also without <i>prep.</i>: v.
<i>supr.</i>); interdiu, Caes.: Liv.: this sense
may sometimes be conveyed by the <i>adj.</i>

by night and by d.</i>, nocturna
versate manu, versate diurna, Hor.
Sometimes used by meton. for <i>the events
of a d.</i>: as, <i>I examine by myself (the
deeds of) the whole day</i>, totum d.
mecum scrutor, Sen.: <i>a great</i> or <i>glorious

2. lux,
lūcis, <i>f.</i> (chiefly, but not solely, poet.):
<i>it is one hundred d.s since the death of
Clodius</i>, centesima l. est ab interitu
Clodii, Cic.: <i>at break of d.</i>, prima luce,
-----File: b0184l.png------------------------------------------------------
Liv.: v. <f>DAWN</f>: <i>before it was fully d.</i>,

3. lūmen,

4.
sol, sōlis, <i>m.</i>: Virg.: Hor. Phr.:

ac reconditarum scientia! <i>d.

Macr. S. S. 7. (Not mentis acies,
subtilitas, which denote <i>acuteness</i> or

ătis, <i>n.</i> (Gr. δίλεμμα): Serv. ad
Aen.: M. L.

2. complexio, Cic.
("complexio est in qua utrum concesseris,
reprehenditur," Inv. 1, 29, 45:
but dilemma is to be preferred as logical
<i>t. t.</i>).

3. bĭceps argūmentum, Apul.

4. syllogismus cornutus, Hier.

II.
<i>A difficulty</i>: angustiae, arum: v.
<f>STRAIT</f>, <f>DIFFICULTY</f>. Phr.: <i>to be in a
d.</i>, haerēre[**P1 "baerere" is not a word], Cic.; haerere in salebra,
Cic.


<b>dilettante</b>: *qui artibus elegantioribus
animi causa studet; elegans
artificiorum existimator, spectator.


<b>dilettantism</b>: ēlĕgantiae (?): v.
<f>REFINEMENT</f>.


<b>diligence</b>:

1. dīlĭgentia (<i>care
and attention</i>): <i>to use, study, d.</i>, d. ad-*
-----File: b0209m.png------------------------------------------------------
*hibere, colere, Cic.: <i>to relax d. in study</i>,
d. in perdiscendo remittere, Caes.

2.
industria: Cic.: Nep.: Suet.: v. <f>INDUSTRY</f>.
Join: diligentia industriaque,
Cic.

3. assĭduĭtas (<i>constant,
untiring attention</i>): <i>to attain an object
by d. and energy</i>, assiduitate et virtute
aliquid consequi, Cic.: v. <f>ASSIDUITY</f>,
<f>ATTENTION</f>.

4. sēdŭlĭtas (<i>zealous,
faithful devotion to an object</i>): Join:
operam et sedulitatem (alicujus laudare),
Cic.; sedulitas ac diligentia, Suet.

5.
gnāvĭtas <i>or</i> nāvĭtas: v. <f>ACTIVITY</f>.
Phr.: <i>to use all one's d.</i>, dare operam
ut (in negative sentence, ne) ..., Sall.:
Cic.; diligenter curare ut (ne), Cic.: v.
<f>TO DEVOTE (ONESELF)</f>.


<b>diligent</b>:

1. dīlĭgens, ntis (<i>careful,
carefully attentive to</i>: usu. with
<i>gen.</i>, also <i>prep.</i>): <i>a very d. student of
ancient literature</i>, vir literarum diligentissimus,
Gell.: <i>d. writing</i>, assidua
et diligens scriptura, Cic.

2. assĭduus
(<i>constantly, untiringly attentive</i>):
v. <f>ASSIDUOUS</f>, <f>CONSTANT</f>.

3. industrius
(<i>industrious</i>: q. v.): Join:
homo gnavus (<i>active</i>) et industrius,
experientissimus (<i>trying every means</i>)
et diligentissimus, Cic.

4. sēdŭlus
(<i>zealously devoted to</i>): <i>d. service</i>, ministerium,
opera s., Apul.: Cic.

5.
gnāvus (nāvus), impĭger: v. <f>ACTIVE</f>.

6. ācer, cris, cre (applicable to any
<i>vigorous</i> action or feeling): <i>so d. care
as this</i>, haec tam a. cura atque diligentia,
Cic.: v. <f>VIGOROUS</f>. See also
<f>ATTENTIVE</f>.


<b>diligently</b>:

1. dīlĭgenter: Cic.:
Caes.: <i>very d.</i>, perdiligenter, Cic.

2.
sēdŭlo: Liv.: Pl.

3. industriē:
Join: diligenter industrieque administrare,
Caes.: v. <f>INDUSTRIOUSLY</f>.

4.
ācrĭter: v. <f>VIGOROUSLY</f>.


<b>dill</b>: ănēthum (*graveolens, L.):
Plin.: Virg.


<b>diluent</b>:

I. Adj.: quod diluit,
dilutum facit: v. <f>TO DILUTE</f>.

II.
Subst.: *dīluens remedium, Krauss
in R. and A.


<b>dilute</b>:

1. dīluo, lui, lūtum, 3:
<i>to d. poison</i>, venenum d., Liv.: <i>to d.
wine</i>, vinum d., Mart.: Virg.

2.
misceo, tempĕro (<i>to combine in due proportion</i>):

3. restinguo,
nxi, nctum, 3 (poet. of <i>wine</i>): <i>to d.

Falerni pocula r. lympha, Hor.


<b>diluted</b>: dīlūtus: <i>d. Falernian</i>, d.

<b>dilution</b>:

I. <i>The act of diluting</i>:

II. <i>The
mixture</i>: dīlūtum: Plin.

<b>dim</b> (<i>adj.</i>):

1. hĕbĕs, ĕtis (both

2.

3. languĭdus: <i>d.

(1) hĕbeo, 2: <i>the planet Venus is d.</i>:
Veneris sidus hebet, Lucan.: Val. Fl.
(2) langueo, 2 (poet.): <i>the (moon) beam
is d. and cloudy</i>, nimbosum languet

hĕbesco, 3: <i>the heavenly bodies grow

Cic. (2) hĕbĕtor, 1: v. <f>TO DIM</f>. (3)
hĕbĕtesco, 3 (late and rare): Plin. (4)

(5) obscūror, 1: v. <f>TO DIM</f>. <i>To make
d.</i>, hĕbĕto, 1: v. foll. art.

<b>diminish</b>:

I. Trans.:

1.
mĭnuo, ui, ūtum, 3: <i>to d. expense</i>, sumptus
m., Cic.: <i>to d. the fear of soldiers</i>,
m. timorem militum, Hirt. Also comps.
(1.) immĭnuo, 3 (not perceptibly different
from minuo in this sense): Cic.
(2.) dēmĭnuo, 3 (<i>to take ever so little

but the MSS. often vary): <i>to d. by ever
so little the brief space of time</i>, aliquid

2. lĕvo, 1 (in certain connexions only;
viz., where <i>weight</i>, <i>value</i>, or <i>dignity</i> are
concerned): <i>authority is d.'d by inconsistency</i>,

Cic.: <i>to d. prices (of corn)</i>, annonam l.,

3. extĕnuo, 1 (<i>to reduce
to little</i>): <i>to d. any one's troubles

<f>TO REDUCE</f>.

4. dētrăho, xi, ctum, 3
(<i>to take</i> aught <i>from</i>: hence usu. foll.

sum total (a little)</i>, aliquid de summa

5. lēnio, 4 (as of <i>care, pain</i>): v.
<f>TO EASE</f>, <f>ASSUAGE</f>.

II. Intrans.:
mĭnuor, immĭnuor, extĕnuor, etc.: v.

<b>disgrace</b> (<i>v.</i>):

I. <i>To put out of
favour</i>: only used in <i>p. part.</i>: v. <f>DISGRACED</f>.

II. <i>To deprive of position or
rank</i>: ignominiâ nŏto, 1 (<i>of a soldier</i>):
ordinem ădĭmo (<i>of a centurion</i>); tribu
mŏveo (<i>of a citizen</i>); etc.: v. <f>TO DEGRADE</f>.

III. (Usual sense): <i>to bring
dishonour upon</i>:

1. dēdĕcŏro,

1: <i>to
d. oneself by a vicious life</i>, se flagitiis d.,
Sall.: Cic.

2. dĕhŏnesto,[**P2: ,|P3--fixed TIA confirms] 1: <i>to stain
and d. any one's good name</i>, alicujus
famam maculare atque d., Liv.: v. <f>TO
DISHONOUR</f>.

3. expr. by means of
turpĭtūdo, etc. (v. <f>DISGRACE</f>, 2): <i>this
order has been d.d</i>, concepta (inusta) est
huic ordini turpitudo, based on Cic.: <i>a
person is not d.d by such a sentence</i>,
tale judicium nullam habet turpitudinem,
based on Cic.: <i>how deeply are we
d.d</i>, quanta turpitudinis labe afficimur!
quanta ignominia atque infamia laboramus!
v. <f>DISGRACE</f>.

4. commăcŭlo, 1
(<i>to blot, stain</i>): <i>to d. oneself by (illegal)
canvassing</i>, se ambitu c., Cic.

5. dēformo,
1 (<i>to mar, spoil</i>): <i>to d. a victory
by a massacre</i>, victoriam clade d., Liv.:
Cic.

6. infāmo, 1 (v. <i>rare</i>): Prop.

7. dēgĕnĕro, 1 (<i>by degeneracy</i>): <i>to
d. one's kin</i>, propinquos d., Prop. (a rare
constr.).

8. trādūco, xi, ctum, 3 (to
expose to <i>disgrace</i>): <i>to d. wives and
children in the eyes of men</i>, conjuges,
liberos tr. per ora hominum, Liv.


<b>disgraced</b>:

I. <i>In disfavour</i>:
*de gratia (principis) dejectus; qui
(principis) frigore percussus est: v.
<f>DISFAVOUR</f>.

II. <i>Covered with disgrace</i>:

1. infāmis, e: <i>d. by vice</i>, flagitiis
(per flagitia, Tac.) inf.,[**P2: inf.,|P3--fixed TIA confirms] Cic.: v.
<f>INFAMOUS</f>.

2. probrōsus (<i>publicly
scandalous</i>): Tac.: v. <f>DISGRACEFUL</f>.
Phr.: <i>deeply d. by abominable crimes</i>,
nefariis sceleribus coopertus, Cic.: Liv.
See also <f>TO DISGRACE</f>.


<b>disgraceful</b>:

1. turpis, e (most
comprehensive word): <i>a d. flight or a
glorious death</i>, turpis fuga aut gloriosa
mors, Cic.: <i>a d. rejection</i>, turpis repulsa,
Hor.: <i>d. morals</i>, turpes mores, Pl.: <i>a
most d. person</i>, homo turpissimus [et
sordidissimus], Cic.: <i>somewhat d.</i>, subturpis,
Cic.

2. ignōmĭniōsus: v.
<f>IGNOMINIOUS</f>.

3. flāgĭtiōsus (<i>marked
by d. conduct</i>): <i>a most d. person</i> (of d.
life), homo flagitiosissimus, Cic.: <i>'tis
less d. for a king to be vanquished in
arms than in generosity</i>, regem armis
quam munificentia vinci minus flagitiosum,
Sall.

4. probrōsus (<i>full of
scandals</i>): <i>d. in (his) life</i>, vitâ pr., Tac.:
<i>d. effeminacy</i>, p. mollities, Plin.

5.
sordĭdus (<i>mean, low, degrading</i>): <i>d. defeat
(in canvass for office)</i>, repulsa s.,
Hor.: <i>a d. adultery</i>, adulterium s., Liv.:
Cic. (v. <i>supr.</i> 1).

6. dēformis, e
(<i>lacking beauty or propriety</i>): <i>a speech
d. to oneself</i>, oratio sibi d., Liv.: <i>d. gains</i>,
d. lucra, Suet.

7. ĭnhŏnestus: v.
<f>DISHONOURABLE</f>.

8. pŭdendus: v.
<f>SHAMEFUL</f>.

9. foedus (a very strong
word): <i>d. terms</i> (of peace), f. conditiones,
Hor.: <i>luxury whilst d. to every
age, is especially d. to old age</i>, luxuria
cum omni aetati turpis, tum senectuti
foedissima est, Cic. Phr.: <i>a d. act</i>,
flāgĭtium, Cic.: still stronger, flagitiosum
facinus, Sall.: <i>to live a d. life</i>, flagitiose
vivere, Cic.: <i>it is not d.</i>, non est flagitium
(foll. by <i>inf.</i>), Ter.: <i>to be d. to
any one</i>, alicui dedecori, opprobrio esse,
etc.: v. <f>DISGRACE</f>.

<b>disguise</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

II. <i>The parts of
a picture which represent more remote

opp. to <i>standing out</i> (eminere) from
the plane: see Quint. 2, 17, 21: in same
sense, abscedentia, ium, Vitr.

by seizing anything</i>, aliquid commisso
vindicare (tollere), Marc. Dig. 39, 4, 16,
§ 8: <i>to be seized on the same ground</i>, in
commissum cadere, ib. § 1. The <i>act.</i>
committere is simply <i>to forfeit</i>: q. v.
Sometimes vendo (in pass. sense veneo)
may be near enough: cf. Dig. l. c., "nec
vendendus est is servus qui in commissum
cecidit, sed," etc.


<b>distraint</b>: nearest single word prob.
vendĭtio: cf. Gai. Inst. 2, 154. Phr.:
<i>to levy a d.</i> (as done <i>by a publican for
non-payment of dues</i>), commisso vindicare
(v. preced. art.): <i>to order a d. to
be levied</i>, constituere ut liceat bona alicujus
vendere, Gai. (in R. and A.).

<b>do</b> (see also <f>DONE</f>):

I. <i>To effect</i>:

1. făcio, fēci, factum; <i>pass.</i> fīo,
fĭĕri,[**P2: ,|P3:yes, checked scan] 3 (the most usu. equiv. for the
Eng.): <i>I cannot do more than I have
done</i>, ego plus quam feci, f. non possum,
Cic.: <i>he begged me to write to you, which
I do</i>, orabat ut ad te scriberem; quod
facio,[**P2: ,|P3:yes, checked scan] Cic.:[** Cic.: @ tia] <i>what am I to do</i>, quid
faciam? Cic.: <i>what would you do with
such a fellow</i>, quid hoc homine faciatis?
Cic.: <i>to do any one a kindness</i>, beneficium
alicui f., Cic.; bene f. alicui, Cic.:
Ter.: <i>to do violence to any one</i>, vim
alicui f.,[**P2: f.,|P3:yes, checked scan] Liv.

2. effĭcio, 3 (stronger
than facio.[**P2: ,] <i>to succeed in doing, to effect</i>):
<i>to do what one has proposed</i>,[**P2: ,|P3:yes, checked scan] quod quis
proposuerit ef., Cic.: v. <f>TO EFFECT</f>.

3.
-----File: b0228l.png------------------------------------------------------
ăgo, ēgi, actum, 3 (the most gen. term
to denote <i>action of any kind</i>: often
used impers. in <i>pass.</i>): <i>to do nothing</i>,[**P2: ,|P3:yes, checked scan]
nihil a., Cic.: <i>what am I to do</i>, quid
agam? Ter.: <i>what is doing</i>, quid agitur?
Ter.: v. <f>TO GO ON</f>.

4. gĕro, gessi,
gestum, 3: v. <f>TO CARRY ON</f>, <f>TRANSACT</f>.
Phr.: <i>to do one's endeavour, do one's
best that ...</i>, id agere, dare operam ut
(ne), or absol., Ter.: Caes.: <i>to do one's
duty (zealously) to the state</i>, navare
operam reipublicae, Cic.: <i>to do any
one's commands sedulously</i> or <i>actively</i>,
mandata alicujus facessere, Virg.: <i>to
have enough to do</i>, sat agere, also satis
agere, or as one word satagere, Pl.:
Cic.: Quint.: <i>to do nothing</i>, nihil agere
et cessare, Cic.: <i>we have long enough
done nothing</i>, cessatum usque adhuc
est, Ter.: <i>to do good to</i>, prodesse, benefacere,
with <i>dat.</i> (v. <f>TO BENEFIT</f>, <f>SERVE</f>):
of medicines, facere: <i>the root does a
great deal of good in cases of colic</i>,
radix coeliacis praeclare facit, Plin.: <i>to
do harm to</i>, obesse, nocere with <i>dat.</i> (v.
<f>TO INJURE</f>): <i>up then and be doing</i>, quin
igitur expergiscimini! Sall.

II. To
do <i>with, have concern with</i>: Phr.: <i>to
have to do with the soil</i> (of farmers),
rationem habere cum terra, Cic.: <i>to
have to do with a person</i>, rem habere
cum aliquo, Ter.: <i>that I have nothing
to do with</i>, (id) nihil ad me attinet, Ter.:
so <i>as far as I have to do with it</i>, quod ad
me attinet, Cic.: Liv.: in short sentences
the verb is sometimes omitted,
<i>what has that to do with the matter</i>,
quid ad rem? nihil ad rem, etc.: <i>to
have as little as possible to do with any
one</i>, *quam minime familiariter uti aliquo:
<i>have thou nothing to do with an
inquisitive man</i>, percontatorem fugito,
Hor.: <i>I have nothing to do with him</i>,
mihi cum illo nihil est, Cic.: <i>what have
I to do with thee</i>, quid mihi et tibi est?
Vulg.

III. As auxiliary verb: not
expressed unless emphatic in Eng.,
when it may often be rendered by vero:
<i>I[** I] do really wish</i>, ego vero cupio,[**P2: ,|P3:yes, checked scan] Cic.:
when in Eng. the auxiliary stands alone,
in Lat. the verb is often expressed: <i>do
you believe? I do</i>, credisne? credo: v.
<f>YES</f>, <f>INDEED</f>. When <i>do</i> expresses urgent
entreaty, it may often be expr. by
amabo: <i>do assist me</i>, amabo, adjuta me!
Ter.: Cic.: or by quaeso, obsecro (v.
<f>PRAY</f>); and sometimes by quin (v. <f>JUST</f>,
<i>adv.</i>).

IV. Intrans.[** ? <g>], <i>to be getting
on</i>, in circumstances <i>or</i> health: Phr.:
<i>how do you do, dearest friend</i>, quid agis,
dulcissime,[**P2: ,|P3:yes, checked scan] rerum? Hor.: <i>they are doing
well</i>, bene est illis, Cic.: Hor.: simly is
used bene habere (Gr. εὖ ἔχειν), Pl.:
Cic.: <i>may you do well</i>, bene rem geras!
Hor.

V. <i>To succeed, answer well</i>:

1. făcio, 3 (of medicines): Plin.:
v. <i>supr.</i> (I., Phr. <i>fin.</i>).

2. respondeo,
2 (of <i>crops</i>): v. <f>TO ANSWER</f> (III.).

VI.
<i>To be enough, satisfactory</i>:

1. expr.
by sătis, sat: <i>it would have done well

doesn't do for poetry to be merely pretty</i>,
non satis est pulchra esse poemata, Hor.:
<i>Hold! that'll do</i>, Ohe jam satis, Hor.

2. in accepting an offer, expr. by
bĕnignē: <i>just take as many as you

Phr.: <i>come, that won't do</i>, *at id non

cănis, is, <i>c.</i> (mostly <i>f.</i> when used generically):
<i>to keep d.s</i>, canes alere, Ter.: <i>he

d.</i>, Plin.; but usu. employed in different

2. cătŭlus, <i>f.</i>

I. <i>Pertaining to
dogmas</i>: dogmătĭcus:
Auson.

II. <i>Prone to dogmatism</i>: in
this sense usu. <f>DOGMATICAL</f>. Phr.: <i>a
d. person</i>, *qui sententias suas ut magister
(auribus) inculcat; qui alienam
sententiam non patitur.


<b>dogmatically</b>: Phr.: <i>to talk d.</i>,
*arroganter et quasi quis magister artis
suae esset loqui; sententias suas praecipientis
modo inculcare; aliter sentientes
non pati: v. <f>DOGMATIZE</f>.


<b>dogmatism</b>: nearest word prob.
arrŏgantia. More fully, *arrogantiae
genus a scholis petitum, quod in sententiis
proferendis cernitur; arrogantia
quasi praecipientis.


<b>dogmatist</b>:

I. <i>One who deals
with dogmas</i>, dogmătistes, ae: Hier.

II. <i>A dogmatical person</i>: v. <f>DOGMATIZER</f>.


<b>dogmatize</b>:

I. <i>To lay down
dogmas</i>: dogmătīzo, 1 (= dogmata trado,
dogmatum auctor sum), Aug.

II. <i>To
speak in an arrogant, positive manner.</i>
Phr.: <i>I am afraid of seeming to d.</i>,
vereor ne quasi praecipientis cujusdam
et docentis esse videatur oratio, Cic. (in
R. and A.): <i>to fall into a d.ing strain</i>,
ad praecipiendi rationem delabi, Cic.


<b>dogmatizer</b>: *qui praecipiendi rationem
amat; qui omnia affirmat quasi
magister esset artis; homo arrogans in
disputationibus, sententiarum alienarum
impatiens.

A. Trans.:

I.
Lit.: <i>to let fall in drops</i>:

1. stillo,

2. instillo, 1 (<i>to d.</i> a fluid <i>upon</i>

-----File: b0236r.png------------------------------------------------------
*lantes odore arbores, Plin.: Tib.

I. <i>To fall

<b>either</b> (<i>conj.</i>):

1. aut ... aut
(<i>either ... or</i>; where the alternatives
are mutually exclusive: L. G. § 570)[** :?]
<i>e. true</i> or <i>false</i>, aut verum aut falsum,
Cic.: the first aut is not always expressed,
unless emphatic.

2. vel (ve)
... vel (where the alternatives are not

Cic.

3. sīve (seu) ... sīve: v.
<f>WHETHER</f>.

4. expr. <i>not ... either
... or</i>, by nĕque (nec) ... nĕque:
<i>death does not affect e. the living or the

ad mortuos, Cic.: the negative is often
doubled: <i>the rest I cannot e. write or

<b>elect</b> (<i>v.</i>):

I. <i>To select for some

<b>ever</b>:

1. expr. by <i>p.
part.</i> of excipio (in making

2. praeter (<i>prep[. --F1]</i> with <i>acc.</i>; also

<i>no one e. Lucullus</i>, nemo p. Lucullum,
Cic.: <i>to be condemned by all the votes e.

those condemned for capital crimes</i>, pr.

praeterquam: cf. Fam. 3, 7. <i>init.</i>:
"nullas iis praeterquam ad te et ad
Brutum dedi literas").

3. extra
(with <i>acc.</i>: much less freq. than prae-*
-----File: b0271m.png------------------------------------------------------
*ter): <i>e. the general and a few others,

reliqui ..., Cic. Fam. 7, 3, <i>ad

4. nĭsi
(only after a negative): <i>that, e. in the

<b>fate</b>:

I. In philosoph. sense, <i>the
necessary connexion of cause and effect</i>:

1. fātum: defined by Cic. thus: fatum

Cic. Fat. 17, 39: <i>if all things happen by
f., they happen in accordance with an
antecedent cause</i>, si omnia fato fiunt,

2. nĕcessĭtas, Cic.: v. <i>supr.</i>: more
fully, fatalis necessitas, Lact.: v. <f>NECESSITY</f>.

<b>fop</b>: no exact word: Cic. thus describes

<b>for</b> (<i>prep.</i>):

I. <i>In place of, in
behalf of</i>: pro (with <i>abl.</i>): <i>they use
oblong pieces of iron f. money</i>, utuntur
ferreis taleis pro nummo, Caes. B. G.
5, 12[** :] <i>I will go f. you, if you don't
like to do so</i>, ego pro te ibo si tibi non
libet, Pl.:[**P2: dot missing] <i>he was left f. dead</i>, pro occiso
relictus est, Cic. Sext. 38, 81: <i>to
fight f. the laws, f. freedom, f. country</i>,
dimicare pro legibus, pro libertate,
-----File: b0313m.png------------------------------------------------------
pro patria, Cic.: <i>to pay f. freight</i>, pro
vectura solvere, Cic. Att. 1, 3: <i>he confesses
that he is under great obligation
to Caesar f. his kindness</i>, confitetur sese
pro Caesaris beneficiis plurimum debere,
Caes. B. G. 5, 27. See also <f>INSTEAD OF</f>.

II. <i>In proportion to, consideration
of</i>:

1. pro: <i>f. their population, they
deemed their territories too limited</i>, pro
multitudine hominum angustos se fines
habere arbitrabantur, Caes. B. G. 1, 2:
<i>a battle very sanguinary for the number
of combatants</i>, proelium atrocius quam
pro numero pugnantium, Liv. 21, 29,
<i>init.</i>

2. expr. by ut: <i>he had considerable
acquaintance with literature
f. a Roman</i>, multae [in eo erant], ut
in homine Romano literae, Cic. Sen. 4,
12: <i>an important and flourishing state,
f. a German one</i>, civitas ampla atque
florens, ut est captus Germanorum, Caes.
B. G. 4, 3. (But Tac. has ut inter,
with a totally different meaning, Agr.
11, <i>init.</i>)

III. <i>Because of</i>:

1. (after
negative expressions) prae (with <i>abl.</i>):
<i>I know not where I am f. joy</i>, prae
gaudio nescio ubi sim, Ter. Heaut. 2, 3,
67: <i>you will not see the sun f. the multitude
of missiles</i>, solem prae jaculorum
multitudine non videbitis, Cic. Tusc. 1,
42, 101.

2. propter (with <i>acc.</i>): <i>f.
that very cause</i>, propter eam ipsam
causam, Cic.: v. <f>ACCOUNT OF (ON)</f>.

3.
ob (with <i>acc.</i>): <i>f. this reason</i>, ob eam
causam, Cic.: <i>to take money f. giving a
verdict</i>, ob rem judicandam pecuniam
accipere, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 32, <i>init.</i>: <i>to encounter
death f. the good of the state</i>,
mortem ob rempublicam obire, Tac.
Ann. 2, 83.

4. de (with <i>abl.</i>: esp.
with causa): <i>to do any thing f. an important
reason</i>, aliquid gravi de causa
facere, Cic. Att. 7, 7, 3: <i>f. these reasons</i>,
his de causis, Caes.: <i>to weep f. the death
of a son</i>, de filii morte flere, Cic. Verr.
2.[**P2: ,] 2, 30, 76.

IV. <i>To the advantage
of</i>: expr. by <i>dat.</i> (L. G. § 288): <i>he
(Pisistratus) conquered Megara not f.
his country, but f. himself</i>, sibi non
patriae Megarenses vicit, Just.: <i>to fear
f. any one</i>, timere alicui, Cic.

V.
<i>With a view to; with a certain result</i>:

1. in (with <i>acc.</i>): <i>to live f. the day
(only)</i>, in diem vivere, Cic. Tusc. 5, 11,
33: <i>she had come f. the funeral</i> (i. e., <i>to
attend it</i>), venerat in funus, Cic. Att.
15, 1, <i>med.</i>: <i>each wished to be the one
whom Fortune might select f. the contest</i>,
se quisque eum optabat quem Fortuna
in id certamen legeret, Liv. 21,
42: <i>to change f. the worse</i>, in deterius
mutare, Tac. Ann. 14, 43.

2. ad
(with <i>acc.</i>): <i>ships ready f. sailing</i>,
naves paratae ad navigandum, Caes.: <i>a
man useful f. nothing</i>, homo ad nullam
rem utilis, Cic.: <i>money is voted f. the
games</i>, pecuniae ad ludos decernuntur,
Cic.: <i>man was made f. intelligence and
action</i>, homo ad intelligendum et ad
agendum natus est, Cic. Fin. 2, 13, 40:
<i>the chamaeleon plant is good f. (curing)
difficulty of urine</i>, facit ad difficultatem
urinae chamaeleon, Plin. (but here the
<i>dat.</i> might have been used: cf. Plin. 22,
18, 21, etc.): <i>he had Licinus f. his
amanuensis</i>,[**P2: ,] Licinum servum sibi habuit
ad manum, Cic.

3. expr. by <i>dat.</i>
(of Purpose <i>or</i> Result, L. G. § 297): <i>to
serve f. a lesson to the rest</i>, ut sint reliquis
documento, Caes.: <i>f. whose advantage</i>,
cui bono? Cic. R. Am. 30, 84.

VI. Of time, <i>during</i> a certain period:

1. expr. by <i>acc.</i> (L. G. § 249):
<i>the matrons mourned him f. a year</i>,
matronae annum eum luxerunt, Liv.:
Cic. (N.B.--This is the usual constr.
when the subs. has an attributive, unless
<i>protraction</i> of time is to be specially
insisted on.)

2. per (insisting
on <i>protraction of time</i>): <i>f. three years,
not a case was adjudged save at his
pleasure</i>, nulla res per triennium nisi
ad nutum istius judicata est, Cic.: <i>f. ten
(whole) days, games were celebrated</i>, ludi
decem per dies facti sunt, Cic. Cat. 3, 8,
20: v. <f>THROUGHOUT</f>.

3. inter (with
<i>acc.</i>: <i>in the course of, from time to
time</i>): <i>all the iniquities which have</i>
-----File: b0313r.png------------------------------------------------------
<i>been perpetrated f. a period of ten
years</i>, omnia quae inter decem annos
nefarie facta sunt, Cic. Verr. Act. 1, 13,
37: Pl. Phr.: <i>f. a little while</i>, paullisper,
Cic.: <i>f. a long while</i>, diu (v.
<f>LONG</f>, <i>adv.</i>): <i>f. the present</i>, in praesens
tempus, Cic.; or simply in praesens,
Hor.: Tac. (v. <f>PRESENT</f>): <i>f. the future</i>,
in posterum, in reliquum (v. <f>FUTURE</f>).

VII. Also of time; to denote <i>the
appointment of a definite time</i>: in (with
<i>acc.</i>): <i>you had arranged the massacre
f. the 28th of October</i>, in a. d. V. Kal.
Novembres caedem te contulisse, Cic.
Cat. 1, 3, 7: <i>he invited the man to
dinner f. the following day</i>, ad coenam
hominem invitavit in posterum diem,
Cic. Also when a <i>period of time</i> is
agreed upon: <i>they obtained a truce f.
thirty years</i>, indutias in triginta annos
impetraverunt, Liv. 9, 37, <i>extr.</i>: <i>to prolong
power f. a year</i>, in annum imperium
prorogare, Liv.

VIII. Of price
<i>or</i> exchange:

1. expr. by <i>abl.</i>:
(L. G. § 316): <i>to buy a pint of water f.
a mina</i>, aquae sextarium minâ emere,
Cic.:[**P2: dot missing] Liv.: <i>he changes round f. square</i>
(or conversely), mutat quadrata rotundis,[**P2: ,]
Hor. Ep. 1, 1, 100: cf. Od. 1, 17, 2. (N.B.--With
mutare, in sense of <i>to exchange</i>, the
price given is regularly put in <i>abl.</i>; but
Hor. puts either of the objects of exchange[** - missing]
in the <i>abl.</i> without difference of
meaning.)

2. (when the sum paid is
indefinite) expr. by such genitives as
tanti, quanti, tantidem, pluris, minoris;
or the ablatives magno [not multo],
permagno, plurimo, nihilo: v. L. G.
§ 316, <i>Obs.</i> 2. <i>F. nothing</i>.[**P2: ,] grātīs, gratuito,
Cic. (v. <f>GRATUITOUSLY</f>)[** .] Miscell.
phr.: <i>to be f.</i>, i. e., <i>in favour of</i>
a party, stŭdeo, făveo (both with <i>dat.</i>):
v. <f>TO FAVOUR</f>: <i>see if this does not altogether
make f. me</i>, vide ni hoc sit totum
a me, Cic. (v. Dr. Smith's Lat. Dict. s. v.
ab, C., IV.) <i>I f. my part think</i>, equidem
censeo, Cic. (v. <f>INDEED</f>): <i>f. all you
may enumerate so many</i>, quamvis multos
enumeres licet, Cic. (v. <f>ALTHOUGH</f>): <i>f.
all I know</i>, quod sciam, Cic. N.B.--<i>For</i>
in English often represents the <i>acc.</i> and
<i>inf.</i> in Latin: <i>it is by no means seemly
f. an orator to get angry</i>,[**P2: ,] oratorem irasci
minime decet, Cic. (v. L. G. § 510): it
also sometimes denotes the relation of
an objective gen. to its governing subs.:
<i>resentment f. an injury</i>, dolor injuriae,
Liv.: <i>grief f. the loss of a wife</i>, dolor
conjugis amissae, Ov. (v. L. G. § 268):
also sometimes the prep. belongs to a
verb immediately preceding it; as <i>to
hope for, to wait for</i>; where see <f>TO
HOPE</f>, <f>WAIT</f>, etc.


<b>for</b> (<i>conj.</i>):

1. nam (introducing a
direct reason; and standing regularly
first in its clause): <i>avoid a questioner</i>:
<i>f. the same is a gossip</i>, percontatorem
fugito; nam garrulus idem est, Hor.:
Caes.: Cic. It is often used elliptically:
<i>what kind of insanity do you think I
have? f. to myself I seem in my senses</i>,
quam me stultitiam insanire putas?
ego <i>nam</i> videor sanus esse, Hor. S. 2,
3, 302 (the position of nam is poet.):
v. L. G. § 581, <i>Obs.</i>

2. namque
(strengthened form of nam): <i>Caesar
came to the rescue in the very nick of
time: f. ...</i>, tempore opportunissimo
Caesar auxilium tulit; namque ...,
Caes. B. G. 4, 34: later authors often put
namque after another word, as, <i>f. they
painted pictures of plants</i>, pinxere namque
effigies herbarum, Plin. 25, 2, 4:
Liv. 3, 44, <i>med.</i>, ibi namque ... ludi
erant.

3. ĕnim (less emphatic than
nam from which it is derived,[**P2: ,] and <i>never
first</i> in a sentence: v. L. G. § 581): <i>he
shouted that they should be of good
cheer, f. he saw the traces of men</i>, exclamavit
ut bono essent animo; videre
enim se hominum vestigia, Cic. Rep. 1,
17, <i>fin.</i>: <i>and yet I did not think of
you; f. I knew,[**P2: ,] etc.</i>, neque tamen de te
cogitavi; sciebam enim, etc.: Cic.

4.
ĕtĕnim (καὶ γὰρ, <i>and in fact</i>; copulative
as well as illative: at the beginning
of a sentence): <i>f. no one can speak
well, saving he have a good understand-*</i>
-----File: b0314l.png------------------------------------------------------
<i>*ing</i>,[**P2: ,] etenim dicere bene nemo potest,
nisi qui prudenter intelligit, Cic. Brut.
6, 23: comp. id. Fin. 1, 9, 30; and v. <f>IN
FACT</f>.

5. quippĕ (at the beginning
of a sentence: in this connection about
equiv. to etenim): <i>not that you can
give me any help; f. the matter is in
hand, and you are at the other end of

<b>force</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

I. <i>Strength, energy</i>:

1. vis, vim, vi; <i>pl.</i> vīres, <i>f.</i> (in most

2.

4. impĕtus, ūs:

II. Military:

1.

<b>----, in</b>:

1. in mănĭbus (of what

<b>----, on the one</b>, <b>the other</b>:

1.
expr. by hic ... ille or the <i>pron. advv.</i>
hic, illic: also by alter ... alter (when
a contrast is intended): cf. Vell. 2, 49,
<i>alterius</i> ducis causa melior videbatur,
<i>alterius</i> erat firmior: <i>hic</i> omnia speciosa,
<i>illic</i> valentia: see also L. G. § 366. The
latter member may be strengthened by
contra: <i>accordingly as on the one h.
these are wretched, so on the other, these
are happy</i>, ergo ut hi miseri, sic illi
<i>contra</i> beati, Cic. Tusc. 5, 6, 16.

2.
et ... et (where <i>enumeration</i> rather
than contrast is intended: v. L. G. § 562):
when one of the clauses is negative, et
may be followed or preceded by neque
(nec), et non (L. G. § 564): <i>(a situation)
which on the one h. the sun does
not scorch, and on the other the dew can
reach</i>, quem et non coquit sol, et tangit
ros, Varr. R. R. 3, 14: Cic.

3. quĭdem
... at sed, autem, etc.: <i>the rest
indeed [on the one h.] have perished
shamefully; Cato, on the other h., nobly</i>,
ceteri quidem foede perierunt, at Cato
praeclare Cic. Fam. 9, 18: cf. id. Sen. 11,
36, et corpora <i>quidem</i> exercitatione et
defatigatione ingravescunt; animi autem
se exercendo levantur: cf. Tursellin.
s. v. <i>quidem</i>.

4. sometimes no word
of contrast is expr. in the former clause
(as often in Eng.): as, <i>it is [on the one
hand] perhaps wrong to say what you
do not think, on the other h., to say no-*</i>
-----File: b0360m.png------------------------------------------------------
<i>*thing is clearly right</i>, dicere fortasse
quae sentias non licet, tacere plane licet,
Cic. Fam. 4, 9, <i>med.</i>: <i>on the one h. rather
more fettered in rhythm, on the
other, more free in dealing with language</i>,
numeris adstrictior paulo, verborum
<i>autem</i> licentia liberior, Cic. de Or.
1, 16, 70.

<b>himself</b>:

1. in agr. with subject:
ipse, īus: <i>he h. said so</i>, ipse dixit (= Gr.
αὐτὸς ἔφα), Quint. 11, 1, 27: Cic.: Sall.
Sometimes strengthened by -met, Pl.
Amph. prol. 102: Cic.: the superl. ipsissimus
also occurs: Pl. Trin. 4, 2, 146.

2. in objective relations, i. e. when
used reflexively: sui, sĭbi, sē <i>or</i> sēsē
-----File: b0373r.png------------------------------------------------------
(referring back to the subject of the
sentence): <i>he devoted h. altogether to
politics</i>, totum se dedidit reipublicae,
Nep. Them. 1: <i>they surrendered themselves
to Caesar</i>, se Caesari dediderunt,
Caes.: Cic. The forms sibi, se, are
often strengthened by the suffix -met;
and the prep. cum is always used enclitically
when joined with se, as secum.

3. when the use of the words <i>himself</i>,
<i>themselves</i>, indicates some opposition
or antithesis: ipse and sui combined:
the ipse agreeing with the subject or
object, according as stress is laid on the
one or the other, cf. Zumpt § 696; St.
L. G. § 617: (i). subjects contrasted:
<i>without trying to move the pity of the
enemy, he laid violent hands on himself</i>,
ne tentata quidem hostis misericordia
se <i>ipse</i> interfecit (i. e. <i>it was not the
enemy who slew him, but himself</i>), Vell.
2, 71, <i>fin.</i>: cf. Tac. H. 1, 46, Praetorii
praefectos sibi <i>ipsi</i> legere (i. e. <i>they
made the appointments themselves, others
did not make them</i>): (ii). objects contrasted:
<i>he cannot control an army who
does not control himself</i>, non potest <i>exercitum</i>
is continere qui <i>se ipsum</i> non
continet, Cic. Man. 13, 38: <i>he slew his
brother, and afterwards himself</i>, fratrem
suum dein seipsum (<i>or</i> se ipsum)
interfecit, Tac. (Key). N.B.--The
former constr. is however more frequent,
and is found even in cases where
there is an antithesis of objects: cf. Cic.
Q. Fr. 1, 1, 2, quid est negotii continere
eos quibus praesis, si te <i>ipse</i> (cf. <i>supr.</i> i.)
contineas? cf. Zumpt, l. c. Phr.: <i>to do
right of h. (freely)</i>, sua sponte recte facere,
Ter. Ad. 1, 1, 50: <i>almost beside h.</i>,
vix compos animi, ib. 3, 2, 12 (v. <f>ONESELF</f>):
<i>one who lives by h.</i>, solitarius
homo, Cic. Off. 2, 11, 39; <i>who keeps by
h. (in political strife)</i>, qui solitarius separatusque
secedit, Gell. 2, 12, <i>init.</i>

<b>his</b> (<i>adj. pron.</i>):

1. expr. by gen.
of is (v. L. G. §§ 370, <i>sqq.</i>): <i>h. father
Neocles was of noble birth</i>, pater ejus
Neocles generosus fuit, Nep. Them. 1:
cf. id. Cim. 1: <i>Numerius h. brother is
dead</i>, Numerius frater ejus, mortuus
est, Cic. Clu. 7, 21. (N.B.--Ejus may
always be so used when <i>his</i> = <i>of the person
aforesaid</i>: cf. L. G. l. c.)

2. expr.
by gen. of hic (when the pron. is used
to denote the principal subject of discourse):
comp. Nep. Them. <i>init.</i>, Themistocles,
Neoclis filius, Atheniensis.[** ,]
<i>Hujus</i> vitia, etc.: also, id. Paus. init., <i>Hujus</i>
illustrissimum proelium, etc. (= <i>of
the subject of this memoir</i>): v. <f>THIS</f>.
(N.B.--Hence hujus is more emphatic
than ejus, giving more prominence to
the person referred to.)

3. expr. by
gen. of ipse (when the <i>his</i> is emphatic,
not referring to the subject): <i>why
should they despair of their own courage
or h. vigilance</i>, cur de sua virtute aut
de ipsius diligentia desperarent? Caes.
B. G. 1, 40: cf. ib. 1, 21, certior factus
hostes consedisse millia passuum ab ipsius
(= <i>his own</i>) castris octo.[** .]

4.
expr. by gen. of qui (when <i>his</i> is preced.
by a conj.; Latin authors freq. using
the rel. pron. as a connective): <i>and he
relieved his exile by sending him money</i>,
cujus fugam pecunia sublevavit, Nep.
Att. 2: cf. ib. 5, <i>cujus</i> sic asperitatem
veritus est: ib. 12, <i>cujus</i> gratia cum
posset (= <i>and though he might ... his</i>).

5. suus (referring to the subject of
the sentence, or sometimes to another
subst. immediately preceding with which
it is closely connected: cf. L. G. § 361):
<i>him his fellow-citizens drove into exile</i>,
hunc sui cives e civitate ejecerunt, Cic.
Sext. 68, 143. Suus is very often more
or less emphatic (= his <i>own</i>), esp. when
used as in preced. ex. with ref. to a
subst. which is not the subject: sometimes
strengthened by -pte, euphony
permitting: Crassum <i>suapte</i> interfectum
manu, Cic. de Or. 3, 3, 10. See
also <f>OWN</f>.

6. whenever the <i>his</i> is
unemphatic, it is usu. not expr. in Lat.:
or if expr. at all, by ejus, suus (referring
to the subject), as quasi-enclitics <i>after</i>
the substt. to which they belong (cf.
L. G. § 673): <i>his father died early</i>, pater
mature decessit, Nep. Att. 2 (where
ejus might have been used): <i>he ordered
his son-in-law Agrippa to be sent for</i>,
Agrippam generum ad se accersi jussit,
ib. 21 (where suum might have been
added): comp. also foll. exx.: Ciceroni
in omnibus <i>ejus</i> periculis singularem
fidem praebuit, ib. 4: quae amicis <i>suis</i>
opus fuerunt, ib. 7: in funere matris
<i>suae</i>, ib. 17: in which cases the pronouns
might have been dispensed with
as above.

<b>how</b>:

I. As adv. of manner, <i>in
what way</i>:

1. quōmŏdŏ <i>or</i> quo mŏdo
(in direct <i>or</i> indirect questions; also in
exclamations): <i>how stands Maecenas
with you</i>, Maecenas q. tecum? Hor. S. 1,
9, 43: Cic. Verr. 3, 10, 25: <i>how these
matters stand, I don't venture to tell</i>,
haec negotia q. se habeant narrare non
audeo, Cic. Fam. 2, 5. Less freq. in exclam.:
<i>h. they are trumping themselves
up to Caesar</i>, q. se venditant Caesari! Cic.
Att. 8, 16[** .] Similar to quomodo is quo
pacto, but more precise and emphatic:
<i>they settle what is to be done, and how</i>,
quid quoque pacto agi placeat constituunt,
Caes. B. G. 7, 83: esp. in phr.
nescio quo pacto, <i>somehow or other</i>: v.
<f>SOMEHOW</f>.

2. quemadmŏdum <i>or</i> quem
ad modum (like preced., but perh. rather
more definite in its reference to <i>manner</i>):
<i>if not, h. [in what way] did you get the
money from him</i>, si non, q. [pecuniam]
ab eo exegisti? Cic. R. Com. 18, 55:
-----File: b0382m.png------------------------------------------------------
Pl.: Plin. jun. (freq.): <i>I know the whole
affair, how it stands</i>, ego omnem rem
scio, q. est, Pl.: Cic. (N.B.--Not used
in exclamations.)

3. quî (strictly
<i>abl.</i> of quis? in direct questions only):
<i>how comes it</i>, quî fit? Hor. S. 1, 1, 1:
<i>how can we think of God as other than
eternal</i>, Deum nisi sempiternum intelligere
quî possumus? Cic. N. D. 1, 10,
25: Caes.

4. ŭt (chiefly after verbs
of <i>hearing, telling, etc.</i>, foll. by <i>subj.</i>:
less freq. in direct questions: also in
exclamations): <i>I believe you have heard
how they pressed round me</i>, credo te
audivisse ut me circumsteterint, Cic. Att.
1, 16, 2: <i>h. does he do</i>, ut valet? Hor.
Ep. 1, 3, 12[** :] Pl.: <i>how they are transported
with joy</i>, ut illi efferuntur laetitia!
Cic. Fin. 5, 22, 61[** :] <i>how I miss
your love and sympathy</i>, ut ego tuum
amorem et dolorem desidero! Cic. Att.
3, 11.

5. quid (interrogative = <i>how
so? how say you?</i> usu. as preliminary
to another question): <i>how now? do you
think I entrusted this to you?</i> quid? tu
me hoc tibi mandasse existimas? Cic.
Fam. 2, 8: also foll. by si = <i>how if ...</i>:
<i>how if I were to alter this</i>, quid si hoc
muto? Caec. in Cic. Fam. 6, 7, <i>med.</i>

II. <i>To what degree</i>:

1. quam
(chiefly in exclamations): <i>how much in
how few words</i>, quam multa quam
paucis! Cic. Fam. 11, 24: <i>see, how long
I stand here and knock</i>, vide, quam
dudum hic adsto et pulto! Pl. St. 2, 2,
39. (N.B.--<i>How much? how many?
how little?</i> must be expr. by quantus,
quot, quantulus: <i>how many are there
of you</i>, quot estis? <i>how much money</i>,
quantum pecuniae? but <i>how many</i> as
an exclam. can only be expr. by quam
multi: v. <i>supr.</i>)

2. quantŏpĕrĕ <i>or</i>
quanto ŏpĕre (<i>how greatly</i>): <i>it is indescribable
how greatly they rejoice</i>, dici
non potest quantopere (<i>al.</i> quanto opere)
gaudeant, Cic. Att. 14, 6: <i>he points out
how greatly it concerns the commonwealth</i>,
docet quanto opere reipublicae
intersit, Caes. B. G. 2, 5. Phr.: <i>how
many times</i>, quoties: <i>how many times
soever</i>, quotiescunque, Cic.: <i>how few there
are found who ...</i>, quotusquisque invenitur
qui ..., Cic. Tusc. 2, 4, 11: <i>how
much more</i>, quanto magis! Cic. Ac. 1, 3,
10: <i>how much less</i>, nedum [non dicam]:
cf. Cic. Clu. 35, 95, optimis temporibus,
nec P. Popillius, nec Q. Metellus ...,
<i>nedum</i> his temporibus ... salvi esse
possimus ("<i>how much less can we be
safe?</i>"): Ter. Heaut. 3, 1, 45 (quanto
minus in this sense appears to be without
authority: quanto magis ... non is
more agreeable to analogy).


<b>howbeit</b> (obsol.): tămen: v. <f>NEVERTHELESS</f>.


<b>however</b>:

I. <i>In whatever way</i>:

1. utcunque: <i>h. he desires the mind
of his hearer to be affected</i>, utc. animum
audientis moveri volet, Cic. Or. 17, 55:
<i>h. that be</i>, utc. erit, Liv. pref. <i>init.</i>

2.

*quae ad falsorum deorum cultum
pertinent; idolorum ritus, caeremonia.


<b>idolatry</b>: īdōlŏlātrīa: Tert.: usu.
better expr. by circuml., *simulacrorum
cultus ac veneratio: <i>to be devoted to i.</i>,
idolis servire, Vulg.: v. <f>IDOLATER</f>.


<b>idolize</b>: i. e. <i>to be passionately fond
of</i>: dēpĕreo, 4, <i>irr.</i> (lit. <i>to be dying for</i>:
with <i>acc.</i>): Ter. Heaut. 3, 2, 14: Join:
deamare, deperire, Pl. Epid. 2, 2, 37.
Comp. <f>IDOL</f> (II.)[** .]


<b>idyl</b>: īdyllium <i>or</i> ēdyllium (Gr. ειδύλλιον):
Auson.


<b>if</b>:

1. sī: (i.) with <i>indic.</i> (mere
assumption: L. G. § 424, 1): <i>if you
wish, I will produce witnesses</i>, si vis,
testes dabo, Cic.: <i>if we follow nature as
our guide, we shall never go wrong</i>, naturam
si sequemur ducem, nunquam
aberrabimus, Cic. (ii.) with <i>subj.</i> (implying
probability or possibility: L. G.
§ 424, 2, <i>sqq.</i>): <i>if I wished, I could not
possibly go away</i>, si velim, abire hinc
nullo facto possim, Pl.: <i>if it had happened
otherwise</i>, si aliter accidisset, Cic.
(N.B.--Si is often used elliptically with
the subj. to express a wish: <i>Oh! if Jupiter
would but restore my past years</i>,
O mihi praeteritos referat si Jupiter annos!
Virg. Aen. 8, 560: Hor.: where,
gaudeam, or some such verb, may be
supplied: comp. Gr. εί γάρ.) (iii.) with
the verb understood (esp. in a negative
alternative, si minus): <i>lead forth with
you all your partisans; if not all, as
many as may be</i>, educ tecum omnes
tuos; si minus, quam plurimos, Cic. Cat.
1, 5, 10 (in which connexion, oft. <i>sin</i>
minus): <i>either nobody, or if any one he
...</i>, aut nemo, aut si quisquam, ille
..., Cic. Am. 2, 9.

2. to introduce
a contrary alternative, sin (= si ne: <i>if
not, if on the contrary</i>): <i>if he had disapproved,
why had he allowed the law
to be passed? if, on the contrary, he had
approved, why ...?</i> si improbasset,
cur ferri passus est? sin probasset, cur
...? Caes. B. C. 1, 32: Cic.: <i>if otherwise</i>,
sin aliter (the verb being understood),
Ter. Ph. 1, 2, 66; sin secus, Pl.:
<i>if not</i>, sin minus (with or without a
verb expr.), Cic. Inv. 2, 29, 88: Att. 9,
15 (the elliptical constr. is better fitted
for colloquial lang.): for which, in the
epist. style occurs also, sin (alone): cf.
Cic. Att. 16, 13, <i>med.</i>, si pares inter se,
quiescendum; sin, latius manabit. Sin
is often strengthened by autem, vero:
Cic.: Col. (N.B.--It is not indispensable
that sin should be preceded by si; but
the preceding member of the sentence
must in some way present an alternative:
cf. Caes. B. C. 1, 32, orat ac postulat,
remp. suscipiant [first alternative]
... sin timore defugiant, <i>if however
they are afraid to do that ...</i>).

3.
sometimes expr. by particip. clause: <i>I
praise her (Fortune) if she remains; if
(on the contrary) she shakes her swift
wings ...</i>, laudo manentem; si celeres
quatit pennas ..., Hor. Od. 3,
29, 55: <i>if admitted to view, could ye refrain
from laughter?</i> spectatum ad-*
-----File: b0388l.png------------------------------------------------------
*missi, risum teneatis? Hor. A. P. 4:
simly. an adject. may be used hypothetically:
<i>if fortune be adverse, he hopes;
if propitious, he fears a change of lot</i>,
sperat infestis, metuit secundis alteram
sortem, Hor. Od. 2, 10, 12.

4. sīve,
seu (<i>whether ... or if</i>): (i.) si ...
sīve (seu): <i>if trunks of trees, or if vessels
were floated down by the barbarians</i>,
si arborum trunci, sive naves essent a
barbaris missae, Caes. B. G. 4, 17, <i>extr.</i>:
Pl.: v. <f>OR</f>. (ii.) sive (seu) without a
preceding si (rare): <i>I demand, or if it
be right (to say so), I entreat you ...</i>,
postulo, sive aequum est, te oro ...,
Ter. Andr. 1, 2, 19: with seu, Virg.
Aen. 11, 327. (iii.) sīve (seu) ...
sīve (seu): cf. Hor. Od. 3, 4, <i>init.</i>, <i>seu
(or if)</i> voce nunc mavis acuta, seu fidibus,
etc.: Cic. (who uses the form sive):
Quint.: v. <f>WHETHER</f>.


<b>if, and</b>: quod si or quodsi, in a negative
sentence, quod nisi, quod ni (denoting
that the hypothesis introduced
depends in some way on what precedes,[** ,?]
may sometimes expr. <i>but if, if indeed</i>;
being chiefly used where a greater emphasis
is to be used): cf. Cic. Mur. 2, 4,
<i>quodsi</i> portu solventibus ii ..., quo
tandem me animo, etc.: ib. 3, 6, <i>quodsi</i>
tum, quum respublica desiderabat, vici
naturam et vehemens fui ... nunc
quanto tandem studio debeo ...:
Nep. Hann. 1, <i>quod nisi</i> domi civium
suorum debilitatus fuisset (<i>if indeed he
had not been weakened</i>), Romanos videtur
superare posse.


<b>---- but</b>: sīn, sīn autem: v. <f>IF</f> (2).


<b>----, even</b>: ĕtiamsi.[**P1: colon not period?|P3 yes] v. <f>ALTHOUGH</f>.


<b>---- indeed</b>:

1. sī quidem <i>or</i> sīquĭdem
(esp. in making a concession,
and parenthetically): <i>O fortunate commonwealth!
if indeed (if really.</i> Gr.
εἴγε) <i>it have ejected this refuse</i>, O fortunatam
remp., si quidem hanc sentinam
ejecerit! Cic. Cat. 2, 4, 7: but
siquidem oftener = <i>seeing that</i>, q. v.

2. quodsi (to introduce a new hypothesis):
v. <f>IF, AND</f>.


<b>---- only</b>: dummŏdo: <i>you will relieve
me of great fear if only there be a wall
between me and you</i>, magno me metu
liberabis, d. inter me atque te murus
intersit, Cic. Cat. 1, 5, 10: v. <f>PROVIDED</f>.

<b>ignorance</b>:

1. ignōrātio (usu.
with ref. to <i>definite things not known</i>,
objectively; whereas ignorantia denotes
<i>a state of the mind</i>, subjectively): <i>i. of
causes</i>, ign. causarum, Cic. When ignorance
<i>in gen. sense</i> is meant, rerum may
be added (cf. L. G. § 595): <i>to be in a
state of extreme i.</i> [in summo errore
atque] ign. maximarum rerum versari,
Cic. N. D. 1, 1, <i>extr.</i>: Curt.

2. ignōrantia
(Cic. prefers ignoratio): <i>i. of literature</i>,
ign. literarum, Cic. Fl. 20, 46: <i>i.
of the ground</i>, ign. loci, Caes. B. C. 3,
68: Ov. (N.B.--Ignorantia is said to
mean <i>culpable ignorance</i>; ignoratio, <i>ignorance
of what one has had no means
of knowing</i>: Habicht, § 522. But?)

3. inscientia (<i>partial ignorance,
imperfect knowledge</i>: cf. Cic. de Or. 1,
46, 203, neque solum <i>inscientiam</i> meam,
sed ne rerum quidem magnitudinem
perspicit): <i>the deity cannot even have
the excuse of i.</i>, Deo ne excusatio quidem
est inscientiae, Cic. N. D. 3, 37,
<i>extr.</i> Join: error atque inscientia,
Cic. Inv. 1, 2, <i>init.</i>

4. inscītia (<i>lack
of judgment</i> or <i>practical knowledge</i>): <i>i.
of business</i>, negotii gerendi ins., Cic.
Prov. Cons. 5, 11: cf. Ter. Phr. 1, 2, 27.
Sometimes appy. = inscientia, cf. Cic.
de Or. 1, 22, 99, earum rerum quae
quasi in arte traduntur <i>inscitia</i>. Phr.:
<i>to keep any one in i.</i>, celare aliquid aliquem
(v. <f>TO CONCEAL</f>; and L. G. § 243):
<i>to be in i.</i>, nescire (v. <f>IGNORANT, TO BE</f>).


<b>ignorant</b>:

I. <i>Not knowing</i> or
<i>acquainted with</i>:

1. ignārus (most
gen. term: usu. with <i>gen.</i>, less freq. with
rel. clause, or <i>acc.</i> and <i>inf.</i>): <i>i. of physical
science</i>, physicorum ign., Cic.: <i>i.
of the worth of virtue</i>, ign. quid virtus
valeret, Cic. Sext. 28, 60. <i>I am not i.
that many will say</i>, non ign. sumus
multos dicturos ..., Cic. Tusc. 2, 1,
3.

2. inscius (used with ref. to different
degrees of ignorance: constr. like
preced.): <i>Socrates pretends to be i. of
everything</i>, S. se omnium rerum ins.
fingit [et rudem], Cic. Br. 85, 292: <i>i. of
what was going on</i>, ins. quid gereretur,
Caes. B. G. 7, 77, <i>init.</i>: <i>nor am I i. that
there is utility in history</i>, nec sum insc.
esse utilitatem in historia, Cic. Fin. 5,
19, 51. Absol., <i>i. persons (<f>opp. to</f> scientific
physicians)</i>, homines inscii imperitique,
Cic. Fin. 2, 5, <i>fin.</i>

3. nescius
(= ignarus: but chiefly poet.: constr.
like preced.): <i>i. of destiny</i>, n. fati, Virg.:
Plin. Ep. Also Cic. has, nescius sum
(= nescio), foll. by <i>acc.</i> and <i>inf.</i>, cf.
Fin. 1, <i>init.</i>, non eram n. ... fore. The
sequence of a rel. clause is poet.: Ov.

4. imprūdens, ntis (<i>not aware of</i>:
esp. used where such ignorance is <i>attended
by some error or mischance</i>): <i>i.
of the law (and so breaking it)</i>, imp.
legis, Cic. Inv. 2, 31, 95: <i>i. of the religious
restriction (and so transgressing)</i>,
imp. religionis, Liv. 31, 14, <i>med.</i> See
also <f>IGNORANT, TO BE</f>.

II. <i>Generally
destitute of knowledge</i>:

1. indoctus:
<i>i. and boorish</i>, ind. et agrestis (opp. to
humanus et politus, Cic. Part. 25, 90):
<i>an i. man, however highly gifted</i>, homo
ind. quamvis sit ingeniosus, Auct. Her.
4, 46, 59. Rarely with <i>gen.</i>, Hor. A. P.
380.

2. impĕrītus (<i>unpractised, not
versed in</i>): v. <f>INEXPERIENCED</f>. Comp.
<i>supr.</i> (I., 2, ex.).

3. rŭdis, e: v. <f>UNACQUAINTED</f>.

<b>important</b>:

I. Of things; <i>weighty,

1. gr[)a]vis (<i>grave, weighty</i>):
<i>i. and serious matters</i>, res gr. seriaeque,

2.

Hor. S. 1, 5, 28: Cic.: Liv.: with some
verbs, as esse, facere, the gen. magni
may be used (L. G[**P2: .] § 281): <i>to be very i.</i>,
magni (maximi) esse, Ant. in Cic. Att.

Cic. Simly, <i>so, how i.</i>, may be
expr. by tantus, quantus (tanti, quanti),
cf. Cic[**P2: .] Dom. <i>l. c.</i>

3. ant[=i]quus (only
in <i>comp.</i> and <i>superl.</i>: of that which <i>takes

4. prior, pr[=i]mus (<i>more, most i.</i>):

5. expr. by
m[=o]mentum, with adj. of quantity: <i>very

II. Of persons or

<b>in</b>:

I. Denoting <i>place where</i>:

1.
in (with <i>abl.</i>): <i>in the heart, in the
brain, in a field, in Italy</i>, in corde, in
cerebro, in agro, in Italia: Cic.: Caes.
(<i>passim</i>). (N.B.--But when stress is
not laid upon[**P1: upon?; P2: yes] the prep., <i>in one's house,
in Rome, etc.</i>, may be expr. as locatives
by <i>gen.</i> or <i>abl.</i>, domi, Romae, etc.: L. G.
§ 257.)

2. when the adj. tōtus is
joined with a subs., the <i>abl.</i> may be
used without prep.: <i>in the whole ocean</i>,
toto mari, Cic. Man. 11, 31; where,
however, the sense is rather <i>throughout</i>:
also lŏcus, rĕgio, terra, are used with
the demonstrative and determinative
prons., and sometimes other adjj. without
a prep.: as, hoc loco, eo loco, eodem
loco, multis locis: cf. Zumpt, L. G.
§ 481. (N.B.--The poets and later
writers freely use all subss. denoting
place in the abl. without a prep., even
though there be no attributive: cf.
Zumpt, l. c.)

3. in certain connexions
only, chiefly where publicity is expressed,
prō (with <i>abl.</i>): cf. Fest. in Paul. Diac.
s. v., <i>pro</i> rostris, id est, <i>in</i> rostris: so pro
contione, <i>in the (public) assembly</i>, Sall.
Jug. 8: Liv. Phr.: <i>in (the writings of)
Plato, Xenophon</i>, apud Platonem, apud
Xenophontem, Cic. Off. 1, 9, 28: de Sen.
22, 79, etc. (For <i>in the presence of</i>, v.
<f>PRESENCE</f>.)

II. Denoting <i>time when</i>:

1. de (with <i>abl.</i>; of a period of time
<i>in the course of which something takes
place</i>): <i>to rise in the night</i>, de nocte
surgere, Hor. Ep. 1, 2, 32: <i>in the course
of the third watch</i>, de tertia vigilia,
Caes. B. G. 1, 12: <i>late in the night</i>,
multa de nocte, Cic. Sext. 35, 75: <i>in the
month of December</i>, de mense Decembri
(rare), Cic. Q. Fr. 2, 1, <i>extr.</i>

2. in
(with <i>abl.</i>; usu. denoting <i>a period of
time during which [<f>not merely</f> in the
course of which] a thing is done)</i>: <i>I did
so too in my youth</i>, feci ego isthaec et
idem in adolescentia, Pl. Bac. 3, 3, 6:
<i>in (throughout) all one's life</i>, in omni
aetate, Cic. Sen. 3, 9: oft. after numeral
advv., <i>twice in a day</i>, bis in die, Cic.
Tusc. 5, 35, 100 (but the abl. occurs also
alone).

3. abl. alone[**P1: alone?|P3 yes]: this occurs
when the subs. of time has an attributive,
as anno tertio, quarto, etc.; mense
Januario, Februario, etc.; also, when a
season[**P1: season?|P3 yes] of the year is particularised, even
without an attributive, as hieme, aestate,
Cic. Div. 1, 42, 94; and in the case of
die, nocte, Cic. N. D. 2, 9, 24 (denoting
continuance; whereas de die, de nocte,
denote merely that something takes
place <i>in the course of the time</i>).

III.
With reference <i>to other circumstances</i>:
in (with <i>abl.</i>): <i>in what position, in
what danger</i>, quo in loco, quanto in
periculo, Caes. B. G. 2, 26: <i>to be in the
wrong</i>, in vitio esse, Cic. Off. 1, 7, 23:
<i>to be heavily in debt</i>, magno in aere
alieno esse, Cic. Cat. 2, 8, 18.

IV.
Denoting <i>direction</i>: in (with <i>acc.</i>): <i>the
camp extended more than 8 miles in
breadth</i>, castra amplius millibus passuum
octo in latitudinem patebant, Caes.
B. G. 2, 7. (This sense may oft. be conveyed
by an adj. with <i>acc.</i> of extent: <i>six
feet in height, breadth, etc.</i>, altus, latus
sex pedes, etc.: v. <f>HIGH</f>, <f>BROAD</f>, etc.)

V. Denoting <i>rule, standard, manner,
etc.</i>:

1. in (with <i>acc.</i>): <i>a decree of
the Senate was passed in these words</i>,
S. C. in haec verba factum est, Liv. 30,
43: <i>in the manner of slaves</i>, servilem
in modum, Cic. Verr. Act. 1, 5, 13.

2.
ad (with <i>acc.</i> = <i>according to</i>): <i>in the
likeness of</i>, ad similitudinem, Cic. N. D.
2, 64, 161: <i>in the same manner (to the
same effect)</i>, ad eundem modum, Ter.
Ad. 3, 3, 70; so ad hunc modum, of <i>the</i>
-----File: b0397r.png------------------------------------------------------
<i>general scope of a speech</i>, Caes. B. G. 2,
31.

3. abl. alone: usu. constr. in the
case of modal substantives: <i>in what
manner, in this manner, in every possible
way</i>, quo modo, hoc modo, omni
modo, omnibus modis, etc., Ter.: Cic.:
<i>passim</i>.

VI. Denoting <i>occasion, state,
means</i> or <i>manner</i>, per (with <i>acc.</i>): <i>to
do anything in anger</i>, facere aliquid per
iram, Cic. Tusc. 4, 37, 79: <i>in sport</i>, per
ludum et jocum, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 60, 155.

VII. Miscell. phr.: <i>in consequence
of the fact that</i>, ex eo quod, Cic.
Fin. 2, 9, 28: <i>in the meanwhile</i>, interim
(v. <f>MEANWHILE</f>): <i>in that</i>, quod, cf. Caes.
B. G. 1, 14, num etiam recentium injuriarum,
<i>quod</i> iter per provinciam per
vim tentassent, quod Haeduos ... memoriam
deponere posse? <i>in proportion as
... so</i>, quo ... eo (with compar.).

ea sunt enim d. non ferenda, Cic. Rep.
2, 15. Less freq. with other words: <i>he

6. dēnĭque (like preced.
but rare): <i>that i. I am wont to deem an

1. vērōnĕ (veron') = <i>is it so,

2.
ain' = aisne? or strengthened ain' tu?

2. ĕquĭdem (usu. =

II. <i>Result</i>:

III. In law, expr.

qua de re agitur (legal form), Cic. Br.

<b>isthmus</b>:

1. isthmus <i>or</i> isthmos,

2. angustiae, arum (<i>any

<b>it</b>: is, ea, id, referring to a thing
before mentioned, cf. L. G. § 370. But
more freq. not expressed, esp. when the
object of a verb, L. G. § 371: also when
it introduces an impers. sentence, it is
left to be understood from the pers. of
the verb, or the gender of an adj., e. g.
<i>it is wearisome, is manifest, etc.</i>, taedet,
manifestum est, etc.


<b>italics</b>: *literae tenuiores ac paullum
inclinatae, Kr.; or simply, literae

Excurs.; typi obliqui quos cursivos vocant,
Nobbe, pref. Cic.; *quos nostrates
Italicos appellant.

2. excēdo,

<b>livelong</b> (<i>adj.</i>): nearest word, tōtus,

longus may serve: v. <f>TEDIOUS</f>.

et f., Cic. Inv[**P1: missing .] 1, 17, <i>extr[**P1: missing .]</i>: <i>to excite l.</i>,
fastidia movere alicui, Ov. Pont. 1, 10,
7; also, fastidium creare, Plin.

2.
nausĕa (<i>sickness</i>, strictly <i>from sailing</i>):
cf. Mart. 4, 37, <i>fin.</i> <i>To feel a l.</i>, fastidio:
v. preced. art.

II. In gen. sense: usu.
best expr. by verb.[**P1: colon, not period?] <i>to feel an utter
l. for baseness</i>, *turpitudinem penitus
animo aspernari atque respuere: v. <f>TO
LOATHE</f>. (Fastīdium in ref. to other
things than food, denotes <i>fastidiousness,

<f>HATRED</f>.


<b>loathsome</b>:

1. foedus (<i>offensive,
revolting</i>): <i>a most l. creature (the bug)</i>,

fastidiendum], Plin. 29, 4, 17[**:] <i>l. tracks

2. tēter (taet.), tra,

stronger than the preced.): <i>l. corpses</i>, t.

3. fastīdiendus
(<i>exciting nausea</i>: v. rare): Plin. 25, 7,
38. (Fastidiosus, <i>of that which one has
no appetite for</i>, Hor. Od. 3, 29, 9; but

4. obscaenus
(strictly <i>of ill omen</i>; hence <i>repulsive</i>:

<b>loathsomeness</b>: foedĭtas: Cic.


<b>lobby</b>: nearest word, vestĭbŭlum

<b>lobe</b>: fibra (<i>of the liver</i>): v. <f>LIVER</f>.


<b>lobster</b>: prob. astăcus: Plin. 9, 31,

<b>lodge</b> (<i>v.</i>):

A. Intrans.:

<i>To have one's abode</i>:

1. dēversor, 1:

<b>man</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

III.
<i>An individual of the male sex</i>: vir,
vĭri: often used in preference to homo,
when the existence of such qualities as
<i>courage, genius, etc.</i>, is implied: <i>he bore

i. e. <i>as man instinctively shrinks from

characters of great men</i>, non satis dignum
summorum virorum personis, Nep.
pref. <i>init.</i> Less freq. with bad epithets,
as turpissimi viri, Sall. Jug. 85. <i>Adv.</i>
vĭrītim, <i>man by man</i> (distributively):
Cic.: Suet. <i>An old man</i>, sĕnex, is (v.
<f>OLD</f>)[** :?|P3 yes] <i>a young m.</i>, adolescens, adolescentulus
(cf. <i>supr.</i> I., 1); juvenis: see also
<f>YOUNG</f>. Phr.: <i>you must play the m.</i>,
vobis necesse est fortibus viris esse, Liv.
21, 44, <i>fin.</i>: <i>I call upon you to play the

m.</i>, omnes (universi, cuncti) ad unum,
Cic. Am. 23, 86: Liv.

IV. <i>A fighting
man</i>: mīles, ĭtis: Caes.: Liv. <i>pass.</i>
But very often, in such exprr. as <i>our
men, his men</i>, the poss. prons. alone are
used: cf. Caes. B. G. 4, 24, quibus rebus
<i>nostri</i> (= nostri milites) perterriti, etc.:
but the subs. may also be expr., cf. ib.
25, nostris <i>militibus</i> cunctantibus. <i>Their
men</i>, i. e. <i>the enemy</i>, may either be expr.
by hostes (Caes.: Liv. <i>pass.</i>), or by illi:
cf. Caes. l. c. 24, quum <i>illi</i> ... audacter
tela conjicerent, etc. In enumerating
losses after an engagement, the subs. is
usu. implied in some other word: <i>the
enemy lost 1500 men slain in the battle</i>,
MD. hostium in acie periere (caesi), Liv.
22, 7, <i>init.</i>

2. lātro, ōnis,
<i>m.</i>: Ov. l. c. 357: Mart. Also, latrunculus:

3. mīles,
ĭtis, <i>m.</i> (the pieces representing <i>soldiers</i>):

consilium imperatorium (= Gr. στρατήγημα,

2. sometimes expr. by convertere

army safe</i>. (But very often not expr.
by any single word: <i>by this m.</i>, quo
facto, qua re, cf. Front. 2, 4, <i>pass.</i>)

<b>march</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

I. <i>Of soldiers</i>:

1. ĭter, ĭtĭnĕris, <i>n.</i> (<i>any journey</i>):
<i>to direct one's m. towards a place</i>, i.
habere (with <i>acc.</i> of name of town <i>to

63; properare, Tac. A. 15, 12: <i>an unsafe,

Cic. Ph. 12, 10, 25: <i>to hasten by

quam potui maximis i., Cic. Fam. 15, 4,
<i>med.</i> See also <f>TO MARCH</f>. (N.B.--<i>To
do anything on</i> or <i>in the course of a
march</i>,[** , or :?] expr. by in itinere, <i>or</i> iter faciens;
<i>ex</i> itinere only to denote the <i>sending[** hyphen msg]
of persons or things</i> from <i>the army
marching</i>: cf. Sall. Cat. 34, Catilina <i>ex</i>
itinere ... litteras mittit.)

2. agmen,
inis, <i>n.</i> (strictly, <i>an army marching</i>:

45: cf. <i>paulo infr.</i>, in agmine = <i>when
the troops were on m.</i>: <i>to harass the

II. As <i>measure of time</i> or <i>distance</i>:
Phr.: <i>one day's m.</i>, iter unius diei, Cic.
Fam. 15, 4, <i>med.</i>: also, diei iter, 44, 7,

secundis castris, Liv. 44, 7, <i>init.</i>;

III. <i>Pace, progress</i>: grădus:

<b>moment</b>:

II. <i>A very brief space of time</i>:

1.

2.

(3). <i>to the m.</i>, i. e. <i>the very m.</i>, ad

very m.</i>, nunc quum maxime (also as one

quum maxime loqueretur, Cic. Verr. 5,
54, 142. Sometimes <i>moment = time</i>:
esp. in such phrr.[** typo or plural?|P2: plural] as <i>a favourable</i> or
<i>unfavourable m.</i>, tempus opportunum,
adversum; <i>at so critical a m.</i>, tali tempore;
<i>at the very m.</i>, ipso tempore: v.
<f>TIME</f>.

[quam] triginta de suis, Nep. Thras. 2.
The pl. occurs in sense of <i>more</i> (as
strict compar. to multi, cf. Cic. Man. 7,
19, non possunt ... <i>multi</i> rem atque
fortunas amittere, ut non <i>plures</i> secum

more freq. = <i>a considerable number</i>:
v. <f>SEVERAL</f>. Note also the use of <i>neut.

verbis[** :?|P3 yes] <i>though I would fain write m.</i>,
plura quum scribere vellem, Sall. Cat.
33, <i>fin.</i>: <i>to pursue at m. length</i>, pluribus
exsequi, Phaedr. 3, 10, <i>extr.</i> <i>Dimin.</i>

<i>med.</i>: Ter. (N.B.--Plus is often an
adv. in Latin, where the corresponding
word in Eng. is regarded as an adj.:

nec esse <i>plus</i> uno, Cic. Ac. 2,

20.)

2. amplius, <i>indecl.</i> (denoting
greater extent of <i>space</i> or <i>time</i>; also

spatium, quod est non a. pedum <sc>DC</sc>,
Caes. B. G.[**P1: missing .] 1, 38: <i>for m. than four hours</i>,
a. quattuor horis, ib. 4, 37: <i>m. than a

Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 5, 14. (N.B.--Plus, amplius,
minus, are often used adverbially
with numeral adjectives, without effecting

3. ultra, <i>adv.</i>
and <i>prep.</i> (to denote excess above a

<b>most</b> (<i>adv.</i>):

I. With adj. and

1. nōmen: <i>to have a n.</i>, n. habere,
Cic. Br. 69, 244 (cf. ib. 69, 238, hujus ...
nomen majus fuisset): <i>to enjoy some n.
and reputation</i>, aliquod n.que decusque
gerere, Virg. Aen. 2, 89: <i>to win an everlasting
n.</i>, n. immortalitatis (better,
aeternum) mereri, Sil. 13, 722: <i>terrified
by the reputation of so great a n.</i>, tanti
n. famâ territus, Vell. 2, 94: <i>to eclipse
any one's n.</i>, alicujus nomini officere,
Liv. prooem.: <i>to lose its n. (of wine)</i>,
n. perdere, Cato R. R. 55: cf. nec Baccho
genus, aut pomis sua n. servat, Virg. G[**P1: missing .]
2, 240.

2. existĭmātio (<i>good n.</i>): <i>to
prefer a good n. to a kingdom</i>, bonam
ex. regno praeponere, Nep. Ages. 4: <i>to
assail or hurt any one's good n.</i>, ex. oppugnare,
Cic. Fam[**P1: missing .] 3, 10; offendere, id.
Planc. 2, 6; ex. lacerare, Suet. Caes. 75;
ex. laedere, id. Ner. 58.

3. fāma (in
good or bad sense): <i>good n. and reputation</i>,
f. et existimatio, Cic[**P1: missing .] Quint. 15, 50
(v. <f>FAME</f>): <i>to take away any one's good
n.</i>, de f. alicujus detrahere, Cic. Fam. 3,
8: alicujus famam laedere, ib. 3, 7.
Phr.: <i>to have a good n.</i>, bene audire:
cf. id. Fin. 3, 17, 57; <i>a bad one</i>, male
audire, ib. 5, 40, 116.

III. <i>Authority</i>:
verba, orum: esp. in phr., <i>in my, your
n.</i>, meis, tuis verbis: <i>you will oblige
me by congratulating your wife in my
n.</i>, gratum mihi feceris, si uxori tuae
meis v. eris gratulatus, Cic. Fam. 15, 8:
<i>in the n. of the Senate</i>, Senatus verbis,
Liv. 9, 36.

IV[**P1: missing .] <i>Name merely, without
the reality</i>: nōmen: <i>friendship is a n.,
fidelity an empty n.</i>, n. amicitia, n. inane
fides, Ov. A. A. 1, 740: <i>the Campanians
brought the n. rather than (the reality
of) strength</i>, Campani n. magis quam
praesidium attulerunt, Liv. 7, 29.

V.
In adjurations; <i>by way of appeal</i>:
Phr.: <i>in the n. of gods and men</i>, per
deos atque homines, Cic. Div. 2, 55, 114:
pro deorum atque hominum fidem, id.
Tusc. 5, 16, 48: <i>in heaven's n.</i>, Di!
vestram fidem, Ter. Andr. 4, 3, 1.


<b>name</b> (<i>v.</i>):

I. <i>To call by a name</i>:

1. nōmĭno, 1: <i>love, from which
friendship is (so) n.d.</i> amor ex quo
amicitia est nominata, Cic. Am. 8, 26:
oftener in sense (II.): v. infr.

2. expr.
by nōmen, ĭnis, <i>n.</i>; and a verb: <i>e. g.</i>
n. alicui dare, Cic. Inv. 1, 24, 34; indere,
Pl. St. 2, 1, 20; facere, id. Men. 1, 1, 1; imponere
(esp. with ref. <i>to things</i>), Cic. Fin.
3, 1, 3. So <i>to be n.d</i>, n. invenire, reperire
[ex aliqua re], v. <f>NAME</f>, <i>subs.</i> (I.).

3.
nuncŭpo, 1 (appy. used, in this sense, to
avoid the repetition of similar syllables):
<i>they n.d (the offspring) after the god
himself</i>, ex nomine ipsius dei nuncupaverunt,
Cic. N. D. 2, 23, 60: Suet. Aug. 31
(Sextilem mensem e suo cognomine
nuncupavit).

4. appello, dīco, etc.:
v. <f>TO CALL</f>.

II. <i>To mention by name</i>:

1. nōmĭno, 1: <i>the Egyptians deem
it an impiety to n. Mercury</i>, (Mercurium)
Aegyptii nefas habent n., Cic. N. D. 3,
22, 56. Esp. in phr. quem honoris causa
nomino = <i>whom I name with all possible
respect</i>, Cic. R. Am. 2, 6: Ter.

2. nuncŭpo,
1 (rare in this sense): <i>to n. (enumerate)
all Pompey's triumphs</i>, Pompeii
omnes triumphos n., Plin. 7, 26, 27.

III.
<i>To designate, appoint, fix</i>: Phr.: <i>to n.
any one heir</i>, heredem aliquem nuncupare,
Ulp. Dig. 28, 1, 21: Tac. (the legal
phr.): <i>to n. a master of the horse</i>, magistrum
equitum dicere (v. <f>TO NOMINATE</f>,
<f>APPOINT</f>): <i>to n. the day for a wedding</i>,
diem nuptiis dicere, Ter. Andr. 1, 1, 75:
Caes.: Cic.

<b>nameless</b>:

I. <i>Not having a name</i>:
nominis expers; nullo vocabulo insignis
<i>s.</i> insignitus: v. <f>NAME</f>.

II. <i>Not mentioned
by name</i>: Phr.: <i>certain persons,
who shall be n.</i>, *certi homines quos
nominare nolo. (N.B.--No such adj. as
anonymus.)


<b>namely</b>:

1. expr. by apposition of
subs.: <i>two most powerful cities, n.,
Carthage and Corinth</i>, duae potentissimae
urbes, Carthago et Corinthus, Cic.
Man. 20, 60: <i>these most base and inconsistent
vices, n., luxury and avarice</i>,
pessuma ac diversa inter se mala, luxuria
atque avaritia, Sall. Cat. 5: cf. ib. 9,
duabus his artibus, audacia in bello;
ubi pax evenerat, aequitate, <i>these two
virtues, namely, ...</i>: et <i>pass.</i>

2.
when greater emphasis is needed: dīco
(<i>I mean to say</i>): cf. Cic. N. D. 1, 31, 86,
ea quae timenda esse negaret, mortem
<i>dico</i> et deos, i. e. <i>namely, death and the
gods</i>: cf. id. Tusc. 1, 32, 78, amicos
nostros Stoicos ..., <i>eos dico</i>, qui dicunt,
etc. In similar sense, Hor. has inquam:
cetera turba, nos inquam (<i>namely, ourselves</i>),
Sat. 2, 8, 27.

3. scīlĭcet (not
so in good authors): cf. Suet. Aug. 29,
quaedam opera alieno nomine, nepotum
<i>scilicet</i> et uxoris sororisque, i. e. <i>namely,
that of his grandsons, etc.</i> (N.B.--A
usage to be sparingly followed.) So also
vĭdēlĭcet is occasionally used, where the
reference to some person or thing is
quite obvious: cf. Cic. Leg. 2, 10, 24,
caste jubet lex adire ad deos, <i>animo
videlicet</i>, in quo sunt omnia (<i>"that is
to say," <f>or</f> "namely" in mind</i>): cf.
Smith's Lat. Dict. s. v. (II.).

4. introducing
an entire sentence illustrative of
something that has gone before, nam:
cf. Cic. Part. 11, 38, rerum bonarum et
malarum tria sunt genera: <i>nam</i> aut in
animis, aut in corporibus, aut extra
esse possunt: i. e. <i>namely, mental,
bodily, or external</i> (Kr.): also Virg. G.
1, 451, hoc etiam ... profuerit meminisse
magis: <i>nam</i> saepe videmus ...[** punct. needed, or four dots?] i. e.
<i>namely, we often see, etc.</i>: v. <f>FOR</f>.

<b>nation</b>:

Cic. Fin. 5, 1, 2: <i>as is n.</i>, sicut natura
fert, id. Part. 7, 24: <i>a n. consequence</i>,
*quod ex ipsa rei natura sequitur (R.
and A.): v. <f>NATURE</f>.

II. <i>Not manufactured</i>:

1. nātīvus: <i>the n. bulwarks

n., Plin. 32, 7, 24: <i>n. hair</i>, n. coma, Ov.

2. vīvus (esp. poet.):
<i>n. rock</i>, v. saxum, Virg. Aen. 1, 167: <i>n.

Phr.: <i>a town with strong n. and artificial

manu munitum, Caes. B. G. 3, 23.

III.
<i>Occurring in the course of nature</i>: nātūrālis:
<i>a n. death</i>, mors n., Plin. 7.[**P2: ,] 53,
54 § 180 (for which, mors sicca, Juv.
10, 113). Phr.: <i>to die a n. death</i> (uti

IV. <i>Born
of mere natural cohabitation</i>: nātūrālis

V. <i>Unaffected</i>:

1. nātūrālis: opp. to fucatus
(<i>false, artificial</i>).[**P2: ,] Cic. Br. 9, 22.

2. perh. sincērus (<i>genuine</i>): cf.
Tac. Dial. 28, <i>fin.</i>, natura sincera et

(<i>genuine, unaffected, uncorrupted</i>).

3.
innātus (strictly, <i>born in any one, not

14. Join: innatus atque insitus (opp.

18, 69; ingenitus et innatus.[**P2: ,] Plin[**P2: .] Pan.
20. Phr.: <i>in a n. manner</i>, sicut

VI. <i>Derived
from natural constitution; not
acquired</i>: Phr.: <i>n. endowments</i>, (1).

indŏles, is, <i>f.</i> (<i>n. disposition</i>): <i>young

n. habuit admirabilem ad dicendum, Cic.

VII. <i>Agreeable</i>

<i>to any one's disposition or nature</i>; or

1. expr.

2. perh. proprius (<i>naturally belonging</i>

VIII.
Theol. term: Phr.: <i>n. religion</i> or <i>theology</i>,
*cognitio Dei (rerum divinarum)

<b>natural</b> (<i>subs.</i>): v. <f>IDIOT</f>.


<b>naturalism</b>: *eorum ratio qui omnia
naturali lege fieri disputant; nihil
supra naturalem legem esse contendunt.
(Avoid naturalismus.)


<b>naturalist</b>: i. e. <i>one who studies
natural history</i>: *animantium <i>s.</i> herbarum
peritus (homo); qui animantium
<i>s.</i> herbarum naturae cognoscendae studet.
(Physicus is rather <i>a natural philosopher</i>
than <i>a naturalist</i>: defined by
Cic. as speculator venatorque naturae,
N. D. 1, 30, <i>init.</i>)


<b>naturalization</b>: cf. foll. art.


<b>naturalize</b>:

I. <i>To confer</i> on an
alien <i>the status of a native subject</i>:
expr. by, civitatem dare, impertire;
civitate donare: v. <f>TO ENFRANCHISE</f>;
<f>FRANCHISE</f>. Fig.: <i>to n. a word</i>, verbo
civitatem dare, Suet. Gr. 22 (Tu, Caesar,
civitatem dare potes hominibus; verbo
non potes): <i>the word sorites is quite
n.d in Latin</i>, sorites satis Latino sermone
tritus est, Cic. Div. 2, 4, 11 (R.
and A.); *hoc verbum omnino jam pro
vernaculo adhibetur; hoc verbo plerique
omnes ut genuino <i>s.</i> domestico utuntur.

II. <i>To accustom</i> a plant or animal
<i>to a new climate</i>: expr. by assuēfăcio,
3: v. <f>TO ACCUSTOM</f>.

III. <i>To search
for specimens of plants, etc.</i>: *herbarum
atque animantium varia genera investigare,
conquirere.


<b>naturally</b>:

I. <i>By nature</i>:

1.
nātūrālĭter: <i>alacrity n. implanted in
all men</i>, alacritas n. innata omnibus,
Caes. B. C. 3, 92: <i>(men) n. very different</i>,
naturaliter dissimillimi, Vell. 2, 60.

2.
nātūrā (modal <i>abl.</i>): <i>n. implanted (in

n. so constituted</i>, n. ita esse factum, id.
Br. 80, 276: et <i>pass.</i> So, when <i>human
nature</i> is intended, ingenio: <i>this is what
we are most of us n. inclined to</i>, ita
plerique ingenio sumus omnes, Ter. Ph.
1, 3, 20: cf. <f>NATURAL</f> (VII.)

II. <i>Agreeably
to nature</i>: secundum naturam, Cic.
Fin. 5, 9, 26; convenienter naturae (<i>e. g.</i>
vivere), id. Tusc. 5, 28, 82; more fully,
congruenter naturae convenienterque, id.

sicut natura fert (<i>in a natural spontaneous

III. <i>Unaffectedly</i>:
simplĭcĭter (Kr.): v. <f>SIMPLY</f>.
Better, sicut natura fert.[**P2: , ?] (v. <i>supr.</i> II.):
or perh. sine mala affectatione, cf. Quint.
8, 3, 56.

IV. <i>As a natural consequence</i>:
nĕcessāriē <i>or</i> -o: v. <f>NECESSARILY</f>.
Or by circuml., *ex ipsa re; (id)
quod (ipsa) res habet (cf. Sall. Cat. 51,
<i>med.</i>, de poena possumus dicere, id quod
res habet = <i>what n. presents itself</i>): <i>it
followed n.</i>, *aliter fieri non potuit quam
factum est.

V. <i>Spontaneously; without
cultivation</i>: (sua) sponte: opp. to alieno
impulsu, Cic. N. D. 2, 12, 32: of <i>plants
not needing to be sown</i>, sp. sua venire,
Virg. G. 2, 11: v. <f>SPONTANEOUSLY</f>.

<b>nature</b>:

I. In wide sense, <i>the

3. ingĕnium, indŏles

V. <i>Natural

<b>nay</b>:

I. As negative answer: non,
non ita: v. <f>NO</f>.

II. <i>Nay more, nay
rather</i>; introducing a remark corrective
of what precedes:[**P2: dot missing]

1. immo <i>or</i> īmo;
esp. strengthened by vēro:[**P2: dot missing] cf. Cic. Cat.
1, 1.[**P2: ,] 2, vivit? <i>immo vero</i> in Senatum
venit, i. e. <i>nay more; he actually comes
into the Senate</i>: also, Suet. Aug. 65,
Agrippam nihilo tractabiliorem.[**P2: ,] <i>immo</i>
in dies amentiorem.[**P2: ,] i. e. <i>nay rather; he
became worse</i>: this use of immo (vero)
is very freq. in conversation, cf. Ter.
Andr. 1, 1, 3.[**P2: :/;] Eun. 2, 3, 38, et <i>pass.</i>

2. atque ădeo (= <i>and more than
that</i>): <i>they hint this; nay more, they
openly show</i>, hoc significant, atque adeo
aperte ostendunt, Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 60, 148:[**P2: dot missing]
v. Smith's Lat. Dict. s. v. adeo (III.).

3. quid? quod ... (an elliptical mode
of speech.[**P2: ,] introducing something <i>that
could hardly have been expected:[** ;? separate markup?] what
of this ... that ...</i>): <i>nay more, if that be
true, all reason is done away with</i>, quid,
quod, si ista vera sunt, ratio omnis tollitur?
Cic. Ac. 2, 8, 26: cf. id. Man. 5,
12, quid, quod salus sociorum summum
in periculum ac discrimen vocatur?
(N.B.--A note of interrogation is often
put immediately after the Quid.) See
also <f>MOREOVER</f>.

<b>neighbour</b>:

I. <i>One living near</i>:

1. vīcīnus; <i>f.</i> -a: <i>your next-door n.</i>,
v. proximus tuus, Pl. Merc. 2, 4, 7: Cic.
Att. 2, 14: <i>a good n.</i>, bonus v., Hor. Ep.
2, 2, 132: Cic. Join: finitimi ac vicini,
Cic. Sull. 20, 58.

2. fīnĭtĭmus (usu.
<i>on a large scale, of nations and tribes
that are adjacent to each other</i>): <i>to wage
wars with n.s</i>, bella cum finitimis gerere,
Cic. Rep. 2, 9: v. <f>NEIGHBOURING</f>. Also,
in narrower sense, with vicinus: v. <i>supr.</i>
(1).

3. proxĭmus (<i>very near neighbour</i>):
esp. with vicinus: v. <i>supr.</i> (1):
<i>the Belgae are very near n.s to the
Germans</i>, Belgae p. sunt Gallis, Caes.
B. G. 1, 1. (N.B.--Propinqui are <i>relatives</i>:
v. Cic. Off. 1, 17.)

4. <i>one's
neighbours</i>, collectively, vīcīnĭtas: Cato
R. R. 4 (si te libenter v. videbit): or,
vīcīnia: Hor. S. 2, 5, 106.

II. <i>Any
other person, brought into relation with
one</i>: alter: <i>to do nothing for the sake of
one's n.</i>, nihil alterius causa facere, Cic.
Leg. 1, 14, 41: Pl. Also sometimes
homo: <i>a man ought not to be a stranger
to his n. (fellow-man)</i>, oportet hominem
ab homine non esse alienum, Cic. Fin. 3,
19, 63: cf. Ter. Heaut. 1, 1, 25, where
humani nil = <i>nothing that concerns my
n.</i>: <i>to attend to one's n.'s affairs</i>, alienas
res curare: v. <f>TO MIND</f>.


<b>neighbourhood</b>:

1. vīcīnĭtas: <i>in

3. expr.
by prŏpinquus: esp. in phr., <i>in the n.</i>,

<i>ad init.</i> So, adv. prope (<i>in the n.</i>):

4. expr. by vīcīnus

<b>neither</b> (<i>conj.</i>):

1. neque (nec)

2. nēve (neu) ... nēve

<b>nerve</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

I. <i>Organ of sensation</i>:

II. Meton., <i>strength, vigour</i>:

orum: Cic. Att. 16, 16, C, <i>extr.</i>, si nervulos
tuos ... adhibebis, <i>strain a n.;

<b>nervous</b>:

I. <i>Full of sinewy vigour</i>:

II.
<i>Having much nervous susceptibility</i>:
Phr.: <i>to feel extremely n. and shaky</i>,

TREMBLE</f>; <f>AGITATED</f>): <i>of a n. temperament</i>,
*ingenio nimis trepido atque
anxio: qui facilius quam opus est

<b>nervously</b>:

I. <i>In a vigorous
manner</i>: nervōsē: Cic. Or. 36, 127.

II. <i>With nervous excitableness</i>:

<b>no</b> (<i>adj.</i>):

1. nullus: used both

2. ullus, with

1, 7.

3. nēmo, of <i>persons</i>: v. <i>supr.</i> (1).

4. nĭhil, <i>indecl.</i> (with <i>part. gen.</i>):

(N.B.--This last use is confined to adjj.[**adj.?|P2: no; plural]
of the first and second declension.) Also
nihil may sometimes be used with intrans.
and other verbs, where in Eng.
the adj. <i>no</i> is used with a verbal subs.:
<i>to make no use of anything</i>, aliqua re
nihil uti, Cic. Agr. 2, 23, <i>init.</i>: <i>I found
no fault with you</i>, nihil te accusavi,[**P2: ,] id.

senectutem, <i>no fault to find with

<b>no</b> (particle of negation):

1. non
(more freq. with verb supplied from the

2. mĭnĭmē (an
emphatic denial): <i>are not you ashamed

3, 2, 42: very often strengthened by

3.
nullo modo (<i>by no means; not at all</i>):
<i>can you not learn that in some other

<b>no one</b>, <b>nobody</b>:

I. In ord. sense:

1. nēmo, ĭnis, <i>c.</i>: for which in <i>gen.</i>
and <i>abl.</i> nullius, nullo, are preferred by
the best authors (Kr.): sometimes in

2.
nē quis (= <i>that no one</i>; after verbs of

Cic. opt. gen. Or. 7, <i>init.</i>: <i>it was enacted
by law that no one should make a tomb
...</i>, lege sanctum est, ne quis sepulcrum

strive hard that no one may surpass me</i>,
*elaborabo (ut) ne quis me vincat,[**P2: ,/:] cf.
Cic. de Or. 2, 72, <i>fin.</i>

II. <i>A person of no
account</i>: terrae filius, Petr. 43, <i>med.</i>: Cic.


<b>nobility</b>:

I. <i>Nobleness of birth</i> or
