<b>not</b>:

I. In direct statements <i>or</i>
interrogative sentences[**P2: :]

1. nōn (most
gen. word: usual position immediately
before the word to be negatived, or
when it qualifies an entire proposition,
at the beginning of it): for the position
of non,[**.?|p2: no] comp. foll. exx.: qui mihi <i>non
id</i> videbantur accusare, quod esset accusandum,[**P2: hyphen missing]
Cic. Sen. 3, 7:[**P2: dot missing] eum colere coepi
<i>non admodum</i> grandem natu, ib. 4, 10:
omnia memoria tenebat, <i>non domestica</i>
solum sed etiam externa bella, ib. 4, <i>fin.</i>
(the words id, admodum, domestica,
bearing in each case the stress of the
negation): non sunt in senectute vires,
ib. 11, <i>init.</i>: at non est voluptatum
tanta quasi titillatio in senibus, ib. 14,
47 (where the entire propositions are to
be negatived). (N.B.--In interrogative
sentences, the particle -nĕ is attached to
the negative, thus: nonne: which in direct
questions begins the sentence, according
to above rule, in indirect ones its
position being more or less a matter of
euphony: <i>did not Lentulus come to you?
did not Sanga?</i> nonne ad te Lentulus
venit? non Sanga? Cic. in Pis. 31.[**P2: ,] 77:
<i>he was asked whether he did not think
Archelaus son of Perdiccas happy?</i> ex eo
quaesitum (est), Archelaum Perdiccae
filium <i>nonne</i> beatum putaret? id. Tusc.
5, 12, <i>init.</i> In compound negative questions,
the -ne is frequently dispensed
with in the later members, as above.)

2. haud (more emphatic than non,
and chiefly joined to adverbs and adjectives;
also used with verbs, especially
in certain phrr.,[**phr?|P2: no, plural form] as haud scio an, haud
dubito): <i>I don't quite understand</i>, haud
sane intelligo, Cic. Off[**.] 2, 2, 5: <i>I did not
so order</i>, haud ita jussi, Ter. Andr. 5, 4,
52: strengthened by -quāquam (<i>not in
any degree</i>): Cic[**.]: Liv.: <i>it is not at
all wonderful</i>, haud mirabile est, Ter.
Heaut. 2, 4, 7: Cic.: <i>thereupon he did
not hesitate to point out ...</i>, tum ille
haud dubitavit docere ..., Cic. Rep. 1,
15.

3. (to be used sparingly, and
only in familiar style) nullus, in agr.
with subject.: <i>Philotimus not only does
not come, but ...</i>, Ph. non modo nullus
venit, sed ..., Cic. Att. 11, 24, 3: <i>I remember;
even were you not to remind
me</i>, memini, tametsi nullus moneas, Ter.
Eun. 2, 1, 10: <i>don't you say</i>, nullus
dixeris, id. Hec. 1, 2, 4. (In this use
nullus is more emphatic than non: cf.
L. G. § 612.)

4. părum, mĭnus (<i>less
than should be</i>; hence = softened negative:
L. G. § 646): <i>my efforts are not
succeeding very well</i>, parum succedit
quod ago, Ter. Andr. 4, 1, 56: <i>Terentia
has not been well</i>, Terentia minus belle
habuit, Cic. Fam. 9, 9. So sometimes
male (with adjj.): <i>not sound in mind</i>,
male sanus, Cic. Att. 9, 15. (N.B.--As
joined with conj. quo [quominus].[**P2: ,] minus
has a purely negative force: v. <f>TO PREVENT</f>,
<f>HINDER</f>.)

5. nĭhil (<i>in no respect,
not at all</i>: only with verbs):[**P2: dot missing] <i>I did not
(by any means) find fault with you
about my brother</i>, de patre nihil te accusavi,
Cic. Fam. 14.[**P2: ,] 1, 6: <i>I don't say
to whom (= say nothing about who it
was)</i>, n. dico, cui, id. Ph. 1, 6, 13.

6.
mĭnĭmē, nullo mŏdo, nullo pacto (<i>by no
means</i>; the two former often[**P2: f unclear] in answer
to questions): v. <f>MEANS</f> (by no). Special
Phr.: (<i>a</i>). <i>and not</i>: nĕque, nec
(cf. L. G. § 564): <i>it delights in a soil
that is poor and not damp</i>, laetatur loco
macro neque humido.[**P2: ,] Col. 2, 11, <i>med.</i>:
<i>a good knowledge of literature, and that
not of a common sort</i>, plurimae litterae,
nec <i>eae</i> vulgares, Cic. Br. 76, 265 (mark
the use of eae; without which pronoun
this use of neque with an adj. is scarcely
elegant): v. <f>NOR</f>. (<i>b</i>). <i>if not</i>: sin mĭnus,
sin: v. <f>IF</f> (2). (<i>c</i>). <i>not even</i>: nē ...
quĭdem (the word emphasized coming
between the two): <i>not to make even the
least sacrifice of glory</i>, gloriae jacturam
ne minimam quidem facere, Cic. Off. 1,
24, 84[**: or .|P2: :] <i>not even ... much less ...</i>, ne
-----File: b0502r.png------------------------------------------------------
quidem ... nedum ut, Liv. 3, 14, <i>fin.</i>
(N.B.--Acc. to Forcell. there is no well
authenticated case of ne quidem occurring
without a word between, though
several have been adduced: v. Tursell.
s. v. ne, No. 36.) (<i>d</i>). <i>not that ... but
...</i>: non quo (quod), with subj. ...
sed ...: <i>not that I like to be ill spoken
of, but because ...</i>, non quo libenter[** unclear]
male audiam, sed ..., Cic. de Or. 2, 75,
305: cf. id. Tusc. 2, 23, <i>fin.</i>, pugiles in

nē: v. <f>THAT</f> (conj.).

II. In dependent
sentences, esp. to denote <i>a purpose</i>;
also in <i>prohibitions</i>:

1. nē (in
dep. sentence = <i>in order that ... not</i>):
<i>let the Consuls see to it that the commonwealth
does not receive damage</i>, videant
Coss. ne quid detrimenti resp. capiat,
Caes. B. C. 1, 5: Sall.: in the case of ne

So after verbs of <i>asking</i>, <i>commanding</i>,
<i>advising</i>, <i>striving</i> (not infin.): v. <f>TO
ASK</f>, etc.

2. in double prohibitions:
nēve (neu) ... nēve (neu).[**P1: should be :] v. <f>NEITHER</f>.
Ne is sometimes used with the first verb:
cf. XII. Tab. in Cic. Leg. 2, 23, <i>init.</i>,
Hominem mortuum in urbe <i>ne</i> sepelito
<i>neve</i> urito.

3. after verbs of <i>fearing</i>,
ut (= <i>that ... not</i>): <i>I fear you will not
live long</i>, ut sis vitalis metuo, Hor. S.
2, 1, 60: but also ne ... non: cf. Cic.

<i>not to say ...</i>, ne dicam: cf. Cic. N. D.

<b>now</b>:

I. <i>At the present time</i>:

1.
nunc: <i>pass.</i>

2. jam (denoting emphasis
and urgency: <i>now, without further
delay</i>): <i>I want (the money) now!--You
shall have it now</i> (directly), jam
opus est--Jam feres, Ter. Ph. 3, 3, 26.
Strengthened by tandem = <i>now at length</i>,
Virg. Aen. 6, 61. Jam and nunc are
often combined = <i>even now</i>: <i>I even now
(in anticipation) fear</i>, jam nunc timeo,
Civ.[** typo? Cic.] Div. Verr. 13, 42. Also jam is
sometimes repeated for emphasis: cf.
Cic. Ph. 2, 34, 87, jam jam minime miror,
i. e. <i>now I no longer wonder</i>: so, Virg.
Aen. 2, 701, jam jam nulla mora est.

3. hŏdiē (<i>in the present day</i>): cf. Cic.
Rep. 2, 2, <i>fin.</i>, omnes qui <i>tum</i> eos agros,
ubi <i>hodie</i> est haec urbs, etc.: Tac. So
in praesenti (less good impraesentiarum),
<i>at present</i>: Cic.: Nep.: v. <f>PRESENT</f>. (In
praesens = <i>for the present</i>.)

II. As
correl., <i>now ... now</i>:

1. mŏdo ...
mŏdo: <i>(to say) n. this, n. that</i>, m. hoc,
m. illud dicere, Cic. N. D. 1, 18, 47:
<i>step n. quick, n. slow</i>, citus m., m. tardus
incessus, Sall. Cat. 15. Instead of the
second modo occurs, interdum, Sall. Jug.
62; aliquando, Tac. A. 1, 81.

2.
nunc ... nunc ...: <i>n. on this side, n.
on that</i>, n. hac parte, n. illac, Liv. 34,
13, <i>init.</i>: Virg.: Curt.

3. ălias in
connexion with alius, aliter: <i>n. one way,
n. another</i>, alias aliter, Cic. Inv. 2, 13,
45. (For which alio tempore may be
used.)

III. As particle of transition:

1. nunc (indicating the matter that
comes immediately after): <i>n. I will reply
to your letters</i>, n. respondebo ad epistolas
tuas, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 2: <i>let us n.
look at what is more recondite</i>, n. interiora
videamus, id. Div. 2, 60, <i>init.</i>: but
nunc is rarely so used as to depart entirely
from its proper sense as an adv.
of time: the foll. is an example of its
doing so: <i>n., I should wish you to understand</i>,
n. velim tibi persuadeas ..., id.
Fam. 15, 4, 2. Note also the phr. age
nunc, <i>come now!</i> in calling attention to
what follows. (N.B.--Nunc vero is not
used merely by way of transition: cf.
Cic. Cat. 1, 7, <i>init.</i>, nunc vero quae tua
est ista vita? i. e. <i>at this very time, etc.</i>:
ib. Verr. 5, 67, nunc vero, quum tibi
loquar ..., i. e. <i>but at the</i> present time:
et <i>pass.</i>

2. jam (implying not <i>merely</i>
a transition of thought, but one in which
what follows is to be emphasised): <i>n.
you are all pretty well aware of this</i>,
jam hoc fere scitis omnes, Cic. Clu. 16,
46: cf. id. Man. 14, 42, <i>jam</i> quantum
consilio valeat, vos, Quirites, etc.: ib.
<i>paulo infr.</i>, humanitate <i>jam</i> tanta est
... (= <i>now</i>; or, <i>and then</i>): also Clu.
-----File: b0504r.png------------------------------------------------------
13, 36, jam, ut Romae vixerint, <i>now, how
they lived at Rome, etc.</i>

3. autem
(esp. in arguments, to indicate the steps
by which a conclusion is reached: never
the first word in a sentence):[**P2: dot missing] cf. Cic.
Top. 14, 56, aut hoc, aut illud; hoc
<i>autem</i>: non igitur illud, <i>it is either this
or that</i>: <i>n., it is this; therefore it is not
that</i>: also in the turns of a narrative:
cf. Cic. Clu. 13, 37, Asinius autem brevi
illo tempore, occiditur, i. e. <i>now, Asinius
shortly afterwards, etc.</i>: v. <f>MOREOVER</f>,
<f>BUT</f>[**F2: is this one phrase, 1 set of tags?].

4. sed (usu. denoting a greater
transition than autem: freq. in Sall.)[** :]
cf. Sall. Cat. 23, <i>init.</i>, sed in his erat
Sempronia, <i>n., among these, etc.</i>: also ib.
41, <i>init.</i>; 43, <i>med.</i>

5. quĭdem, or, with
<i>1 pers. sing.</i> and <i>pl.</i>, ĕquĭdem (= <i>it is
true, no doubt</i>; and indicating a counter

51, <i>ad med.</i>: ib. <i>paulo infr.</i>, de poena
possumus equidem dicere ...: sed, per
deos immortales! ..., <i>n., it is true, we
might say, etc.</i>: v. <f>INDEED</f>.

6. stronger
than quidem, and usu. denoting contrast
with something before, vēro (never first
in a sentence): cf. Liv. 26, 11, <i>med.</i>, id
vero adeo superbum atque indignum
visum, <i>n., this (really) seemed so insulting,
etc.</i>: also in exhortation and calling
attention, age vero! <i>come n.!</i> Cic. Man.
14.[**P2: ,] 40.

7. only as enclit., dum (in
calling attention): <i>Sosia, come n.! I

4, 27: Cic.

8. porro: esp. in phr., age
porro! <i>come n.!</i> (to call attention): Cic.

9. tandem: v. <f>PRAY</f>.


<b>now and then</b>: ălĭquando, nonnunquam,

O.


<b>O</b>, <b>OH</b>:

1. O: (i). used in addressing
a deity or (less freq.) any other
person (with <i>voc.</i>): <i>O Romulus,
Romulus divine!</i> O Romule, Romule
die! Enn.: <i>O thou light of Dardan
land!</i> O lux Dardaniae! Virg. Aen. 2,
281: <i>O my (dear) Furnius!</i> O mi Furni!
Cic. Fam. 10, 26. (ii). in exclamations
(usu. with <i>acc.</i>): <i>oh, fine guardian of
the sheep!</i> O praeclarum ovium custodem!
Cic. Ph. 3, 11, 27: <i>oh, wretched
me!</i> O me perditum! id. Fam. 14, 4.
Less freq. with <i>nom.</i>: <i>oh, what a figure!</i>
O qualis facies! Juv. 10, 157: Ter.
(iii). in wishes, with si, utinam: = <i>oh
if[**space?]...! oh that[**space?]...! oh, if Jove would
recal[** recall|P2: no] my past years!</i> O mihi praeteritos
referat si Jupiter annos! Virg. Aen. 8,
560: Ov. M. 1, 363 (O utinam possim...!).

2. oh (not to be confounded
with preced.: it denotes <i>surprise,
joy,[**P2: ,] grief</i>, acc. to the intonation:
only in the comic writers): <i>oh! you
are unfair ...</i>, oh! iniquus es, Ter.
Heaut. 5,[**P2: ,] 3, 8: repeated, as <i>a lament</i>,
oh,[**P2: ,] oh, oh! Pl. Capt. 2, 1, 6.

3. ŏhē[** ŏbē?]
-----File: b0506r.png------------------------------------------------------
(<i>ho! holla!</i>): <i>oh! that's enough!</i> ohe!
jam satis est! Hor. S. 1, 5, 12.

4.
proh, pro (denoting <i>wonder</i> or <i>lamentation</i>:
with <i>voc.</i> to denote an appeal;
otherwise with <i>acc.</i>): <i>O ye immortal
gods!</i> pro dii immortales! Cic. Man. 12,
33.[**P1: should be :] <i>O Jupiter! the folly of the man!</i>
pro Jupiter! hominis stultitiam, Ter.
Ad. 3, 3, 12.

5. expr. by <i>voc.</i> alone
to denote <i>address</i>; by <i>acc.</i> alone to denote
<i>surprise, indignation, etc.</i>: <i>O thou
fostering Sun!</i> alme Sol! Hor. Car.
Saec. 9[**P1: missing :] Virg.: <i>O admirable witnesses</i>,
testes egregios! Cic. Coel. 26, 63: <i>O once
happy Roman generals!</i> beatos quondam
duces Romanos! Tac. A. 11, 20.

<b>object</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

I. <i>That about which

II.
<i>Any external thing</i>: res; or expr. by

III. <i>That on which any

1. expr.

<i>to be the o. of any one's hatred</i>, esse

Sall. Jug. 75, <i>fin.</i>: <i>to be an o. of mockery</i>,
ludibrio esse alicui, Liv. 2, 23: cf. L. G.
§ 297.

2. expr. by verbal subs. in

3.

voice: <i>Alexis was the o. of Corydon's

<b>object</b> (<i>v.</i>):

I. <i>To offer an objection</i>:

1. expr. by dīco, xi, ctum, 3:

<b>objection</b>:

I. <i>A counter statement</i>:

1. expr. by dīco, 3: <i>the o.s

2. <i>a quibbling o.</i>, captio:

II. <i>Difficulty</i> or

1.
expr. <i>to have no o.</i>, by non recusare, non

2.

3.
mŏra (strictly, <i>delay</i>; hence, <i>cause of

13. (Not Cic. in this sense.)

v. <f>HINDRANCE</f>. Phr.: <i>I

<b>of</b>:

I. Denoting the relation of one
subs. to another:

1. expr. by gen.:
<i>pass.</i> N.B.--This constr. cannot be used
(<i>a</i>) when the latter subs. denotes the
same thing as the former (apposition:
as, urbs Roma, insula Tenedos, where
the gen. can never stand): nor (<i>b</i>) when
the latter subs. denotes a <i>quality</i> of the
former, except when an adj. is attached
to the latter (hence, <i>a man of genius</i>,
vir ingeniosus <i>or</i> vir magni ingenii:
<i>never</i> vir ingenii): nor (<i>c</i>) when the
latter subs. denotes the <i>material</i> of
which the former is made (<i>a statue of
marble</i>, statua marmorea, never statua
marmoris): nor (<i>d</i>) in indicating the
place of any one's birth (<i>a man of
Athens</i>, Atheniensis; never vir Athenarum).

2. sometimes instead of gen.
a prep. may be used, to define more
exactly the relation between the two
subss.: e. g. <i>the news of (= concerning)
the death of Titurius had not yet reached
him</i>, nondum ad eum fama de Titurii
morte perlata, Caes. B. G. 5, 39: <i>much
flattery of (= addressed to) Augusta on
the part of the Senate</i>, multa patrum in
Augustam adulatio, Tac. A. 1[** ,?|P3 yes] 14: <i>fear
of (arising from, caused by) the Emperor</i>,
metus ex Imperatore, ib. 11, 20
(a constr. not to be imitated).

II. In
partitive sense:

1. expr. by <i>gen.</i>
(after all words which denote <i>a part of
a number</i>; including comparatives and
superlatives, Zumpt § 429): <i>that at
least one of the consuls should be appointed
from the commons</i>, ut consulum
utique alter ex plebe crearetur, Liv. 6,
35, <i>med.</i>: so also with uterque: <i>you
will greatly oblige both of us</i>, utrique
nostrum gratum admodum feceris, Cic.
Am. 4, 16 (but in <i>pl.</i>, hi utrique, <i>both
of these</i>; not horum utrique): <i>thou
mightiest of princes</i>, maxime principum!
Hor. Od. 4, 14, 6: <i>the elder of (two)
young men</i>, major juvenum, id. A. P.
366: Cic.[** :?|P3 yes] <i>(to do anything) best of all</i>,
optime omnium, Cic. Fam. 4, 13, <i>extr.</i>
(N.B.--This constr. is not used with
words signifying <i>a part of a single
whole</i>; in which case an adj. usu. occurs
in agr. with subs.: e. g. <i>the top, bottom
of a tree</i>, summa, ima arbor, etc.: L. G.
§ 341.)

2. expr. by preps. de, ex, and
less freq. inter: <i>a few of our men are
slain</i>, pauci de nostris cadunt, Caes. B. G.
1, 15: <i>one of them</i>, unus de illis, Cic. Mil.
24, 65: <i>one of the many (the common
herd)</i>, unus de multis, id. Off. 1, 30, 109
(also, unus e multis, id. Fin. 2, 20, <i>fin.</i>):
<i>the keenest of all the senses</i>, acerrimus ex
omnibus sensibus, id. de Or. 2, 87, 357:
<i>one of the soldiers</i>, quidam ex militibus,
Caes. B. G. 1, 42: <i>Croesus richest of
kings</i>, ille Croesus opulentissimus inter
reges, Sen. Contr.: Mela. N.B.--(1).
Instead of either the gen. or a prep.,
must be used an adj. in agreement with
its subs., when <i>the whole are included</i>:
e. g., <i>but a few of us survive</i>, nos pauci
supersumus: cf. Cic. Ph. 2, 6, 13, veniamus
ad vivos, <i>qui duo</i> e consularium
numero reliqui sunt, i. e. <i>two of whom</i>:
so, <i>how many are there of you?</i> quot
estis? the prep. <i>of</i> denoting a kind of
apposition, not separation. (2). After
the dualizing words alter, uter, neuter,
uterque, the <i>gen.</i> is preferred: after a
superlative, the <i>gen.</i> denotes absolute,
unqualified superiority, as a thing beyond
doubt: when de <i>or</i> ex is used, the
objects compared are placed more on a
level. (3). After words not included in
the preced. two cases, the use of a prep.
is usual in prose, not of a genitive.

III. To denote <i>the material of which
a thing is made</i>:

1. ex: esp. after
the verb facio: <i>a statue of bronze</i>, statua
ex aere facta, Cic. Verr. 2, 21, 50: Varr.:
also without facio: <i>cups of gold</i>, pocula
ex auro, ib. 4, 27, 62 (but this constr. is
less fit for common prose).

2. de
(mostly poet.: constr. like preced.): <i>a</i>
-----File: b0513l.png------------------------------------------------------
<i>statue (made) of marble</i>, factum de
marmore signum, Ov. M. 14, 313: <i>I will
build a temple of marble</i>, templum de
marmore ponam, Virg. G. 3, 13: Tib.
So of transformations: <i>to make a captive
of a king</i>, captivum de rege facere,
Just. 7, 2.

3. expr. by adjj. in -eus,
-nus: e. g. <i>made of wood, marble, fir,
oak</i>, ligneus, marmoreus, abiegnus, ilignus,
etc.: v. <f>WOODEN</f>, etc.

IV. Denoting
quality <i>or</i> description:

1.
expr. by <i>gen.</i> or <i>abl.</i>, but only when the
latter subs. has an adj. joined with it
(L. G. §§ 274, 318): <i>a man of the highest
talents</i>, vir summae indolis <i>or</i> summa
indole; summi ingenii <i>or</i> summo ingenio:
<i>pass.</i>

2. when the second subs.
has no <i>adj.</i>, represent the Eng. subs. by
an adj.: thus, <i>a thing of beauty</i>, res
pulchra; id quod pulchrum est: see corresponding
adjj.

V. To denote cause:
expr. by <i>abl.</i>: <i>e[**P1: missing .] g.</i> <i>to die of a disease,
of hunger, of cold</i>, morbo, inedia, frigore
perire: L. G. § 311.

VI. = <i>About,
with reference to</i>: de: v. <f>CONCERNING</f>.

VII. Inseparable from certain verbs;
as <i>to smell of, taste of, consist of</i>: v. <f>TO
SMELL</f>, etc.


<b>off</b> (<i>prep.</i> and <i>adv.</i>):

I. Adv., <i>at
a distance</i>: usu. with words denoting
distance: as, <i>far off, a long way off</i>,
prŏcul, longē: <i>to be a long way off</i>,
longe abesse: v. <f>FAR</f>, <f>DISTANT</f>.

II.
As modifying the sense of certain verbs:
e. g. <i>to bear off</i>, auferre; <i>to come off
(victorious, etc.)</i>, discedere; <i>to make off</i>,
se in pedes conjicere, etc.: see the
several verbs.

III. As <i>interj.</i>: Phr.:
<i>off with you!</i> aufer te modo! Pl. Rud.
4, 3, 104: hinc vos amolimini! Ter.
Andr. 4, 2, 24. See also <f>AWAY</f>.

IV.
Of geographical position, <i>lying at a little
distance from the coast</i>:

1. expr. by
objăceo, ui, 2 (<i>to lie opposite</i> or <i>off</i>); in
connexion with which may be used
<i>p. part.</i> objectus, <i>lying off</i> (with <i>dat.</i> or
contra and <i>acc.</i>): <i>(islands) which lie off
the promontory of Taurus</i>, quae contra
Tauri promontorium objacent, Mela 2,
7: <i>these (islands) lie off the coasts of
Thracia and Greece</i>, hae Thracum Graiorumque
terris objacent, ib.: <i>Leuce, lying
off the mouth of the Borysthenes</i>, Leuce
Borysthenis ostio objecta, ib. In sim.
sense, adjaceo, <i>to lie close to</i>: <i>they lie off
the coasts of Asia</i>, Asiaticis regionibus
adjacent, ib.

2. contra: v. <f>OPPOSITE
TO</f>.

3. prŏcul: usu. denoting <i>a considerable
distance</i>, but used by Virg. of
places <i>lying off, but in view</i> (pro oculis):
cf. Aen. 5, 124, est procul in pelago
saxum spumantia contra littora: also
id. E. 6, 16.

V. Denoting <i>condition,
supplies, etc.</i>: Phr.: <i>to be well off for
provisions, for the necessaries of life</i>,
frumento commeatuque abundare; iis
rebus quae sunt necessariae (ad vitam)
abundare, cf. Cic. Sen. 16, 56 (villa
abundat porco, etc.): <i>to be badly off for
provisions</i>, a re frumentaria laborare,
Caes. B. G. 7, 10: <i>he was poorly off even
for fodder</i>, ne pabuli quidem satis magna
copia suppetebat, ib. 1, 16: <i>to see that
(the community) are well off for all the
necessaries of life</i>, consulere ut earum
copia rerum sit, quae sunt necessariae,
Cic. Off. 2, 21, 74: <i>to be well off for leisure</i>,
otio abundare, id. de Or. 1, 6, 22:
<i>Athens was well off for writers of genius</i>,
provenere (Athenis) scriptorum magna
ingenia, Sall. Cat. 8 (so, <i>to be badly off</i>
may be expr. by minus provenire).

3. expr. by such

<i>something to rest on</i>): e. g. <i>on

when that which supports is at the

<b>on</b> (<i>adv.</i>):

I. <i>Forward</i>: porro: v.
<f>FORWARD</f>. <i>To go or move on</i>, procedo,
pergo: v. <f>TO PROCEED</f>.

II. <i>Continually</i>:
usque: <i>we will drink on till daylight</i>,
usque ad diurnam stellam potabimus,
Pl. Men. 1, 2, 62: also absol., <i>I with being
beaten on, and he with beating on, are
pretty well tired</i>, ego vapulando ille verberando
usque, ambo defessi sumus,
Ter. Ad. 2, 2, 5. Sometimes expr. by
de, ex, in comp.: cf. deproeliantes venti,
<i>the winds battling on</i>, Hor. Od. 1, 9, 11.

V. In
contrast to <i>the other</i>:

1. hic, foll. by
ille (when hic denotes <i>that which is at
present under consideration</i>): cf. Cic.
Am. 2, 10, <i>hujus</i> facta, <i>illius</i> dicta laudantur,
i. e. <i>the deeds of the one (<f>viz.</f>
Cato; who is the subject of discourse),
the speeches of the other</i>: Smith's Lat.
Dict. s. v. hic (4).

2. alter ... alter;
or when more than two persons (or
things) are spoken of, ălius ... ălius:
<i>the o. (mind) is shared by us with the
gods, the other (body) with brutes</i>, alterum
nobis cum dis, alterum cum beluis commune
est, Sall. Cat. <i>init.</i>: <i>o. thing is
nature to a horse, another to an ox,
another to a man</i>, aliud equo est natura,
aliud bovi, aliud homini, Cic. Fin. 5, 9,
26: when <i>difference</i> or <i>contrast</i> is indicated,
alius ... alius may even be used
of two objects: cf. Cic. Coel. 3, 6, aliud
est maledicere, aliud accusare (where
alterum would have been much less
forcible). Alius also sometimes follows
aliquis: cf. Cic. Tusc. 4, 28, 60, putat
<i>aliquis</i>, esse voluptatem bonum: <i>alius</i>
autem pecuniam (where aliquis is however
more definite than alius would be.[**P1: really :?|P3 yes]
referring to Epicurus). (N.B.--Alius
often occurs in different cases in the
same sentence = <i>one ... one; other ...
other</i>: e. g. alium alio mittit: <i>he sends
o. in o. direction, and another in another</i>,
alium alio mittit, Sall. Cat. 27: see L. G.
§§ 629, 692.)

3. expr. <i>one ... the other,
one another</i>, either by (1). inter se [se
inter se, in Cic. Am. 22, 82, is prob. a
false reading]: <i>the young Ciceros love o.
another</i>, Cicerones pueri amant inter se,
Cic. Att. 6, 1, 9: <i>the soldiers embrace o.
another with tears</i>, complecti inter se
lacrimantes milites, Liv. 7, 42, <i>med.</i>: or
by (2). alter, alius ... with another case
of the same pronoun: <i>the o. needs the
help of the other</i>, alterum alterius auxilio
eget, Sall. Cat. 1, <i>extr.</i>: <i>o. stimulates
the other</i>, alius alium hortari, ib. 6.

4. expr. <i>one or the other</i> by altĕrŭter,
tra, trum (also with both parts of the
word decl.: rare): <i>you must be either
the o[**P1: missing .] or the other</i>, est necesse alterutrum
(te esse), Cic. Div. Verr. 18, 58: Hor.
Phr.: <i>o. good turn deserves another</i>

12, pref.: cf. Ter. Ph. 2, 1, 37, tradunt

<f>MUTUALLY</f>, <f>IN TURN</f>): <i>at o. time ... at

1, 18, 47: Ter. (v. <f>NOW</f>): <i>to love o.

VI. Equivalent to German <f>man</f>[**fraktur?];

2. expr.
by <i>impers. pass.</i> (of intrans. verbs), and

VII. In strictly

aut; = <i>either ... or</i>: a preceding aut
is not found when what follows is rather
an afterthought than an alternative primarily
entertained: cf. Cels. 1, 2, exercitationis
plerumque finis esse debet
sudor, <i>aut</i> certe lassitudo, <i>a perspiration;
or, at least, fatigue</i>: add Cic. Div.
2, 26, <i>init.</i> Sometimes aut = <i>or else</i>;
when a sudden turn is given to the discourse:
cf. Cic. de Or. 2, 2, 5, omnia ...
bene ei sunt dicenda, qui hoc se posse
profitetur, <i>aut</i> eloquentiae nomen relinquendum
est, <i>or else he must abandon, etc.</i>

2. vĕl, freq. following another
vel; = <i>whether ... or</i>: denoting not, as
aut usually does, a distinct alternative,
but rather one which is compatible with
the former one: L. G. § 570. -ve is
simply an abbreviated form of vel,
being used enclitically: L. G. § 570,
<i>Obs.</i> 2.

3. sīve (seu): both with and
without an antecedent sive (seu):
usually indicating an indifference between
two alternatives: v. <f>WHETHER</f>.
[Kr. thus sums up the uses of the
above:--The particle <i>aut</i> distinguishes
-----File: b0522m.png------------------------------------------------------
objects or sentences, which are either
actually opposed, or at least regarded
as quite different: <i>vel</i> indicates that it
is, <i>in the given case</i>, indifferent which of
the objects or predications is accepted;
whether they differ or not in themselves
being another question: <i>-ve</i> distinguishes
mostly single words, less
frequently sentences; and denotes a less
important verbal or real difference:
<i>sive</i> is used (1) when an option is given
between two or more names or predicates
of the same thing; and (2) when
the writer, himself hesitating between
two or more causes, conditions, etc.,
leaves the reader to accept which alternative
he chooses.]

II. In interrogative
sentences:

1. ăn, following utrum
or -ne in the former part of the double
question: <i>is it money that makes you
prouder, or (the fact) that the commander
consults you?</i> utrum te superbiorem
pecunia facit, an quod te imperator
consulit? Cic. Fam. 7, 13: <i>am I
to go to Rome, or stay here?</i> Romamne
venio, an hic maneo? id. Att. 16, 8:
sometimes, esp. in dependent questions,
the antecedent <i>whether</i> is not expressed:
<i>shall I speak out or hold my peace?</i>
eloquar an sileam? Virg. Aen. 3, 39:
<i>to doubt whether anything be right or
wrong</i>, dubitare aequum sit quicquam
an iniquum, Cic. Off. 1, 9, <i>fin.</i>

2. -nĕ
(infreq.): <i>it was uncertain whether they
had conquered or been conquered</i>, incertum
fuit vicerint, victine essent, Liv.
5, 28, <i>med.</i>: Nep. Esp. in the expr.,
<i>or no</i>, necne: v. <i>infr.</i> (4, 2).

3. pleonastically,
annĕ (infreq.)[** :?|P3 yes] <i>to ask whether
there are few or many</i>, interrogare pauca
sint anne multa, Cic. Ac. 2, 29[**P1: missing ,] 93.

4.
expr. <i>or not, or no</i>, by (1). annon (or as
two words): <i>is it the person I am in
search of or not?</i> isne est quem quaero
annon? Ter. Ph. 5, 6, 12: Cic. (2). less
freq. necnĕ (in questions expressed by
<i>whether ... or no</i>): <i>the question arises,
whether or no there are gods</i>, quaeritur
sintne dii necne sint.[**P1: should be ,] Cic. N. D. 1, 22, 61:
also without the verb being repeated:
<i>whether battle could be advantageously
joined or no</i>, utrum proelium committi
ex usu esset, necne, Caes. B. G. 1, 50.
(N.B.--Never aut in questions.)

<b>ought</b> (<i>v.</i>):

1. dēbeo, 2 (denoting
<i>obligation</i>, in the most general way):
Cic.: Caes. (<i>pass.</i>).

2.[**P2: .] ŏportet, uit,[**P2: ,] 2
(of <i>moral obligation</i>: with Eng. subject
in <i>acc.</i>, foll. by <i>infin.</i>): <i>those who o. to have
been put to the sword</i>, quos ferro trucidari

to have humoured the young man</i>, adolescenti
gestum (fuisse) morem oportuit,
Ter. Ad. 2, 2, 6. Less freq. is subj. after
oportet, <f>WITHOUT CONJ.</f>: cf. Cic. de Or.
1, 6, 20, ex rerum cognitione efflorescat
et redundet oratio oportet: Hor. Ep. 1,
2, 49. N.B.--(1). <i>Ought to have ...</i> is
regularly expr. by perf. of debeo or
oportet, foll. by <i>imperf. infin.</i>, as pecunia
quam his oportuit <i>dari</i> (not datam
esse), <i>the money which o. to have been
given</i>. The use of the <i>perf. infin.</i> in
such cases refers to <i>the completion of the</i>
-----File: b0526m.png------------------------------------------------------
<i>act</i> referred to rather than the doing of it:
cf. Cic. Cat. 1, 2, 6, hoc quod jam pridem
factum esse oportuit[**unclear], <i>which o. to have
been done out of hand long since</i>. (2).
The use of the <i>past imperf. indic.</i>,
debebam, oportebat.[**P2: ,] is often conditional,
indicating that something <i>o. to have been
done which has not been done</i> (= Gr.
ἐχρῆν): cf. L. G. § 428, <i>Obs.</i>

3. expr.
by <i>gerund. part.</i>: v. <f>MUST</f> (2).

4.
sometimes.[**P2: ,] dĕcet, 2: v. <f>BECOMES</f> (it).
(N.B.--Ought <i>not</i> may be expr. by non
lĭcet.[**P2: ,] nĕfas est: v. <f>LAWFUL</f>, <f>UNLAWFUL</f>.)


<b>ought</b> (<i>pron.</i>): more correctly, <i>aught</i>:

<b>own</b> (<i>adj.</i>): always preceded by
<i>my</i>, <i>thy</i>, <i>his</i>, <i>our</i>, <i>your</i>, <i>their</i>, or some
other possessive word:

1. expr. by
<i>gen.</i> of ipse: <i>with my, his, o. hand</i>, mea,

ipsorum sanguine, Cic. Man. 11, 30,
et <i>pass.</i> Also the <i>pron.</i> ipse freq. stands
in apposition with subject, instead of
being put in <i>gen.</i>: <i>he cut off his o. legs</i>,
*ipse sua crura amputavit (not sua
ipsius crura): for rules applying to such
cases, comp. <f>HIMSELF</f>.

2. when a
contrast gives prominence to the <i>pron.</i>
-----File: b0531m.png------------------------------------------------------
<i>adj.</i>, meus, tuus, suus, etc. are sufficiently
emphatic without any addition: e. g. <i>to
defend the interests of their allies, not

<i>grasping what belonged to others; lavish

3. the <i>pron. adj.</i> is
sometimes strengthened by suffixes,

<b>person</b>:

I. <i>A human being</i>:

1.
hŏmo, ĭnis, <i>c.</i>; which, esp. in <i>pl.</i>, is often
sufficiently indicated by the gender of
an <i>adj.</i> or <i>pron.</i>: <i>one of the advocati,
a p. of the highest character</i>, quidam ex
advocatis, homo summa virtute praeditus,
Cic. Clu. 63, 177: <i>many p.s</i>,
multi; <i>some p.s</i>, nonnulli, etc.: <i>passim</i>.

2. esp. in enumerations, căput, ĭtis,
<i>n.</i>: <i>8000 p.s, free and slaves</i>, octo millia
liberorum servorumque capitum, Liv.
29, 29: Caes.: <i>common p.s (the mass of
the people)</i>, ignota c., Liv. 3, 7, <i>init.</i> Also
comicé: <i>a nice, jolly p.</i>, lepidum c., Ter.
Ad. 5, 9, 9, etc.

3. similar to caput,
and used chiefly in general descriptions,
corpus, ŏris, <i>n.</i>: <i>free p.s</i>, libera c., Liv.
29, 21, <i>med.</i>: <i>to consign a free p. to
bondage</i>, liberum c. in servitutem addicere,
id. 3, 56, <i>med.</i>

4. persōna (denoting
<i>not</i> a person <i>individually</i>, but <i>as
coming under a certain description</i>): <i>he
did away with the use of litters except
for certain p.s and ages</i>, lecticarum
usum nisi certis p. et aetatibus ademit,
Suet. Caes. 43: <i>p.s in humbler rank</i>,
minores p., id. Tib. 32.

II. In legal
sense, as opp. to <i>things</i>: persōna: cf.
Paul. Dig. 1, 5, 1, omne jus vel ad personas
pertinet vel ad res: cf. Smith's Ant.
s. v. actio.

III. With ref. to <i>rank</i> or
<i>importance</i>: Phr.: <i>to have respect to
p.s</i>, in personam (hominum) per gratiam
et preces exorabilem esse, Suet. Aug.
27, <i>init.</i>: *dignitatis hominum magis
quam aequi et boni rationem habere, cf.
Cic. de Or. 2, 4, 17 (dignitatis habere
rationem alone does not necessarily
denote anything improper): personam
accipere (not class.), Vulg. Jac. ii. 9
(= Gr. προσωπολημπτεῖν); *dignitatis
nobilitatisque magis quam justitiae observantem
esse. (Personae servire [R.
and A.], in Cic. Off. 3, 29, 106 = <i>to adhere
faithfully to a character</i>.)

IV.
<i>The body</i>:

1. corpus, ŏris, <i>n.</i>: <i>(Dionysius)
entrusted the keeping of his p.
to barbarians</i>, barbaris corporis custodiam

<i>to prostitute the p. for hire</i>, quaestum
corpore facere, Pl. Poen. 5, 3, 21: <i>attention
to the p. (personal habits)</i>, corporis
cura, Suet. Caes. 45.

2. forma
(<i>exterior, shape</i>; usu. implying <i>comeliness
or beauty</i>): <i>a maiden of remarkable
beauty of p.</i>, virgo formâ excellens,
Liv. 3, 44: <i>p. and exterior worthy of a
gentleman</i>, f. ac species liberalis, Cic.
Coel. 3, 6: Plin. In sim. sense, facies:
<i>a woman of singular beauty of p.</i>, mulier
f. eximiâ, Cic. Verr. 5, 31, 82.

3.
spĕcies, ēi (<i>exterior</i>): esp. with other
subss. descriptive of the person: e. g.
species et motus atque ipse amictus, id.
Br. 62, 224; forma et species et statura

[apposita ad dignitatem], Auct. Her. 4,
47, 60.

V. Periphrastically, usu. with
ref. to <i>people of rank</i>: expr. by <i>pers.
pron.</i>: <i>he had 300 unarmed youths in
attendance upon his p.</i>, trecentos inermes
juvenes circa se habebat, Liv. 29, 1,
<i>init.</i>: Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 48, 126: in similar

VI. <i>Actual self</i>; esp. in phr[**P1: missing .], <i>in
person</i>: expr. by ipse: <i>only with the

non nisi cum ipso coram duce Romano,

<b>personally</b>:

1. phĭlŏlŏgus (<i>a man

1. phĭlŏsŏphĭcus

2. phĭlŏsŏphus

Cic. (?): v. <i>supr.</i> (N.B.--Not to be
used = <i>pertaining to philosophy</i>; which

3. expr. by
phĭlŏsŏphia, phĭlŏsŏphi: <i>p. works</i>, libri

<b>philosophy</b>:

I. <i>Reasoned truth</i>:

1. phĭlŏsŏphia (Gk. φιλοσοφία):
defined by Cic. as, studium sapientiae,
de Off. 2, 2, 5: also used to denote
<i>different departments or schools of philosophy</i>:
<i>moral p.</i>, p. moralis, Sen. Ep.
89, 8 (suggested by Cic. Fat. <i>init.</i>, as a
substitute for the circuml., ea pars philosophiae
quae de moribus est): <i>natural
p.</i>, p. naturalis, Sen. l. c.: <i>theoretical or
practical p.</i>, p. contemplativa (= Gk.
θεωρητική), activa (Gk. πρακτική), Sen.
Ep. 95, 10: <i>two (different) p.s</i>, duae p.,
Cic. Off. 3, 27, 107.

2. săpientia
(strictly, <i>that wisdom or knowledge of
which <f>philosophia is</f> the desire and aim</i>:
cf. Cic. Leg. 1, 22, 58: hence = <i>p. on its
practical side, as wisdom attained</i>): <i>p.
offers herself as the surest guide to pleasure</i>,
p. certissimam se ducem praebet
ad voluptatem, Cic. Fin. 1, 13, 43:
<i>ancient p. taught only what was to be
done and what avoided</i>, antiqua s. nihil
aliud nisi facienda et vitanda praecepit,
Sen. Ep. 95, 13.

3. rătio (<i>theory</i>):
<i>impious principles of p.</i>, impia rationis
elementa, Lucr. 1, 82: <i>the Epicurean p.
(system) which is well known to most</i>,
Epicuri r. quae plerisque notissima est,
Cic. Fin. 1, 5, <i>init.</i>: so, Stoicorum ratio
disciplinaque, id. Off. 3, 4, 20.

II.
<i>The principle of anything</i>: rătio: v.
<f>THEORY</f>, <f>PRINCIPLE</f>.

<b>police</b>:

I. <i>The entire regulations
for maintaining order, etc., in a city</i>:
*securitatis urbanae cura, custodia,
tutela: cf. Vell. 2, 98, <i>init.</i>

II. <i>The
officials</i>: no term exactly corresponding
to Eng., the duties of our police being
distributed: <i>night p.</i>, vĭgĭles, Suet. Aug.
30: <i>their controlling officer</i>, praefectus
vigilum, Dig. 1, 15: by day, the lictors
and apparitors of the magistrates acted
as a kind of police (v. Smith's Dict. Ant.
s. vv.[** typo? v.|P2: no; plural]): also the vigiles had certain <i>day
duties</i>, as for example, <i>to keep watch
over the clothes of bathers</i>, Paul. Dig. 1,
15, 3 § 5: <i>the care of the markets</i> under
the emperors was assigned to the Praefectus
urbis, Ulp. Dig. 1,[**P2: ,] 12, 1 § 11
(originally under the aediles and their
officials): <i>the infliction of punishments</i>
devolved upon the triumviri capitales
(v. Dict. Ant. s. v.): and all these terms
may serve in their place. N.B.--Perhaps
the best word for gen. use is vigiles.

etc.: v. <f>TO MAINTAIN</f> (VII.).


<b>positive</b>:

I. <i>Explicit, peremptory</i>:
perh. dīrectus (<i>straightforward</i>): cf.
Liv. 21, 19, <i>init.</i>, d. percunctatio et denuntiatio
belli. Join: directum, simplex,
Cic. R. Com. 4, 11. See also
<f>EXPLICIT</f>.

II. <i>Having certainty</i>:
certus, firmus: v. <f>CERTAIN</f>, <f>SURE</f>. Phr.:
<i>I cannot give any p. information about
them</i>, de iis haud facile compertum narraverim,
Sall. Jug. 17. As tech. term in
phil.: *positivus: <i>p. philosophy</i>, *philosophia
positiva quam volunt, perhibent.

III. Opp. <i>negative</i>: affirmātīvus
(late): Diom. (Cic. uses aiens, opp.
negans: Top. 11, 49).

IV. <i>Confident
in assertion</i>: expr. by affirmo, 1: <i>not
to be p. about anything</i>, nihil af., Cic.
Div. 2, 2, 8. <i>A p. statement</i>, affirmatio,
id. Off. 3, 29, 104: v. <f>POSITIVELY</f>.

V.
In grammar: pŏsĭtīvus: Prisc. 3, <i>init.</i>
(The older term was absolutus; as epith.
of substantives: e. g. abs. nomen, <i>a noun
in the p. degree</i>, cf. Quint. 9, 3, 19; but
positivus is required as gram. term <i>only</i>.)


<b>positively</b>:

I. <i>Expressly</i>: dĭsertē:
Liv.: v. <f>EXPLICITLY</f>.

II. <i>With strong
asseveration</i>:

1. affirmātē: Cic. Off.
3, 29, 104: Gell.

2. affirmanter
(rare): Gell.

3. with verbs of <i>affirming</i>,
firmĭter, firmē: <i>to assert most p.</i>,
firmissime asseverare, Cic. Att. 10, 14.

4. constanter (like preced.): Suet.
Vesp. 5 (constantissime asseverare).
Phr.: <i>to assert p.</i>, affirmare, asseverare
(v. <f>TO ASSERT</f>, <f>MAINTAIN</f>): <i>to deny most p.</i>,
[cum] multa affirmatione negare, Curt. 6,
11, <i>fin.</i>

III. <i>Certainly</i>:

1. certo (<i>of
a certainty</i>): <i>not to expect anything as
if it must p. come to pass</i>, nihil ita exspectare
quasi c. futurum, Cic. Tusc. 5,
28, 81.

2. expr. by compertus, certus:
<i>to know nothing whatever p.</i>, nihil habere
cogniti, nihil comperti, Cic. Clu. 47, 131:
<i>to promise p.</i>, pro comperto polliceri,
Suet. Ner. 31.[**P1: unclear|P3 clear on TIA]

IV. Opp. to <i>negatively</i>:
perh. *affirmātīvē (as logical term).
Phr.: <i>To be negatively rather than p.
virtuous</i>, *magis carere vitiis quam virtutibus
ornari. <i>In positive degree</i>: absolūtē;
or expr. by <i>part. adj.</i> absolutus:
v. <f>POSITIVE</f> (<i>fin.</i>)

<b>positiveness</b>: in assertion, affirmātio:
v. <f>POSITIVELY</f> (I.).


<b>possess</b>:

I. <i>To have as one's own</i>:

1. expr. by sum, with <i>dat.</i> of Eng.
subject, or in the case of bodily or mental
features, by <i>gen.</i> or <i>abl.</i> of quality: v.
<f>TO HAVE</f>.

2. possĭdeo, sēdi, ssum, 2
(in strict legal sense, denoting no more
than <i>the holding of property</i>: also in
gen. sense): <i>to p. much wealth</i>, multa
p., Hor. Od. 4, 9, 45. Absol., <i>to p. landed
property</i>: Callist. Dig. 47, 9, 7 (juxta
littora p.).

3. tĕneo, 2: v. <f>TO HOLD</f>,
<f>OCCUPY</f>.

II. <i>To seize, occupy the mind;
of emotions</i>: invādo, căpio, incesso, etc.:
v. <f>POSSESSION</f> (to take).

III. <i>To have
entire control and influence over</i> (fig.):
tĕneo, 2: Virg. E. 1, 32 (of <i>the object of
affection</i>): Ov. Or expr. by tōtus: cf.
Ter. Eun. 5, 8, 10, fratris igitur tota
Thais est? <i>then does my brother possess
the affections of Thais?</i> so, of <i>one entirely
devoted to some deity</i>, Dei totus, Val. Fl.;
*quem totum Deus tenet.


<b>possessed</b> (<i>part. adj.</i>): perh. lymphātus
(<i>maddened</i>), lymphātĭcus (<i>suffering
from madness</i>): v. <f>MADDENED</f>.
(In Vulg. usu., daemonium habens, a
daemonio vexatus: <i>pass.</i>) Sometimes,
furibundus, vēcors, may serve: v. <f>MAD</f>,
<f>PASSION</f> (IV.).


<b>possession</b>:

I. <i>Holding, occupation</i>:
possessio (not necessarily implying
<i>ownership</i>): <i>to come into p.</i>, in p.
venire, Cic. Att. 4, 2, <i>ad init.</i>: <i>to proceed
to take p.</i>, in p. proficisci, id. Quint.
27, 85: <i>to be in p.</i>, in p. esse, ib. § 84: <i>to
send (any one) to take p.</i>, in p. mittere,
ib. 26, <i>extr.</i>: <i>to dislodge from p.</i>, de p.
deturbare, ib. Esp. in phr., <i>to take or
obtain p.</i>: (i.) lit.: (1). possĭdeo, sēdi,
ssum, 2 (as legal term = in possessionem

Or. 2, 70, 283: id. Quint. 6. (2). occŭpo,
1: v. <f>TO SEIZE</f>, <f>OCCUPY</f>. (3). pŏtior, 4
(<i>to obtain p. of; become master of</i>):
foll. by <i>abl.</i> or <i>gen.</i>: <i>to obtain p. of the
sovereignty</i>, imperio p., Cic.[** typo? Caes.?] B. G. 1, 2:
also, (illius) regni p., Cic. Fam. 1, 7: less
freq. with <i>acc.</i>, e. g. summam imperii p.,
Nep. Eum. 3: v. <f>MASTER</f>, <i>subs.</i> (I., <i>fin.</i>).
(ii.). fig., as of <i>emotion</i>: (1). căpio, 3:
<i>fear took p. of the senate</i>, metus senatum
cepit, Liv. 23, 14, <i>med.</i>: Ter. (but no
less freq. is the inverse statement, capere
desiderium, inimicitias, etc.: Ter.: Cic.).
(2). invādo, si, sum, 3 (<i>to fall upon</i>:
with <i>acc.</i> or <i>dat.</i>): v. <f>TO FALL ON</f> (II.).
(3). incēdo, ssi, 3 (usu. with <i>dat.</i>; less
freq. <i>acc.</i>): <i>resentment seized on the
whole army</i>, dolor toti exercitui incessit,
Caes. B. C. 3, 74: Sall.: <i>fear took p. of
the senate</i>, timor patres incessit, Liv. 1,
17: Just. Phr.: <i>p.[**P1: missing .] is nine points in
law</i>, perh., occupantis melior est conditio,
Ulp. Dig. 14, 5, 3.

II. <i>That which is
possessed</i>:

1. possessio: <i>he promises
the soldiers lands out of his own p.s</i>,
militibus agros ex suis p. pollicetur,
Caes. B. C. 1, 17: Cic. Par. 6, 1, 44.

2. bŏna, orum; fundus: v. <f>PROPERTY</f>,
<f>ESTATE</f>. Phr.: <i>to have great
p.s</i>, multa possidēre, Hor.

III. <i>By
evil spirits</i>: expr. by daemonia (<i>pl.</i>)

IV. <i>Control
of one's emotions</i>: v. <f>SELF-POSSESSION</f>.


<b>possessive</b>: possessīvus (in grammar):
Quint. 1, 5, 45: Prisc.


<b>possessively</b>: *possessīvē (in

<b>possessor</b>:

1. possessor (not involving
<i>ownership</i>): Cic. Ph. 5, 7, 20:

2. dŏmĭnus: v. <f>OWNER</f>, <f>PROPRIETOR</f>.
(Or expr. by verb: v. <f>TO
POSSESS</f>.)


<b>possibility</b>: *possĭbĭlĭtas (very late
and only to be used in philos. lang., for
precision, <i>if at all</i>): Arn. Usu. expr.
by fieri posse: <i>to inquire into the p. of
anything</i>, *quaerere fieri quid possit

ut ...: v. <f>POSSIBLE</f>. Sometimes conditio
may serve; esp. as opp. to eventus
(<i>actuality</i>): cf. Cic. Rab. perd. 5, 16,
harum omnium rerum non solum
<i>eventus</i> sed etiam <i>conditio</i> ... indigna

<b>possible</b>:

1. *possĭbĭlis, e (a late
and harsh word, appellatio dura: only
fit for technical lang.): Quint. 3, 8, 25
(δυνατόν[**unclear], quod nostri <i>possibile</i> nominant).

2. usu. better expr. by posse: <i>it is
p. I am mistaken</i>, potest fieri ut fallar,
Cic. Fam. 13, 73: <i>as far as p.</i>, ut potest
(<i>sc.</i> fieri), ib. 1, 2, <i>fin.</i> (colloq.): oftener
as verb pers.: <i>(I did it) with all p. earnestness
and care</i>, ut gravissime diligentissimeque
potui, ib. 7, 17.

3.
expr. <i>as ... as possible</i>, by quam, with superl.
of adjj. and advv.: <i>to sow the largest
amount p.</i>, quam maximas sementes facere,
Caes. B. G. 1, 3 (or with posse expr.):
<i>as often as p.</i>, quam saepissime, Cic.
Fam. 13, 6, <i>fin.</i>: et <i>pass.</i> Phr.: <i>every
p. torture, mental and bodily</i>, omnes

Fin. 2, 30, <i>init.</i>: <i>what p. crime have I
committed?</i> quid <i>tandem</i> (like Gr. πότε)
admisi in me? Pl. Men. 5, 1, 12: Cic.


<b>possibly</b>: usu. expr. by posse: <i>as far
as I p. can</i>, quantum valeo quantumque
possum, Cic. Fam. 6, 5, <i>init.</i>: <i>as carefully
as I p. could</i>, quam diligentissime potui,
id. 7, 17: <i>so that the law might not p.

v. <f>POSSIBLE</f>. Sometimes =
<i>perchance</i>: fortasse: v. <f>PERCHANCE</f>.

1. sĭmĭlis vēri, or in

<b>pronounce</b>:

I. <i>To utter formally

III. <i>To articulate syllables</i>:

2. lŏquor, lŏcūtus,
3 (sufficiently precise for ordinary lang.):

3. exprĭmo,

1, 2, 6. Phr.: <i>to p. a syllable with the

Cf. foll. art.

2. appellātio (<i>enunciation</i>): <i>a soft
(pleasing) p.</i>, lenis a. litterarum, Cic.
Br. 74, 259 (so, suavitas litterarum appellandarum,
ib. 35, 133).

3. meton.[**,?]
os, ōris, <i>n.</i> <i>(utterance): to correct faults
of p. (<f>e. g.</f> a broad or affected way of
speaking)</i>, oris vitia emendare, Quint.
1, 11, 4 (so, vitia oris et linguae, ib. 1, 5,
32): <i>a distinct p.</i>, os explanatum, id.
11, 3, 30: <i>a bad foreign p.</i>, os in peregrinum
sonum corruptum, ib. 1, 1, 13.

4. explānātio (<i>distinct</i> p. or utterance):
ib. 1, 5, 33: Plin.

5. prōlātio
(<i>act of uttering</i>): Liv. 22, 13, <i>med.</i>
(Punicum abhorrens os ab Latinorum
nominum prolatione).

II. <i>More of
enunciating particular words or syllables</i>:
perh. sŏnus, i: Quint. 1, 5, 33.
Usu. better expr. by verb: <i>to write
words according to their p.</i>, verba sicut
sonant scribere; verba sicut loquimur
scribere, etc.: v. <f>TO PRONOUNCE</f> (III.).


<b>proof</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

I. <i>That which
proves or makes certain</i>:

1. dŏcŭmentum:
<i>most convincing p.s</i>, maxima
d., Sall. Cat. 9[**P2: :] <i>to be a p. (of something)</i>,
-----File: b0584m.png------------------------------------------------------
documento esse (foll. by rel. clause),
Caes. B. C. 3, 10. (Documentum more
freq. carries with it the sense of <i>a lesson
or instance from which one may learn</i>.)

2. argūmentum (<i>evidence, convincing
token</i>): <i>that is a convincing[** smudge?|P3 yes] p.
that</i>, id magno a. est (foll. by <i>acc.</i> and
<i>inf.</i>), Cic. Ph. 2, 16, 40: so, <i>it is sufficient
p. that ...</i>, satis est argumenti, id.
Quint. 12, <i>extr.</i> Join: [certissima] argumenta
atque indicia [sceleris], id. Cat.
3, 6, 13.

3. indĭcium (<i>token, indication</i>;
esp. <i>of guilt</i>): <i>p.s and traces of
poison</i>, ind. atque vestigia veneni, id.
Clu. 10, 30: cf. <i>supr.</i> (2). Also in good
sense, indicium benevolentiae, id. Fam.
7, 6.

4. signum: v. <f>SIGN</f>.

II. <i>A
course or mode of demonstration</i>: perh.
rătio demonstrandi <i>s.</i> probandi: v. <f>TO
PROVE</f>. Sometimes, argumentum may
serve (when there is <i>one main point in
the demonstration</i>): so in <i>pl.</i>, <i>the points
(leading heads) in a p.</i>, puncta argumentorum,
Cic. de Or. 2, 41, 177: v.
<f>ARGUMENT</f>.

III. <i>Act of proving</i>: in
phr., <i>difficult of proof</i>; difficile probatu:
Cic. Tusc. 5, <i>init.</i>: <i>a statement
difficult of p.</i>, *quod vix satis firmis argumentis
probari possit: v. <f>TO PROVE</f>.

IV. <i>Trial</i>; expĕrīmentum; or expr.
by experior, 4 (<i>to make proof of</i>): v.
<f>TRIAL</f>; <f>TO TRY</f>. Phr.: <i>armour of p.</i>,
*arma quae usu comprobata sunt (?).

V. <i>Specimen sheet struck off by a
printer</i>: plăgŭla: Schneider pref. Vitr.:
Orell.: <i>to correct p.s</i>, p. corrigere.


<b>proof</b> (<i>adj.</i>): expr. by verb: <i>p.
against argument</i>, *quem nulla argumenta
movere possunt: <i>p. against corruption</i>,
*qui nullo pretio labefactari
potest, cf. Cic. Clu. 68, 194: <i>intrepidity
p. against all terrors</i>, *animi praesentia
quam nulli metus frangere neque debilitare
possunt: v. <f>TO PREVAIL ON</f>; <f>SHAKE</f>,
<f>OVERCOME</f>, etc.


<b>proof-sheets</b>: v. <f>PROOF</f>, <i>subs.
(extr.)</i>.


<b>prop</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

I. Lit.:

1. cŏlūmen,
ĭnis, <i>n.</i> (<i>gable-prop, mainstay</i>):

2. pĕdāmen, pĕdāmentum

3. admĭnĭcŭlum (more elegant

4. stătūmen, ĭnis, <i>n.</i> (<i>any

II.
Fig.: <i>main support</i>: cŏlūmen: <i>the p.

Also praesĭdium may serve: cf. Hor.

<b>prop</b> (<i>v.</i>):

1. fulcio, si, ltum, 4:
<i>to p. a vine</i>, vitem f., Cic. Sen. 15, 52:

2.
pĕdo, 1 (<i>in horticulture</i>): <i>to p. vines</i>,

3. expr.
<i>to be p.'d</i> by, innītor, subnītor (as it were,

Cic. Rep. 6, 20. (N.B.--These
two verbs are chiefly used in present
sense, in <i>p. part.</i>; subnixus mostly fig.:
v. <f>RELYING ON</f>.)


<b>propaganda</b>: "Societas de propaganda

<b>propagate</b>:

A. Trans.:

I.
<i>To reproduce</i>.[**P1: should be :?]

1. propāgo, 1 (as horticultural

2. expr. <i>to be

-----File: b0584r.png------------------------------------------------------
nascuntur, Virg. G. 2, 65: <i>trees that

II. <i>To spread</i>:

2. dissēmĭno, 1 (<i>to

<b>propense</b>: v. <f>INCLINED</f>.


<b>propensity</b>:

1. prōclīvĭtas (rare):
Cic. Tusc. 4, 12, 28, where it is used as
special term to denote <i>an evil tendency</i>
(haec in bonis rebus facilitas, <i>in malis
proclivitas</i> nominetur).

2. cŭpĭdĭtas
(<i>a ruling desire, passion</i>): <i>the mind
becomes enslaved by an evil p.</i>, animus
se cupiditate devincit mala, Ter. Heaut.
1, 2, 34: <i>to have the passions bridled, to
control evil p.s</i>, domitas habere libidines,
coercere cupiditates, Cic. de Or. 1, 43,
<i>extr.</i>: v. <f>DESIRE</f>, <f>PASSION</f>. (Still stronger
than cupiditas is libido: cf. Cic. Off. 2,
24, 84, tanta in eo peccandi libido fuit,
<i>such an inordinate propensity</i> or passion
for wrong-doing.)

3. often expr. by
<i>adj.</i>: <i>one person has a p. to one vice
and another to another</i>, animus alius ad
alia vitia propensior, Cic. Tusc. 4, 37, 81:
<i>to have a p. towards ...</i>, animo esse propenso
ad ...: v. <f>INCLINED</f>. (N.B.--Various
<i>evil p.s</i> may be denoted by special
terms; as, <i>p. to lying</i>, mendācĭtas;
<i>to slander or reviling</i>, maledicentia; <i>to
drinking</i>, vinolentia; etc.: where see
the names of the several vices.)


<b>proper</b>:

I. <i>Peculiar; not common</i>:
proprius: v. <f>PECULIAR</f>. Esp. as

Prisc. 2, 5, 22. Phr.: <i>the p. signification

Quint. 8, 2, <i>init.</i>

II. <i>Fit, suitable</i>:
aptus, accommŏdātus (ad aliquam rem):
v. <f>FIT</f>.

III. <i>Right, becoming</i>: dĕcōrus:
Cic. Off. 1, 31, 111: see also <f>PROPRIETY</f>.
<i>It is p.</i>: dĕcet, 2 (with <i>acc.</i>
and <i>inf.</i>): <i>it is not at all p. for an
orator to get into a passion</i>, oratorem
minime decet irasci, Cic. Tusc. 4, 25,
<i>init.</i>: so, dedecet (= non decet): v.
<f>BECOMING</f>; <f>TO BECOME</f>. See also <f>RIGHT</f>.


<b>properly</b>:

I. <i>Strictly, in strict
sense</i>: propriē: Cic. Off. 3, 3, 13 (proprie
vereque): Gell.

II. <i>Fitly, rightly</i>:
aptē, rectē, commŏdē: v. <f>RIGHTLY</f>, <f>WELL</f>.
Phr.: <i>you have not acted p.</i>, non te
dignum fecisti, Ter. Eun. 5, 2, 25; *non

I. <i>Special quality,

<b>property-tax</b>: Phr.: <i>to impose a

<b>prove</b>:

A. Trans.:

I. <i>To
test</i>: expĕrior, 4: v. <f>TO TRY</f>.

II. <i>To
render certain by evidence, argument,
etc.</i>:

1. prŏbo, 1 (<i>to make good, substantiate</i>):
<i>he p.s to them that the thing
is perfectly easy</i>, perfacile factu esse
illis probat, Caes. B. G. 1, 3: <i>this is hard
to p.</i>, hoc difficile est probatu, Cic. Tusc.
5, 1, 2: <i>to p. (substantiate) a charge</i>,
crimen p., id. Fl. 37, 93: Ov.

2.
dŏceo, 2 (<i>to show or inform in any way</i>):
more exactly, argumentis docere, Cic.
N. D. 3, 4, 9: and again, argumentis et
rationibus, id. Div. 2, 11, 27. (But doceo
is often = simply, <i>to inform</i>.)

3.
effĭcio, fēci, fectum, 3 (<i>to make out by

is mortal</i>, vult e. animos esse mortales,
Cic. Tusc. 1, 31, <i>fin.</i> Esp. in <i>pass.</i>, efficitur,
<i>it is p.d, it follows</i>: with <i>acc.</i> and
<i>inf.</i>, or ut and <i>subj.</i> (id. N. D. 3,[**P2: ,] 12, 30).

4. vinco, vīci, victum, 3 (a strong
expr., <i>to p. triumphantly or irrefragably</i>:
cf. Gr. ὁ λόγος καθαιρει): <i>if I
show (that it was not done) by Avitus, I
p. conclusively that it was by Oppianicus</i>,
si doceo non ab Avito, vinco ab
Oppianico, Cic. Clu. 23,[**P2: ,] 64: Hor.

5.
confirmo, 1 (<i>to establish, make out surely
and certainly</i>): <i>to p. our own (position)
by arguments</i>, c. nostra argumentis et
rationibus, Cic. de Or. 2, 19, 80: Quint.
(Confirmo refers rather to the <i>manner</i>
of proof, as <i>strong and conclusive</i>, than
simply to the <i>fact of demonstration</i>.
Hence it cannot be used of mathematical
proof.) So also firmo, 1: Cic. Fat. 5, 11.
(N.B.--Demonstro, monstro, signify simply
<i>to point out, state, show</i>; and do not
necessarily imply argument.)

III. <i>To

1. praebeo, 2

12.

2. praesto, stĭti, stĭtum and
stātum, 1; <i>fut. part.</i> praestāturus: <i>to

3. exhĭbeo, 2 (with direct <i>acc.</i>

B. Intrans., <i>to turn out

1. of persons,

2. of things, expr. by esse,

4. where the reference is

<b>prudence</b>:

1. prūdentia (a more

pulse</i> (with pl. <i>pulses</i>):

1. pulsus
venārum: Plin. 29, 1, 5. (N.B.--The
ancients called the <i>arteries</i> venae; and
they believed <i>wind-pipes</i> [arteriae] to
be distributed through the whole body:
[v. <f>ARTERY</f>]: then, ascribing the pulsations
of the true <i>arteries</i> to these
"arteriae," they also called the <i>pulse</i>
arteriarum pulsus: <i>the pulse, which is
most felt at the extremities of the limbs</i>,
arteriarum p. in cacumine maxume
membrorum evidens [index fere morborum],
Plin. 11, 37, 88: an <i>even, quick,
<f>or</f> slow p.</i>, art. pulsus per aetates stabilis
aut citatus aut tardus, ib.)

2. expr.
by vēnae alone: <i>if the p. beats so,
he has a fever</i>, si v. sic moventur, is
habet febrem, Cic. Fat. 8, 15: Cels. 3, 6:
<i>the p. has quite failed</i>, protinus v. conciderunt,
id. 3, 5: <i>we trust the p. most,
which is very misleading</i>, venis maxime
credimus, fallacissimae rei, id. 3, 6: <i>the
p. is natural</i>, venae naturaliter sunt ordinatae,
ib.: <i>the p. is slower or quicker
according to age, sex, and temperament</i>,
venae leniores celerioresve sunt et aetate
et sexu et corporum natura, Cels. ib.:
<i>to quicken the p.</i>, venas concitare, resolvere,
movere, turbare, ib.: <i>to feel the
p.</i>, venas tentare, Suet. Tib. 72, <i>fin.</i>;
v. tangere, Pers. 3, 107; pulsum venarum
attingere, Tac.; venarum pulsum et
momenta captare, Apul. Fig.: <i>to
feel one's p. (= to sound one)</i>, *alicujus
voluntatem, mentem, tentare; or, with
<i>acc.</i> of person: cf. Tac. H. 1, 75: v. <f>TO
SOUND</f>. Phr.: <i>the p. of life</i> (Shaksp.),
*pulsus vitales: <i>the p. of states</i> (Clarendon),
*quasi venae quaedam civitatum:
<i>My temperate p. does regularly beat</i> (Dryden),
*pulsus venarum stabiles in corde
moventur.

3. ictus, ūs (<i>sc.</i> arteriarum),
<i>a stroke of the p.</i>: <i>a quick or
slow p.</i>, crebri aut languidi ictus [gubernacula
vitae temperat], Plin. 11, 37, 88.

II. <i>Any similar movement, <f>as</f> of
sound, light, etc.</i>: <i>the vibrations or p.s
of this medium</i> (said <i>of light</i>, Newton):
pulsus, ictus, vibrātio (all by analogy):
v. <f>OSCILLATION</f>.

III. <i>Any leguminous
esculent vegetable</i> (generally constructed
as plural): lĕgūmen, ĭnis, <i>n.</i>, also <i>pl.</i>:
<i>let them give us p. to eat</i>, dentur nobis l.
ad vescendum, Vulg. Dan. i. 12: <i>the
earth abounds in fruits and various
sorts of pulse</i>, terra feta frugibus et vario
leguminum genere, Cic. N. D. 2, 62.
Also legumentum, Gell. 4, 11. Adj. leguminarius
(Inscr. Orell. No. 3093): as
subs. a <i>pulse-seller</i> (ὀσπριοπώλης), Gloss.
Philox.


<b>pulsion</b>, obsol. (More, Bentley): <i>the
act or motion of driving or drawing</i>:
v. <f>PROPULSION</f>.


<b>pulverisation</b>: v. <f>PULVERISE</f>.


<b>pulverise</b>: <i>to crush or grind to
powder</i>:

1. (full expression) in pulverem
contĕro, 3: <i>the dry root of baccar
p.d</i>, baccaris radix arida in pulverem
contrita, Plin. 26, 11, 70. Also tĕro,
contĕro, obtĕro, commĭnuo (absol.): v.
<f>TO POUND</f>, <f>GRIND</f>.

2. in late Lat.
only, pulvĕro, 1 (prop. <i>to scatter dust, to
dust over</i>): Calp. Ecl. 5, 88: and pulvĕrīzo,
1: <i>a drachm of p.d frankincense</i>,
turis pulverizati drachma, Veg.
Vet. 1, 54. The act of <i>p.ing <f>or</f> pulverisation
(<f>e. g.</f> by digging up the soil
round vines)</i>, pulveratio: <i>it (the vine)
is made more fruitful by p.ing the soil</i>,
tum et crebris fossionibus implere [convenit]:
nam fit uberior pulverationibus,
Col. 4, 28.


<b>puma</b>: <i>a feline beast of prey</i>, inhabiting
the warm regions of America:
being unknown to the ancients, can only
be expr. (according to their frequent
usage) by the name of its genus, f[=e]les,
is, <i>f.</i>, or *f. Americana.


<b>pumice</b>, <b>pumice-stone</b>: <i>a light

ĭcis, <i>m.</i>: Hor. Ep. 1, 20, 2 (<i>f.</i> Cat. 1, 2):

<b>pummel</b>: v. <f>POMMEL</f>.


<b>pump</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

I. <i>A machine for
raising water</i>: antlia, <i>f.</i> (gen. term):
<i>the p. raises water obtained with toil, for
the thirsty gardens</i>, quas det sitientibus
hortis curva laboratas a. tollit aquas,
Mart. 9, 19, 3-4 (curva points to the
<i>swinging pole and bucket</i>, which was
also called tollēno, ōnis, <i>m.</i>: Plin. 19, 4,
20). The following sorts are distinguished:
(1.) orgănum pneumătĭcum,
Plin. 19, 4, 20. (2.) haustrum: <i>as we
see rivers turn wheels and pumps</i>, ut
fluvios versare rotas atque haustra videmus,
Lucr. 5, 517. (3.) tympănum
(<i>the lift-pump</i>, a wheel <i>turned by water,
or by manual labour, with buckets or
jars round it</i>): also called hydromūla,
<i>f.</i>, Vitr. 10, 9, 10: and rota, Plin. <i>l. c.</i>:
tympănum also denotes a kind of <i>chain-pump</i>.
(4.) <i>the Archimedean screw p.</i>,
cochlĕa, <i>f.</i>: Vitr. 10, 11, 4. (5.) <i>a sort
of force-pump</i>, Ctēsĭbĭca māchĭna, Vitr.
10, 12. (6.) <i>a ship's p.</i>, sentīnācŭlum
(prop. <i>a sort of scoop for raising the
bilge-water out of the well of the hold</i>,
sentīna): Paul. Non. Ep. 36, 3. (7.) <i>a
fire-p.</i>, or <i>fire-engine</i>, sĭpho, ōnis, <i>m.</i>
(Gk.), Plin. Ep. 10, 42: Ulp. Dig. 33, 7,
12: v. <f>WATERWORKS</f> (cf. Dict. of Ant.
s. v. Antlia).

II. <i>A light thin-soled
shoe</i>: soccus, <i>m.</i>, Cic. de Or. 3, 32, 127:
Cat. 61, 10: Suet. Cal. 52. <i>Dimin.</i>
soccŭlus, <i>m.</i>, Suet. Vit. 2, <i>fin.</i>


<b>pump</b> (<i>v.</i>):

A. Trans.:

I. <i>To
pump, pump up or out (<f>object</f>, water)</i>:

1. haurio, si, stum, 4: <i>machines
for p.ing water</i>, organa, quae ad hauriendam
aquam inventa sunt, Vitr. 10, 9,
1.

2. tollo, 3: <i>the plan of the screw,
which raises a great body of water, but
does not p. it up so high as the wheel</i>,
cochleae ratio, quae magnam vim haurit
aquae, sed non tam alte tollit quam
rota, Vitr. 10, 11, 1.

3. ēgĕro, ssi,
stum, 3: <i>one p.s out the water</i> (from a
ship), egerit hic fluctus, Ov. M. 11, 488.
Also, antliâ haurire, tollere, egerere,
aquam, undam, etc.: v. <f>TO DRAW OFF
AND OUT</f>, <f>RAISE</f> (water). (N.B.--Antlo
and exantlo or -clo, doubtful: their use
depends partly on their true etymology,
see Smith's Lat. Dict. s. vv.) Fig.: <i>to
pump a person, <f>or</f> a thing out of a person</i>:
expiscor, 1: proinde expiscare,
quasi non nosses, Ter. Ph. 2, 3, 35: nescis
me ab illo omnia expiscatum? Cic.
Fam. 9, 19.

II. <i>To pump, pump out,
pump dry (<f>object</f>, the vessel, <f>e. g.</f> a ship)</i>:
exhaurio, 4: <i>others p. out the hold</i>, alii
sentinam ex., Cic. Sen. 6, 17: v. <f>DRAIN</f>.
Exhaurio may also be used with acc. of
<i>that which is removed by pumping</i>, cf.
Tac. A. 2, 23, non adhaerere ancoris,
non exhaurire irrumpentes undas poterant
(<i>could not p. the ships dry</i>).

B.
Intrans.: usu. translate by supplying
the object: v. <i>supr.</i> <i>The act of pumping</i>,
haustus, ūs, <i>m.</i>: <i>(gardens) watered
from a well by the wheel, or engines,
pumping by lifting machines</i>, (hortos)
e puteo rota organisve pneumaticis vel
tollenorum haustu rigatos, Plin. 19, 4,
20.


<b>pumpkin</b> (Cucurbita Pepo, Linn.):

<b>pun</b> (<i>subs.</i>): difficult to find an exact
Latin equivalent: several gen. terms
for <i>jest, point, wit, etc.</i>[**or treat as a list? except etc. kind of messes that up], may be used.

1. perh. most specific lŏgi (λόγοι):

omnes logos, qui ludis dicti sunt, animadvertisse,

2. Cicero, himself an inveterate punster,

facetiis, maxime nostratibus, Cic. Fam.

quod in similitudine verborum vertitur.)

3. <i>puns</i> are at least included under

And this suits the probable etymology
(from Fr. <i>pointe</i>), as does ăcūleus, <i>m.</i>

4. argūtĭŏla,
<i>f.</i> (?): prop[**P1: missing .] <i>a quibble</i>, Gell. 9, 14.
Other terms, perhaps more or less admissible,

<b>punch</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

I. <i>A pointed instrument,
which, when struck, pierces a
hole</i>, distinguished from a <f>DRILL</f>, which
pierces by boring: no known word; but,
this distinction not being always exact,
we may perh. use tĕrĕbra (<i>gimlet</i>),
<i>pierce with a p. the vine-stock you are
going to graft</i>, terebra vitem quam inseres

word is commonly used for an instrument
which punches out a piece of the
stuff, *terebra cavata. Ferrum may also
be used with the verb. Sometimes for
an instrument which indents a mark,
without penetration, forma: v. <f>STAMP</f>.

II. <i>The stroke of a punch</i>, ictus, ūs:
v. <f>BLOW</f>, <f>STROKE</f>: also (vulg.) <i>a blow
with the fist (or elbow, etc.)</i>:

1. pugnus:
<i>to give one a p.</i>, pugnum ducere
alicui, Paul. Dig. 47, 10, 4.

2. obtūsio:
Lampr. Comm. 10.

3. percussio: <i>p.s
on the head</i>, capitis percussiones, Cic.
Tusc. 3, 26, 62 (adapted): v. <f>BLOW</f>.

III. <i>The beverage</i>: untranslatable.[**P1: should be : or ,|P3 s/b ,]
unless perh. călĭdum (caldum), or călĭda
(calda) (denoting <i>some warm drink</i>),
may serve: <i>they drink p. in the gin-shop</i>,
in thermopolio caldum bibunt,
Plaut. Curc. 2, 3, 14 (adapted): cf. Varr.
L. L. 5, 27, 36. <i>A p.-bowl</i>: crātēr, ēris,
m. (κράτηρ, i. e. <i>mixing-bowl</i>), prop. a
bowl for <i>mixing wine with water</i>, Ov.
M. 8, 669: crātēra, <i>f.</i>, Hor. Od. 3, 18,
7: also authepsa, <i>f.</i>, <i>a vessel in which

v. Smith's Dict. of Ant. s. v. Calida:
<i>a p.-ladle</i>, trulla, <i>f.</i>, trulla vinaria, Cic.
Verr. 4, 27, 62: Hor. S. 2, 3, 144: and
perhaps cy̆ăthus, Hor. Od. 3, 8, 13: v.
Dict. of Ant. s. v.

IV. <i>The hero of
the puppet-show</i>: untrans.: perhaps we
may Latinize the original Italian <i>Puncinello</i>,
or <i>Policinello</i>, *Puncinellus <i>or</i>

<b>punctilio</b> (dim. of puncto, which is
used in the same sense by Bacon,
Henry VII.): <i>a small nicety in conduct,

1. usu. expr. by circuml.: <i>mindful

atque studiosus: cf. <f>PUNCTILIOUSNESS</f>.

2. perh. căvillātio (<i>a captious nicety</i>):
<i>silly p.s</i>, c. ineptae, Quint. 7, 9, 4: <i>a thousand
p.s of law</i>, mille juris c., id. 7.[**P1: should be ,?] 4,
37.

3. spīna (<i>a thorny subtlety</i>):
esp. <i>in philosophy and dialectics</i> (cf.
Cic. Fin. 4, 28, 79, nec acerbitatem

id. Tusc. 4, 5, (Peripatetici) partiendi
et definiendi spinas praetermittunt: v.
<f>QUIBBLE</f>).

4. a proud <i>nicety as to
points of conduct</i>: fastīdium, Cic. de Or.
1, 61, 258: "<i>punctilio is out of doors,
the moment a daughter clandestinely
quits her father's house</i>" (Richardson),
*fastidii nihil superest, simul ac, etc.

<b>punctual</b>:

I. <i>Consisting in a point</i>
(obs.), as, "Round this opacous earth,

II. <i>Exact, coinciding to
a point</i> (obs.): accūrātus, esp. in <i>superl.</i>:
<i>the punctual exactness</i> (of description in

<f>EXACT</f>, <f>PRECISE</f>.

III. <i>Exact in keeping
engagements</i>: dīlĭgens: "<i>punctually</i>

<i>just (<f>or</f> punctual) to perform what he
knew requisite</i>" (Raleigh), omnis officii

IV.
Esp., <i>exact in keeping to time</i>:

1.

2. dīlĭgens,

3. promptus: cf. Nep.

<b>punctuality</b> (in older writers, <i>punctualness</i>):

1. <i>Exactness, observance
of minute points</i>; esp. <i>of time</i>: dīlĭgentia,
Cic. de Or. 2, 35, 150: <i>punctualities</i>

1. mundus: v. <f>CLEAN</f>.

<b>purifying</b> (<i>adj.</i>):

1. purgātor
(cf. L. G. § 598); of course only <i>masc.</i>:

2. purgātōrius:

3. pūrĭfĭcus (late and rare):

4. expr. by rel.
clause and predicate purgo; with which
an object must be expr.: <i>p. fire</i>, ignis
qui omnia purgat, etc.


<b>purifying</b> (<i>subs.</i>): purgātio; pūrĭfĭcātio;

<b>purism</b>, <b>purist</b>: in language: the

<b>puritanism</b>: *Puritanismus qui appellatur;

<i>pousser</i>, fr. Lat. pulso), <i>to thrust at</i> or
<i>away</i>, usu. <i>with a weapon</i> (as, "<i>push</i>
with biting point," Dryden), esp. of an
animal <i>pushing with its horns</i>.[**P1: should be :] pĕto,
īvi and ĭi, ītum, 3: cf. Ov. 5, 185, Pectora
Lyncidae gladio petit (<i>p.s</i> or <i>thrusts

ram)[**P1: missing ,] cornu petere, Virg. E. 3, 87 (cf.
id. G. 3, 526, Inter se adversis <i>luctantur</i>

(N.B.--Also late Lat. [esp. Vulg.] ventĭlo,
ventĭlor, 1; <i>to wave in the air</i>;
hence, to <i>toss about</i>: <i>with these [horns]

<b>put</b>: (N.B.--1. In translating this
word, care must be taken to distinguish
the cases in which it is followed by a
true <i>preposition</i>, governing a noun, from
those in which it is <i>compounded with a
separable particle</i>, the noun being the
object to the compound verb: <i>e. g.</i>
Case 1, <i>the load was put on the horse</i>:
Case 2, <i>he put on his hat</i>: but, for convenience
of reference, we shall put most
examples of the former kind under the
heads of the latter. 2. The word is so
general in its use, that in many passages
it must be expressed with the context,
and not by any verbal equivalent. 3.
Its two chief uses, referring to <i>state and
place</i>, are too much mixed up in Latin
to be put under separate heads: cf. esp.
<f>TO PLACE</f>.)

<b>qualitative</b> (<i>adj.</i>): only used in

of the kind of substance, not
of its quantity (v. <f>QUANTITIVE</f>): perh.
*ănăly̆sis quālĭtīva or quālĭtātīva, (<i>t. t.</i>).


<b>quality</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

I. Abstr. <i>the
nature or kind of anything</i>; concr.
<i>the property or properties that determine
its nature or kind</i>: hence, of persons,
<i>character</i> or <i>disposition</i> (these meanings
are mingled in the Latin words):

1.
the etym. equiv. quālĭtas, ātis, <i>f.</i>, is
only used in the best Latin as a <i>t. t.</i> of
philosophy: cf. qualitates igitur appellavi
quas ποιότητας Graeci vocant:
quod ipsum apud Graecos non est
vulgi verbum, sed philosophorum, Cic.
Ac. 1, 7, 25, <i>et seqq.</i>, as opp. to <i>a thing
in its essence</i>: cf. aut de substantia controversiam
esse, aut de qualitate, Quint.
3, 6, 39 (cf. esp. 7, 4, 1): in later writers
as a common word: cf. ager aliis qualitatibus
aestimandus est, Col. 2, 2, 17.
Expr. by tālis (<i>of such a q.</i>), and quālis,
<i>rel.</i>, <i>inter.</i>, and <i>indef.</i>: <i>(that) we naturally
shew the q.s which we really have</i>,
ut facillime quales simus tales esse videamur,
Cic. Off. 2, 13, 44: as depend.
interr., <i>tell me what are their bodily q.s</i>,
doce me quales sint corpore, id. N. D. 1,
23: as indef., <i>a thing must first be, and
then have some q.</i>, prius aliquid esse
debet, deinde quale esse, Sen. Ep. 117:
<i>pl.</i> quālĭa (<i>the q.s of things</i>, dist. fr.
quālĭtas, their common principle): cf.
Cic. Ac. 1, 7, 28, quum ita moveatur illa
vis, quam <i>qualitatem</i> esse diximus ...,
illa effici quae appellant <i>qualia</i> (freely,
<i>their q.s are developed</i>): <i>of what q.
(adv.)</i>, qualiter: <i>of whatever q. (of what
q. soever)</i>, qualis qualis, Tryphon. Dig.
20, 5, 12: qualiscunque, Cic. Leg. 3, 14:
id. Att. 14, 14: <i>of what q. you please</i>,
qualislibet, Apic. 4, 2: cf. <f>SORT</f>, <f>SUCH</f>.
N.B. The proper use of these terms can
only be acquired by knowledge and experience.

2. vis, <i>f.</i> (rare in this
sense, but expressive: <i>special q. or
virtue</i>); <i>the q. of virtue</i>, v. virtutis, Cic.
Fam. 9, 16: cf. in quo est omnis vis
amicitiae, id. A. 4, 15: <i>the q. of mercy
is not strained</i> (Shaksp.), *non éluctábitúr
vis mísericórdiaé.

3. nātūra,
<i>f.</i> (lit. <i>in-born q.</i>): <i>the essential q. of
life</i>, n. propria animae et vis, Cic. Rep.
6, 26: <i>the q.s with which J. has endowed
bees</i>, naturas apibus quas Juppiter ipse
addidit, Virg. G. 4, 149: <i>the subtle q. of
air</i>, n. tenuis aeris, Lucr. 2, 232: <i>pl.</i>,
<i>qualities (= endowments); a man of
varied and manifold q.s</i>, homo varia
multiplicique natura, Cic. Coel. 6: cf.
<f>NATURE</f>. Phr.: <i>this q. is implanted
by nature</i>, hoc natura est insitum, Cic.
Sull. 30, 83.

4. ingĕnĭum, <i>n.</i> (same
meaning): <i>the q.s of soils</i>, ingenia arvorum,
Virg. G. 2, 177. Join: lactis
ingenia et proprietates, Gell. 12, 1: esp.
of <i>mental and moral q.s</i>: <i>q. of mind</i>,
animi ing., Cic. Inv. 1, 45, 83: <i>I have
tried (tested) the q. of your character</i>,
tentavi vestrum ingenium ingenii (perh.
intens[**P1: missing .] redupl., <i>your inmost q.s or nature</i>),
Pl. Stich. 1, 2, 69.[**P1: should be :] esp. for <i>high
qualities</i>: <i>men with the most excellent
q.s</i>, praestantissimis ingeniis homines,
Cic. Fin. 2, 16, 51: <i>to be urged (to shew

q.s</i>, sollicitari vel ing. hominis pulcherrimo

<b>quarantine</b> (formerly and prop.
<i>quarantain</i>: from the orig. term of

as <i>defin.</i> only, *mora quadragenaria in
statione propter pestem (or, propter
suspectam valetudinem): <i>a tedious q.</i>,
segnis q. (like segnis mora, Liv. 34, 9).
<i>To perform q.</i>, *q. agĕre: <i>to be put in
q.</i>, *XL. dies morāri or retineri: (<i>intr.</i>)
<i>to put a ship into q.</i>, navem retinere,
morāri (<i>trans.</i>); or, more fully, *quadragenariam
(moram) navi inferre, imponere,
facere: <i>to break q.</i>, *q. (moram)
rumpere (like moram rumpere, Virg.
Aen. 4, 569).

<b>quarterly</b> (<i>adj.</i>):

I. <i>Containing
a quarter</i>: or, <i>consisting of, <f>or</f> divided
into, 4 parts</i>.

1. Gen. quadrĭpartītus:
<i>the q. changes of the seasons</i>, commutationes
temporum q., Cic. Tusc. 1, 28, 68:
also, quadrĭfărius: cf. q. divisio, Cass.
Varr. 3, 51: also, quadrĭfĭdus: cf. (fig.)
q. labor, Claud. Cons. Probr. et Olybr.
268.

2. specific case: <i>containing a
q. of a year</i>: trĭmestris: trimestre spatium
(<i>a period of three months</i>), Plin. 37,
10, 59.

II. <i>Recurring every q. of a
year</i>: *tertio quoque mense (by analogy):
<i>or rather</i>, according to the Latin
computation, *quarto quoque mense
(every 4th month, <i>i. e.</i> at the end of

account</i> or <i>settlement of money</i>, *ratio,
computatio, trimestris: *ratio tertio quoque
mense confecta: <i>a q. payment</i>, <i>i. e.</i>
(1) <i>a q.'s pay</i>, *quarta pars annuae mercedis:
(2) <i>a sum to be paid q.</i>, pensiones
trimestres (Ai.): *pecunia tertio quoque
mense solvenda, or quolibet spatio trimestri
(Ai.), or tertio quoque mense.


<b>quarterly</b> (<i>adv.</i>):

I. In gen. sense,
<i>by quarters</i>: quadrĭfărĭam (v. <i>supra</i>);
quadrĭfărĭter, Paul. Dig. 38, 10, 10, § 14:
quadrĭpartito, Col. 4, 26, 3.

II. <i>Every
three months</i>: *quarto quoque mense
(like quinto quoque anno, <i>every four
years</i>: Cic. Verr. 2, 2, 56): <i>to make up
an account q.ly</i>, quarto post mense rationem
ductare (cf. Pl. Am. 2, 2, 38);
or, ducere, Cic[**P1: missing .] Verr. 2, 2, 52; or, inire,
Caes. B. G. 7, 71 (cf. id. ib. 6, 19, <i>the acc.

quarto post mense r. reddere, Pl. Men.
1, 3, 23; referre, Cic. Verr. 2, 1, 39;
rationes referre, id. ib. 5, 24.


<b>quartern</b>: <i>a measure of capacity</i>:

I. <i>Of liquids</i>: 1-4th of a pint (= <i>a
gill</i>):

1. quartārius, <i>m.</i> (1-4th of the
sextarius, which was almost a pint, v.

II. <i>Of solids</i>:
(1) <i>of flour</i> (= 1/4th <i>of a peck</i>, by measure,
or 1/4th of a stone, <i>i. e.</i> 3-1/2 lbs.
by weight), quartarius farris, Plin. 18,
3, 3 (the etym. equiv. in the sense of
<i>a quarter</i> of the unit understood): more
exactly (as equiv. measure) *quadrans
modii, or *quarta pars modii: (2) <i>a
quartern loaf</i> (= 4 lbs. of bread), pānis
quadrĭlībris: cf. Pl. Aul. 5, 2.

<b>should</b>:

I. <i>As auxiliary verb in
the conditional</i>: expr. by <i>subj.</i> the pres.
and perf. tenses of which are used of an
hypothesis which is conceived as possible:
<i>if I s. deny</i>, si negem; <i>if I s. be
disposed</i>, si velim; <i>if you s. be aware</i>, si
scieris, etc., L. G. § 426: and the <i>imperf.</i>
and <i>pluperf.</i> of an hypothesis contrary
to fact and therefore not conceived as
now possible: <i>I s. not say so did I not
believe it</i>, non ita dicerem nisi mihi persuasum
esset: <i>I s. not have said so unless</i>
..., non ita dixissem nisi ... etc.,
L. G. § 427.

II. <i>As a softened form</i>
to avoid too positive a statement: use
<i>pres.</i> or <i>perf. subj.</i>: <i>I s. think</i>, censeam;
<i>I should be inclined to believe</i>, crediderim,
etc.: L. G. § 430.

III. As sign
of future after past tenses; where in a
direct statement the future indic. would
be found: e. g. <i>he said he s. sail to-morrow</i>
(direct statement, <i>I shall sail
to-morrow</i>), dixit se cras navigaturum:
<i>what do you suppose I should have done?</i>
quid me facturum fuisse arbitraris?
L. G. § 507.

IV. As denoting obligation:

1. expr. by <i>fut. imperat.</i>: <i>this
you s. do ... this you s. shun</i>, hoc facito,
hoc fugito, Ter. Ad. 3, 3, 63: <i>you s. beware
of such</i>, hunc tu caveto, Hor. 1, 4,
85: <i>all commands s. be just</i>, imperia
justa sunto, Lex in Cic. Leg. 3, 3, <i>init.</i>

2. expr. by gerundive; used personally
in the case of trans. verbs and

<b>since</b> (<i>conj.</i>):

I. Temporal:

1.
