Or expr. by <i>adj.</i> (v. <f>SNUG</f>).


<b>so</b> (<i>adv.</i> and <i>conj.</i>):

I. Demonstrative:

A. With reference to
what precedes: <i>in the manner described,
in this manner</i>:

1. sīc: <i>a blessing on
thy valour, boy! so do men go heavenwards</i>[**P3  * removed],
macte virtute puer: s. itur ad
astra, Virg. Aen. 9, 641: <i>Laelius, a
philosopher; for so he was</i>, L. sapiens,
sic enim est habitus, Cic.

2. ĭtă:
<i>I say that the young man in question
was ill several days, and so died</i>, dico
illum adolescentem aliquot dies aegrotasse
et i. esse mortuum, id. Clu. 60,
168: <i>I do not see any reason why it
should be so</i>, non video causam cur i.
sit, Cic. Att. 9,[**P1: should be ,] 2 (b.), 2. Special
Phr.: (i.) <i>to be so</i>: <i>it is s.</i>, ita est, Cic.
<i>pass.</i>: sic est, Hor.: sic res est, Ter.:
res ita se habet, Cic.: sic res se habet,
id.: sic habet, Hor. S. 1, 9, 53: <i>matters
being so</i>, quae quum ita sint, Cic.: quae
cum res ita se haberet, id.: <i>to be not so</i>,
aliter esse, id.: aliter se habere, Caes.:
<i>it must be so</i>, fieri non potest aliter, Cic.
(ii.) <i>be it so</i> (or <i>so be it</i>). (1.) esto: v. <f>TO
GRANT</f> (II.). (2.) fiat: <i>go with me this
way, I beg</i>. <i>Be it so</i>, i mecum hac, obsecro.
Fiat, Plaut.: v. also <f>TO GRANT</f> (II.)
(iii.) <i>to do so</i>: (α.) Expressed: (1.)
expr. by facere id (esp. to avoid <i>repetition</i>
of a previous statement): <i>it would
be tedious were I to tell you why I do so</i>,
longum est si tibi narrem quamobrem
id faciam, Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 94. Also
facio, <i>absol.</i>: <i>I have done so before, and
I do so now</i>, et feci ante et facio nunc,
Cic. Fam. 15, 14, 3: v. also <i>infr.</i> (IX.).
(2.) when a verb is repeated, the latter
verb may be rendered "<i>to do so</i>": <i>the
senate decreed that those should preside
over the provinces who had not already
done so</i>, senatus eos voluit praeesse
provinciis qui non praefuissent, Cic.
Att. 6, 6, 3. (β.) Unexpressed:
N.B.--<i>To do so</i> may sometimes be <i>implied</i>
in Latin from the context: e. g.,
<i>the woman believes she cannot on any
account do so</i>, illa enim se negat (supply
<i>facturam esse</i> from a previous <i>facere</i>),
Ter. Ph. 1, 2, 63 (L. G. § 654): <i>he was
just plunging his sword into his bosom
(<f>supply</f> and would have done so), had
not, etc.</i>, gladium in pectus deferebat,
ni, etc., Tac. (L. G. § 396): <i>how are you
to find men of that class who love you
sincerely, instead of pretending to do so
for their own advantage?</i> qui potes reperire
ex eo genere hominum qui te
ament ex animo ac non sui commodi
causa simulent? (supply <i>te amare</i>), Cic.
Q. Fr. 1, 1, 5, 15. (iv.) <i>how <f>or</f> why so?</i>
quid ita? Cic.: or simply, quid (v. <f>HOW</f>,
I., 5): quamobrem tandem? (Ainsw.).
(v.) <i>just so</i> or <i>precisely so</i> (in answers):
-----File: b0764r.png------------------------------------------------------
ita plane, etc. (v. <f>EXACTLY</f>, III.). (vi.)
Miscell.: <i>by chance, say you</i>: <i>do
you really think so</i> (or <i>is it really so</i>),
casu, inquis? itane vero? Cic.: <i>you
don't say so</i>, quid ais: <i>others perhaps do
not think so</i>, aliis fortasse non idem videtur
(Ainsw.): <i>he thinks he may do so</i>,
idem sibi arbitratur licere (Ainsw.): <i>if
that be true, then this is so</i>, si illud, hoc,
Cic. Fin. 4, 19, 55: <i>there is a class of
people who will have it that they are
first in everything, but are not so</i>, est
genus hominum qui esse primos se omnium
rerum volunt, nec sunt, Ter. (cf.
L. G. § 432): D. <i>Is this as I say?</i>
L. <i>It is even so</i>, Estne hoc ut dico?
Ea res est, Pl. Asin. 1, 1, 41: <i>Heaven
grant it may be so</i>, Dii faxint: Dii faciant:
utinam Dii faxint ut <i>s.</i> ne, etc.:
Dii bene vertant: Cic. <i>pass.</i>

B. With
reference to what follows: <i>in the following
manner, as follows</i>:

1. sīc (with
<i>acc.</i> and <i>inf.</i> clause): <i>strive and so hold
(the theory) that thou art not mortal,
but that this body is</i>, enitere et s. habeto,
non esse te mortalem, sed corpus hoc,
Cic. Rep. 6, 24 (8), 26: <i>he replies that in
the oracular books, in Etruscan lore it
is so recorded that, etc.</i>, respondit sic
libris fatalibus, sic disciplina Etrusca
traditum esse (folld. by <i>acc.</i> and <i>inf.</i>),
Liv. 5, 15, <i>ad fin.</i>

2. ĭtă (with <i>acc.</i>
and <i>inf.</i> clause): <i>for so he wrote to me
that, etc.</i>, i. enim scripsit ad me (folld.
by <i>acc.</i> and <i>inf.</i>), Cic. Fam. 13, 24, 1.

3. tālia (<i>neut. absol.</i>: poet.)[** :?|P3 yes] <i>so
speaks he</i>, t. fatur, Virg. pass. (N.B.--In
prose, in hunc modum, ad hunc modum
would be used.)

II. Correlative:
<i>as ... so</i>:

1. ut ... (folld. by ita,
sic): <i>as the laws preside over magistrates,
so do magistrates over the people</i>,
ut magistratibus leges, ita populo praesunt
magistratus, Cic. Leg. 3, 1, 2: <i>as
there are two species of kings (queen-bees),
so there are two sorts among their
subjects</i>, ut binae regum facies, ita corpora
gentis, Virg. G. 4, 95: <i>as you must
walk, must anoint yourself, so must I
sleep</i>, ut tibi ambulandum, unguendum,
sic mihi dormiendum (est), Cic. Att. 9,
7, 7. For velut ... sic, v. <f>AS</f> (I., 9): for
sicut ... ita, item, v. Smith's Lat. Dict.
s. v. sicut, I., 2, ii.: I., 1, ii.: and for
prout ... ita, ita ... prout, v. id. s. v.
prout.

2. ita ... ut (not sic ... ut,
wh. = <i>as ... as</i> or <i>as</i>: cf. Smith's Lat.
Dict. s. v. sic, II.): <i>and so may Heaven
love me as I am delighted not so much
on my own account as on his</i>, atque i.
me di ament ut ego nunc non tam meapte
causa laetor quam illius, Ter. Heaut. 4,
3, 8.

3. quemadmŏdum ... sic: <i>if,
as you generally argue on other subjects,
so you should have argued about friendship</i>,
si q. soles de ceteris rebus, sic de
amicitia disputaris, Cic. Am. 4, 16. For
quemadmodum (with ita, item, etc.), v.
Smith's Dict. s. v. II., 2: and for quomodo
... sic, v. id. s. v. quomodo, II., ii.

4. tālis ... quālis: <i>in order that
as we really are, so we may seem to be</i>,
ut q. simus, t. esse videamur, Cic.

5.
quum ... tum: v. <f>AS</f> (I., 13). [May
also be freq. expr. by such phrr. as,
tum ... tum, et ... et, where the
usual rendering "<i>both ... and</i>" would
be clumsy.] N.B.--<i>(In proportion) as
... so</i>, expr. by quo ... eo (with
<i>comp.</i>): also by tanto ... quanto (with
<i>comp.</i>), Hor. S. 2, 7, 18.

III. Consecutive:
<i>and so, so then</i>:

1. ĭtăque
(<i>and so</i>)[**P1: missing :?|P3 no] v. <f>ACCORDINGLY</f>: and Smith's
Lat. Dict. s. v.

2. ĭtă (used <i>logically</i>):
<i>now virtue is full of activity, and your
deity inactive</i>: <i>consequently without
share in virtue, and so not even happy</i>,
virtus autem actuosa est,[**P1: should be ,?] et deus vester
nihil agens: expers igitur virtutis: ita
ne beatus quidem,[**P1: should be ,] Cic. N. D. 1, 40, 110.

3. ergō (in Ov. and the post-Aug.
poets sometimes ergŏ), Cic. <i>pass.</i> Join:
itaque e., Liv. 9, 31: Ter.

4. ĭgĭtur:
<i>but the postman is pressing, so good-bye</i>,
sed flagitat tabellarius, valebis igitur,
Cic. Ep. (L. G. § 398). Join: ergo i.,
Plaut.: Ter. (N.B.--<i>Itaque</i> differs from
<i>igitur, ergo, etc.</i>, in not being used like
-----File: b0765l.png------------------------------------------------------
them to draw a strictly <i>logical</i> conclusion.)

5. quĕ: <i>and you do not find
an escape, and so the whole state staggers</i>,
nec vos exitum reperitis, totaque res
vacillat, Cic. N. D. 1, 38, 107: cf. pubescant

oriuntur e terra, ib. 2, 19, 50. Cf. too,

ideoque (Georg.): v. also <f>THEREFORE</f>.
(N.B.--<i>So then</i> may be expr. by quamobrem,
quapropter, quare, quocirca, etc.:
v. <f>WHEREFORE</f>.)

IV. Of Manner or
Result: <i>so ... that, so ... as, so that,
so as</i>:

1. ĭtă ... ut: <i>so it results that
reason presides, passion obeys</i>, i. fit ut
ratio praesit, appetitus obtemperet, Cic.
Off. 1, 28, 101: v. also <f>THUS</f>: <i>let us
always so live as to believe that we must
render up an account</i>, semper i. vivamus
ut rationem reddendam (esse) nobis arbitremur,
Cic. (L. G. § 294).

2. sīc
... ut (more rarely): <i>so (= in such a
manner), Scipio, practise virtue as thy
grandsire did</i>, sic, S., ut avus hic tuus
justitiam cole, Cic. Rep. 6, 15, 15, <i>fin.</i>

3. ut: <i>by exercise Demosthenes succeeded
so that no one was considered to
have been a plainer speaker than he</i>,
D. perfecit meditando, ut nemo planius
eo locutus putaretur, Cic. (L. G. § 457).
Phr.: <i>the infantry were hurrying along
so as to look like a body of runaways</i>,
peditum agmen in modum fugientium
agebatur, Liv. 21, 41, <i>post init.</i>: <i>and
so</i>, quo factum est ut, qua re factum
est ut.

V. Of the Purpose:

A.
Affirmative: <i>so that = in order
that, so as to</i>:

1. ŭt: <i>they resolved
to make as large sowings as possible
so that (= in order that) there might
be a supply of corn at hand on the
march</i>, constituerunt sementes quam
maximas facere, ut in itinere copia frumenti
suppeteret, Caes. B. G. 1, 3.

2.
quō: <i>a law ought to be short, so that
(= in order that) it may the more easily
be grasped by the unlettered</i>, legem
brevem esse oportet, quo facilius ab
imperitis teneatur, Cic.

3. qui (quae,
quod): <i>words were invented so as to
denote the will</i>, verba reperta sunt quae
indicarent voluntatem, Cic.

4. dum
(= <i>so that meanwhile</i>): <i>the siege then
took the form of a blockade rather than
an assault for a few days, so that meanwhile
the general's wound might be cured</i>,
obsidio deinde per paucos dies magis
quam oppugnatio fuit dum vulnus ducis
curaretur, Liv. (L. G. § 497). See also
<f>THAT, UNTIL</f>.

B. Negative:

1.
nē (= ut non, quo non): <i>I am reluctant
to be an applauder, so that I may not
seem a flatterer</i>, nolo esse laudator ne
videar adulator, Auct. Her. 4, 21, 29.

2. ut ne (more rarely: v. Smith's
Lat. Dict. s. v. ne, 5).

3. quīn, quōmĭnus:
<i>nor did he think that savages as
they were, they would keep a check upon
themselves, so as not, etc.</i>, neque sibi homines
feros temperaturos existimabat,
quin, etc., Caes. B. G. 1, 33: v. also L. G.
§§ 461, 463.

VI. Of Extent or Degree:

A. <i>So</i> (followed by <i>as</i> or <i>that</i>):

1. ĭta ... ut (ĭta gen. with <i>verbs</i>,
<i>adjj.</i>, or <i>advv.</i>): (<i>a.</i>) <i>so exceedingly</i>:
<i>all the news that is bought from your
quarter is so uncertain that I cannot
tell what to write</i>, i. erant omnia quae
isthinc afferebantur incerta ut quid ad
te scriberem non occurreret, Cic. Ep.
(L. G. §§ 398, 404, q. v., for the <i>epistolary
tenses</i>): <i>but there are some so unmusical
that they cannot come into the number
of orators</i>, sed sunt quidam i. voce absoni
ut in oratorum numerum venire
non possint, Cic.: <i>this indeed so inflames
their minds that, etc.</i>, id vero i. accendit
animos ut, etc., Liv. 6, 14, <i>post med.</i>: cf.
Cic. Verr. 1, 4, 12. (<i>b.</i>) <i>so little</i>: <i>they
triumphed, it is true, yet so (little) that
the other, routed and overpowered though
he was, was still a sovereign</i>, i. triumpharunt
ut ille pulsus superatusque regnaret,
Cic. Manil. 3, 8: <i>that the state
is not so (little) ill that it can be
propped up by usual remedies</i>, non
i. civitatem aegram esse ut consuetis
remediis sisti possit, Liv. 3, 20, <i>fin.</i>
-----File: b0765m.png------------------------------------------------------

2. sīc ... ŭt (very seldom found
with <i>adjj.</i>): <i>his province is full of the
bravest men so (= to such an extent)
that none in the whole of Italy can be
called more peopled (with them)</i>, hujus
praefectura plena est virorum fortissimorum
sic, ut nulla tota Italia frequentior
dici possit, Cic.

3. ădeō ... ŭt:
<i>so inexperienced in matters as to trust,
etc.</i>, a. imperitus rerum, ut,[**P2: ,] etc., Caes.
B. G. 5, 27, <i>med.</i>: <i>Hannibal was so

22, 32,[**P2: ,] <i>post init.</i>: but v. Smith's

4. tam ... (folld. by quam, qui,
or ut): <i>nothing seems to Xenophon so
princely as the pursuit of tilling the

q. studium agri colendi, Cic.: <i>who is so

5. tantus ...
(folld. by quantus, ut, qui): <i>I never saw

nullam unquam vidi tantam (contionem)
quanta nunc vestra est, Cic.: <i>he was not
so great a man that, etc.</i>, non fuit t.
homo ut,[**P2: ,] etc., id.: <i>they determined that
that crime was so atrocious that it ought
not to be concealed</i>, statuerunt t. illud
esse maleficium quod non occultari deberet,
id. (N.B.--In Cic. Fam. 1, 7,[**P2: ,] 4,

t. vim habet ut, etc.)[**P1: missing .|P2: no ?|P3 no]

6.
aeque (with atque, ac, et, ac si: v.
Smith's Lat. Dict. s. v. aeque): but
very rarely with quam or ut: e. g.,
<i>nothing frightened them so much as the
vigour and complexion of the general</i>,
nihil a. eos terruit quam robur ac color
imperatoris, Liv. (v. <f>AS</f>, I., 3): <i>in
pleading nothing pleases him so much
as brevity</i>, ei nihil a. in causis agendis

Phr.: <i>I am not so strong as either of

uterque (Ainsw.): <i>not so large as was

<i>hanc</i> sibi populoque gratiam referret

<i>id</i> tempus esse <i>ut</i>, etc., Liv. 2, 29, <i>post
med.</i>: <i>by this time the state of affairs
in Latium was so sad that, etc.</i>, jam Latio
<i>is</i> status erat rerum <i>ut</i>, etc., id. 8, 13,
<i>init.</i> Special Phr.: <i>be so good as,
etc.</i>: expr. by amabo <i>s.</i> amabo te (parenthetically):
<i>assist me in this, be so
good</i> (or <i>be so good as to, etc.</i>), id, amabo,

<i>be so good as to cross over to there</i>, a. ut

Also less colloq. by circuml.: <i>be so good

<i>subj.</i> of volo (foll. by a verb in the

as to answer me this</i>, velim uti respondeas,[**P2: ,]
Cic.

B. <i>So</i> (<i>absol.</i>, without
<i>as</i> or <i>that</i>: = <i>so very, so much</i>,
some clause being understood):

1.
ĭtă (after non, haud = admodum): <i>those
statues are very magnificent and admirable,
but not so (very) old</i>, sunt ea
(simulacra) perampla et praeclara sed
non i. antiqua, Cic.: <i>not so much corn</i>,
haud i. multum frumenti, Liv.

2.
-----File: b0765r.png------------------------------------------------------
sīc (very rarely): <i>they were unwilling
to throw a body to wild beasts, not
so (much so) to fling naked persons
into the river</i>, noluerunt feris corpus
objicere, non s. nudos in flumen dejicere,
Cic. Rosc. Am. 26, 71. Cf. sīccĭnĕ:
<i>will you go so untidy as you are?</i>
s. immunda ibis?[**this question mark should not be italicized/F2] Plaut.: <i>s. (<f>or</f> to such
an extent) do you allow your soldier
and chieftain to be harassed by personal

3. ădeō (with the <i>indic.</i>: the

<b>---- as, as</b>:

1. sĭmul atque,

<b>sooner</b>:

I. <i>Earlier</i>: tempĕrius,
mātūrius (v. <f>EARLY</f>): tempestīvius, Hor.

Phr.: <i>the s. the better (= as soon as

II.
<i>More quickly</i>: expr. by <i>compar. adv.</i>
(v. <f>SOON</f>, II.: <f>QUICKLY</f>, <f>SPEEDILY</f>).
Phr.: <i>no s. said than done</i>, dictum ac

III. <i>More willingly</i> (= <i>rather</i>:
q. v.): expr. by lĭbentius, pŏtius, măgis,
etc. foll. by quam: or by some verb
denoting <i>preference</i> (v. <f>TO PREFER</f>).
In Cic. Off. 1, 18, we find even citius =
potius: simly. in id. Tusc. 5, 27, 77,
prius = potius.

IV. <i>More easily</i>:

1. ōcius: <i>that nook of yours will s.
produce pepper and frankincense than
the grape</i>, angulus iste feret piper et
tus ocius uva, Hor. Ep. 1, 14, 23.

2.
făcĭlius: <i>nothing is s. said</i>, nil est dictu
f., Ter. Ph. 2, 1, 70: and gen. by a <i>compar.
adv.</i> (see also <f>EASILY</f>).


<b>soonest</b>: expr. by a <i>superl. adv.</i> (v.
<f>SOON</f>): or by periphr.: e. g. <i>at the s.</i>,
primo quoque tempore, etc. (v. <f>SOON AS
POSSIBLE, AS</f>). Often best expr. by <i>adj.</i>:
<i>pears the s. ripe</i>, ocissima pira, Plin.

1. fūlīgo, ĭnis, <i>f.</i>: <i>the door-*posts

2. cămīnorum

I. <i>To utter articulate

1. lŏquor, cūtus, 3: cf. Virg. G. 1,
478, pecudesque locutae, infandum!
(<i>articulate speech</i> being the peculiarity
of <i>human beings</i>): <i>to s. in good pure
Latin</i>, pure et Latine l., Cic. de Or. 1,
32, <i>init.</i>: <i>to s. spitefully</i>, infeste l., Liv.
21, 11, <i>init.</i>: <i>the facts s. for themselves</i>,
res ipsa l., Cic. Mil. 20, <i>med.</i>: also, res
pro se ipsa l., id. 3, 2, <i>extr.</i>: <i>to s. before
any one (as before a judge)</i>, apud aliquem
l., id. Fin. 2, 22, <i>extr.</i> Freq. with
<i>acc.</i> of <i>adj.</i> or <i>neut. pron.</i>: <i>having spoken
these words, many words, etc.</i>, haec locutus,
multa locutus, etc. Also with
noun as direct obj. = <i>to speak of</i>, v. foll.
art.

2. fāri, fātus, 1 (old verb, and
chiefly poet. = preced.): <i>infants unable
to speak</i>, nescios fari pueros, Hor. Od. 4,
6, 18: <i>hardly had I spoken these words</i>,
vix ea fatus eram, Virg. <i>pass.</i>

3. dīco,
xi, ctum, 3 (<i>to give expression to thought</i>;
implying not only the use of the organs
of speech, but also the <i>exercise of the
rational powers</i>: thus, bene loqui, is to
<i>speak accurately, with correct accent,
etc.</i>: bene dicere, to be <i>a good speaker</i>):
v. <f>TO SAY</f>.

4. fābŭlor, 1: v. <f>TO TALK</f>.
<i>Not able to s.</i>, infans, tis: Cic.: Hor.

II. <i>To make a speech</i>:

1. expr.
by phr.: verba facere (not necessarily
implying <i>a set speech</i>), Caes. B. G. 2, 14;
more fully, verba atque orationem
facere, id. B. C. 2, 18: orationem habere,
Sall. Cat. 31; and in somewhat diff.
sense, <i>to s. at length on any subject</i>,
multam orationem de aliqua re habere,
Cic. Tusc. 5, 33; contionem [esp. apud
populum, apud milites] habere, Caes.
B. C. 3, 73: <i>he spoke as follows</i>, talem
orationem exorsus est, Liv. 21, 39, <i>extr.</i>

2. contiōnor, 1 (<i>to deliver an oration
to a public assembly</i>): <i>to s. before the
people</i>, ad populum c., Suet. Aug. 84;
<i>before troops</i>, apud milites, Caes. B. C.
1, 7: <i>to s. as from a higher platform</i>,
c. tanquam superiore e loco, Cic. Tusc.
1, 49, 117.

3. ōro, 1 (rare in this
sense): <i>the art of s.ing (oratory)</i>, ars
orandi, Quint. prooem. § 4. <i>Comp.</i> pĕrōro,
1 (<i>to finish s.ing, come to a conclusion</i>),
Liv. 21, 11.

4. also in referring
generally to a speech, dico or
loquor may suffice; esp. <i>ger.</i>: <i>as soon
as Caesar had done s.ing</i>, postquam
Caesar dicendi finem fecit, Sall. C. 52,
<i>init.</i>


<b>---- against</b>:

I. <i>To speak in opposition
to</i>: expr. by contra and <i>acc.</i>,
with dico or loquor: <i>to s. against any
one's civil status</i>, c. caput alicujus dicere,
Cic. Quint. 13, 44 (contradicere with <i>dat.</i>
= <i>to contradict</i>): v. <f>AGAINST</f>.

II. <i>To
use hostile or reproachful language
against any one</i>:

1. mălĕdīco, 3 (with
<i>dat.</i>): v. <f>TO REVILE</f>, <f>ABUSE</f>. Also, male
loqui alicui, Pl.: not so constr. in Cic.:
but comp. id. R. Am. 48, 140, where m.
loqui [absol.] = maledicta dicere.

2.
oblŏquor, cūtus, 3 (usu. rather to <i>interrupt
a person who is speaking</i>: with
dat.): Cat. 83, 4.

3. invĕhor, ctus,
3 (<i>to launch out in attack of any one</i>:
with <i>acc.</i>): <i>to s. bitterly and insultingly
against any one</i>, acerbe contumelioseque
in aliquem i., Cic. de Or. 2, 75, 304: v.
<f>TO INVEIGH AGAINST</f>.

4. expr. by
maledicta in aliquem dicere, Cic. Fam.
2, 3: conferre, id. Att. 11, 8.


<b>---- of</b>:

1. dīco, 3: in prose usu.
foll. by de and <i>abl.</i>: <i>to s. of Scipio</i>, de
Scipione d., Cic. <i>pass.</i>: freq. in poets
with direct obj. = <i>to tell of; sing,</i>
-----File: b0782m.png------------------------------------------------------
<i>praise</i>: <i>to s. of Diana, Hercules, etc.</i>,
Dianam, Alciden d., Hor. This constr.
even occurs in prose: cf. Liv. 7, 29, <i>init.</i>,
majora jam hinc bella ... dicentur.
(Dico also occurs in prose with direct
obj. = <i>to name, mention, refer to</i>: cf.
Cic. Fin. 3, 2, <i>extr.</i>, quod autem meum
munus dicis, but not = <i>to speak concerning</i>.)

2. lŏquor, 3 (same constr.
as preced., except that it is freq. used in
prose with <i>acc.</i> of <i>neut. prons., etc.</i>): <i>to
s. with any one of any subject</i>, l. cum
aliquo de aliqua re, Cic. pass.: <i>we will
s. of these subjects together</i>, ista loquemur
inter nos, Cic. Fin. 3, 2, <i>extr.</i>: <i>to s. of
battles</i>, proelia l., Hor. Od. 4, 15, 1: Sen.:
Plin.

3. mĕmŏro, 1: v. <f>TO MENTION</f>.
See also <f>TO DISCUSS</f>. Phr.: <i>to s. well
of</i>, benedicere, with <i>dat.</i>, Cic. Sext. 52,
<i>init.</i>; praedicare (constr. with <i>acc.</i> or de
and <i>abl.</i>); esp. with bene, optime: cf.
Cic. Arch. 9, 20, a quo sua virtus optime
praedicaretur (v. <f>TO PRAISE</f>, <f>PUBLISH</f>):
<i>to s. ill of</i>,[**P1: should be ,|P2 checked original - corrected to ,] maledicere (v. <f>TO SPEAK
AGAINST</f>): <i>not to s. of</i> (inserted in a kind
of parenthetical way), ut omittam ...,
Cic. Br. 76, <i>fin.</i>: Nep. (better than ut
praetermittam): so, ut taceam (poet.),
Ov. M. 13, 177.


<b>speak out</b>:

1. ēlŏquor, 3: Cic.:
Quint.

2. prōlŏquor, 3: Auct. B. Afr.
Phr.: <i>to s. out plainly</i>, plane et Latine
loqui, Cic. Ph. 7, 6, 17: vere ac libere
loqui, id. R. Am. 48, 140.


<b>---- to</b>:

1. appello, 1 (<i>to address,
accost</i>): with <i>acc.</i>: Ter.: Cic. In same
sense also, compello, 1 (chiefly poet.):
Virg.

2. allŏquor, 3 (<i>to talk to</i>:
whereas appello is simply <i>to address</i>:
also with <i>acc.</i>): <i>no one was willing to
s. to him</i>, quem nemo a. vellet, Cic. Clu.
61, 170: Pl.: Ter.

3. affāri, 1: only
used in <i>pres. ind.</i> (but not <i>1 pers.</i>),
<i>perf. part.</i>, <i>infin.</i>, and <i>2 pers. sing.
imperat.</i> (<i>to address</i>): <i>to s. to any one
by name</i>, nomine a. aliquem, Cic. Br.
72, 253.


<b>---- together</b>:

1. collŏquor, or
simply lŏquor, 3 (with inter and <i>pron.
refl.</i>): <i>they spoke a great deal t.</i>, multum
inter se collocuti sunt, Cic. de Or. 1,[**P1: should be ,|P2 checked original - corrected to ,] 7,
26: so, loquemur inter nos, id. Fin. 3, 2,
<i>extr.</i>

2. confābŭlor, 1 (rare): Ter.
See also <f>TO CONVERSE</f>.


<b>---- with</b>: collŏquor, 3: usu. foll.
by cum: Cic.


<b>speaker</b>:

I. <i>One who makes
speeches</i>: ōrātor: v. <f>ORATOR</f>. Phr.:
<i>a good s.</i>, homo disertus, Cic. de Or. 1,
21, 94: <i>to be a good s.</i>, aptum esse ad
dicendum, id. Tusc. 1, 3, 5: multum
valere dicendo, id. Br. 7, 27.

II. <i>One
at the time speaking</i>: use <i>imperf. part.</i>
of dico (except in <i>nom. sing.</i>: L. G.
§ 638): or rel. clause, is qui dicit,
loquitur, etc.: v. <f>TO SPEAK</f>.

III. <i>The
president of the House of Commons</i>:
ōrātor (in class. sense of <i>spokesman</i>).


<b>speaking</b> (<i>subs.</i>): expr. by dīco, lŏquor,
verba făcio: <i>artfully to take up
the time by s.</i>, calumnia dicendi diem
eximere, Cic. Att. 4, 3, 3: <i>to refrain
from evil s.</i>, temperare a maledicendo,
male loquendo (also, a maledictis): <i>unaccustomed
to public s.</i>, *insolens verba
ad populum (ad coetus hominum) faciendi:
<i>they think they shall be heard
for their much s.</i>, *propterea se exauditum
iri putant quod multa loquuntur.
See also <f>ORATORY</f>.


<b>speaking</b> (<i>adj.</i>): perh. argūtus, signĭfĭcans:
v. <f>SIGNIFICANT</f>.


<b>speaking-trumpet</b>: perh. cornu
(gen. term for any such instrument).


<b>spear</b> (<i>subs.</i>);[**P1: typo for :]

1. hasta: <i>pass.</i>
(N.B.--This is the regular word to represent
Eng.)

2. lancea (<i>a light s.
with a leathern thong fastened to the
middle</i>): Hirt.: Tac.

3. sărissa (<i>the
long Macedonian pike used by the phalangites</i>):
Liv. (Pilum is not a spear,
but <i>the regular javelin of the Roman
legionary</i>: v. <f>JAVELIN</f>.)


<b>spear</b> (<i>v.</i>): Phr.: hasta configere,
transfigere: v. <f>TO TRANSFIX</f>.


<b>spearman</b>: hastātus: Curt. 3, 3.
Or by circuml.: *miles hasta armatus,
qui hastam fert.

<b>spear-mint</b>: *mentha viridis: Bot.


<b>special</b>:

I. <i>Confined to one species
or class</i>:

1. pĕcūliāris, e (<i>relating to
a particular case</i>): <i>a s. edict</i>, p. edictum,
Cic. Verr. 3, 14, 36: v. <f>PECULIAR</f>.

2.
spĕciālis, e (not in Cic., but good as <i>t.t.</i>[** t. t. below]):
Quint. 5, 10, 43 (opp. generalis): Sen.

3. proprius (<i>belonging peculiarly
to</i>: with <i>gen.</i>): cf. Suet. Aug. 5, quasi
proprio suo et peculiari deo (<i>his own s.
divinity</i>).

4. praecĭpuus (a legal
phr.): Dig.: v. Smith's Lat. Dict. s. v.
Phr.: <i>a s. law directed against a person</i>,
privilegium, Cic. Leg. 3, 19, 44: <i>to confer
a province by s. decree</i>, provinciam
extra ordinem decernere, id. Prov. Cons.
8. See also <f>PARTICULAR</f>.

II. <i>Standing
out from the rest</i>:

1. praecĭpuus:
<i>to hold in s. honour</i>, p. honore habere,
Caes. B. G. 5, 52: Cic.

2. pĕcūliāris:
<i>for s. desert</i>, p. merito, Suet. Vit. 4. See
also <f>SINGULAR</f>, <f>SIGNAL</f>, <f>REMARKABLE</f>.

III. In phr. <i>special jury</i>: perh.
judices extraordinarii.

<b>specially</b>:

I. <i>With reference to
species</i>: spĕciālĭter (only as <i>t. t.</i>): opp.
generatim: Col. 12, 2.

II. <i>In an especial
manner</i>:

1. praecĭpuē: Cic.

2. pĕcūliārĭter (late): Plin. See

<b>specie</b>: aurum argentumve signatum:
v. <f>TO COIN</f>, <f>STAMP</f>.


<b>species</b>:

I. In strict sense: spĕcies,
ēi (not so used in Cic., but necessary
for precise expression): Sen. Ep. 58, 7,
where the genus is represented as containing
a variety of species: M. L.
(N.B.--Cic. makes an approach to this
use of the word, de Or. 1, 42.[**P2: ,] 189, genus
est id quod sui similes ... <i>specie</i> autem
differentes duas aut plures complectitur
partes.)

II. In looser sense, <i>a sort or
kind</i>: gĕnus: v. <f>KIND</f>.


<b>specific</b> (<i>adj.</i>):

I. <i>Relating to a
species</i>: Phr.: <i>s. features</i>, quae alicujus
rei propria [ac peculiaria] sunt[**P2: :]
v. <f>PECULIAR</f>, <f>PROPER</f>. <i>S. name</i> (scient.
<i>t. t.</i>), perh. *speciei nomen, nomen speciale.

II. <i>Precise and definite</i>: v.
<f>EXPLICIT</f>,[**P2: ,] <f>EXPLICITLY</f>.


<b>specific</b> (<i>subs.</i>): expr. by singŭlāris,

singulare serpentibus abigendis, id. 8,
32, 50 § 118. Also expr. by facere (ad),
prodesse: v. <f>GOOD</f>, <i>adj.</i> (II.).


<b>specifically</b>: dĭsertē: v. <f>EXPLICITLY</f>.


<b>specify</b>: subtiliter enumerare: v.
<f>PRECISELY</f>.


<b>specimen</b>: exemplum (<i>sample to
judge from</i>): <i>the following will suffice

Quint. 9.[**P2: ,] 2, 56: so, in exemplum

specimen in this sense: specimen dare
is <i>to furnish proof, give practical demonstration

Verr. 8, 27.) See also <f>PROOF</f>. Phr.:
<i>learn what they all are from a single s.</i>,
ex uno disce omnes, Virg.


<b>specious</b>: prŏbābĭlis: or expr. by
spĕcies: v. <f>PLAUSIBLE</f>, <f>SHOWY</f>. Sometimes
fūcātus may serve; but it expresses
more than Eng.: v. <f>FALSE</f>,
<f>COUNTERFEIT</f>. Also, vendĭbĭlis, e (<i>that
makes the most of itself</i>): Cic. Am,[**P2: .] 25,
96. (Not speciosus; which has a good
sense.)


<b>speciously</b>: prŏbābĭlĭter: v. <f>PLAUSIBLY</f>.


<b>speciousness</b>: captiosa probabilitas:
v. <f>PLAUSIBILITY</f>.

<b>speculate</b>:

<b>speculation</b>:

I. <i>Philosophical</i>:

III. <i>A guess</i>: conjectūra: v. <f>GUESS</f>.

<b>speech</b>:

I. <i>The faculty of speaking</i>:
ōrātio: Cic. Off. 1, 4, 12: <i>deprived

53, 121. Phr.: <i>to take away the faculty

II. <i>Utterance</i>: Phr.:

III. <i>An address, oration</i>:

1. ōrātio: <i>dimin.</i> ōrātiuncŭla (<i>a short
s.</i>): <i>a powerful, polished, admirable s.</i>,
o. gravis, polita, admirabilis, Cic. de Or. 3,
25: <i>a clever and oratorical s.</i>, o. diserta
et oratoria, ib. 1, 54, 231: <i>a brilliant s.</i>,
o. luculenta, Sall. C. 31. The foll. epithets
are taken from Kr. (e Cic.): oratio
fortis et virilis: compta, polita, composita
et ornata: diligenter elaborata,
accurate commentata (<i>carefully studied</i>):
gravissimis verbis sententiisque
plena: accurata et facta quodam modo.
<i>To deliver a s.</i>, o. habere, Cic. <i>pass.</i>: <i>from
MS.</i>, o. de scripto dicere, id. Pl. 30, 74:
<i>to study a s.</i>, o. commentari, id. R. Am.
29, 82.

2. contio, ōnis, <i>f.</i> (<i>a s. before
the people, or to troops</i>): <i>he delivered a
s. to the soldiers</i>, c. ad milites habuit,
Caes. B. C. 3, 73: <i>in the s. to the people
against Catiline</i>, in c. contra Catilinam,
Quint. 5, 11, 42. <i>To deliver such a s.</i>,
contionari: v. <f>TO SPEAK</f> (II.).

3. actio
(<i>a legal s. or pleading</i>): thus <i>the speeches
against Verres are called</i> actiones, Cic.
Verr. 2, 1, 30, 75, etc.: Suet.: Quint.
Phr.: <i>to make a s.</i>, verba facere, Caes.
B. G. 2, 14: <i>to wind up a s., finish it</i>,
perorare, Cic.

<f>TO SPIN</f> (I.). Also meton.[** s/b ,] stāmen, ĭnis,
<i>n.</i>: <i>I beguiled sleep by s.</i>, fallebam stamine
somnum, Prop. 1, 3, 41. Phr.: <i>to
earn a living by s.</i>, *colo fusoque victum
quaeritare: staminibus ducendis
quaestum facere.


<b>---- wheel</b>: *rota ad fila (stamina)
deducenda.


<b>spinosity</b>: fig. of argument or style,
spinosum disserendi [orationis] genus.


<b>spinous</b>: spīnōsus: v. <f>THORNY</f>.


<b>spinster</b>: virgo: quae nondum viro
nupsit: innupta: v. <f>MAID</f>, <f>UNMARRIED</f>.


<b>spiracle</b>: spīrāmentum, spīrācŭlum:
v. <f>PORE</f>.


<b>spiral</b> (<i>adj.</i>):

1. spirae <i>s.</i> cochleae
formam habens (spira denotes <i>any
kind of twist or coil</i>: cochlea, <i>the form
of a snail-shell or screw</i>): so, <i>to wind
in a s. direction</i>, in cochleam serpere,
Cels. 8, 10, 1.

2. less precisely: invŏlūtus,
convŏlūtus, intortus, rĕtortus,
tortĭlis: <i>they form s. channels</i>, involutos
faciunt canales [et justam cochleae
naturalemque imitationem], Vitr. 10, 6
(11), 2: <i>(shells) with a s. top</i>, vertice
muricatim (= <i>like the shell of the murex</i>)
intorto, Plin. 9, 33, 52: <i>a s. or winding
cave</i>, specus in cochleam retortus, Col.
8, 17, <i>init.</i>: <i>a s. horn</i>, buccina tortilis,
Ov. Met. 1, 336 (where is added an exact
description of <i>an expanding s. form</i>, in
latum quae turbine crescit ab imo).
(N.B.--Spiralis is without authority:
Forcell. gives the foll. definition of <i>a s.
line</i>, linea flexuosa quae orbes facit non
redeuntes in se: s. v. spira.)


<b>spiral</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

1. cochlea, spīra:
v. preced. art.

2. invŏlūtio: Vitr.
10, 6 (11), 3.


<b>spire</b>:

I. <i>A coil</i>: spīra, orbis: v.
<f>COIL</f>.

II. <i>Of a church, etc.</i>: perh.
turris genus quae meta in fastigium
convoluta exsurgit: cf. Plin. 16, 33, 60
(where the description is of <i>a kind of
tapering cypress</i>): *culmen undique
acute fastigatum: in acutum excelsumque
fastigium eductum [qualis Anglice
<i>spira</i> dicitur].


<b>spirit</b>:

I. Orig. sense: <i>the breath</i>:
spīrĭtus, ūs: v. <f>BREATH</f>.

II. <i>Animating
principle</i>:

1. ănĭma (<i>vital
principle; in man or in brutes</i>): v.
<f>SOUL</f>.

2. spīrĭtus (not class. in this
sense): Vulg. Eccl. iii. 21: et <i>pass.</i>
(= Gr. πνεῦμα). See also <f>SOUL</f>.

III.
<i>Intelligence apart from body; an immaterial
being, human or otherwise</i>:

1.
mens, ntis, <i>f.</i>: <i>God is a pure s.</i>, Deus est
mens soluta quaedam et libera [segregata
ab omni concretione mortali], Cic.
Tusc. 1, 27, 66: <i>the stars are animated
by divine s.s</i>, stellae divinis m. animatae
sunt, id. Rep. 6, 15, <i>med.</i>

2. spīrĭtus
(not class. in this sense): <i>God is a s.</i>,
s. est Deus, Vulg. Joh. iv. 24: <i>the Holy S.</i>,
Sanctus S., ib. <i>pass.</i>

3. ănĭma: Virg.
Aen. 6, 713: v. <f>SOUL</f>.

IV. Esp. in <i>pl.,
the dead as living in another state; disembodied
spirits</i>:

1. ănĭmae: <i>the s.s
of the blest</i>, piae a., Hor. Od. 1, 10, 17:
Virg.

2. mānes, ium, <i>m.</i> (used both
-----File: b0785l.png------------------------------------------------------
of <i>the departed spirit of an individual
and of the community of spirits</i>): v.
<f>SHADE</f> (IV.). <i>The world of s.s</i>, infĕri,
orum; later, Orcus: v. <f>SHADE</f> (V.).

V.
As syn. for <i>mind or soul</i>, but usu. with
a <i>somewhat higher conception</i>:

1. ănĭmus:
<i>a lofty s.</i>, animus excelsus magnificusque,
Cic. Off. 1, 23, <i>init.</i>: a magnus
elatusque, ib. 1, 18, 61:[**P1: should be :|P3 visible in TIA] cf. Sall. Cat. 5,
a. vastus, <i>an unbounded (ambitious) s.</i>:
v. <f>MIND</f>, <f>SOUL</f>.

2. ingĕnium: <i>a lofty
and elevated s.</i>, sublime et erectum i.,
Tac. Agr. 4: so, i. excelsum, Plin. Ep.

VI. <i>Vivacity and energy of mind</i>:

1. ănĭmus: <i>our men are imbued
with fresh s.</i>, nostris augetur animus,
Caes. B. G. 7, 70: <i>be of good s. (courage)</i>,
ades animo! Cic. Rep. 6, 10: also <i>pl.</i>:
<i>(the goddess) imparts s.</i>, animos dat,
Ov. M. 5, 47. Hence, <i>full of s.</i>, ănĭmōsus
(whether <i>of men or animals</i>): Cic.:
Ov.: v. <f>SPIRITED</f>.

2. spīrĭtus, ūs
(<i>high s.</i>): <i>a man of immense s.</i> (with
the accessory idea of <i>pride and ambition</i>),
ingentis s. vir, Liv. 21, 1: esp. <i>pl.</i>,
of <i>an overbearing and arrogant s.</i>:
Cic. Clu. 39, 109 (noratis animos ejus ac
s. tribunicios): Liv.

3. vis, vĭgor: v.
<f>VIGOUR</f>, <f>ENERGY</f>. <i>Lacking s.</i>: ignāvus:
v. <f>SPIRITLESS</f>, <f>COWARDLY</f>. Phr.: <i>I am
in wonderful s.s for fighting</i>, sum mira
alacritate ad pugnandum, Cic. Att. 2, 7.

VII. <i>Animation and energy of style</i>:

1. vĭgor (appy. not in Cic.): Join:
quantum vigoris, quantum animi [in illo
libro], Sen. Ep. 64, 2.

2. ănĭmus (late
in this use): <i>plenty of thought and of s.
(in an orator)</i>, et consilii et animi satis,
Quint. 10, 1, 113: cf. Sen. l. c.

3.
nervi, orum (<i>sinew</i>, i. e. <i>force and
energy</i>: a stronger term than Eng.):
cf. Cic. Or. 19, 62, horum oratio neque
nervos neque aculeos (<i>pungency</i>) oratorios
ac forenses habet.

4. very oft. expr.
by <i>adj.</i>: <i>full of spirit</i>, acer, vehemens,
animosus: v. <f>SPIRITED</f>. <i>Lacking s.</i>, frigidus,
lentus: v. <f>FLAT</f>, <f>DULL</f>, <f>SPIRITLESS</f>.

VIII. <i>Temper or disposition</i>:

1. ingĕnium,
indŏles (both denoting <i>natural,
and so permanent character</i>): <i>a manly
s.</i>, ingenium virile, Sall. C. 20: <i>a virtuous
s.</i>, virtutis indoles, Cic. Off. 3, 4,
16: v. <f>DISPOSITION</f>, <f>TEMPER</f>, <f>MIND</f>.

2.
ănĭmus (<i>attitude of mind at any given
time</i>): <i>you ought to display this s. towards
me</i>, hoc a. in nos esse debebis,
Cic. Fam. 2, 1, <i>extr.</i>: <i>animated by a
friendly s. towards the R. people</i>, bono
a. in P. R., Caes. B. G. 1, 6: Suet. So
animatus (<i>influenced by a certain s.</i>):
<i>entertaining a bad s. (disaffected) towards</i>,
male animatus erga ..., Suet.
Vit. 7: so, bene animatus, Nep. Cim. 2.

3. stŭdium (<i>strong or eager bent of
mind</i>): <i>a warlike s.</i>, s. bellicae gloriae,
Cic. Off. 1, 18, 61: <i>the s. of inquiry after
truth</i>, s. ad investigandam veritatem incitatum,
id. Tusc. 5, 24, 68: <i>a revolutionary
s.</i>, novandi <i>s.</i> rerum novarum s.
(cupiditas): v. <f>REVOLUTION</f> (III.).

4.
mens (<i>both of permanent and temporary
features of mind</i>): <i>a virtuous s.</i>, m.
bona, Liv. 39, 16, <i>med.</i>: Ter.: <i>the s. of
(prevailing in) the armies</i>, m. exercituum,
Tac. H. 1, 4.

5. often such
phrr. as <i>a kindly s., a hostile s.</i>, may be
expr. by a single word: v. <f>KINDNESS</f>,
<f>HOSTILITY</f>, etc.

IX. <i>Peculiar or prevailing
sentiment and complexion</i>; esp.
of <i>an age or a nation</i>:

1. perh. rătio:
cf. Cic. Verr. 5, 69, 177, ratio atque inclinatio
temporum (<i>the s. and tendency
of the age</i>): <i>the s. of the oratory of each
age</i>, cujusque aetatis dicendi ratio voluntasque,
id. de Or. 2, 22, 92.

2.
mōres: <i>since the s. of the age inclines
to ...</i>, quum hi mores ad ... incubuerint,
id. Q. Fr. 1, 1, 3: so, quum ita
se mores habent, Sall. Cat. 52, <i>med.</i>

3. sēcŭlum (<i>fashion or s. of the
age</i>; in unfavourable sense): cf. Tac.
Ger., nec corrumpere et corrumpi <i>seculum</i>
vocatur: also Pl. Trin. 2, 2, 7, novi
ego hoc s. quibus moribus slet[** siet? unclear|P3 s/b siet]. Phr.:
<i>he exercised office in the same s. in
which he had sought it</i>, quibus artibus
petierat magistratus, iisdem gerebat,
Liv. 7, 33. (See Nägels. Stil. § 67, 2.)

X. <i>Intention</i>; as <i>distinguished
from mere verbal expression</i>:

1. vŏluntas:
<i>whether to abide by the letter or
s. of laws</i>, verbis legum an voluntate
standum sit, Quint. 7, 10, 6: Cic. Join:
voluntas et sententia (legis), Cic. Verr.
3, 84, 193: voluntas et consilium et sententia
(interdicti), id. Caec. 18, 50.

2.
consĭlium (<i>intention</i>): Cic. Caec. l. c.:
cf. ib. <i>paulo infr.</i>, ad <i>verba</i> rem deflectere,
<i>consilium</i> autem eorum qui
scripserunt relinquere (<i>to sacrifice the
spirit to the letter</i>).

3. sententia
(<i>meaning</i>): like consilium, may be
strengthened by a synonym: v. <i>supr.</i>
Phr.: <i>to obey the letter <f>or</f> the s. of a
command</i>, ad verba obedire, ad id quod
ex verbis intelligitur obtemperare, Cic.
Caec. 18, 52: <i>not to translate literally,
but to give the s. of an author</i>, *non
verbum verbo reddere sed mentem sententiamque
scriptoris referre; *potius
ex mente scriptoris quam ex verbis interpretari.

XI. Meton., <i>a person, as
marked by certain intellectual qualities</i>:
ingĕnium: cf. Tac. Agr. 2, monumenta
clarissimorum ingeniorum (<i>of those
illustrious spirits</i>): also Sall. Cat. 8,
scriptorum magna ingenia. Phr.: <i>a
choice s.</i>, *singulari virtute atque ingenio
vir: eximiae mentis indolis homo:
<i>a generous s.</i>, *vir generosus ac liberalis
(v. <f>GENEROUS</f>): <i>a beautiful s.</i>, *venustissimi
candidissimique ingenii homo.

XII. Theol., <i>the renewed nature of
man</i>: spīrĭtus: Vulg.

XIII. Chem.,
<i>a distilled fluid</i>: spīrĭtus: used as
scient. <i>t. t.</i>: also lĭquor (tenuissimus,
nobilissimus, efficacissimus): Bauer in
Kr.


<b>spirited</b>:

1. ănĭmōsus (<i>full of
life and energy</i>; of horses, <i>mettlesome</i>):
<i>the s. Accius</i>, animosi oris Accius, Hor.:
Varr.: Cic. Join: fortis et animosus,
Cic.: animosus atque fortis, Hor. See
also <f>METTLESOME</f>.

2. gĕnĕrōsus (<i>high-*bred,
high-spirited</i>): <i>a s. and powerful
king</i>, rex g. et potens, Cic. Off. 3, 22, 86.
More fully, generosi spiritus (<i>gen.</i> of
quality), <i>high-s.</i>: Plin. 8, 40, 61.

3.
ācer, cris, cre (rather stronger than Eng.:
<i>full of energy and vigour</i>: <i>eager, brave,
fierce</i>): <i>a most s. champion</i>, acerrimus
defensor, Cic. Fam. 1, 1, 1: <i>a s. horse</i>,
a. equus, Virg. Aen. 4, 156: v. <f>EAGER</f>,
<f>FIERCE</f>.

4. ălăcer, cris, cre (weaker
than preced. and than Eng.: <i>brisk,
lively</i>): Caes. B. G. 3, 24 (alacriores
ad pugnandum): see also <f>CHEERFUL</f>,
<f>ACTIVE</f>.


<b>spiritedly</b>:

1. ănĭmōsē (<i>courageously</i>):
Join: animose et fortiter,
Cic.

2. ācrĭter (<i>keenly, vigorously</i>):
Caes.: Cic.

3. ălăcrĭter (<i>briskly</i>):
Amm. (Or by circuml., acri or alacri
animo: v. <f>SPIRITED</f>.)


<b>spiritless</b>:

1. ignāvus (<i>lacking
courage or energy</i>): <i>bees s. with hunger</i>
(apes) fame ignavae, Virg. G. 4, 259:
<i>s. and feeble</i>, i. et imbecillus, Cic. Rep.
1, 32: v. <f>COWARDLY</f>, <f>SLOTHFUL</f>.

2.
pĭger, gra, grum (<i>slow, inactive</i>): <i>s. look</i>,
p. vultus, Mart. 2, 11. Join: piger
tristisque, Apul.

3. imbellis (<i>unwar-*like</i>):
Join: ignavus et imbellis, Liv.;
timidus et imbellis, Quint.

4. by phr.,
imbecillus animo, Cic. Am. 19, 70: animo
demisso atque humili, id. Font. 11, 23:
animo abjecto fractoque, cf. id. Am. 16,
59. See also <f>DULL</f>, <f>FLAT</f>.


<b>spiritlessly</b>:

1. ignāvē (for <i>syn.</i>
v. <i>adj.</i>): <i>to crop the herbage s.</i>, (of ailing
cattle), i. carpere herbas, Virg. G.
3, 465: with ref. to style, Hor. Ep. 2, 1,
67 (= <i>tamely, without life or expressiveness</i>).

2. abjectē (<i>in a despairing,
unmanly way</i>): Join: abjecte, timide[**P1: missing ,?|P3 yes]
ignave, Cic. Tusc. 2, 23, 55.

3. frīgĭdē
(esp. of style, <i>flatly, tamely</i>):
Quint.: Gell.

4. expr. by circuml.
parum acriter <i>s.</i> alacriter: haud (parum)
alacri animo, etc.: v. <f>SPIRITED</f>, <f>SPIRITEDLY</f>.


<b>spiritlessness</b>: animus abjectus,
(nimis) demissus atque humilis: ignāvia:
v. <f>SPIRITLESS</f>.


<b>spiritual</b>:

I. <i>Incorporeal</i>: corporis
expers: ab omni corpore sejunctus,
-----File: b0785r.png------------------------------------------------------
etc.: v. <f>IMMATERIAL</f>. Phr.: <i>s. beings</i>,
animi per se ipsos viventes, Cic. Tusc.
1, 16, 37.

II. <i>Relating to the spirit or
mind</i>: expr. by animus, mens: <i>bodily
and s. goods</i>, corporis animique bona[**P1: missing :]
<i>s. pleasures</i>, voluptates ab animo profectae,

III. <i>Not secular</i>:

<b>spiritualism</b>: *spiritualismus (qui

<b>spiritualist</b>: *spiritualis (qui dicitur).


<b>spirituality</b>: no exact word: perh.

<b>spiritually</b>: animo, mente: v. <f>MIND</f>.

<b>spiritualty</b>: clērus, clērĭci: v.

<b>spit</b> (<i>v.</i>):

II. <i>To eject (saliva) from the

2. spūto, 1 (freq. of spuo): <i>to

3. exscreo, 1
(<i>to cough out, clearing the throat</i>): <i>to s.

4. expr. by spūtum, sălīva, with

<b>spite</b> (<i>subs.</i>):

1. līvor (<i>jealous,

2. mălĕvŏlentia (<i>the disposition

3. obtrectātio (<i>ill-natured disparagement</i>):

4. mălignĭtas
(<i>that evil and malicious disposition

5. also ŏdium may sometimes
serve: v. <f>HATRED</f>. (Simultas = <i>feud</i>:
<i>estranged and bitter feeling</i>.) Phr.[** :?|P3 yes]
<i>in s. of</i>: no exact word or phr.: usu.

allurements of pleasure, etc.</i>, Hercules,

omnibus voluptatum illecebris contemptis,
etc., Kr. (not quanquam with

1. mălĕvŏlus (not

<i>3rd pers.</i>): both of which may be
strengthened by the dem. particle -ce,
v. Lat. Gr. § 78, <i>Obs.</i> 1: or by is, which
is the logical and determinative <i>pron.</i>,
and weaker than either of the preced.;
hence it is often omitted: it is the proper
antecedent to qui. For the use of
these <i>prons.</i> see Lat. Gr[**P1: missing .] §§ 365, 368,
370-374, 616, 619. Remarks:--(i.) since
is is not a proper demons. it should not
be used in such sentences as the foll.,
epistolae Ciceronis placent non <i>eae</i> Plinii;
<i>hae</i> or <i>illae</i> must be used (Nägelsb.
Styl. p. 243): with a <i>rel. clause</i>, however,
we find Cic. Off. 3, begin thus:
P. Scipionem, Marce fili, <i>eum</i>, qui primus
Africanus appellatus sit, dicere
solitum scripsit Cato.... (ii.) ille is
often emph.: <i>Xenophon, t. famous follower
of Socrates</i>, Xenophon Socraticus
ille, Cic. de Or. 2, 14, 58. (iii.) iste is
sometimes contemptuous: Lat. Gr. § 369.
(iv.) the Eng. and Lat. idioms do not
correspond in the use of the demons.:
hic is not unfreq. used in pref. to is or
even ille: sometimes the converse is the
case. This is a mere point of style.
In historians, esp. Caesar, hic is used to
put a thing before the eyes of the reader:
huic rei (<i>for that purpose</i>) quod satis
est visum militum reliquit, Caes. B. G.
5, 2: and almost always in explanations,
"<i>t. is to say</i>" = hoc est: cf. Cic.
Mil. 9, 24: for id est, see id. Fin. 2, 1, 1:
(it may also be rendered videlicet, v.
<f>NAMELY</f>): the mere unemphatic this is
"is": idque ejus rei causa (<i>for this
reason</i>) antiquitus institutum videtur
ne ...: Caes. B. G. 6, 11: cf. 7, 1, id esse
facile. (v.) <i>and t.</i> (emphatic) = et is,
-----File: b0849r.png------------------------------------------------------
isque, atque is, et is quidem: Lat. Gr[**P1: missing .]
§§ 374, 619, 638, <i>Obs.</i> 2: <i>devoted to the
noblest pursuits, and t. from a boy</i>,
studiis optimis deditus idque a puero, Cic.
Fam. 13, 16, 4: <i>t. very thing</i> = id adeo,
Lat. Gr. § 614: so, id demum, maxime,
quidem: <i>I had t. moment come into the
Appian road when he met me</i>, emerseram
commode in Appiam (ex Antiati)
quum in me incurrit, Cic. Att. 2, 12, <i>ad
init.</i> (so, tantum quod, v. <f>JUST</f>). (vi.)
<i>this ... t.</i>: v. under <f>THIS</f>.

II. <i>Relative
pronoun</i>: qui, quae, quod: v. <f>WHO</f>.

III. <i>Conjunction</i>:

A. <i>Introducing
noun clauses</i>:

1. expr. by <i>acc.</i>
and <i>inf.</i>: this is the case after verbs of
<i>thinking, knowing, perceiving, saying,
hearing</i>[**F2: or treat as list & mark individually?], or equiv. phr.: Lat. Gr. §§ 507,
508: <i>news was brought t. the ambassadors
had arrived from Rome</i>, ab Roma
legatos venisse nuntiatum est, Liv. 21,
9.

2. expr. by quod (<i>as to the fact
t.</i>): esp. freq. after verbs or phr. of
<i>mental emotion</i>: <i>rejoice t. a thousand
eyes behold thee speaking</i>, gaude quod
mille oculi spectant te loquentem, Hor.
Ep. 1, 6, 19: cf. <f>BECAUSE</f>.

3. expr.
by ut (negatively by ne): esp. after
verbs of <i>entreating, commanding, effecting,
resolve, fear</i>[**F2: same question], v. Lat. Gr. §§ 451, 452,
460. It must be remembered that after
any verb of fearing ut expr. <i>t. not</i>, ne,
<i>t.</i>: <i>I fear he will not come</i>, vereor ut
veniat: <i>I fear he will come</i>, vereor ne
veniat. [N.B.--All such clauses are properly
final clauses, denoting either purpose
or result: a large number of verbs
take either the <i>acc.</i> and <i>inf.</i> or ut with
the <i>subj.</i>, according as the clause is
viewed simply as the <i>object</i> of the verb,
or as <i>depending</i> upon it as <i>purpose</i>
or <i>result</i>: thus impero admits either
constr.: the admissible constr. must
therefore be sought under each verb or
phr. The constr. with ut after many
<i>adjs.</i> goes to support the view that it is
in origin a <i>rel. pron.</i>: thus, non est
verisimile ut literas adamarit, Cic. Rosc.
Am. 41, 121: sometimes the sentence
gives exactly the Eng. idiom (<i>t.</i> being
orig. a dem.): nec minus id contendunt
et laborant ne ea quae dixerint enuntientur,
Caes. B. G. 1, 31: id egi ne interessem
rebus gerendis = <i>I took care t. I
was not mixed up with public transactions</i>,
Cic. Fam. 4, 7, 2.[** ]? closing bracket missing]

4. <i>Granting
t.</i> = ut (ellipt. for fac ut): ut ita sit, Cic.
Verr. 3, 64, 151: <i>to think t.!</i> is expr.
ellipt. by the <i>inf.</i>: as, mene incepto
desistere victam, Virg. Aen. 1, 37: v.
Lat. Gr. § 516.

B. <i>Introducing final
clauses</i>: <i>in order t., so t.</i>:

1. when
<i>purpose</i> is denoted, ut (uti), quo, negatively
ne (less freq. ut ne): hence instead
of ut nemo, ne quis, etc., must be
used.

2. When <i>result</i> is denoted, ut
(uti): negatively, ut non: after verbs
of prevention, quominus, quin, the latter
also after verbs of doubting. See Lat.
Gr. §§ 450-463. The rel. qui may be
subst. for ut: Lat. Gr. §§ 478-481.

C.
<i>Oh t.!</i> (in wishes):

1. ŭtĭnam: Lat.
Gr. §§ 444, 446. O utinam occurs in
Ov. H. 1, 5.

2. O si: <i>Oh t. fortune
would show me a jar of money!</i> O si
urnam argenti fors mihi monstret, Hor.
S. 2, 6, 10.

<b>the</b>:

I. <i>The article</i>: no equiv.:
the foll. sentences should be observed,
in which the constr. partly expr. the
art., or an equiv. dem. pron. is used:
<i>t. people of Achaia and also t. people
of Asia</i>, Achaici itemque in Asia (οἱ
ἐν τῆ Ἀσίᾳ), Cic. Att. 11, 15, 1: <i>t.
last two letters of t. word optimus</i>,
postremae duae literae quae sunt in
"optimus," id. Orat. 48, 161: <i>they pretend
that it is a votive offering for their
return</i>: <i>t. report spreads</i>, votum pro
reditu simulant: ea fama vagatur, Virg.
Aen. 2, 17: <i>t. Hercules of Xenophon</i>,
Hercules Xenophontius ille, Cic. Fam.
5, 12 (here we have the ille of celebrity,
Lat. Gr. § 365): <i>I wish we could say t.
same with truth</i>, vellem nobis hoc idem
vere dicere liceret, id. Off. 3, 1,[**P2: ,] 1: <i>I am
in the enjoyment of repose, but not t.
repose which he ought to enjoy who
formerly gave repose to the state</i>, otio
fruor, non illo quidem, quo debebat is,
qui quondam peperisset otium civitati,
id. ib. 3, 1, 3. [N.B.[**P2: .]--The practice of
some modern Latinists, who use the
Greek article on emergency, is always
to be avoided: see Nägelsb. Styl. p. 21,
sq.]

II. <i>The abl. of the demonstrative</i>:
expr. by the <i>abl.</i> of manner (Lat. Gr.
§ 321), eo, hoc, etc.: <i>he persuades them
t. more easily to this</i>, id hoc facilius iis
persuasit, Caes. B. G. 1, 2: for quo = ut
eo, see Lat. Gr. § 453. Usu. it has a
correl., <i>t. ... t.</i>: it is then expr. by (i.)
eo ... quo; hoc ... quo; tanto ... quanto;
the rel. clause usu. preced.: <i>t. less he
sought glory t. more it followed him</i>,
quo minus gloriam petebat illo magis
eum sequebatur, Sall. C. 54: <i>t. more
clever and gifted a man is t. more
laboriously does he teach</i>,[**P2: ,] quo quisque
est sollertior et ingeniosior eo docet
laboriosius, Cic. Rosc. Com. 11, 31: <i>t.
longer he is away t. more I wish for
him</i>, quanto diutius abest magis cupio
tanto, Ter. Heaut[**P2: .] 3, 1, 15 (quantum
magis ... eo acrius occurs in Liv. 3, 15)[**P2: ./:]
(ii.) it may also be expr. by ut ... ita
(Lat. Gr. § 356), ut being mostly foll.
by quisque, and both clauses usu. having
a <i>superl.</i>: but the <i>comp.</i> and even
the <i>pos.</i> are used sometimes: at times
the force of the <i>superl.</i> is expr. by the
<i>verb</i> or <i>subs.</i>: also ita is sometimes
omitted. <i>T. better a man is t. less inclined
is he to suspect others to be wicked</i>,
ut quisque est vir optimus ita difficillime
esse alios improbos suspicatur, Cic. Q.
Fr.[** unclear] 1, 1, 4, 12: <i>we are so framed by
nature that there is a bond of union</i>
-----File: b0850m.png------------------------------------------------------
<i>amongst all, but it is t. stronger t. more
nearly we are related</i>, ita natos esse nos
ut inter omnes esset societas quaedam,
major autem ut quisque proxime accederet,
id. Am. 5, 19:[**P2: dot missing] see Lat.-Eng. Dict.
under ut, A, II., iii. Sometimes both
correlatives are omitted, and only quisque
retained with the <i>superl.</i> in both
clauses: <i>t. wiser a man is t. more calmly
he dies</i>, sapientissimus quisque aequissimo
animo moritur, Cic. Sen. 22, 83.
(iii.) it is much less freq[**P2: .] expr. by quam
... tam: <i>t. more ... t. more</i>, quam magis ...
tam magis, Virg. Aen. 7,[**P2: ,] 787
(without tam, id. G. 3, 309): quam magis ...
tanto (artius), Pl. Men. 1, 1, 19:
<i>t. worse a man acts t. safer is he</i>, quam
quisque pessime fecit tam maxime tutus
est, Sall. J. 31. [N.B.--quantocius, <i>t.
sooner t. better</i>, occurs only in Sulp.
Sev.]

<b>theme</b>:

1. propŏsĭtio or propŏsĭtum

2. quaestio:
Cic. Top. 21, 79, says there are two

<b>then</b>:

I. <i>At that time</i>, denoting
coincidence:

1. tum (used <i>absol.</i> or
as <i>correl.</i> to <i>quum</i>, <i>postquam</i>, <i>ubi</i>, <i>si</i>, or
<i>abl. abs.</i>: it may be strengthened by
demum, denique, vero, maxime): <i>Curio
was t. tribune of the plebs</i>, erat tribunus
plebis t. Curio, Cic. Brut. 89, 305: <i>praise
is most honourable when it follows (our
endeavours), not when it is sought</i>, laus
t. est pulcherrima cum sequitur non
cum arcessitur, Quint. 10, 2, 27: here <i>t.</i>
is better omitted in Engl.: in Lat. it
gives more force and precision to the
sentence. It may be, and often is
omitted: so in Liv. 26, 11, ubi recepissent
se in castra mira serenitas oriebatur.
This is a mere point of style.

2. tunc
(emph. form of preced.: prop. opp. to
nunc or hodie; <i>at that particular moment
or conjuncture of circumstances</i>:
rarely as <i>correl[**P2: . ?]</i> of <i>quum</i> or <i>si</i>: it may
be strengthened by demum): <i>t.</i> (seeing
that the camp of Hannibal was pitched
just outside Rome) <i>they took refuge in
their houses</i>, t. in domos refugiebant,[**P2: ,]
Liv. 26, 10: <i>(t.) when all has been said</i>,
t. cum omnia dicta sunt, Cic. Verr. Act[** .]
1, 18, 55.

3. expr. by eo tempore,[**P2: ,]
Cic. Brut. 91, 313, or phr. of similar
import. [N.B.--Tum ... tum, means
<i>now ... t.</i>: <i>he did not say first this
t. that, but always the same thing</i>, non
t. hoc t. illud sed idem semper dicebat[** ,]
Cic. Am. 4, 13: v. <f>NOW</f> (II.): t. is repeated
9 times in Cic. N. D. 2, 20, 51:
<i>now and t.</i> is expr. by aliquando, v.
<f>SOMETIMES</f>, <f>OCCASIONALLY</f>. Avoid such
combinations as t. temporis, Just.]

II.
<i>Thereupon</i>, denoting succession.

1. tum
(strengthened by vero, deinde, postea,

..., inquit, Cic. de Or. 3, 24, 91: <i>what
t[**P2: .]?</i> quid t.? id. Mur. 12, 26: Ter.:
<i>t. he sent a part of his forces</i>, t. demum

2. dĕinde, dĕin (constantly scanned

III. The chief
combinations used in enumerations are:[** checked TIA]
primum ... deinde ... postremo, Cic.:[** checked TIA]
primum ... deinde ... deinde ... deinde,
id.[** :?] primum ... deinde ... tum ...
postremo, id.: primum ... tum etiam,
Caes. Without primum or equiv. phr.:
... deinde ... inde ... deinde, Cic.:
deinde ... deinde ... postremo, Cic.:
deinde ... post autem ... tum vero,
Cic. Also, in enumerations dehinc becomes
a syn. of deinde: primum ...
dehinc, Virg.: Sall.: without primum:
dehinc ... tum ... inde, Sen.

IV.
<i>Now</i>, in introducing a new argument:
jam, v. <f>NOW</f> (III., 2), <f>AGAIN</f>, <f>MOREOVER</f>.

V. <i>Therefore</i>, denoting logical consequence:

1. ĭgĭtur (rarely first,
unless emph.: however this position is
freq. given to it in Sall., Tac., Liv., and
the com. poets: it draws an inference,
introduces consecutive interrogations,
or resumes after a digression): <i>I am not
so dull as to say that.</i> M. <i>What do you
say t.?</i> Non sum ita hebes ut istud
dicam. <i>M.</i> Quid dicis i.? Cic. Tusc. 1,
6, 12. (For its ordinary use, v. id. Acad.
2, 30, 96.) <i>Let us return to the point
whence we have digressed</i>: <i>Hortensius t.
whilst quite a youth ...</i>, ad id unde
digressi sumus revertamur: Hortensius
i., cum admodum adolescens ..., id.
Brut. 88, 301.

2. ergo (in Ov. and
later poets ergŏ: stronger than preced.:
it is usu. put first: it often occurs in
<i>inter. phr.</i>: sometimes with an <i>imper.</i>
or as a resumptive word):[** :?] <i>to-morrow t.
punctually by the clock</i>, cras e. ad clepsydram,
Cic. Tusc. 2, 27, 67: <i>so t. eternal
sleep overpowers Quintilius</i>, e. Quintilium
perpetuus sopor urget, Hor. Od. 1,
24, 5: <i>cease t.</i>, desinite e., Caes. B. C. 3,
19, <i>ad fin.</i>: <i>why t. do we hesitate ...?[**close up space?]</i>
quid e. dubitamus ...?[**close up space?] Cic. Fin. 4, 14,
36 (cf. quid dubitas igitur? id. ib. 4, 13,
34): <i>there are t. three roads, as I said</i>,
tres e., ut dixi, viae, id. Phil. 12, 9, 22:
v. <f>THEREFORE</f>.

<b>there</b>:

I. <i>In that place, at that

<i>compd.</i> with <i>per</i> expr. the notion in many

or perdoctus: in <i>com.</i> or <i>colloq.</i> language
tri- has a like force: <i>a t.[** space?|P2: no]-paced knave</i>,
trifurcifer: see also <f>THOROUGHLY</f>. Phr.:
<i>t. friendship</i>, vera et perfecta amicitia,
Cic. Am. 6, 22: <i>nothing worthy of t.
knowledge</i>, nihil magna cognitione dignum,
id. Fin. 5, 19, 50.


<b>---- -bred</b>: gĕnĕrosus: <i>a t. horse</i>,
g. equus, Quint. 5, 11, 4: Virg.


<b>---- -fare</b>:

I. <i>A road through</i>:
pervium: <i>a t. for armies</i>, p. exercitibus,
Tac. H. 3, 8: more usu. expr. by means
of the <i>adj.</i> pervius, of which the preced.
is the <i>neut.</i> used <i>subst.</i>: <i>t.s</i>, perviae
transitiones, Cic. N. D. 2, 27,[**P2: ,] 67: v.
<f>PASSAGE</f>, No. V.: <i>a house through which
there is a t.</i>, transitoria domus, Suet. Ner.
31 (as a name orig. given to the Golden
Palace). Arcades, leading out from the
forum as passages, are called Jani, in Cic.
l. c.: cf. Hor. S. 2, 3, 18: "<i>no t.</i>", fundula
(defined in Varr. L. L. 5, 32, 40, § 145, as
"a fundo, quod exitum non habeat ac
pervium non est iter").

II. <i>A right
of way</i>: there were three legal <i>t. t.</i>,
iter, actus, via, Ulp. Dig. 8, 3, 1: the
first was the mere <i>right of passing
through</i>; the second implied the <i>right
of driving</i> cattle, vehicles, etc.; the
third implied the existence of a <i>road
through a man's property</i>: cf. Cic. Caecin.
26, 74: v. Dict. Ant. 1030, "servitutes
praediorum rusticorum." It may also
be expr. by jus eundi et agendi, Ulp. Dig.
43,[**P2: ,] 8, 2, § 21: (or without et, Just. Inst.
4, 6, 2).


<b>thoroughly</b>:

1. pĕnĭtus (once
with <i>sup.</i> in Vell.): <i>to shave the head t.</i>,
caput p. abradere, Cic. Rosc. Com. 7, 20:
<i>to make oneself t. acquainted with the
case</i>, p. in causam insinuare, id. de Or.
2, 35, 149: <i>to give himself up t. to the
society of that fellow</i>, bene p. in istius
familiaritatem se dare,[**P2: ,] id. Verr. 2, 70,
169 (R. and A.): <i>to understand anything
t.</i>, p. intelligere aliquid, id. Att. 8, 12.

2. planē (<i>entirely, without any reservation</i>):
<i>to be t. devoid of common
sense</i>, communi sensu p. carere, Hor. S.
1, 3, 66: v. <f>ENTIRELY</f>, <f>QUITE</f>.

3. omnīno
(<i>in all points, completely</i>): <i>to be t.
ignorant</i>, o. omnis eruditionis expertem
esse, Cic. de Or. 2, 1, 1: v. <f>ALTOGETHER</f>.

4. plēne (<i>fully</i>): <i>t. wise men</i>, p.
sapientes homines, Cic. Off. 1, 15, 46: v.
<f>COMPLETELY</f>.

5. prorsus: v. <f>WHOLLY</f>,
<f>ABSOLUTELY</f>.

6. fundĭtus: v. <f>UTTERLY</f>.
Phr.: <i>a t. praiseworthy man</i>, vir per
omnia laudabilis, Vell. 2, 33, 1: Quint.:
<i>Octavius is t. devoted to me</i>, Octavius
mihi totus deditus est, Cic. Att. 14, 11,
<i>extr.</i>: <i>nothing is t. happy</i>, nihil est ab
omni parte beatum,[**P2: ,] Hor. Od. 2, 16, 27: <i>to
stick at Brundusium is t. irksome</i>, jacere
-----File: b0856m.png------------------------------------------------------
Brundusii in omnes partes est molestum,
Cic. Att. 11, 6: <i>to scrutinize t. every
man's countenance</i>, perspicere omnes
vultus, id. de Or. 2, 35, 148.


<b>thou</b>: tu: the <i>pron.</i> is not expr.
except for emph.: L. Gr. §§ 357, 615:
the emph. forms are tute (tute ipse,
Cic.), tete, tutemet, tibimet, the suffix
-met being more freq. employed with the
<i>pl.</i>: sometimes, though rarely, the <i>pron.</i>
vos is used with a <i>sing. subs.</i>: Cic. Deiot.
10, 29: Virg. Aen. 9, 525: also, by a
singular idiom, the <i>voc. adj.</i> agrees with
the <i>nom.</i> tu in Pers. 3, 28. Occasionally
tu is replaced by other <i>pron.</i> in the
poets: exoriare aliquis nostris ex ossibus
ultor, Virg. Aen. 4, 625 (= <i>thou, my
particular, yet unknown avenger</i>): at
nunc aeterna silentia lethes ille canorus
habes, Stat. S. 2, 4, 9 (= <i>t., the famous
bird of song</i>): cf. Tib. 4, 3, 1 and 2: but
the supposed use of is for tu in Cic. Phil.
2, 30, 76, rests on a false reading. Tu,
not vos, is the ordinary <i>pron. of address</i>
in Latin: hence there is no phr. corresponding
to "<i>thou and thee</i>" any one:
Erasm. coined the <i>v.</i> tuisso, 1: the Romans
in similar circumstances used
pater, frater, filius, as terms of familiarity:
see Hor. Ep. 1, 6, 54, and Orell.
<i>ad loc.</i>: <i>after thy fashion</i>, tuatim,
Pl. Am. 2, 1, 4.


<b>though</b>: etsi, etiamsi: v. <f>ALTHOUGH</f>.


<b>thought</b>:

<b>thrash</b>:

I. <i>To beat out corn</i>:

1. tĕro, trīvi, trītum, 3 (<i>to rub out

flails</i>, or lastly by <i>thrashing-machines</i>:

6, 23. [N. B.--The three processes are
mentioned in Plin. 18, 30, 72: "messis

<b>to</b>:

A. In space:

I. <i>Direction
towards without motion</i>:

1. ad (antith.
to <i>ab</i>): <i>(part of Gaul) lies to the north</i>,
vergit ad septentriones, Caes. B. G. 1, 1:
<i>the part which looked to the strait</i>, pars
quae ad fretum spectaret, Cic. Verr. 5,
66, 169: sometimes specto is used with
<i>acc.</i> without the <i>prep.</i>: <i>Acarnania lies
to the west</i>, Acarnania solem occidentem
spectat, Liv. 33, 17. Fig.: <i>he looks to
his own glory rather than the safety of
the state</i>, ad suam magis gloriam spectat
quam ad salutem rei publicae, Cic. Sest.
16, 37: v. <f>TO REGARD</f>. Joined with
<i>versus</i>: <i>that part of the Esquiliae which
looks to the vicus patricius</i>, ea pars
Esquiliarum quae jacet ad vicum patricium
v., Fest.: Varr.

2. in (with
<i>acc.</i> antith. to <i>ex</i>): <i>the Belgae lie to the
north west</i>, Belgae spectant in septen-*
-----File: b0865m.png------------------------------------------------------
*triones et occidentem solem, Caes. B. G.
1, 1.

3. versus (<i>looking towards</i>);
<i>looking to the temple of Quirinus</i>,[**P2: ,] v.
aedem Quirini, Liv. 8, 20.

4. sometimes
adversus (-versus, <i>or</i> -sum): v.
<f>OPPOSITE TO</f>.

5. ergā (<i>looking towards</i>,
rare): Plaut. Truc. 2, 4, 52.

6. expr.
by <i>adv.</i> of <i>direction</i>, huc, illuc, eo, etc.:
<i>looking this way and that</i>, huc atque
illuc intuens, Cic. de Or. 1, 40, 184.
Fig.: <i>to what do all these words tend?</i>
quorsum haec omnis spectat oratio? id.
Phil. 7, 9, 26.

II. <i>Direction towards
with motion</i> (<i>with</i> or <i>without</i> the idea of
<i>arrival</i>):

1. ad: (i.) <i>without</i> the idea
of <i>arrival</i>: <i>the hills and plains seem
flying to the ships</i>, fugere ad puppes
colles campique videntur, Lucr. 4, 390:
with <i>versus</i>: <i>he bids Labienus direct
his march to the ocean</i>, Labienum ad
oceanum v. proficisci jubet, Caes. B. G.
6, 33: v. <f>TOWARDS</f>. (ii.) <i>with</i> the idea
of <i>arrival</i>: <i>since the time I came to
Rome</i>, ut veni ad urbem, Cic. Fam. 16,
12, 2: with <i>usque</i> (<i>all the way</i>): <i>he
came up to the enemy's camp</i>, u. ad
castra hostium accessit, Caes. B. G. 1, 51.
Fig.: <i>to be scourged to death</i>, virgis
ad necem caedi, Cic. Verr. 3, 29, 70:
usque ad necem deverberasse,[**P2: ,] Ter. Ph.
2, 2,[**P2: ,] 13: <i>he unroofed the temple to the
half</i>, aedem ad dimidiam partem detexit,
Liv. 42, 3. The whole space
traversed is indicated by the words
dependent on <i>ab</i> and <i>ad</i>: <i>they sailed
from Dianium to Sinope</i>, usque a
Dianio ad Sinopen navigarunt, Cic. Verr.
1, 34, 87. <i>To my, thy, etc., house</i>:
ad me, te, etc.: <i>let us go to my house</i>,
eamus ad me, Ter. Eun. 3, 5, 64: sometimes
domum is expr.: domum ad
me (al. lect. meos) literas mittam, Cic.
Fam. 3, 8, 10: so with a proper name:
<i>crowds thronged to the house of Afranius</i>,
magni domum concursus ad Afranium
fiebant, Caes. B. C. 1, 53. The repetition
of <i>ad</i> to denote motion to a place, and
to a person there present, is occasionally
found: <i>the soldiers being summoned to
the meeting before the tribunes</i>, vocatis
militibus ad concilium ad tribunos, Liv.
5, 47: abi ad forum ad herum, Plaut.
As. 2, 2, 100. Ad, with the name of a
deity in the <i>gen.</i>, is elliptical for ad
templum, aedem: <i>we had reached Vesta's
(temple)</i>, ventum erat ad Vestae, Hor. S.
1, 9, 35: ad Opis, Cic. Att. 6, 1, 17. In
answer to the question <i>Whither?</i> names
of towns and small islands (rarely of
large ones), domus in the sense of <i>home</i>,
and rus in the sense of <i>to the country</i>,
are put in the <i>acc.</i> without a <i>prep.</i>:
<i>I am in doubt whether to go to Venusia</i>,
dubito an Venusiam tendam, Cic. Att.
16, 5, 3: the poets use this constr. with
names of countries and <i>subs.</i> generally:
<i>he came to Italy</i>, Italiam venit, Virg.
Aen. 1, 2. The poets use both constr.
with names of towns: ad doctas proficisci
cogor Athenas, Prop. 3, 21, 1: doctas jam
nunc eat, inquit, Athenas, Ov. H. 2, 83.
<i>Ad</i> is sometimes used with the name of
a town in prose: <i>I went to Capua</i>, profectus
sum ad Capuam, Cic. de Sen. 4, 10.
The <i>prep.</i> is also expr. (i.) when there
is an antithesis: <i>they sailed from Dianium
to Sinope</i>, usque a Dianio ad Sinopen
navigarunt, Cic. Verr. 1, 34, 87: this
rule is however not always observed:
<i>they came from Ardea to Rome</i>, ab Ardea
Romam venerunt, Liv. 4, 7. (ii.) if <i>urbs,
oppidum, etc.</i>, is added in apposition: <i>the
consul arrived in the town of Cirta</i>, consul
pervenit ad Cirtam oppidum,[**P2: ,] Sall. J.
81. (iii.) when the <i>neighbourhood</i> of a
town or <i>part</i> of it is meant: <i>all the
Gauls march to (the neighbourhood of)
Alesia</i>, omnes Galli ad Alesiam proficiscuntur,
Caes. B. G. 7,[**P2: ,] 76: v. Lat.
Gram. § 259. With words compounded
with <i>ad</i>, which denote <i>going, bringing,
etc., near</i>, instead of repeating the
<i>prep.</i>, the noun is put in the <i>dat.</i> or
<i>acc.</i>, though chiefly in the post-Aug.
period, and in the poets: <i>to approach
the rocks</i>, accedere scopulos, Virg. Aen.
1, 201: v. <f>TO APPROACH</f>, <f>ACCOST</f>, etc.:
v. the constr. of such verbs as adeo, in
-----File: b0865r.png------------------------------------------------------
Lat.-Eng. Dict.

2. in (with <i>acc.</i>, to
or <i>into</i>). (i.) <i>without</i> the idea of <i>arrival</i>:
with <i>versus</i>: <i>he moves his camp to the
district of the Arverni</i>, castra movet in
Arvernos v., Caes. B. G. 7, 8, <i>fin.</i>: v.
<f>TOWARDS</f>. (ii.) <i>with</i> the idea of <i>arrival</i>:
<i>I will go to the Piraeus</i>, ibo in Piraeum,
Plaut. Bac. 2, 3, 2: <i>to send ambassadors
to the Ubii</i>, legatos in Ubios mittere,
Caes. B. G. 4, 11. Joined with <i>ad</i>:
<i>you fly for refuge to God as to an altar</i>,
tamquam in aram confugitis ad deum,
Cic. N. D. 3, 10, 25: <i>when we had gone
to law before the praetor</i>, quum ad praetorem
in jus adissemus, id. Verr. 4, 65[**P2: ,]
147. For constr. with names of towns,
in answer to the question <i>Whither?</i> v.
under <i>ad</i> (8): <i>to have gone to Tarquinii,
the most flourishing town in Etruria</i>,
se contulisse Tarquinios in urbem Etruriae
florentissimam, Cic. Rep. 2, 19, 34.
For constr. of words compounded with
<i>in</i>, v. such words as infero in Lat.-Eng.
Dict.: <i>to set fire to the temples</i>, templis
ignes inferre, Cic. Cat. 3, 9, 22. Fig.:
<i>to boil down to one-half</i>, decoquere in
dimidiam partem, Col. 12, 24, 1: with
<i>usque</i>: u. in quartam partem, id. 12, 12,
3: hence, denoting a <i>change</i>: <i>rivers
change to leaves</i>, vortunt se fluvii in
frondes, Lucr. 2, 880.

3. versus (as
<i>prep.</i>, <i>towards</i>): <i>to march to Massilia</i>,
Massiliam v. iter facere, Caes. B. C. 3,
36: for constr. as <i>adv.</i> with <i>ad</i>, etc.,
v. <i>supr.</i>

4. adversus (-vorsus, <i>or</i> -sum)
(as <i>prep.</i>): <i>who is this coming to me?</i>
quis est haec quae me adversum incedit?
Plaut. Pers. 2, 2, 18: v. <f>TOWARDS</f>,
<f>AGAINST</f>: for <i>adv.</i> constr. v. <i>supr.</i>

5.
usque (<i>adv.</i>, <i>all the way</i>, with <i>prep.</i>, or
<i>acc. of motion</i>): <i>to go from the upper
sea to Rome</i>, a mari supero u. Romam
proficisci, Cic. Clu. 68, 192: v. under <i>ad</i>,
<i>supr.</i>

6. tĕnus (<i>reaching to</i>, always
placed after its case, constr. with <i>gen.</i>,
or more usu. <i>abl.</i>):[**P2: dot missing] <i>its dewlap hangs
down to its legs</i>, crurum t. laquearia
pendent, Virg. G. 3.[**P2: ,] 53: <i>his kingdom
extends to Taurus</i>, Tauro t. regnat, Cic.
Deiot. 13, 36: <i>he plunged his sword to
the hilt in his side</i>, lateri capulo t. abdidit
ensem, Virg. Aen. 2, 553: hac
tenus as <i>adv.</i>: <i>to this point</i>, hac Trojana
tenus fuerit fortuna secuta, ib. 6.[**P2: ,] 62.

7. fīne (or -i, <i>abl.</i> used as <i>adv.</i>, rare):
<i>projecting from the wall up to the breast</i>.[**P2: ,]
de muro pectoris f. prominentes, Caes.
B. G. 7, 47.

8. The question <i>Whither?</i>
is answered by <i>advs.</i> of <i>motion</i>, huc,
illuc, eo, etc.: <i>they hastened to the point
with all speed</i>, huc magno cursu contenderunt,
Caes. B. G. 3, 19: with <i>ad</i>:
<i>to come to you here</i>, huc ad vos venire,
Cic. Rep. 6, 15, 15: with <i>in</i>: <i>to this city</i>,
huc in urbem, Ter. Hec. 1, 2, 100: with
<i>gen.</i>: <i>she removed to this neighbourhood</i>,
huc viciniae commigravit, id. Andr. 1, 1,
43: <i>to and fro</i>, huc illuc, huc atque
illuc, etc.: also, huc et illo, Sen.: huc et
huc, Hor. Epod. 4, 9. Fig.: <i>I have
brought affairs to this point</i>, rem huc
deduxi, Cic. Cat. 2.[**P2: ,] 2, 4: <i>to this must be
added a certain sweetness</i>, huc accedat
oportet suavitas quaedam, id. Am. 18,
66: sometimes accedit, etc., is used
without the <i>adv.</i>: <i>add to this death</i>,
acc. mors, id. Fin. 1.[**P2: ,] 18.[**P2: ,] 60: <i>to proceed
to such a pitch</i>, huc usque proficisci.[**P2: ,]
Plin. 26, 4, 9, § 20: <i>they came to
such extremity of want</i>, eo inopiae
venere, Tac. Agr[**P2: .] 28: <i>to this point
(thus far) I could write with prudence</i>,
hactenus fuit quod caute a me scribi
posset, Cic. Att. 11, 4, 2: <i>his wishes
had extended to this</i>, hactenus voluerat.[**P2: ,]
Tac. A. 12, 42, <i>fin.</i>: v. <f>SO FAR</f>.

B. In time:

1. ad: with or
without usque: <i>to that time I was honest
and virtuous</i>, ad id frugi usque et probus
fui, Plaut. Most. 1, 2, 50: <i>Sophocles
wrote tragedies to the end of his life</i>, Sophocles
ad summam aetatem tragoedias
fecit, Cic. Tusc. 1, 3, 5: (the employment
of a <i>past</i> tense shows that the action has
ceased, otherwise the <i>present</i> would be
used): <i>to this time</i>, ad id, Liv. 3, 22; ad
id locorum.[**P2: ,] id. 9, 45.

2. in (with <i>acc.</i>,
<i>till</i>): <i>they stood in battle array to a late</i>
-----File: b0866l.png------------------------------------------------------
<i>hour</i>, in multum diei in acie constiterunt,[**p2 proofed as ","][**P1: should be ,]
Liv. 27, 2: <i>they learned these things
to old age</i>, usque in senectutem didicerunt
haec, Quint. 12, 11,[**P1: should be ,] 20: <i>to live
from day to day (regardless of the
future)</i>, in diem vivere, Cic. Tusc. 5, 11,
33: so = <i>daily</i>, Liv. 22, 39.

3. expr.
by <i>advs.</i>, quoad, quousque[**p2 typo for quousque|P3 clear in TIA], etc.: v. <f>UNTIL</f>,
etc.: <i>up to this time the outposts
were quiet</i>, hactenus quietae stationes
fuere, Liv. 7, 26.

C. In other relations:

I. <i>Of number</i>: ad: (i.)
denoting an <i>approximation</i>: <i>men to the
number of (<f>i. e.</f> about) 2300 were slain</i>,[**p2 proofed as ","][**P1: should be ,]
ad duo milia et trecenti occisi, Liv. 10, 17.
(ii.) denoting the <i>limit reached</i>: <i>to the
last farthing</i>, ad assem, Hor. Ep. 2, 2,
27: <i>they all agree to a man (all together)</i>,
omnes ad unum idem sentiunt, Cic. Am.
23, 86: so, ad unum, Cic.: Caes. (iii.)
denoting <i>addition</i>: <i>in addition to the
traitors of Falerii and Pyrrhus a third
example should be added</i>, ad Faleriorum
Pyrrhive proditores tertium exemplum
esset, Liv. 24, 45: <i>to crown all</i>, ad omnia,
id. 35, 32.

II. <i>Of conduct, etc.,
towards</i>:

1. in (with <i>acc.</i>): <i>dutiful
to his parents</i>, pius in parentes, Cic. Off.
3, 23, 90: <i>indulgence to our children</i>,[**P1: should be ,] in
liberos nostros indulgentia, id. de Or. 2,
40, 168: sometimes with <i>abl.</i> (<i>in the
case of</i>): <i>such was he to Priam his foe</i>,
talis in hoste fuit Priamo, Virg. Aen. 2,
541.

2. adversus (-um): <i>the greater
justice to others</i>, summa adversus alios
justitia, Liv. 3, 33: <i>pleasing to you</i>,
gratum adversum te, Ter. Andr. 1, 1, 15.

3. ergā: <i>the divine goodness to
mankind</i>, divina bonitas e. homines, Cic.
N. D. 2, 23, 60: <i>unbroken fidelity to the
Roman people</i>, perpetua e. populum Romanum
fides, Caes. B. G. 5, 54.

III. <i>Generally
of relation</i>:

1. ad: (i.) of letters,
books, etc.: <i>addressed <f>or</f> dedicated to</i> any
one: <i>he wrote to me from Egypt</i>, ad me
ex Aegypto literas misit, Cic. Lig. 3,[**p2 proofed as ","][**P1: should be ,] 7:
(literas dare alicui = to intrust a letter
<i>to any one's hands</i> as messenger: v.
<i>infr.</i>) M. Tulli Ciceronis ad M. Brutum
Orator. (ii.) of <i>adaptation <f>or</f> intention
for</i>: <i>a place suitable to land at</i>, locus ad
egrediendum idoneus, Caes. B. G. 4, 23:
<i>a thing difficult to believe</i>, difficilis res
ad credendum, Lucr. 2, 1027: <i>man is
born to reason</i>, homo ad intelligendum
natus, Cic. Fin. 2, 13, 40: <i>an opportunity
to act</i>, occasio ad rem gerendam, Liv. 37,
26. (iii.) of a standard, <i>according to</i>:
<i>they adapt themselves to their will and
pleasure</i>, ad eorum arbitrium et nutum
totos se fingunt, Cic. Or. 8, 24. (iv.)
<i>concerning, affecting</i>: <i>I found it was
nothing to Pamphilus</i>, comperiebam
nihil ad Pamphilum quicquam attinere,
Ter. Andr. 1, 1, 64: <i>as to the provinces</i>,
quod ad provincias attinet, Liv. 42, 10:
<i>your feelings in regard to the marriage</i>,
animus tuus ad nuptias, Ter. Andr. 2,
3, 4.

2. in (with <i>acc.</i>): (i.) of <i>adaptation</i>
or <i>intention, aim</i>, etc., <i>for</i>: <i>a
Greek verse to this effect</i>, Graecus in eam
sententiam versus, Cic. Div. 2, 10, 25:
<i>what is useful to the purpose</i>, quae in
rem sunt, Liv. 26, 44. (ii.) in adverbial
expr.: <i>to a greater extent</i>, in majus, Sall.
J. 73: <i>changed to barbarism</i>, in barbarum
corruptum, Tac. A. 6, 42: v.
Lat.-Eng. Dict. <f>IN</f> (B., III.). Instead of
<i>prep.</i> the idea of <i>to</i>, denoting <i>aim, purpose</i>,
etc., is expr. in various ways. (i.)
after verbs of <i>giving</i> and the like, by
<i>dat.</i>: <i>he gives to him his daughter in
marriage</i>, ei filiam in matrimonium dat,
Caes. B. G. 1, 3. (ii.) after verbs compounded
with <i>ad</i>, by <i>dat.</i> or <i>acc.</i>: <i>his
mind was constant to no fortune</i>, nulli
fortunae adhaerebat animus, Liv. 41,
20: <i>to speak kindly to the man</i>, hominem
blande alloqui, Ter. Ph. 2, 1, 22. (iii.)
with idea of <i>advantage</i>, etc., by <i>dat.</i>:
usui esse, Caes. B. G. 5, 1 (so, ex usu,
ib. 1, 50): est utilitati, emolumento,
detrimento, etc. (iv.) by <i>subj.</i> in <i>final</i>
or <i>consecutive</i> sense: <i>I came to greet
you</i>, veni ut te salutarem: <i>they sent
men to carry the news</i>, miserunt qui
nuntiarent: <i>here is something to see</i>,
hic est quod spectetur: <i>worthy to com-*</i>
-----File: b0866m.png------------------------------------------------------
<i>*mand</i>, dignus qui imperet: v. Lat.
Gram., § 449, <i>seqq.</i> (v.) as the sign of
<i>inf.</i> by <i>inf.</i>: <i>to love</i>, amare: <i>to err is
human</i>, humanum est errare: so, after
verbs of <i>beginning</i>, <i>ceasing</i>, <i>desiring</i>,
<i>ordering</i>, <i>forbidding</i>, etc.: <i>he ceased to
sing</i>, canere desiit: <i>he bade him to approach</i>,
accedere jussit (in such cases it is
necessary to refer to Lat.-Eng. Dict. to
ascertain what verbs take the <i>inf.</i>, <i>subj.</i>
with <i>ut</i>, etc.): <i>it is time to attempt</i>, tempus
est conari, Liv. 6, 18 (constr. also
with <i>ut</i>, etc.). (vi.) with <i>gerund</i>, <i>supine</i>,
<i>fut. partic.</i>, etc.: <i>a desire to contend</i>,
certandi cupiditas: <i>he gave me books to
read</i>, dedit mihi libros legendos: <i>born
to endure sorrow</i>, miseriis natus ferendis:
<i>what are we to do?</i> quid faciendum
est? <i>I came to greet you</i>, veni te salutatum,
or, te salutaturus, or, salutandi
causâ: <i>he said that he should vote for
his condemnation</i>, dixit sua illum sententia
condemnatum iri: <i>nothing is
easier to say</i>, nihil est dictu facilius: <i>I
am ashamed to say it</i>, pudet dictu.
(vii.) by <i>adv.</i>, expr., eo, adeo, etc.: <i>I
speak to the end that</i>, eo dico ne, Plaut.
Aul. 2, 2, 62 (so, eo consilio, etc.): <i>to
that end was I born</i>, eo natus sum, Sall.
J. 24: <i>to such an extent did these words
fail of effect</i>, adeo haec dicta nihil
moverunt quemquam, Liv. 3, 2. (viii.)
the idea is contained in a word employed:
<i>let him see to that himself</i>,
viderit ipse, Cic. Att. 12, 21, 1, <i>fin.</i>
