I. Denoting
motion <i>in the
direction of</i> any object:

1. adversus
(with <i>acc.</i>): <i>they charge t. the hill</i>, impetum
a. montem faciunt, Caes. B. C. 1,
46: <i>who is coming t. me?</i> quis me a.
incedit? Plaut. Pers. 2, 2, 18.

2.
versus (following its case, used chiefly
with names of towns; with other
<i>subs.</i> in or ad are used, and versus is
added adverbially): <i>I turned from
Minturnae t. Arpinum</i>, verti me a
Minturnis Arpinum v., Cic. Att. 16,
10: <i>to shift his quarters at one
time t. the city at another t. Gaul</i>,
modo ad urbem modo in Galliam versus
castra movere, Sall. Cat. 56.

3. ad
(rare in this sense): <i>hills and fields
seem to fly t. the ship</i>, fugere ad puppim
colles campique videntur, Lucr. 4,
390 (v. <f>TO</f>). <i>T.</i> is often expr. in Latin
by ad or ob in comp. with a verb:
v. L. G. § 556.

4. obviam: v. <f>TO
MEET</f>. <i>T. some place</i>, aliquo vorsum,
Plaut.: <i>t. the right</i>, dextrorsum or -sus
(v. <f>RIGHT</f>): <i>t. the left</i>,[**P2: ,] sinistrorsum or
-sus (v. <f>LEFT</f>).

II. Of direction without
any idea of motion, often of geogr.
position:

1. ăd: <i>Gaul turns t. the
north</i>, Gallia vergit ad septentriones,
Caes. B. G. 1, 1: freq. in Plin.

2.
ĭn: <i>the Belgians lie t. the north and east</i>,
Belgae spectant in septentriones et
orientem solem, Caes. B. G. 1, 1: Tac.:
<i>windows turned t. the road</i>, fenestrae
in viam versae, Liv. 1, 41.

3. adversus:
v. <f>OPPOSITE TO</f>.

III. Of time,
denoting approximation:

1. sŭb: <i>t.
night</i>, sub noctem, Caes. B. C. 1, 28: <i>t.
early dawn</i>,[**P2: ,] sub lumina prima, Hor. Sat.
2, 7, 33.

2. ĭn: <i>if the fever increases
t. night</i>, si febris in noctem augetur,
Cels. 7, 27.

IV. Fig.: of inclination
or action directed to a person or personified
object:

1. erga (generally
of friendly feelings and after <i>subs.</i>): <i>the
kindness of our friends t. us</i>, benevolentia
amicorum e. nos, Cic. N. D. 2, 23,
60.

2. adversus: <i>the greatest fairness
t. others</i>, summa a. alios aequitas,
Liv. 3, 33: Tac.

3. ĭn (with <i>acc.</i>):
<i>faithful and kind t. her</i>, fidelis et benignus
in illam,[**P2: ,] Ter. Hec. 3, 5, 22: <i>most
generous t. every class of men</i>, in omne
genus hominum liberalissimus, Suet.
Vesp. 7: <i>a fatherly feeling t. his
brothers</i>, in fratres animus paternus, Hor.
Od. 2.[**P2: ,] 2, 6: <i>brotherly love t. me</i>, amor
in nos fraternus, Cic. Q. Fr. 1, 1 (v. <f>FOR</f>):
<i>forbearance [** t.?] suppliants</i>, clementia in
supplices, Plin. 8, 16, 19.

4. contra
(rare): <i>the elephant's forbearance t.
weaker creatures</i>, clementia elephanti
contra minus validos, ib. 7, 7.

5. ĭn
(with <i>abl.</i>, usu. after expressions signifying
hatred, rage, cruelty, etc.): <i>he was
cruel t. a foe</i>, saevus in hoste fuit, Ov.
Am. 1, 7, 34: also gen. when the disposition
is represented in connection
with the object, but not in reference to
any particular manifestation: e. g. <i>to
show pity t. human misfortunes</i>, adhibere
in hominum fortunis misericordiam,
Cic. Rab. Perd. 2, 5.

6. adversus:
<i>his old hatred t. the Armenians</i>, vetus a.
Armenios odium, Tac. Ann. 13, 37 (v.
<f>FOR</f>, <f>AGAINST</f>). <i>T.</i> may freq. be rendered
in Latin after a <i>subs.</i> by the objective
<i>gen.</i>, when there is no danger of
-----File: b0870r.png------------------------------------------------------
ambiguity: e. g. <i>love t. one's country</i>,
caritas patriae, Cic. Off. 3, 27, 100: <i>compassion
t. the masses</i>, misericordia vulgi,
Caes. B. G. 7, 15: v. <f>FOR</f>, and L. G. § 268.
Also <i>to entertain any feeling t. any one</i>
may be expr. by the corresponding
Latin verb governing the case of the
object: e. g. <i>to feel affection t. any one</i>,
aliquem amare.

<b>un____.</b>[**P2: prefix so short hyphen|F2: disagree, dash represents rest of word] This prefix gives a negative
signification to the word before which
it stands, and may be prefixed at pleasure
to almost any Eng. <i>subs.</i>, <i>adj.</i>, or
<i>verb</i>. In many cases there is no single
Lat. equivalent to the neg. word thus
formed, but the neg. force may be given
by prefixing a Lat. neg. <i>part.</i>, as non,
haud, minus, minime, parum, nequaquam,[**P2: ,]
sine, nondum, etc., or some word
denoting defect, as careo, desum, etc., to
the word of positive signification, to
which word the reader will in many of
the foll. arts. be referred.

facere quod populi voluntatem offendat:
v. <f>UNPOPULAR</f>.


<b>unpractised</b>: rŭdis, ĭnexpertus: v.
<f>RAW</f>, <f>INEXPERIENCED</f>.


<b>unpraised</b>: illaudātus: Plin. Ep. 9,
26, 4: in Virg. G. 3, 5 = <i>odious, detestable</i>.


<b>unprecedented</b>: nŏvus, ĭnaudītus:
v. <f>NOVEL</f>, <f>UNHEARD OF</f>. See also <f>EXTRAORDINARY</f>.


<b>unprejudiced</b>: candĭdus: <i>an u.
judge</i>, c. judex, Hor. Ep. 1, 4, 1. Phr.:
<i>to be quite u.</i>, *nullam praejudicatam
opinionem secum afferre; praejudicatis
opinionibus omnino liberum esse.


<b>unpremeditated</b>: sŭbĭtus: v. <f>EXTEMPORARY</f>.
(Or expr. by meditatus,
cogitatus, with a negative: v. <f>PREMEDITATED</f>.)


<b>unprepared</b>: impărātus: both <i>absol.</i>
and foll. by a, ab, of the thing with
ref. to which a person is unprepared:
<i>e. g.</i> imparatus a militibus, a pecunia:
Cic. Att. 7, 15.


<b>unprepossessed</b>: v. <f>UNPREJUDICED</f>.


<b>unprepossessing</b>: perh. injūcundus,
ŏdiōsus: v. <f>UNPLEASANT</f>, <f>OFFENSIVE</f>.
Phr.: <i>an u. appearance</i>, aspectus
deformis [atque turpis], Cic. Off. 1,
35, 126 (rather stronger than Eng.):
*aspectus parum ad conciliandam hominum
benevolentiam aptus, accommodatus.


<b>unpretending</b>: minime ambitiosus:
v. <f>PRETENTIOUS</f>, <f>OSTENTATIOUS</f>. <i>An u.
monument</i>, *monumentum omni ostentatione
vacuum.


<b>unprincipled</b>: malis <i>s.</i> corruptis
moribus: Sall. Cat. 37, <i>ad fin.</i> Sometimes
imprŏbus, nēquam, injustus, may
be precise enough: v. <f>UNJUST</f>, <f>WICKED</f>.


<b>unproductive</b>: infēcundus, infructuōsus:
v. <f>UNFRUITFUL</f>.


<b>unprofitable</b>: expr. by nullum
fructum (or <i>pl.</i>) afferre; nil prodesse:
v. <f>PROFIT</f>, <f>PROFITABLE</f>. Also inūtĭlis
may serve: v. <f>USELESS</f>. (Infructuosus,
late.)

<b>unprotected</b>: indēfensus: Join:

<b>unproved</b>: *quod non probatum

<b>unpruned</b>: impŭtātus: Hor. Epod.

<b>unpublished</b>: *(liber) qui non (nondum)

<b>unpunctual</b>: *temporibus suis parum

<b>unpunished</b>: impūnītus: Join:

Phr.: <i>to escape (get off) u.</i>, aliquid

<b>unpurified</b>: perh. crūdus, rŭdis (<i>in
its natural state</i>): v. <f>RAW</f> (III.).


<b>unqualified</b>:

I. <i>Not possessing
proper qualifications</i>: haud idoneus,
aptus, habilis, etc.: v. <f>QUALIFIED</f>.

II.
<i>Not limited in any way</i>: Phr.: <i>to
praise any one in the most u. manner</i>,
perh. *cumulatissime laudare; cumulatissimis
laudibus aliquem onerare: <i>to
speak in too u. a manner</i>, *nimis simpliciter
absoluteque rem ponere (for this
use of absolute, cf. Scaev. Dig. 33, 1, 13.
Respondi non posse absolute responderi,
i. e. <i>not without qualifications</i>).

III.
<i>Without legal authorization</i>: *nullis
litteris; nullo diplomate instructus.


<b>unquenchable</b>: inexstinctus: Ov.
F. 6, 297 (ignis). See also <f>INSATIABLE</f>.


<b>unquestionable</b>: *certus, certissimus;

<b>unquestionably</b>: făcĭlĕ: <i>u. the

<f>CERTAINLY</f>.


<b>unquestioned</b>: certus, certissimus;

v. <f>CERTAIN</f>, and <f>TO QUESTION</f> (II.).


<b>unquestioning</b>: Phr.: <i>u. confidence</i>,
*fides (fiducia) omni dubitatione
vacua, libera.


<b>unquiet</b>: inquiētus, sollĭcĭtus, etc.:

<b>unquietly</b>: inquiētē: v. <f>RESTLESSLY</f>.


<b>unransomed</b>: non redemptus: v.

<b>unreasonable</b>:

<b>until</b> (<i>conj.</i>):

1. dum: with <i>indic.</i>

36, 78: Caesar, however, always uses

2. dōnĕc (rare in Cic.: not
in Caes. or Sall.): same construction as

of facts.

3. quŏăd: with <i>ind.</i> or
<i>subj.</i> according as it refers to actual fact

5. usque dum: Cic.
Verr. 1, 5, 12: Plaut.

6. adeo usque
dum; Plaut. Am. 1, 2, 10. The idea of the
continuance of action up to the specified

v. L. G. §§ 496-499.

word): <i>to entertain one and
the same v.</i>, unum atque idem sentire,
Cic.: <i>who entertained most noble and
generous v.s respecting the state</i>, qui de
republica praeclara atque egregia sentirent,
Cic. Cat. 3, 2, 5: <i>to entertain v.s
hostile to the state</i>, contra rempublicam
sentire, Cic.: but v. also <f>OPINION</f>.
(I., phr.). Also expr. by videtur with
<i>dat.</i>: e. g. <i>this is the v. I take</i>, hoc mihi
videtur (with <i>acc.</i> and <i>inf.</i>), Cic.: <i>different
people entertain different v.s of
the honourable and the base</i>, non eadem
omnibus sunt honesta atque turpia
(Quich.): v. also <f>TO THINK</f>, <f>TO JUDGE</f>.

V. <i>End in v., design</i>: prōpŏsĭtum,
consĭlium, etc. (v. <f>PURPOSE</f>, <i>subs.</i>).
Expr. also by periphrasis of such verbs
as volo, specto, peto, sequor, valeo, with
id, quod, quid, and other pronouns: v.
<f>PURPOSE</f> (<i>subs.</i>, 11.). Phr.: <i>with what
v.?</i> quo consilio? Ter. Eun. 5, 7, 1:
quorsum (v. Smith's Lat. Dict. s. v.:
and art. <f>WHEREFORE</f>): <i>with a good v.</i>,
bono consilio, Cic. N. D. 3, 31, 78: <i>with
this v. that</i>,[** ,] or <i>with a v. to</i>, eo consilio ut,
Caes. B. G. 1, 48, <i>init.</i>: ea mente ... ut,
Cic. Fam. 12, 14, 1.[** s/b :] ad eam rem ... ut,
id. Verr. 4, 15, 33.[** s/b :] idcirco s. ideo ... ut,
id.: v. also SO (V., throughout). Also
expr. by ad or in, foll. by <i>pron.</i> or
<i>gerund</i>: or by ad simply.[** s/b :] e. g. confingis
falsas causas ad discordiam, Ter. Hec.
4, 4, 71: v. also <f>FOR</f> (<i>prep.</i>, V.). Also
expr. by causa, gratia (in <i>abl.</i>): v.
Smith's Lat. Dict. s. vv. Special
Phr.: <i>to have in v.</i>: spectare (v. <f>END</f>,
<i>subs.</i>, IV., 3, 4): also expr. by, in animo
est, cōgĭto, etc. (v. <f>TO INTEND</f>, <f>TO PURPOSE</f>):
<i>to have in v. one's interests</i>, alicui
servīre, consŭlere, prospĭcere (v. <f>TO
CONSULT</f>, III.).

<b>virtue</b>:

I. As a gen. term, <i>moral</i>

1. virtus, ūtis, <i>f.</i>: <i>v. is

<b>what</b> (<i>pron.</i>):

I. Interrogative,
independent or dependent:

1. quid
(used substantively): <i>what do you
want?</i> quid tibi vis? Hor.: <i>take care
what you do</i>, vide quid agas,[**P2: ,] Ter.: <i>what
if he restore it?</i> quid si reddet? Ter.:
<i>what? have you brought your daughter?</i>
quid? adduxtin' filiam? Ter.

2.
quidnam (<i>what, pray?</i> the termination
"nam" adds liveliness to the question):
<i>I come back to see what Chaerea is doing
here</i>, reviso quidnam Chaerea hic agat,
Ter.

3. ecquid (asks with expectation
of negative): <i>what hope is there further?</i>
ecquid[**beginning char. msg.?|P3 correct as shown] spei porrost? Ter.

4. quis
-----File: b0944m.png------------------------------------------------------
(used adjectively for <i>what</i>, chiefly with
substantives which denote a person:
cf. Madvig Lat. Gr. 88, 1: <i>what senator?</i>
quis senator? Cic.: in such cases
the inquiry seems after the name only,
and not, as with "qui," after the character.

5. qui, quae, quod (an inquiry
after <i>character, kind, etc.</i> is usually implied):
<i>what Chaerea?</i> qui Chaerea?
Ter.: <i>what sweeter song can be found?
what more pleasant actor?</i> qui cantus
dulcior inveniri potest? qui actor jucundior?
Cic.: <i>what power have I?</i> quae in
me est facultas? Cic.

6. quinam (a
mere strengthening of qui).

7. quālis
(<i>of what kind, sort</i>): <i>what honour, what
natural affection think you that they
possess?</i> quali fide,[** ,] quali pietate existimatis
eos esse? Cic.

8. quantus (<i>of
what an amount, how great</i>): <i>for what
did he buy it?</i> quanti emit? Ter.


II. Exclamatory:[** :] quid (substantive);
qui,[** ,] qualis, quantus (adjectives),
with distinctions as given above: <i>O
what embracings, what joys there were!</i>
O qui complexus, et gaudia quanta
fuerunt! Hor. S. 1, 5, 43: <i>O what an
appearance,[** ,] and worthy of what a
picture!</i> O qualis facies et quali digna
tabella! Juv. 10, 157. <i>What</i> in this
use may also be rendered by "quam"
with adj.: <i>what a shameful deed!</i>
quam indignum facinus! Ter.

III.
Relative: equivalent to <i>that which</i>:

1. quod: <i>why do you wish for
what you possess?</i> cur optas quod
habes? Hor.

2. quae, <i>n. pl.</i> (if, as
frequently in English, the relative <i>what</i>
sums up several things): <i>what you have
written to me I feel to be true</i>, quae ad
me scripsisti ea sentio esse vera, Cic.


<b>whatever</b>:

1. quīcunque: used
both adjectively and, in the neuter, substantively:
<i>by whatever method I could</i>,
quacunque potui ratione,[** ,] Cic.: <i>whatever
you see</i>, quodcunque vides, Prop.: with
genitive of noun: <i>whatever soldiers you
can gather</i>, quodcunque militum contrahere
poteritis, Cic. Att. 8, 12, A.

2. quisquis: the neuter quicquid is
chiefly substantive, constr. like quodcunque;
but in other genders and cases
it is used adjectively: <i>whatever man</i>,
quisquis homo, Pl.: <i>with whatever design
he did it</i>, quoquo consilio fecit, Cic.
("Quicunque" and "quisquis" are both
used when among a number of specimens
in a class none is excepted; but
"quisquis" appears more summarily to
dismiss the specimens as equal among
themselves: e. g.: quodcunque est, tibi
habe, <i>take all that there is</i>: quicquid
est tibi habe, <i>take anything or everything
that there is,[** ,] it is all the same</i>. Perhaps
too "quicquid" leaves it more uncertain
whether there is much or little).

<b>when</b>:

1. quum: the most gen.
word for the varying shades of meaning
of <i>when</i>: it denotes the coincidence of
two facts, or the sequence of one after
the other. When used purely of <i>time</i>
with no idea of <i>cause and effect</i>, quum
is constr. with <i>indic.</i> of any tense (v.
Lat. Gr. § 485): so too with indic. of
repeated actions, when it means <i>as
often as</i>. Where <i>cause and effect</i> are
implied, constr. with <i>subj.</i>: hence in historical
sequence it usually takes <i>subj.</i>
(v. Lat. Gr. §§ 483, 484), <i>some relation
of cause and effect</i> being almost
necessarily implied: with <i>subj.</i>, if for
<i>when</i> we might substitute <i>since, whereas,
etc.</i>: or if it is used by periphr. to supply
the lack of a <i>past part. active</i> in Latin.

2. ŭbi: denotes a point of time
from which some other takes its be-*
-----File: b0945l.png------------------------------------------------------
*ginning: <i>w. (as soon as) the Helvetii
were informed they sent ambassadors</i>,
ubi Helvetii certiores facti sunt, legatos
mittunt, Caes. B. G. 1, 7: it is constr.
with <i>indic.</i> usually; the <i>subj.</i>, where it
occurs, being hardly attributable to
"ubi:" e. g., <i>w. once a man has perjured
himself he must not henceforth be
believed</i>, ubi semel quis pejeraverit, ei
credi postea non oportet[**,] Cic. Rab. Post.
13, 36: where the <i>subj.</i> s[** is] used because
it is a supposed case.

3. ŭt: <i>as soon
as ever</i>: to mark an occurrence immediately
preceding the main action: <i>w. I
had read your letter, immediately I
wrote mine</i>,[** ,] litteras scripsi statim ut
tuas legeram, Cic. Att. 2, 12, 3.

4.
quando: interrogative, direct, and in dependent
sentences: <i>O country, w. shall
I see you?</i> O rus, quando ego te aspiciam?
Hor. S. 2, 6, 60: <i>we do not see
w. old age is creeping over us</i>, non intelligitur
quando obrepat senectus, Cic.
Phr.: <i>Caesar, when he had landed his
army, hastened against the enemy</i>, Caesar
exposito exercitu ad hostes contendit,
Caes.: <i>Sabinus w. he had encouraged
his men, gave the signal</i>, Sabinus suos
hortatus signum dat, id.: <i>Tarquinius,
w. besieging Ardea, lost his kingdom</i>,
Tarquinius Ardeam oppugnans regnum
perdidit, Liv.: <i>since the time w[** .] Deucalion
climbed the mountain</i>, ex quo
Deucalion montem ascendit, Juv. 1, 81:
<i>w. (what time) first Deucalion cast the
stones into an empty world</i>, quo tempore
primum Deucalion vacuum lapides jactavit
in orbem, Virg. G. 1, 62.


<b>whence</b>: unde: <i>nor does he come
thence w. I would have preferred</i>, nec
inde venit unde mallem, Cic.: <i>w. has
Cinna been dislodged?</i> unde dejectus
est Cinna? id.: <i>that he might answer
me, w. he came</i>, ut mihi responderet unde
esset, id.: <i>I do not recal to mind w. I
have fallen, but w. I have risen</i>, non
recordor unde ceciderim, sed unde surrexerim,
Cic. Att. 4, 16, 10: <i>the relation
will be brief if the beginning be made w.
it must needs be</i>, brevis erit narratio si
unde necesse est inde initium sumetur,
Cic. Inv. 1, 20, 28: <i>who had killed the
man w. (from whom) he himself was
born</i>, qui eum necasset unde ipse natus
esset, id. Rosc. Am. 26, 71.

2. unde unde: Tert.

2. utcunque: <i>w.
morals have failed</i>, utcunque defecere

3. quŏties
(<i>as often as</i>, of repeated actions): <i>w. it

<b>where</b>:

I. Interrogative:

1.
ŭbi: <i>w. am I to find Pamphilus?</i> ubi
inveniam Pamphilum? Ter.: <i>w. in the
world?</i> ubi gentium? Pl.: <i>I could not
even guess w. on earth you were</i>, ne suspicabar
quidem ubi terrarum esses, Cic.

2. ŭbĭnam: <i>w. is the man?</i> ubinam
est homo? Pl.: <i>I see not where the mind
can take its stand</i>, non video ubinam
mens insistere possit, Cic.

II. Relative:

1. quā: <i>I shall be spoken of
w. violent Aufidus roars</i>, dicar qua
violens obstrepit Aufidus, Hor. Od. 3,
30, 10.

2. ŭbi: <i>w. a tyrant is, there
we must say there is absolutely no commonwealth</i>,
ubi tyrannus est, ibi dicendum
est plane nullam esse rempublicam,
Cic. <i>Where</i> may often be turned by the
cases of the relative "qui": e. g., <i>the
house w.</i>, domus in qua; <i>the place w.</i>,
locus in quo, apud quem; <i>a matter w.</i>,
res in qua: etc.


<b>whereas</b>: quoniam, quando, quandoquidem,
quum: v. <f>SINCE</f>, <f>WHILE</f>.
<i>Whereas</i>, when serving to shew an adversative
relation of two clauses, is often
not expressed in Latin: e. g., <i>we heard</i>
-----File: b0945m.png------------------------------------------------------
<i>you say that we thought all men enemies
who were not with us, w. you thought
all men friends who were not against you</i>,
te dicere audiebamus,[** ,] nos omnes adversarios
putare nisi qui nobiscum essent,
te omnes qui contra te non essent tuos,
Cic.


<b>whereby</b>:

I. Interrogative: quā
re, ratione, viā; quo pacto: Cic.

II.
Relative: quo, quā viā, etc.; per quod,
per quae, Cic.


<b>wherefore</b>:

I. Interrogative:

1. quāre, quamobrem, cur, quid:
Cic.

2. quāpropter: Pl.: Ter.

II. Relative: expressing a conclusion
from grounds distinctly stated:

1. quāre: <i>w. I thus recommend
him to you</i>, quare sic tibi eum commendo,
Cic.

2. quamobrem (referring
<i>to one distinctly stated reason</i>): <i>conceit
of power is odious, w. I say nothing of
my own powers</i>, arrogantia ingenii odiosa
est, quamobrem nihil dico de meo
ingenio, Cic.

3. quāpropter (in
transitions, referring to <i>several reasons</i>):
<i>w. I shall say this</i>, quapropter hoc
dicam, Cic.

4. quōcirca: <i>w. the
senate in our ancestors' time rightly
decreed</i>, quocirca bene apud majores
nostros senatus decrevit, Cic.

5.
proinde (<i>consequently</i>: used in <i>animated
exhortation</i> esp.): <i>w. let them
either depart, or keep quiet</i>, proinde aut
exeant, aut quiescant, Cic.


<b>wherein</b>: in quo, in quā re,[** ,] in quibus
(if many things are referred to).


<b>whereof</b>: cujus, cujus rei, quorum:
de quo, qua re, quibus (if in <i>whereof</i> the
<i>of</i> means <i>concerning</i>).

1.

2.
quorsum: <i>will you not say w. this

II. Relative: <i>to
which</i>: cui, cui rei: ad quod, ad quam
rem: acc. to the context.


<b>whereupon</b>:

1. quo facto (<i>after

2. post quae
(<i>after which</i>).


<b>wherever</b>:

1. quācunque: <i>wherever

<b>whether</b> (<i>conj.</i>):

I. In single

1. nĕ (attached to the

2. num:
<i>I ask w. things would happen differently

3. an (after verbs of <i>doubting, not

-----File: b0945r.png------------------------------------------------------
Lig. 9, 26: there is really no ellipse of a[** a ?|P3 yes, clear @TIA]
negative here; it is only that <i>I am not
sure w.</i>, in Latin,[** ,] conveyed a leaning to
the affirmative, whereas in English it
leans to the negative: <i>I doubt w. I

4.
si (after verbs of <i>seeing, trying</i>): <i>I will

5. utrum (very rare in this

II. In double questions,
<i>whether ... or</i>:

1. utrum ... an,
anne, ne: <i>w. he spoke in a Roman sense,

2. ne ... an: <i>w. in the whole

3.
... an, ne, the Latin word for <i>whether</i>
being not expressed: <i>w. wounded or

saucius an sanus numquid tua signa
reliqui? Ov.: <i>so that it was uncertain

Liv.

III. <i>Whether ... or</i>, where a
matter is left undecided, but a conclusion
drawn whichever way it be:
sive ... sive, seu ... seu (the former
Ciceronian, the latter, as also sive ...
seu, seu ... sive, in Caes. and in the

lego, illo loco libentissime soleo uti,

sic fata ferebant, Virg.: <i>w. it is madness
or any one has harmed you</i>, seu
furor est, sive aliquis nocuit, Ov.

<b>while</b> (<i>conj.</i>):

1. dum (the present

II. By cases of the

1.
Ablative: of the instrument, manner,

Latin cases the ablative most frequently

for <i>with</i> might be brought: but it is
often optional whether the <i>prep.</i> cum

2. Dative: after verbs of

3. Genitive: with a
